However, for Part 135 operations, 14 CFR 135.225 and company operations specifications establish the minimum weather requirements, and operations below those are prohibited. The inverse is also true: a company cannot legally require a pilot to operate below what the pilot's own sound judgment and 91.3 authority dictates is safe. If a company pressures a pilot to fly below personal minimums, this represents a classic 'external pressure' hazardous attitude scenario, and the pilot's correct response is to refuse the flight and document the pressure appropriately. The FAA's position is clear — certificate holders and their personal ADM authority are never subordinated to commercial pressure when safety is at stake.

questions.question: What is the fundamental difference between anti-icing and deicing systems on a helicopter, and why does that distinction matter before an IFR flight?
questions.answer: Anti-icing systems prevent ice from forming in the first place — they apply heat or fluid continuously to keep surfaces above freezing. Deicing systems remove ice that has already accumulated, typically in cycles. The distinction matters for preflight planning because anti-icing must be activated before entering icing conditions, while deicing is reactive. If you select the wrong approach — using a deicing system after ice has already critically degraded rotor or engine performance — you may be too late. Pilots must know exactly which system their helicopter is equipped with and follow the manufacturer's specific activation procedures.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 4; 14 CFR 91.9 (operating limitations); POH/RFM Anti-ice/De-ice Section

questions.question: Where in the helicopter's flight manual or Rotorcraft Flight Manual would you find the manufacturer's approved procedures for operating the anti-ice system, and what type of information should you expect to find there?
questions.answer: Anti-ice and deice procedures are found in the Normal Procedures section and the Limitations section of the RFM (Rotorcraft Flight Manual) or POH. The Limitations section will specify conditions under which the system must be on, any airspeed or altitude restrictions when ice protection is active, and whether the helicopter is certified for flight into known icing (FIKI). The Normal Procedures section will cover step-by-step activation sequences — such as which systems to turn on first (e.g., pitot heat, engine inlet, rotor blade leading edges), when to activate them relative to entering IMC or icing conditions, and any associated electrical load or generator considerations.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 27.1419 (icing certification rotorcraft); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 4; RFM Limitations and Normal Procedures sections

questions.question: Name at least four helicopter components or systems that typically have dedicated anti-icing or deicing protection and briefly explain why each one is critical.
questions.answer: 1. Main rotor blade leading edges — ice accumulation changes blade airfoil shape, increases drag, reduces lift, and causes asymmetric shedding that creates severe vibration. 2. Engine inlet/air intake — ice ingestion can cause compressor damage or flameout in turbine engines; inlet blockage reduces power available. 3. Pitot tube — ice blocks pitot pressure, rendering the airspeed indicator unreliable or inoperative during IFR flight. 4. Tail rotor blades — similar to main rotor but asymmetric ice shedding can cause loss of antitorque authority or catastrophic vibration. 5. Windshield — ice accumulation on the windshield prevents visual reference and is critical in IMC for situational awareness. Each of these directly affects continued safe flight if compromised.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 4; 14 CFR 91.205 (required equipment); RFM ice protection systems

questions.question: You are conducting a preflight for an IFR flight in forecast IMC with temperatures between -2°C and +2°C at cruise altitude. Walk me through how you would use the manufacturer's information in the RFM to determine whether your helicopter is legal and operationally ready to depart into those conditions.
questions.answer: First, I check the Limitations section of the RFM to confirm whether the helicopter holds a FIKI (flight into known icing) certification under 14 CFR 27.1419. If it is not FIKI certified, I cannot legally depart into known icing conditions regardless of whether anti-ice equipment is installed. Second, I verify all ice protection systems are functional during preflight — pitot heat, engine inlet anti-ice, rotor blade systems, and windshield heat — per the RFM checklist. Third, I check for any operational limitations tied to ice protection use, such as electrical load restrictions, generator requirements, or reduced performance charts. Fourth, I verify the systems are operationally tested — for example, pitot heat verified warm to the touch, inlet heat confirmed via cockpit annunciator. Temperatures between -2°C and +2°C are in the prime icing range, so all systems must be on prior to entering cloud. If any system is inoperative, I am not legal or safe to depart into those conditions.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 27.1419; 14 CFR 91.9; 14 CFR 91.213; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 4; RFM Limitations

questions.question: During your IFR flight at 6,000 feet MSL in IMC, you notice a slight but progressive vibration developing and your airspeed is slightly lower than expected at the same power setting. The OAT is -4°C and you are in visible moisture. What do you suspect and what does the RFM tell you to do?
questions.answer: These are classic early symptoms of rotor blade icing. Ice accumulation changes blade aerodynamic profile, increases drag (explaining the airspeed reduction at constant power), and if shedding asymmetrically, creates vibration. I immediately reference the Emergency or Abnormal Procedures section of the RFM for rotor icing. Typical manufacturer guidance includes: confirm all rotor anti-ice systems are on and operating (check annunciators), increase power as needed to maintain airspeed, exit icing conditions immediately by descending to a warmer altitude or turning to exit the cloud if possible, and avoid abrupt control inputs if blade ice shedding is occurring. Many RFMs prohibit continued flight in icing once vibration is detected. I would also declare an emergency if the situation is deteriorating and ATC coordination is needed to descend.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (emergencies); RFM Abnormal/Emergency Procedures — Rotor Icing; 14 CFR 91.3

questions.question: Your helicopter's RFM states the pitot heat must be on any time the aircraft is in IMC or when the OAT is below 5°C. You are flying VFR in clear air at 4,000 feet and the OAT is 3°C. Are you required to have pitot heat on, and what failure mode occurs if you don't and inadvertently pick up icing?
questions.answer: Yes — the RFM limitation specifies below 5°C OAT, regardless of VMC or IMC conditions. That is an operating limitation under 14 CFR 91.9, which requires flight within the limitations established by the manufacturer. Pitot heat must be on. If pitot heat is off and the pitot tube ices over, the failure mode depends on whether the drain hole also freezes. If only the pitot inlet ices (drain hole open), static pressure equalizes and the ASI slowly drops to zero — you lose airspeed indication. If both the inlet and drain hole freeze, the pitot tube acts like a sealed chamber — as you climb, static pressure decreases but pitot pressure (trapped) does not change, causing ASI to incorrectly read an increase in airspeed, and on descent it reads a false decrease. This is particularly dangerous in IMC where the ASI is a primary reference.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.9; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5 (pitot-static failures); RFM Limitations

questions.question: You are flying a helicopter with pneumatic rotor blade deicing boots. The RFM specifies a specific cycling sequence for the boots and warns against activating them before a minimum ice accretion has occurred. Why would the manufacturer restrict you from turning on the boots immediately upon entering icing conditions, and what aerodynamic risk does premature activation create?
questions.answer: Pneumatic deicing boots work by inflating and cracking accumulated ice off the blade leading edge. The manufacturer restricts premature activation because if you inflate the boots before sufficient ice has built up, the thin layer of ice can conform to the shape of the inflated boot rather than cracking off. When the boot then deflates, a void or ridge is left between the boot surface and the remaining ice — subsequent ice then accumulates on top of this irregular shape (called ice bridging), creating a far worse aerodynamic contaminant than if you had waited for proper accretion first. The resulting irregular ice shape significantly disrupts boundary layer airflow over the blade, increases drag, reduces lift, and cannot be removed by subsequent boot cycles. Manufacturer-specified minimum accretion time (often visually observed at the blade leading edge reference point in the cockpit) must be followed precisely.
questions.follow_up: If you suspect ice bridging has already occurred on the main rotor blades and your deicing boots are no longer effective, what are your remaining options and priorities?
questions.follow_up_answer: Once ice bridging has occurred and boots cannot remove the ice, the priority is to exit icing conditions immediately — descend to a warmer altitude (above 0°C OAT), divert to a lower altitude or VFR conditions, or reverse course. There is no in-flight fix for bridged rotor ice. I would reference the RFM emergency section for rotor icing, declare an emergency if necessary, keep power up to maintain rotor RPM, minimize cyclic inputs to reduce asymmetric loading risk, and land as soon as practicable. I would not attempt an autorotation unless forced — bridged ice causing asymmetric blade loading can create uncontrollable vibration at reduced rotor RPM during autorotation descent.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 4 (anti-icing/deicing systems); RFM Abnormal/Emergency Procedures; 14 CFR 91.3

questions.question: A student tells you the helicopter is equipped with engine inlet anti-ice and rotor anti-ice, so it is approved for flight into known icing. As the examiner, what is wrong with that reasoning and how would you use the RFM to correct it?
questions.answer: Having anti-icing equipment installed does not automatically confer FIKI certification. 14 CFR 27.1419 requires that the FAA specifically evaluate and certify the helicopter's ice protection system for flight into known icing as part of the type certificate or supplemental type certificate (STC) process. The RFM Limitations section will explicitly state whether the aircraft is 'Approved for Flight in Known Icing Conditions' — if that statement is not present, the aircraft is not FIKI certified regardless of what equipment is installed. Anti-ice equipment may be present only for incidental icing protection (e.g., pitot heat required under Part 91), not for sustained flight in known icing. I would direct the student to the RFM Limitations section and have them read the specific language. If it says 'flight into known icing is prohibited' or has no FIKI approval statement, that ends the discussion — we do not depart into known icing.
questions.follow_up: If the helicopter has an STC for FIKI installed, but the original RFM has not been updated with the STC supplement, can you legally fly into known icing?
questions.follow_up_answer: No. An STC approval must be accompanied by a corresponding RFM Supplement (RFMS) that is physically incorporated into the aircraft's RFM. The RFMS establishes the specific procedures, limitations, and equipment checks required under the STC. Without the RFMS incorporated, the pilot has no approved limitations or procedures to operate under, and the FIKI approval is not valid for that specific aircraft operation. I would need to confirm the STC paperwork, the RFMS, and the aircraft logbook entries showing the STC equipment was properly installed before I could consider that aircraft FIKI-legal.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 27.1419; 14 CFR 21.113 (STC); 14 CFR 91.9; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 4; RFM Limitations and STC Supplements

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of an Automatic Flight Control System (AFCS) in a helicopter, and how does it differ from a simple stability augmentation system?
questions.answer: An AFCS is an integrated system that provides both stability augmentation and autopilot functions, allowing the helicopter to maintain selected flight parameters such as heading, altitude, airspeed, and navigation tracking with reduced pilot workload. A simple stability augmentation system (SAS) only dampens unwanted aircraft motions and attitude deviations without holding specific flight parameters. The AFCS typically builds on SAS by adding attitude hold, heading hold, altitude hold, and navigation coupling modes. The specific modes and their functions will be defined in the Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) for the aircraft used on the practical test.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 4; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5; Applicable RFM/POH

questions.question: Where is the authoritative source for AFCS operating procedures and limitations for the specific helicopter being used on your practical test, and why is that source considered authoritative?
questions.answer: The authoritative source is the manufacturer-published Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) or Pilot's Operating Handbook (POH) specific to the aircraft's make, model, and serial number configuration. It is authoritative because the FAA approves the RFM as part of the type certification process, and the AFCS procedures, mode descriptions, limitations, and abnormal/emergency procedures contained within it are FAA-accepted data. Generic descriptions in handbooks like the FAA-H-8083-21B are supplemental; the RFM governs. Pilots must be familiar with their specific aircraft's RFM before flying IFR.

questions.question: During preflight for an IFR flight, what AFCS-related items should you typically verify before departure, based on manufacturer guidance?
questions.answer: Based on manufacturer guidance (RFM), a pilot should typically verify: (1) AFCS circuit breakers are set and system receives power; (2) AFCS self-test or built-in test equipment (BITE) completes successfully with no fault annunciations; (3) all mode controllers, mode select switches, and annunciator lights are functional; (4) flight director bars or command bars display and respond correctly; (5) any required AFCS engagement conditions are met (e.g., minimum airspeed, rotor RPM within limits); and (6) trim actuators respond correctly to controller inputs. The specific checklist steps are always defined by the manufacturer in the normal procedures section of the RFM.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.103; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 4; Applicable RFM Normal Procedures

questions.question: You are established in cruise at 4,500 feet MSL on an IFR flight plan with the AFCS in altitude hold and heading modes. The altitude hold mode unexpectedly disengages and an amber caution light illuminates on the AFCS controller. Walk me through your thought process and actions.
questions.answer: First, maintain aircraft control manually — immediately take over pitch and collective inputs to hold altitude. Aviate before troubleshooting. Next, confirm what mode actually disengaged by checking the mode annunciator panel. Reference the RFM abnormal procedures section for the specific caution light that illuminated — it will identify whether this is a degraded mode, sensor fault, or full AFCS failure. Determine if a lower-authority mode (such as SAS or attitude hold) remains available and re-engage only what the RFM permits. Notify ATC of any deviation if altitude was lost. Consider whether the remaining system is adequate for continued IFR flight or if a diversion is appropriate. Do not attempt to re-engage a failed mode without RFM authorization to do so. Document the fault for maintenance.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.187; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (emergency decision-making); Applicable RFM Abnormal Procedures

questions.question: Your helicopter's AFCS has a flight director but no autopilot servos — the flight director only. How does this affect your IFR workload compared to a fully coupled AFCS, and what skill does the pilot need to demonstrate to use the flight director effectively?
questions.answer: With a flight director only (no servo coupling), the pilot must manually follow the command bars — the system does not physically move the controls. Workload remains high because the pilot must continuously scan the flight director and make precise cyclic, collective, and pedal inputs to keep command bars centered. The key skill is disciplined cross-check and precise aircraft control: the pilot must treat the command bar as the primary pitch and bank reference, integrating it into the standard instrument scan, and respond to command bar movement with smooth, calibrated control inputs rather than chasing the bars aggressively. Compared to a fully coupled system, manual following of a flight director demands higher concentration, especially during approaches in IMC. The RFM will define the specific flight director modes available and any operating limitations.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 4; Applicable RFM

questions.question: You are flying an IFR approach coupled to the AFCS with the navigation mode tracking the localizer. On short final, a trim runaway occurs — the cyclic trim system begins moving the cyclic aft without pilot input. What is the immediate action and what is the underlying system principle you are relying on?
questions.answer: The immediate action for a trim runaway, per most manufacturers, is to disengage the AFCS/trim system using the primary disconnect switch (typically a force trim release or AFCS disconnect button on the cyclic), simultaneously apply opposing control pressure to maintain the desired flight path, and fly the remainder of the approach manually. The underlying principle is that all AFCS designs include a disconnect mechanism that allows the pilot to override or disengage the system rapidly — the pilot always has final authority over the controls. After disconnecting, the pilot must reassess whether to continue the approach with manual control or execute a missed approach depending on aircraft position, altitude, workload, and conditions. The specific disconnect procedure and subsequent checklist steps are defined in the RFM emergency procedures section.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 4; Applicable RFM Emergency Procedures

questions.question: Some helicopter AFCS installations have an airspeed limitation below which certain modes, such as altitude hold, are not authorized to be engaged. Why does this limitation exist from a flight dynamics standpoint, and what is the risk of attempting to engage altitude hold below that airspeed in a helicopter?
questions.answer: Altitude hold in a helicopter typically uses barometric altitude and vertical speed sensor inputs to drive collective servo movements. At very low airspeeds, especially near or in the hover regime, the relationship between collective position and altitude becomes highly nonlinear and sensitive to power changes, translational lift effects, ground effect variations, and wind gusts. The AFCS control laws may not be tuned to handle the rapid, large-amplitude collective movements required at low speed, potentially causing altitude excursions, oscillations, or pilot-induced oscillations (PIO) as the system hunts for a stable altitude reference. Additionally, some aircraft use airspeed-dependent blending between different control law modes — below the minimum engagement speed, the control law may be invalid. Attempting to engage altitude hold below the RFM-specified minimum airspeed risks loss of control authority, unexpected pitch or collective transients, and in extreme cases, entry into vortex ring state if the system commands an aggressive descent to re-capture altitude.
questions.follow_up: If the altitude hold AFCS mode disengages automatically during a deceleration to a hover, such as during a missed approach transition, what must the pilot be prepared to do immediately and what instrument scan priority shifts?
questions.follow_up_answer: The pilot must immediately assume manual control and revert to raw data instrument flying without the command bar or servo assistance. The priority scan shifts to the altimeter, VSI, and torque/collective position as primary references to arrest any altitude deviation that may have begun during the transition. The pilot must also maintain rotor RPM awareness since the system is no longer managing power distribution indirectly. Simultaneously, the pilot must manage the go-around power application, cyclic attitude, and heading — all manually. This transition represents one of the highest workload moments in IFR helicopter flight and underscores why AFCS mode awareness and manual instrument proficiency must be maintained regardless of automation availability.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 4; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5; Applicable RFM Limitations Section

questions.question: During the oral portion of the practical test, you tell me you have 800 hours total time but only 50 hours in this specific helicopter with the AFCS installed. Research shows that accident rates decrease significantly after 100 hours in type. Given that AFCS-equipped helicopters can mask developing aircraft control deficiencies in early flight hours, how should a pilot with limited hours in type approach AFCS use during IFR flight, and what does the manufacturer's guidance require you to demonstrate regardless of automation?
questions.answer: A pilot with limited hours in type should treat the AFCS as a workload management tool rather than a substitute for manual flying proficiency. The FAA-H-8083-21B notes that accident rates correlate more strongly with hours in a specific aircraft model than with total hours, and that errors most often stem from accumulated poor decisions — not single catastrophic events. Practically, this means the pilot should: (1) regularly practice manual IFR flying in the aircraft to maintain proficiency without AFCS, so a failure does not result in a surprise; (2) thoroughly understand every mode, limitation, and abnormal procedure in the RFM before any IFR flight; (3) never exceed AFCS-imposed limitations believing automation will compensate for them; and (4) maintain an active monitoring role even when the AFCS is engaged, since the system can fail without warning. The ACS requires the pilot to demonstrate familiarity with manufacturer-specific AFCS procedures — meaning the examiner expects the applicant to know mode logic, engagement conditions, annunciator meanings, and disconnect procedures from the RFM, not just that an autopilot exists. Automation complacency is an identified human factors risk, and SRM principles require the pilot to manage automation actively, not passively.
questions.follow_up: If I asked you to disconnect the AFCS and fly the last 500 feet of an ILS approach to minimums manually in actual IMC, what would your biggest concern be, and how does your pre-IFR training address that scenario?
questions.follow_up_answer: The biggest concern is the abrupt transition from servo-assisted, stabilized flight to manual control with no stabilization or command guidance — especially at low altitude, low airspeed, in degraded visual conditions, and with high workload. The pilot must be current and proficient in manual IFR flight in this specific aircraft before flying IFR in IMC, which is both an ACS requirement and a safety imperative. Pre-IFR training should include intentional AFCS-off instrument approaches in simulated IMC until the pilot can maintain instrument tolerances without automation. This is not optional; it represents the baseline competency level — automation is an enhancement, not the floor of capability.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM/SRM); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 4; 14 CFR 61.57 (IFR currency); Applicable RFM

tasks.title: Task B. Helicopter Flight Instruments and Navigation Equipment

questions.question: Which flight instruments are driven by the pitot-static system, and what is the sole source of input for each one?
questions.answer: Three instruments use the pitot-static system: (1) the Airspeed Indicator (ASI), which uses both pitot (impact) pressure and static pressure; (2) the Altimeter, which uses static pressure only; and (3) the Vertical Speed Indicator (VSI), which uses static pressure only. The pitot port measures ram air pressure from forward movement, while the static port measures ambient atmospheric pressure.

questions.question: What does the magnetic compass measure, and what are the two main compass errors a helicopter pilot should know about for IFR operations?
questions.answer: The magnetic compass directly measures the aircraft's magnetic heading by sensing the Earth's magnetic field. The two main errors are: (1) Magnetic Dip (Northerly Turning Error and Acceleration/Deceleration Error) — caused by the compass card tilting toward the Earth's magnetic field lines; turns through north and south show lagging or leading indications depending on hemisphere and direction. (2) Variation — the angular difference between true north and magnetic north, which varies by geographic location and must be applied to convert between true and magnetic headings. Additional errors include deviation (caused by aircraft magnetic fields) and oscillation error from turbulence or rotor vibration.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the transponder Mode C, and what squawk code is assigned for an ATC communication failure in VFR conditions?
questions.answer: A Mode C transponder automatically reports the aircraft's pressure altitude to ATC in 100-foot increments, along with the 4-digit squawk code, allowing controllers to identify the aircraft and its altitude on radar. In VFR conditions, the code 1200 is the standard VFR squawk. For a radio communication failure, pilots squawk 7600. Code 7700 is for emergencies, and 7500 is for hijacking. Under 14 CFR 91.215, Mode C transponders are required in Class A, B, and C airspace, and within 30 NM of Class B primary airports.

questions.question: You are in cruise flight in your IFR helicopter and you notice your airspeed indicator is reading unusually high while your altimeter and VSI appear normal. What is the most likely cause, and how do you confirm it?
questions.answer: The most likely cause is a blocked static port with an open pitot drain hole, or more commonly, a blocked pitot tube with the drain hole also blocked — but if only the pitot tube is blocked and the drain is open, the ASI will slowly bleed down to zero because the trapped ram air escapes through the drain. If the pitot tube is completely blocked (both tube and drain), the ASI acts like an altimeter — it increases as you climb and decreases as you descend because the static pressure continues to act on the reference side. If the altimeter and VSI are working normally, the static system is intact. To confirm, cross-check with GPS groundspeed (adjusting for wind) and check whether the indication changes with altitude changes in the manner described. Activate pitot heat if icing is suspected as the cause of pitot blockage.

questions.question: Your helicopter is equipped with an AHRS-based glass cockpit (PFD/MFD). During preflight, you notice the PFD attitude indicator shows a slight bank when the helicopter is sitting level. What does this indicate, and what is your course of action before an IFR departure?
questions.answer: This indicates that the AHRS has not completed its initialization and alignment process, or it has an erroneous reference stored. AHRS systems require the aircraft to be stationary during the alignment phase to establish accurate attitude and heading references using accelerometers and gyroscopic sensors. A residual bank indication on the ground means the system has not aligned correctly or is malfunctioning. The correct course of action is: (1) Do not depart IFR — this is an unairworthy condition. (2) Allow the system additional time to complete initialization per the AFM/POH, as some systems require several minutes. (3) If the error persists, consult the avionics system manual for a reset procedure. (4) If the error cannot be resolved, the aircraft is not legal for IFR flight under 14 CFR 91.205(d) requirements for functional flight instruments. Document the discrepancy in the maintenance log.

questions.question: ADS-B Out is required in certain airspace as of January 1, 2020. As an IFR helicopter pilot, describe the specific airspace where ADS-B Out is required and what equipage standard must be met.
questions.answer: Per 14 CFR 91.225, ADS-B Out is required in: (1) Class A airspace; (2) Class B airspace and within 30 NM of Class B primary airports (the 'Mode C veil'); (3) Class C airspace; (4) Class E airspace at or above 10,000 ft MSL, excluding airspace at or below 2,500 ft AGL; (5) above the ceiling and within the lateral boundaries of Class B or C airspace up to 10,000 ft MSL; (6) Class E airspace over the Gulf of Mexico at or above 3,000 ft MSL within 12 NM of the U.S. coast. The equipage standard requires either a 1090 MHz extended squitter (1090ES) transmitter or a Universal Access Transceiver (UAT) operating on 978 MHz, both capable of broadcasting GPS-derived position. The position source must meet the performance requirements of TSO-C166b (1090ES) or TSO-C154c (UAT). ADS-B In (reception) is not required but enables TIS-B and FIS-B services on the MFD.

questions.question: Your IFR helicopter loses electrical power in IMC. Walk me through the immediate implications for your flight instruments, navigation capability, and what options you have to maintain instrument flight.
questions.answer: A complete electrical failure in an IFR helicopter with a modern glass cockpit is extremely serious. Immediate implications: (1) PFD and MFD go dark — all AHRS-derived attitude, heading, and air data information is lost simultaneously; (2) GPS navigation, autopilot, and FMS are lost; (3) Transponder and ADS-B Out cease transmitting — ATC loses your position and altitude; (4) Radio communications are lost — you cannot declare an emergency or receive vectors. Options depend on aircraft equipment: (a) If the helicopter has a standby battery or emergency bus, non-essential loads shed automatically and a standby attitude indicator, one radio, and transponder may remain powered — prioritize those; (b) If equipped with vacuum-driven or mechanically driven standby gyros (rare in modern helicopters), those may remain functional; (c) The magnetic compass remains operational — it requires no electrical power and provides heading reference; (d) The altimeter and VSI remain functional as they are pitot-static only — no electrical input needed; (e) ASI also remains functional. With compass, altimeter, ASI, and VSI, a pilot can maintain controlled flight using the 'partial panel' technique and execute a descent to VFR conditions or a precautionary landing. Declare 7600 on the transponder if any electrical power is restored.
questions.follow_up: You mentioned the magnetic compass remains functional. What specific errors will you encounter using the magnetic compass in IMC in a helicopter, and how do you compensate for the most critical one during a turn to a specific heading?
questions.follow_up_answer: In a helicopter the magnetic compass has several error sources: (1) Northerly Turning Error (magnetic dip error) — the most critical in IMC. In the Northern Hemisphere, when turning through north the compass lags behind actual heading; when turning through south it leads. The memory aid is 'UNOS' (Undershoot North, Overshoot South). To compensate during a timed turn: when turning to north, roll out when the compass reads approximately 30° (your latitude) before the desired heading; when turning to south, roll out when the compass shows approximately 30° past the desired heading. (2) Acceleration/Deceleration Error — on easterly or westerly headings, acceleration causes a false indication of turning north; deceleration causes a false indication of turning south. (3) Deviation — caused by aircraft electrical equipment and magnetic fields; the deviation card in the cockpit shows corrections for magnetic headings. (4) Rotor/vibration oscillation — helicopter rotor vibration causes the compass card to oscillate, requiring the pilot to average readings. Use a standard rate turn (3°/sec) with timed turns as the most reliable technique when the compass is the only heading reference.

questions.question: During an IFR approach in your glass-cockpit helicopter, you activate the alternate static source. Describe exactly how each of the three pitot-static instruments will be affected and why, and how you would correct for the error on the altimeter.
questions.answer: When the alternate static source is activated (typically drawing from inside the cabin), the cabin pressure is slightly lower than outside ambient pressure because the fuselage venturi effect and pressurization reduce cabin static pressure. This causes the following effects on each instrument: (1) Altimeter — indicates slightly higher than actual altitude. The lower cabin static pressure causes the aneroid wafers to expand more than they should, showing a higher reading. The error is typically 50–100 feet in unpressurized aircraft/helicopters, but the exact value is published in the AFM/POH for the specific aircraft — pilots must reference that correction factor and apply it. (2) VSI — shows a momentary climb indication as the pressure transitions, then returns to approximately correct trend indications. It may be slightly inaccurate in precise rate terms due to the sustained pressure differential. (3) ASI — indicates slightly faster than actual airspeed. The lower static reference pressure used in the differential calculation (pitot minus static) results in a larger differential, causing an over-reading. The correction value is also published in the AFM/POH. To correct for the altimeter error: reference the specific correction table in the AFM/POH, then mentally subtract the published error value from the indicated altitude to determine true altitude. On an approach, this means you may be lower than your altimeter shows — a critical safety consideration for obstacle clearance and MDA/DH compliance.
questions.follow_up: You said the altimeter reads higher with the alternate static source. On an ILS approach to minimums, how does this specific error affect your decision height (DH) and what is the safety implication?
questions.follow_up_answer: If the altimeter is reading higher than actual altitude due to alternate static source use, then when the altimeter shows your published DH — for example, 200 ft HAT — you are actually lower than 200 feet above the touchdown zone. This means you may be at or below DH in terms of actual aircraft position while the instrument still reads at DH. The safety implication is severe: if you continue the approach to the altimeter-indicated DH, you are flying closer to terrain and obstacles than you believe. The correct procedure is to reference the AFM/POH correction for the alternate static source, then add that correction value to your published DH to determine the corrected altimeter reading at which you should execute the missed approach. For example, if the published DH is 200 ft and the alternate static error is +60 ft, you should execute the missed approach when the altimeter reads 260 ft to ensure you do not descend below the actual 200 ft HAT. Always know your aircraft's specific correction values before flight.

questions.question: When flying inbound on a VOR radial, your CDI shows a full-scale deflection to the right. What does that tell you about your position, and approximately how far off course are you?
questions.answer: A full-scale CDI deflection on a VOR indicates you are at least 12 degrees off the selected course. Since VOR radials are oriented FROM the station, a full deflection to the right while flying inbound means you are to the left of the centerline. The actual distance off course depends on your distance from the station — 12 degrees at 10 NM is approximately 2 NM off course. By comparison, a full ILS localizer deflection represents only about 2.5 degrees, making the localizer roughly 4–5 times more sensitive than a VOR CDI.

questions.question: What is the primary function of Distance Measuring Equipment (DME), and what type of information does it provide to the pilot?
questions.answer: DME provides the pilot with slant-range distance in nautical miles to a collocated VORTAC or VOR/DME ground station. It interrogates a ground transponder and measures the time delay of the reply to calculate distance. DME also computes groundspeed and time-to-station when tracking directly to or from the facility. The distance shown is slant range, not horizontal distance — this distinction is most significant when flying directly overhead at high altitude. DME is often paired with VOR to provide both azimuth and distance, enabling a fix without a second VOR.

questions.question: What are the three components of an Instrument Landing System (ILS), and what does each one provide to the pilot?
questions.answer: The three primary components of the ILS are: (1) Localizer — a VHF signal that provides lateral course guidance, centered on the runway extended centerline, with a total width of approximately 5 degrees (full deflection = ~2.5 degrees off course); (2) Glideslope — a UHF signal that provides vertical descent guidance at approximately 3 degrees above horizontal, with full deflection representing about 0.7 degrees deviation; (3) Marker Beacons — outer, middle, and inner markers that provide distance-to-threshold information through audio tones and cockpit light indications (outer = blue/dashes, middle = amber/alternating dots and dashes, inner = white/dots). DME may substitute for marker beacons on some ILS approaches.

questions.question: You are flying a helicopter IFR in IMC and your GPS navigator annunciates 'RAIM NOT AVAILABLE' as you approach the final approach fix for a GPS approach. What does this mean, and what are your options?
questions.answer: RAIM (Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring) is the GPS receiver's self-check that verifies enough satellites are available and providing consistent signals to support the integrity required for the current phase of flight. 'RAIM NOT AVAILABLE' means the receiver cannot confirm the accuracy of the position solution — it does not necessarily mean the position is wrong, but you cannot trust it for navigation. You may not continue the GPS approach if RAIM is unavailable at or before the FAF. Options include: executing a missed approach and holding until RAIM is restored; diverting to an alternate where WAAS or another approach type (VOR, ILS) is available; or, if WAAS-equipped and the approach is LPV/LNAV+V, understand that WAAS uses a different integrity method (SBAS) — but if the WAAS signal itself is flagged, the same restriction applies. Pre-flight RAIM prediction is required for GPS approaches under 14 CFR 91.175.

questions.question: Your helicopter is WAAS-equipped and you're flying an RNAV (GPS) approach. The approach plate shows minimums for LPV, LNAV/VNAV, and LNAV. At briefing, your navigator shows 'LP+V' rather than 'LPV.' Can you use LPV minimums, and what is the practical difference?
questions.answer: No — 'LP+V' is not the same as 'LPV.' LP (Localizer Performance) provides lateral guidance only, similar to a localizer, and the '+V' suffix indicates an advisory vertical path is displayed for situational awareness only — it is not a precision or approved vertical guidance approach. LPV (Localizer Performance with Vertical guidance) is an approach with approved vertical guidance and uses WAAS to meet the required integrity for a decision altitude (DA). LP+V minimums are LNAV-style (MDA), not LPV minimums. The pilot must use the LP or LNAV line of minimums, not the LPV line, if the navigator is showing LP+V. This is a common confusion on the checkride and operationally significant.

questions.question: You're flying a helicopter equipped with an FMS and autopilot coupled to an ILS approach. At 500 feet AGL, the glideslope needle suddenly deflects full-scale up. What are the possible causes, and what is your immediate response?
questions.answer: A full-scale upward glideslope deflection below 500 feet on a coupled ILS approach is a critical situation requiring immediate action. Possible causes include: (1) false glideslope lobe capture — the glideslope transmits multiple lobes, and the false lobe at approximately 9 degrees can capture the receiver; (2) glideslope signal interruption or failure; (3) aircraft deviation far below the glideslope; (4) autopilot or FMS malfunction driving the aircraft off profile. Immediate response: disconnect the autopilot, cross-check all instruments (altimeter, VSI, radar altimeter if equipped), assess aircraft energy state, and execute a missed approach if visual contact with the runway environment has not been established or if safe continuation cannot be confirmed. Below DH/DA, if runway is not in sight or the approach cannot be continued safely, execute the missed approach immediately. Do not chase a full-scale glideslope deflection at low altitude.

questions.question: A pilot flying a helicopter IFR asks you why their GPS position appears accurate on the moving map but the approach mode will not arm for an RNAV (GPS) approach they've loaded. Walk through the possible reasons why an approach might fail to arm even with a valid GPS signal.
questions.answer: Several distinct conditions can prevent approach mode from arming even with a valid GPS position display: (1) Database currency — if the navigation database is expired, many certified GPS units will inhibit approach mode per the AFM/POH supplement; (2) Distance from FAF — most units require the aircraft to be within a defined distance (typically 30 NM) of the destination and within the terminal area before approach mode is selectable; (3) RAIM/integrity prediction — if the unit predicts insufficient integrity will exist at the FAF ETA, it may block arming; (4) Incorrect approach loaded or wrong airport selected — subtle errors like selecting the wrong runway or approach type; (5) Sequencing or activation issue — the approach may be loaded but not 'activated' as the active flight plan leg; (6) WAAS signal unavailable on an LPV approach — the unit may revert to LNAV-only and not arm for LPV; (7) Unit in a degraded mode (e.g., demo mode, simulation mode). The pilot must consult the specific unit's AFM supplement to understand the arming criteria for that installation.
questions.follow_up: If the database is expired by one day, can the pilot legally use the GPS for the RNAV approach under IFR?
questions.follow_up_answer: Not without specific authorization. 14 CFR 91.175 and the AFM supplement govern this. Per AIM 1-1-17, a pilot may use an expired database only if the pilot verifies that the procedures and relevant data have not changed. In practice, most avionics manufacturers and the AFM supplement prohibit IFR approach use with an expired database. Additionally, many certified units will automatically inhibit approach mode when the database expires. The practical answer for a checkride: if the database is expired, the pilot should not fly the RNAV approach — they should either update the database or use a non-GPS approach.
questions.regulatory_ref: AIM 1-1-17; 14 CFR 91.175; AC 90-100A; applicable GPS AFM supplement

questions.question: Your helicopter is conducting an IFR flight with an AHRS-based glass cockpit (no traditional gyros) and an FMS coupled to an autopilot. During cruise, you notice the HSI heading slowly drifting and the autopilot is making progressively larger corrections. The ADC appears normal. What is the most likely cause, what instrument cross-checks would you perform, and how does this scenario differ from a vacuum-driven heading indicator failure in a traditional cockpit?
questions.answer: In an AHRS-based system, the heading source is a solid-state magnetometer and accelerometer array — there is no vacuum-driven gyro to precess. A slow heading drift in an AHRS system most likely indicates: (1) AHRS magnetometer calibration error or local magnetic interference (e.g., cargo, electronics near the sensor); (2) AHRS internal fault beginning to affect the heading channel while the attitude channel remains valid (AHRS failures are not always total); (3) a software or sensor weighting issue in the AHRS unit. Cross-checks: compare AHRS heading to the magnetic compass (the only truly independent heading reference), compare to GPS track (groundspeed must be sufficient for GPS track to be meaningful), and assess whether attitude indications are also suspect. If heading is unreliable, declare it failed and fly using GPS track and magnetic compass as primary heading references. Engage autopilot heading hold cautiously or disconnect. The key difference from a vacuum failure: in a traditional cockpit, heading indicator failure is typically sudden (vacuum loss) and affects the HI distinctly from the attitude indicator. In a glass AHRS system, a partial AHRS failure may affect heading and attitude simultaneously and insidiously — the pilot may not have independent gyro attitude backup unless a standby attitude indicator is installed. This makes AHRS failure more dangerous and harder to detect than a simple vacuum pump failure.
questions.follow_up: If both the primary AHRS heading and the backup magnetic compass are disagreeing with GPS track by 30 degrees, which do you trust, and what are the limitations of using GPS track as a heading substitute?
questions.follow_up_answer: GPS track (course over ground) is a reliable indicator of actual aircraft direction of movement relative to the ground — but it is NOT the same as magnetic heading. GPS track does not account for wind correction angle. In a crosswind, the aircraft heading will differ from GPS track by the wind correction angle. Therefore, if you are flying a heading of 090 with a 20-knot crosswind from the north, your GPS track might show 100 degrees. For navigating in IMC, you can use GPS track to maintain a desired ground track, but you must mentally account for wind drift if heading needs to be precise (e.g., for ATC instructions). Trust GPS track over both a suspect AHRS and a suspect compass only if you have confirmed GPS is functioning normally (no RAIM errors, reasonable groundspeed). The magnetic compass should be used carefully — it is only accurate in straight, unaccelerated, wings-level flight, and at cruise it should be cross-checked after a stabilized straight segment.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B, Chapter 5 (AHRS, ADC, HSI); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9; 14 CFR 91.205

questions.question: What is an Electronic Flight Bag (EFB), and what are the three classes of EFB hardware recognized by the FAA?
questions.answer: An EFB is an electronic device used by flight crew to perform flight planning, display aeronautical charts, reference aircraft performance data, and access other operational information traditionally carried in paper form. The FAA recognizes three hardware classes: Class 1 EFBs are portable, commercially available devices not mounted to the aircraft; Class 2 EFBs are portable devices that may use aircraft power or data ports and may have a mounting system; Class 3 EFBs are installed as part of the aircraft avionics and must meet airworthiness approval standards.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA AC 120-76D (Authorization for Use of Electronic Flight Bags)

questions.question: When using an EFB as your primary aeronautical chart source during an IFR helicopter flight, what is the minimum backup requirement the FAA recommends to ensure continued navigation capability if the EFB fails?
questions.answer: The FAA recommends that pilots have a means to revert to an alternate source of aeronautical information if the EFB fails. This can include a second independent EFB, paper charts, or access to onboard approved navigation equipment. AC 120-76D states that EFB applications used for IFR operations should have redundancy so that a single failure does not leave the crew without required navigation data. At minimum, the pilot should have a current backup source — either paper or a second device — readily accessible.

questions.question: Are pilots required by regulation to have an EFB onboard for IFR helicopter operations, and what currency requirement applies to the aeronautical data loaded on an EFB?
questions.answer: No, an EFB is not required by regulation for IFR operations. However, if an EFB is used in lieu of paper charts, the aeronautical data — including approach plates, terminal procedures, and en route charts — must be current. Under 14 CFR 91.103, a pilot must have all available information concerning the flight. Chart data on an EFB must be within the effective dates of the current chart cycle (updated every 28 days for approach plates via the AIRAC cycle) to be considered current and usable for IFR operations.

questions.question: You are on an IFR cross-country in a helicopter and your EFB loses power and cannot be restarted just as you are cleared for an RNAV (GPS) approach at your destination. You have no paper charts onboard. What should you do, and what does this scenario tell you about EFB risk management?
questions.answer: You should immediately notify ATC that you have lost your EFB and request an alternate means of completing the approach — for example, ATC can provide advisory information, or you can divert to an alternate airport where you have other means of chart access. You should declare the situation to ATC and coordinate accordingly. This scenario illustrates the critical risk management principle that an EFB used as a sole-source chart replacement creates a single point of failure. Pilots using EFBs without backup charts or a second device violate the spirit of 14 CFR 91.103 (preflight planning) and AC 120-76D guidance on redundancy. Proper risk management requires either a second EFB, paper backups, or confirmed onboard avionics capable of executing the approach independently.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.103; FAA AC 120-76D; 14 CFR 91.167 (alternate airport requirements)

questions.question: A helicopter pilot uses a tablet EFB with a GPS receiver for moving map navigation during an IFR flight. ATC asks for your position and your installed panel GPS has failed. Can you legally use the EFB's GPS position for IFR navigation, and what limitations apply?
questions.answer: A Class 1 or Class 2 EFB with an integrated or attached GPS is generally not approved as a primary IFR navigation source unless the device and its GPS meet specific airworthiness requirements. The GPS in a commercial tablet typically does not meet TSO-C146 or TSO-C129 standards required for IFR navigation. Therefore, the EFB's GPS moving map can be used as a situational awareness tool but cannot substitute for an approved IFR navigation system. The pilot must use installed, certified navigation equipment for IFR navigation. If installed avionics have failed to a degree that IFR navigation is not possible, the pilot should declare the situation to ATC and proceed accordingly under 14 CFR 91.187.

questions.question: During your preflight planning for an IFR helicopter flight, you notice that your EFB app shows approach plates that expired two days ago and a database update is available but not yet downloaded. The weather at your destination is IMC. How should you handle this situation, and what regulatory principle applies?
questions.answer: You must not depart on an IFR flight relying on expired approach plate data. Under 14 CFR 91.103, the pilot in command must become familiar with all available information concerning the flight, which includes using current charts. Expired approach plate data may not reflect current NOTAMs, frequency changes, minimums revisions, or procedure amendments, all of which are safety-critical for IFR operations. The correct action is to download and install the current database update before flight, verify the effective dates, and confirm all approach data is current. If internet connectivity is unavailable to update the EFB, you must obtain current approach information through another means — paper charts, a second updated device, or delaying departure until the update can be completed.

questions.question: An operator wants to use a Class 2 EFB with an aircraft-specific performance application to replace the helicopter's paper AFM performance charts during operations. Under what conditions is this permissible, and who has authority to approve the EFB software application for this purpose?
questions.answer: Using an EFB application to replace AFM performance charts is classified as a Type C (aircraft airworthiness-related) application under AC 120-76D. Type C applications require formal airworthiness approval because they directly affect aircraft operations and airworthiness decisions. This approval is granted by the FAA's Aircraft Certification Office (ACO) or through an amended FAA-approved AFM supplement. The operator cannot self-authorize Type C applications — they require an Supplemental Type Certificate (STC) or AFM amendment. The FSDO or appropriate certification office must evaluate the software for accuracy, data integrity, and operational suitability before it can legally replace paper AFM performance charts. Simply loading a performance app on a tablet and using it in lieu of the AFM is not permissible without this approval.
questions.follow_up: If the EFB performance application is approved and the helicopter pilot notices that the app's computed hover ceiling differs significantly from what the paper AFM charts show for the same conditions, what should the pilot do?
questions.follow_up_answer: The pilot must not use the EFB application and should immediately ground the aircraft from operations relying on that performance data. A discrepancy between an approved EFB performance application and the paper AFM charts indicates a potential software error, data corruption, or input error that must be resolved before flight. The pilot should document the discrepancy, report it to the operator and the EFB application developer or vendor, and revert to the paper AFM as the authoritative source. Under 14 CFR 91.9, the PIC is responsible for not exceeding aircraft limitations, which requires relying only on verified, accurate performance data. Operating on suspect performance data — especially for hover operations where power margins are critical — is unacceptable from both a regulatory and safety standpoint.

questions.question: During an IFR checkride, an instrument helicopter applicant references their EFB during a simulated partial panel scenario to pull up the approach chart. As the examiner, what specific concerns would you probe regarding EFB use and workload management in a degraded aircraft state, and what standard must the applicant demonstrate?
questions.answer: As an examiner, the primary concerns are: (1) whether the applicant loses aircraft control or allows critical attitude deviations while manipulating the EFB — especially on partial panel where workload is already elevated; (2) whether the applicant has pre-briefed the approach and loaded the chart before the degraded scenario began, demonstrating proper workload management; (3) whether the applicant knows the approach details well enough to cross-reference the EFB with the garbled or failed instruments. The ACS standard requires that EFB use not compromise the pilot's ability to aviate, navigate, and communicate in priority order. An applicant who drops below ACS tolerances (e.g., ±100 feet altitude, ±10 knots airspeed, ±10° heading for partial panel) while fumbling with an EFB demonstrates a workload management failure. The applicant must also show awareness that if the EFB fails at this moment, a backup plan must exist.
questions.follow_up: If the applicant tells you they always use the EFB as their sole chart source and never carry paper backups, how would you evaluate whether this is an acceptable risk management strategy for a helicopter IFR pilot?
questions.follow_up_answer: This is not an acceptable risk management strategy without a second independent EFB or equivalent redundancy. AC 120-76D specifically advises that when an EFB is used in lieu of paper products for IFR operations, there should be a means to revert to an alternate source if the EFB fails. A single EFB with no backup represents a single point of failure at a critical phase of flight. Under the PAVE and SRM frameworks taught in the Helicopter Flying Handbook, the pilot must identify and mitigate equipment risks. Relying solely on one electronic device — subject to battery failure, software crashes, screen damage, or RF interference — without any fallback violates sound risk management principles. During the checkride debrief, this would be identified as a risk management deficiency even if the applicant flew proficiently, and it would be addressed as a teaching point if not an unsatisfactory item depending on the overall evaluation context.

questions.question: In a helicopter equipped with an autopilot or Flight Management System, what is the primary risk associated with over-reliance on automated systems during IFR flight?
questions.answer: Over-reliance on automated systems — sometimes called 'automation complacency' — can cause the pilot to lose situational awareness, degrade manual flying skills, and fail to detect system malfunctions or data errors in time to take corrective action. The pilot in command is always responsible for the safety of the flight regardless of what automation is doing, and automation must be actively monitored, not passively trusted.

questions.question: What does the term 'automation management' mean in the context of Single-Pilot Resource Management for helicopter IFR operations?
questions.answer: Automation management is the ability to control and use automated systems — such as autopilots, GPS navigators, flight directors, and FMS — at the appropriate level of capability for the phase of flight, while continuously monitoring their status and outputs. It includes knowing when to engage, disengage, or reduce the automation level, and maintaining the manual skills needed to fly the helicopter safely if automation fails or gives erroneous guidance.

questions.question: When a helicopter's AHRS provides attitude and heading data to the autopilot and PFD, what single-point failure risk does the pilot need to manage, and how?
questions.answer: Because a single AHRS unit feeds multiple downstream systems — the PFD, HSI, autopilot, and possibly the FMS — a failure or error in the AHRS can simultaneously corrupt attitude, heading, and navigation displays without being immediately obvious. The pilot must cross-check AHRS-driven displays against independent backup instruments (e.g., a standby attitude indicator, magnetic compass), monitor for any disagreement flags or annunciations, and know how to disconnect the autopilot and revert to raw instrument flight if needed.

questions.question: You are flying a helicopter IFR en route and notice the autopilot-coupled GPS course deviation bar is centered, but a quick glance at the map page shows you are several miles off your expected track. What risk does this scenario illustrate, and what should you do?
questions.answer: This scenario illustrates the risk of 'automation mode confusion' — the autopilot may be tracking a wrong waypoint, an outdated flight plan leg, or a database error, while displaying a falsely reassuring centered needle. The risk is CFIT or airspace deviation due to trusting the automated system without independent verification. The pilot should immediately cross-check position using raw VOR/DME data or a secondary GPS source, confirm the active leg and waypoint in the FMS/GPS, and be prepared to disconnect the autopilot and fly manually while resolving the discrepancy. Never assume centered = correct without confirming what the system is actually tracking.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9 (GPS/FMS errors); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (CFIT awareness, SA)

questions.question: During a helicopter IFR approach in IMC, the flight director suddenly provides pitch guidance that seems to command a steeper descent than expected. You are single pilot. Describe how you manage the risk of this automated system anomaly in real time.
questions.answer: First, do not blindly follow the flight director command bars — cross-check the raw approach data (glideslope needle, altimeter, VSI) against what the flight director is commanding. If they disagree, the raw data takes precedence. Immediately reduce workload on secondary tasks, verbalize the discrepancy to yourself as part of SRM, and consider disconnecting the flight director and flying raw instrument data for the remainder of the approach. If the approach is destabilized or you cannot confirm your position and rate of descent, execute a missed approach. Per ADM principles, if you're only 'probably' going to make this work, choose the option you know works — the missed approach.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5 (FDS/flight director); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (Trescott Tip, ADM)

questions.question: A helicopter pilot transitioning from a steam-gauge aircraft to a glass cockpit helicopter with an integrated AHRS and ADC has 2,000 total flight hours but only 15 hours in the new aircraft. What specific risk management concern does this situation create regarding automated system monitoring?
questions.answer: Research cited in the FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook shows that accident rates correlate more strongly with hours in a specific aircraft model than with total hours — pilots with low time in type are at higher risk regardless of experience. With only 15 hours in type, this pilot may not yet recognize normal versus abnormal system behaviors, may be slower to detect automation failures or annunciations, and may not be proficient at recovering to manual IFR flight if the automation fails. Risk mitigation includes additional training focused on automation failures, practicing manual reversions under IMC conditions, and avoiding high-risk operations (e.g., single-pilot IMC approaches to minimums) until type proficiency is established.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (hours in type correlation); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5 (AHRS/ADC)

questions.question: A helicopter with a coupled autopilot is flying a GPS approach in LNAV mode. The GPS receiver silently loses WAAS augmentation mid-approach and downgrades to non-WAAS GPS accuracy, but the autopilot remains coupled and the pilot does not notice the mode change. What layered risks are present, and what monitoring protocols should have prevented this situation?
questions.answer: The layered risks include: (1) the pilot flying an approach to LNAV minimums that the system may now lack the accuracy to support; (2) autopilot coupling continuing to a degraded navigation source without the pilot's awareness; (3) potential CFIT if the descent is continued to minimums with insufficient lateral or vertical accuracy. Prevention requires active monitoring of the GPS annunciation panel and PFD for RAIM alerts, WAAS integrity flags, or approach mode downgrade messages throughout the approach — not just at the FAF. The pilot should verify that the GPS approach mode (LNAV, LNAV/VNAV, LPV) displayed matches the approach being flown and the minimums being used, and confirm this at each step-down fix and prior to the FAF. Autopilot coupling does not reduce the pilot's responsibility to monitor navigation source integrity.
questions.follow_up: If the GPS downgrades from LPV to LNAV mid-approach and you are already below LPV decision altitude but above LNAV MDA, what is the correct action?
questions.follow_up_answer: The pilot must immediately execute a missed approach. The aircraft has descended below an altitude that is only protected under LPV approach criteria, and continuing the approach using LNAV minimums when you are already below the LNAV MDA is not permitted. The missed approach must be initiated without delay, and the situation should be reported to ATC. This scenario underscores why the pilot must monitor GPS integrity annunciations continuously — not just at approach initiation.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9 (WAAS, GPS approach modes, RAIM); 14 CFR 91.175

questions.question: In the context of automated system management, explain the risk created when a helicopter pilot uses the 'set it and forget it' approach to the autopilot during a long IFR cruise leg, and describe how the error chain concept applies if conditions begin to deteriorate.
questions.answer: The 'set it and forget it' mindset leads to progressive erosion of situational awareness — the pilot stops actively monitoring position, fuel state, weather, system annunciations, and airspace. If conditions deteriorate (e.g., weather moves in, fuel burn is higher than planned, an automated system begins to degrade), the pilot is now behind the aircraft and has reduced cognitive capacity to detect and respond. The error chain concept from ADM describes how accidents are rarely caused by a single failure but rather by a sequence of compounding poor decisions or missed cues — automation complacency is often an early link in that chain. Breaking the chain requires scheduled scan discipline: the pilot should perform systematic checks of navigation accuracy, fuel, weather, system annunciations, and terrain clearance at defined intervals regardless of how smoothly automation appears to be performing.
questions.follow_up: If you're single pilot in IMC and you realize the autopilot has been tracking the wrong VOR radial for the past 10 minutes, walk me through your immediate priority sequence.
questions.follow_up_answer: First, maintain aircraft control — verify attitude and altitude are stable, and if not, correct them first. Second, determine actual position using all available cross-checks (DME, second VOR, GPS, ATC radar). Third, advise ATC immediately — declare a problem if necessary and request vectors if positional uncertainty is high. Fourth, re-evaluate the flight plan to confirm a safe route forward. Fifth, investigate why the autopilot tracked the wrong radial — wrong course set in the HSI, wrong station selected, or system error — and correct or disable the erroneous automation. Throughout, apply SRM: prioritize tasks, manage workload, and avoid fixating on troubleshooting while neglecting aircraft control.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (error chain, SRM, ADM, workload management); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9 (VOR tracking)

questions.question: What is the fundamental regulatory difference between an approved and a non-approved navigation device for IFR flight in a helicopter?
questions.answer: An approved navigation device has been certified under TSO (Technical Standard Order) standards and is installed in accordance with an FAA-approved avionics installation, making it legal for use as a primary navigation source under IFR. A non-approved device — such as a consumer-grade tablet or handheld GPS running EFB software — has not been certified to TSO standards and cannot be used as a primary navigation source for IFR operations. It may be used as a supplemental or situational awareness tool only. The distinction matters because approved equipment must meet accuracy, reliability, and integrity standards that non-approved devices are not required to meet.

questions.question: What does TSO stand for, and why does it matter when determining whether a navigation device is approved for IFR use?
questions.answer: TSO stands for Technical Standard Order. It is an FAA minimum performance standard that avionics manufacturers must meet for their equipment to be considered airworthy and approved for installation and use in certificated aircraft. Navigation devices that hold a TSO authorization — such as GPS receivers certified under TSO-C129 or TSO-C145/C146 — have been tested and verified to meet specific accuracy, integrity, and reliability requirements. Devices without TSO authorization, such as consumer GPS units or tablet applications, have not been evaluated to these standards and are therefore not approved for use as a primary IFR navigation source.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR Part 21 Subpart O; TSO-C129; TSO-C145; TSO-C146

questions.question: Can a pilot legally use a tablet or smartphone running an aviation navigation app — such as ForeFlight or Garmin Pilot — as the sole navigation source for an IFR helicopter flight? Why or why not?
questions.answer: No. A tablet or smartphone running an aviation navigation app is considered a non-approved device because it is not certified to any FAA TSO standard and is not installed as part of the type-certificated avionics system. These devices are classified as Electronic Flight Bags (EFBs) and may be used as a supplemental situational awareness tool — for example, to cross-check position or display charts — but they cannot legally serve as the primary or sole navigation source for IFR flight. Primary IFR navigation must be accomplished using approved, TSO-certified equipment that is properly installed and maintained in the aircraft.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.205; AC 91-78 (Use of Class 1 or Class 2 Electronic Flight Bag); AIM 1-1-17

questions.question: You are flying an IFR helicopter flight and your panel-mounted, TSO-certified GPS fails enroute. You have a current tablet with ForeFlight and a portable ADS-B receiver showing your GPS position. Describe the risks of relying on the tablet as your primary navigation tool for the remainder of the flight.
questions.answer: The primary risk is that you are now navigating without an approved navigation source, which may constitute a regulatory violation and — more critically — places you in a high-risk situation from a safety standpoint. Non-approved devices like tablets are not subject to the same database currency, signal integrity monitoring, or fault alerting requirements as TSO-certified avionics. The portable ADS-B receiver provides GPS position data but has not been certified for primary IFR navigation use. Additionally, if ATC is providing radar services, you may be able to continue with ATC guidance, but you must declare the situation and coordinate an appropriate course of action — including diversion to a suitable airport. The 'error chain' risk here is relying on a device whose accuracy and reliability have not been verified to IFR standards, potentially leading to CFIT or navigational error especially in IMC or mountainous terrain.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.205; AC 91-78; AIM 6-1-2 (Declaring an Emergency); Instrument Flying Handbook FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9

questions.question: A helicopter operator tells you that the installed GPS in the aircraft has an expired database, but the portable tablet has a current database and subscription. For an IFR flight using a GPS approach, what are the risks of relying on the tablet for the approach and why can't it substitute for the panel-mounted unit?
questions.answer: A GPS approach requires an approved, TSO-certified GPS receiver with a current navigation database. An expired database in the panel-mounted GPS means it cannot legally be used for that GPS approach unless the pilot verifies that the procedure has not changed and receives an appropriate authorization — but in practice the expired database is a significant risk and typically precludes its use for approaches. The tablet cannot substitute because it is not an approved navigation system certified to TSO-C129, TSO-C145, or TSO-C146, and it has not been integrated into the aircraft's avionics in an FAA-approved manner. Using the tablet as the sole means of flying the approach would be a regulatory violation and introduces safety risks including lack of integrity monitoring, receiver autonomous integrity monitoring (RAIM) equivalent functionality, and no verified obstacle clearance assurance. The correct action is to select an approach for which approved equipment is current and legal, or divert.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.205; AIM 1-1-17; TSO-C129/C145/C146; AC 90-94; Instrument Flying Handbook FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9

questions.question: During preflight planning for an IFR helicopter flight, how do you confirm that the navigation equipment installed in the aircraft is actually approved for the type of IFR operations you intend to fly — such as GPS RNAV approaches?
questions.answer: You should confirm approval through several steps: First, check the aircraft's Approved Flight Manual (AFM) or AFM Supplement for the specific navigation equipment installed — it will list what operations the avionics are authorized for. Second, verify the equipment holds a valid TSO authorization (TSO-C129a for non-WAAS GPS, or TSO-C145/C146 for WAAS-capable GPS) by checking the equipment manual or avionics documentation. Third, confirm the navigation database is current for the intended date of flight. Fourth, verify the installation was accomplished via a Supplemental Type Certificate (STC) or FAA Form 337 field approval, making it part of the legal avionics system. Fifth, for WAAS GPS approaches (LPV or LNAV/VNAV), confirm the unit is WAAS-capable and that WAAS is available and functional via NOTAMs. Without these verifications, you risk attempting an approach with equipment that is not authorized for that operation.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.205; 14 CFR 91.9; AC 90-100A (RNAV operations); AIM 1-1-18; TSO-C145/C146

questions.question: A student tells you: 'My tablet has WAAS GPS built in and shows accuracy of less than 3 meters — it's more accurate than the certified GPS in the panel, so it should be fine to use for IFR approaches.' How do you respond, and what is the fundamental flaw in their reasoning?
questions.answer: The student is confusing accuracy with integrity and airworthiness approval. Accuracy alone does not make a device approved for IFR use. The flaw is that TSO certification evaluates not just positional accuracy under normal conditions, but also signal integrity monitoring, fault detection and exclusion, alerting capability (RAIM or WAAS integrity), resistance to interference and spoofing, and the reliability of performance under adverse conditions. A consumer WAAS chip in a tablet may report high accuracy on a clear day, but it provides no certified integrity alerts if the signal degrades below IFR requirements, no independent cross-checking, and no guaranteed performance under all conditions the FAA requires. Additionally, approved avionics must be installed in accordance with FAA-approved data, maintained under Part 43, and documented in the aircraft records. A tablet meets none of these requirements regardless of its raw GPS accuracy. The risk is that the pilot may fly an approach believing they have reliable guidance when in fact they have no certified safety net if the data degrades.
questions.follow_up: If accuracy doesn't determine approval, what specific integrity concept does the FAA use to evaluate whether GPS-based navigation is safe for a given phase of flight or approach type?
questions.follow_up_answer: The FAA uses the concept of Required Navigation Performance (RNP) and specifically Horizontal Protection Level (HPL) versus Horizontal Alert Limit (HAL). RAIM (Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring) continuously monitors the GPS signal and alerts the pilot if integrity cannot be assured within the limits required for the current operation. For WAAS, the system uses a ground-based correction and integrity monitoring network (SBAS) to compute protection levels. If the HPL exceeds the HAL for the intended operation, the system alerts the pilot that GPS cannot be used for that phase. This entire integrity monitoring architecture is part of what TSO-C129/C145/C146 requires — and it is completely absent in consumer-grade GPS devices regardless of their advertised positional accuracy.
questions.regulatory_ref: TSO-C129a; TSO-C145c; TSO-C146c; AIM 1-1-17; AC 90-105A (RNP Operations); Instrument Flying Handbook FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9

questions.question: You are conducting a helicopter IFR checkride and discover the helicopter has a panel-mounted GPS that was installed without a Supplemental Type Certificate (STC) or FAA Form 337 field approval — the owner just had an avionics shop plug it in. The unit has a current TSO and a current database. What are the airworthiness and risk management implications, and can this flight legally proceed?
questions.answer: The flight cannot legally proceed under IFR using that GPS as a navigation source. While the unit itself holds a valid TSO authorization, the installation must also be FAA-approved to be considered part of the legal avionics suite. Without an STC or FAA Form 337 field approval documenting the installation, the modification is unapproved, making the aircraft potentially unairworthy. Under 14 CFR 91.7, the pilot in command is responsible for ensuring the aircraft is in airworthy condition before flight. Under 14 CFR 43.3, only properly certificated personnel using FAA-approved data may perform maintenance and alterations. An unapproved installation means there has been no FAA review of wiring, interference, antenna placement, or compatibility with other aircraft systems. Even if the GPS functions correctly, the aircraft's airworthiness certificate is potentially compromised by the unapproved alteration. The risk management implication is that relying on this GPS introduces not just regulatory risk but genuine safety risk — no one has certified that this particular installation performs correctly in this aircraft's environment. The checkride cannot proceed; the aircraft owner must obtain proper authorization for the installation before it can be used legally for IFR operations.
questions.follow_up: Suppose the shop claimed they used an existing, valid STC but cannot produce the paperwork. What document should be in the aircraft records to prove an STC-based installation was performed, and where would you find it?
questions.follow_up_answer: The aircraft maintenance records (logbooks) must contain an entry documenting the avionics installation, referencing the specific STC number (e.g., SA-XXXX) used to authorize the work. Additionally, if the STC added new limitations or required changes to the AFM, a copy of the STC approval holder's FAA-approved AFM Supplement must be in the aircraft with the flight manual. The STC holder's installation manual should also be on file. You would find the logbook entry in the airframe maintenance log, and the AFM Supplement in the aircraft document package.
