If neither the logbook entry nor the AFM Supplement can be produced, there is no legal evidence the installation was performed under an approved STC, and the aircraft should be treated as having an unapproved modification until the documentation is located or the installation is properly re-authorized.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.7; 14 CFR 43.3; 14 CFR 43.9; 14 CFR 21.113 (STC requirements); 14 CFR 91.9; AC 43-9C (Maintenance Records)

questions.question: Your static system becomes blocked during an IFR flight in your helicopter. What happens to your altimeter, VSI, and airspeed indicator?
questions.answer: With a blocked static system, the altimeter freezes and shows the altitude at which the blockage occurred — it will not update as you climb or descend. The VSI will show a continuous zero, giving no climb or descent information. The ASI will become inaccurate because it relies on static pressure to compute the differential with pitot pressure. If the helicopter is equipped with an alternate static source, you should switch to it — but note that cabin static is slightly lower than ambient, so the alternate source will give a slightly higher indicated altitude, a faster indicated airspeed, and a momentary climb indication on the VSI.

questions.question: What is the difference between 'homing' and 'tracking' to an NDB station, and why does homing to a station represent a navigation risk in IMC?
questions.answer: Homing means simply keeping the ADF needle pointed to 0° relative bearing — the pilot uses any heading necessary to keep the needle centered. In a crosswind, this causes the aircraft to fly a curved, arcing path toward the station rather than a straight track. Tracking means establishing a specific magnetic bearing to the station by correcting for wind drift, resulting in a straight-line ground track. Homing is a risk in IMC because the curved path may take you into terrain, obstacles, or airspace that a direct straight-line track would have avoided, and the approach geometry will be unpredictable — especially critical during final approach segments.

questions.question: On your helicopter's PFD, the AHRS fails in flight. Which instruments lose their primary source of information, and what is your backup strategy?
questions.answer: The AHRS (Attitude and Heading Reference System) is a solid-state system that replaces the traditional attitude indicator, heading indicator, and turn indicator. If the AHRS fails, the PFD will lose attitude, heading, and turn rate information. The risk is significant because all three of those indications disappear from a single point of failure — unlike older systems where each had a separate gyro. The backup strategy depends on the specific aircraft and avionics suite, but typically includes a standby attitude indicator (often battery-powered), a standby magnetic compass, and potentially a secondary AHRS source if installed. The pilot should immediately cross-check the standby instruments, declare the failure to ATC, and if necessary, request vectors or a clearance to VMC to reduce workload.

questions.question: You're flying your helicopter IFR on a GPS approach and the navigator annunciates 'RAIM NOT AVAILABLE' just as you reach the FAF. What does this mean operationally, and what should you do?
questions.answer: RAIM stands for Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring — it is the GPS receiver's ability to self-check that the satellite geometry and signal quality are sufficient to support navigation accuracy. If RAIM is not available at the FAF, the GPS cannot guarantee the accuracy required for the approach. Operationally, this means you cannot continue the GPS approach because the system cannot verify its own integrity. You should execute the published missed approach immediately, notify ATC, and request an alternate approach procedure (such as an ILS, VOR, or NDB approach if available) or request vectors to an alternate airport. RAIM availability should be checked during preflight planning — GPS RAIM prediction tools allow you to verify availability for the planned approach window before departure.

questions.question: During an IFR flight in your helicopter, you notice your VOR CDI is showing a full deflection even though you are tracking what you believe is the correct radial. What are three possible failure conditions you should consider, and how would you differentiate between them?
questions.answer: Three possible failure conditions are: (1) VOR receiver failure — the CDI may go to full deflection if the receiver loses the signal or fails; check the NAV flag, which should appear if the signal is lost. (2) You are actually significantly off course — a full VOR CDI deflection indicates 12 degrees or more off the selected radial. Cross-check your heading indicator and GPS if available to confirm your actual position. (3) Incorrect course selection — verify the OBS is set to the correct radial/course. To differentiate: check the NAV flag first (flag = signal loss or receiver failure), then compare with GPS position to determine if you are truly off course, then verify the OBS setting. If GPS confirms you are on course and the flag is not showing, suspect receiver failure and notify ATC. Note that VOR CDI full deflection equals roughly 12 degrees, while a localizer full deflection is only 2.5 degrees — much more sensitive.

questions.question: You are conducting an IFR flight in a helicopter equipped with an autopilot coupled to the FMS. Partway through the flight, you notice the helicopter has deviated significantly from the programmed route and the autopilot is still engaged. What risk does this scenario illustrate, and how should you manage it?
questions.answer: This scenario illustrates automation complacency and loss of situational awareness — a significant risk associated with highly automated flight management systems. When pilots over-rely on automation, they can lose awareness of what the aircraft is actually doing, a concept sometimes called 'automation surprise.' The risk is compounded in IMC because the pilot may not detect the deviation visually. Management steps: First, disconnect the autopilot and fly the aircraft manually to regain direct control. Cross-check your actual position using all available navigation sources (GPS, VOR, DME). Determine the cause of the deviation — possible causes include incorrect FMS programming, a database error, an entered waypoint error, or an autopilot mode that was not what the pilot intended. Notify ATC of the deviation and your current position. The FAA and SRM principles emphasize that automation should be monitored continuously and that pilots must remain actively engaged even when the autopilot is flying.

questions.question: Your helicopter's pitot tube becomes blocked with ice, but the drain hole remains open. Describe precisely how the ASI will behave during a climb, descent, and level flight — and explain why this specific failure mode is more insidious than a fully blocked pitot system in terms of pilot risk.
questions.answer: When the pitot tube is blocked but the drain hole remains open, the pitot chamber drains to ambient pressure. This means the ASI receives only static pressure on the pitot side, which equals the static pressure on the static side — resulting in zero differential pressure. The ASI will slowly bleed off to zero regardless of actual airspeed, in all phases of flight. It does not respond to climbs or descents. This is more insidious than a fully blocked pitot system (both tube and drain blocked) because: with both holes blocked, the pitot chamber maintains the trapped pressure, causing the ASI to behave like an altimeter — it increases in a climb and decreases in a descent, giving the pilot an obvious and dramatic indication that something is wrong. A pilot noticing the ASI increasing as they descend will quickly recognize instrument failure. However, with just the drain hole open, the ASI slowly drops to zero in a way that can initially look like an airspeed deceleration, potentially leading a pilot to add power inappropriately or to accept the zero reading as valid for longer before diagnosing the failure — especially under high workload in IMC.
questions.follow_up: If this pitot failure occurred during a coupled autopilot approach and the autopilot uses ASI data from the ADC, what additional risk is introduced and how might it manifest?
questions.follow_up_answer: If the autopilot's Air Data Computer (ADC) feeds on the faulty pitot data, the autopilot may attempt to correct for what it perceives as a continuously decelerating or zero-airspeed condition. Depending on the autopilot's logic, it could command nose-down pitch and/or increase power to 'recover' from the perceived airspeed loss — potentially putting the helicopter into a dangerous attitude or configuration, especially during a low-altitude instrument approach. The pilot must be aware that in integrated glass cockpit systems, a pitot failure can cascade through the ADC to affect autopilot behavior, and any unexpected autopilot or flight director command should trigger a cross-check of all raw data sources and potentially a disconnect of the automation.

questions.question: A helicopter pilot reports that during a night IFR flight, all gyroscopic instruments appeared normal but heading indications drifted significantly, causing a deviation from the assigned airway. The aircraft had no obvious mechanical failures. What failure mode could explain this, and what does it mean for risk management when planning IFR flights in this aircraft?
questions.answer: The most likely explanation is a vacuum system failure — either a failed vacuum pump or a broken drive coupling — that allowed the gyroscopic instruments to slowly tumble or precess without triggering an obvious cockpit warning. In aircraft with wet-type vacuum pumps, failure can be gradual, and if the vacuum gauge is not actively monitored, the pilot may not detect the loss until significant instrument error has developed. In aircraft using AHRS (solid-state), a heading drift could suggest a magnetometer calibration error, magnetic interference, or AHRS initialization error. For risk management: the pilot should include vacuum gauge (or AHRS health page) in the regular instrument scan, not just during preflight. Cross-checking heading against GPS track and magnetic compass periodically is essential. Operationally, the risk is that a gradual vacuum or AHRS failure can produce a false sense of confidence — all needles appear to be moving normally, just pointing in the wrong direction. IFR flight planning should include briefing alternate vacuum sources (electric standby gyros), knowing the AHRS failure indications specific to the installed avionics, and having a plan for the failure before it happens.
questions.follow_up: If the helicopter has a single vacuum pump with no backup electric gyro and the pump fails in IMC, what are the pilot's options and what does 14 CFR 91.205 say about required equipment for IFR?
questions.follow_up_answer: Under 14 CFR 91.205(d), IFR operations require a gyroscopic rate-of-turn indicator, slip-skid indicator, gyroscopic pitch-and-bank indicator, and gyroscopic direction indicator among other instruments. If the vacuum pump fails and there is no backup, the pilot has lost multiple required instruments simultaneously. Options include: immediately declaring an emergency, requesting ATC assistance and radar vectors, attempting to climb to VMC if feasible, or executing a partial-panel approach using only the magnetic compass, ASI, altimeter, and VSI — which is very demanding. If the aircraft is not equipped and maintained to meet 91.205(d) requirements with a working backup, it should not depart IFR. This failure scenario underscores the importance of a pre-flight vacuum system check and the risk of operating IFR with a single-source gyro system.

questions.question: What is an Electronic Flight Bag (EFB), and what are the three classes the FAA recognizes for EFB equipment?
questions.answer: An EFB is an electronic device that helps flight crews perform flight management tasks more easily and efficiently, replacing traditional paper-based reference materials. The FAA recognizes three classes: Class 1 EFBs are portable, commercially available devices (e.g., tablets/iPads) not mounted to the aircraft; Class 2 EFBs are portable but use aircraft power or data ports and may be mounted on a fixed mount; Class 3 EFBs are installed aircraft components certified under TSO and treated as avionics. Most GA helicopter pilots use Class 1 or Class 2 devices running EFB software applications.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA AC 120-76D (Authorization for Use of Electronic Flight Bags); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5

questions.question: What does the FAA require a pilot to verify about an EFB's navigation data before using it for IFR flight?
questions.answer: The pilot must verify that all navigation databases loaded in the EFB are current and within their expiration date. Navigation databases (including approach plates, charts, and GPS databases) are typically updated on a 28-day AIRAC cycle. Using outdated database information can result in incorrect procedure depictions, missing NOTAMs, or inaccurate obstacle data. Additionally, the pilot should confirm the EFB software version is current and the device is functioning properly during preflight.

questions.question: Under what circumstances may a pilot use an EFB in place of paper charts for IFR operations, and is this always permitted?
questions.answer: A pilot may use an EFB in place of paper charts when authorized under FAA AC 120-76D for Part 91 operations, provided the EFB application is approved for that use, the database is current, and the device has been tested for the operational environment. However, this is not automatically permitted in all contexts — air carrier operations (Parts 121/135) require specific OpSpec or Letter of Authorization approval. For Part 91 IFR operations in a helicopter, a Class 1 or 2 EFB with current charts is generally acceptable, but the pilot must ensure the device is reliable and have a contingency plan if it fails.

questions.question: You are conducting an IFR helicopter flight in IMC at cruise altitude. Your EFB tablet suddenly loses power and will not restart. You have no paper charts aboard. How do you manage this situation, and what risk does it highlight?
questions.answer: This situation highlights the risk of over-reliance on a single electronic device without a backup. Immediate actions: declare the situation to ATC, request radar vectors or assistance, and use the aircraft's installed avionics (GPS/FMS, CDIs, and any installed approach capability) to continue safely. The risk is that if the EFB is the sole reference for approach plates, the pilot may be unable to execute an instrument approach safely without ATC assistance. Best practice is to always carry a backup — either paper charts for the route of flight, a second EFB/tablet, or ensure ForeFlight/similar apps are pre-loaded and downloaded offline. This underscores the ADM principle of not relying on a system that will only 'probably' keep working.

questions.question: During your preflight planning, you notice your EFB shows an instrument approach procedure for your destination that looks slightly different from what you recalled briefing last week. What risk management steps should you take before accepting that approach data as accurate?
questions.answer: First, verify the navigation database cycle date on the EFB — if it was recently updated (28-day AIRAC cycle), the procedure may have legitimately changed. Cross-check against an official, current source such as the FAA's Instrument Approach Procedures (IAP) published on AeroNav/FAA charts or a second EFB with a verified current database. Check NOTAMs for the destination airport and the specific navaid or procedure, as NOTAMs may amend procedure notes, minimums, or availability. Never fly a procedure that cannot be verified as current from an authoritative source. This scenario also illustrates the risk of complacency — assuming familiarity with a procedure without re-checking currency.

questions.question: You are flying an IFR helicopter tour operation under Part 135. Your company has not issued an OpSpec authorizing EFB use, but your personal tablet has all current charts loaded. Can you use it as your primary chart reference on this flight, and what are the risk implications if you do?
questions.answer: No — under Part 135, you may not substitute an EFB for required paper charts or approved electronic chart systems without specific OpSpec authorization from the FAA. Using an unauthorized EFB as your primary chart reference is a regulatory violation under 14 CFR Part 135 and the applicable OpSpecs. The risk implications are significant: if an incident or accident occurs, using non-approved equipment could result in certificate action, company liability, and insurance issues. Additionally, without company vetting of the EFB software and procedures, there is no assurance the device meets operational standards. The correct course is to use approved, authorized chart sources and work with your company's operations department to obtain proper EFB authorization.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR Part 135; FAA AC 120-76D; OpSpec A061 (EFB authorization for Part 135)

questions.question: A helicopter pilot uses a tablet EFB mounted on the cyclic for in-flight reference. During a single-pilot IFR approach in a turbine helicopter, the pilot spends significant time head-down manipulating the EFB to zoom in on the approach plate. What specific risk does this create in the helicopter IFR environment that may be more pronounced than in a fixed-wing aircraft, and how should it be mitigated?
questions.answer: In the single-pilot helicopter IFR environment, extended head-down time with the EFB creates a severe workload and situational awareness risk that is more acute than in fixed-wing because: (1) helicopters require more continuous, coordinated control inputs — even momentary inattention can result in rapid attitude deviation; (2) the high vibration environment of helicopters can make small-screen touch inputs more difficult and time-consuming; (3) transition to/from the EFB competes directly with scan of the primary flight instruments at the most critical phase of flight. This directly increases the risk of spatial disorientation and controlled flight into terrain (CFIT). Mitigation includes: pre-loading and fully briefing the approach before entering IMC, setting the EFB to the correct approach plate at the IAF so no manipulation is needed during the approach, using autopilot where installed to reduce stick-and-rudder workload, and never using the EFB as a substitute for primary instrument scan during critical flight phases.
questions.follow_up: If the helicopter is equipped with a certified installed GPS/FMS that displays the same approach, and the pilot is using the EFB only as a backup chart reference, does the risk profile change? What should the pilot's primary reference be?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, the risk profile changes significantly. When the aircraft has a certified installed avionics suite displaying the approach (e.g., a Garmin GTN or G500/G600), the EFB should serve only as a supplemental reference — not the primary course of guidance. The pilot's primary reference should be the installed, certified flight instruments and navigation displays. The EFB should be pre-set before the approach and only briefly referenced if needed to confirm a missed approach procedure or minimum altitude. This division of roles reduces head-down time and maintains instrument scan discipline. The ADM concept of workload management (part of SRM per FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13) directly supports this: pre-planning eliminates in-flight EFB manipulation during high-workload phases.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA AC 120-76D; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (SRM/ADM, workload management, CFIT awareness); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5

questions.question: A pilot completes a thorough preflight with their EFB showing current databases and all systems working. During the flight, ATC issues a clearance amendment involving a departure procedure the pilot has not briefed. The pilot quickly pulls up the procedure on the EFB while maintaining IMC. What human factors risks are present, and how does this scenario relate to the 'error chain' concept discussed in helicopter ADM?
questions.answer: This scenario presents multiple compounding human factors risks that form a classic error chain: (1) surprise and task saturation — an unexpected clearance change while already managing flight in IMC spikes workload suddenly; (2) attention tunneling — focusing on the EFB to interpret the new procedure may cause the pilot to neglect primary flight instruments, risking attitude deviation; (3) confirmation bias — the pilot may quickly skim the procedure and misread a constraint under time pressure; (4) plan continuation bias — the pilot may feel committed to accepting and flying the amended clearance rather than requesting delay or clarification. Per FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13, each of these represents a link in the error chain. Breaking any one link — such as telling ATC 'unable, request vectors' to buy time — can prevent the chain from becoming an accident. The EFB itself is not the hazard; it is the interaction between EFB use, unexpected task demand, and degraded situational awareness in IMC that creates the risk.
questions.follow_up: If the pilot had used the autopilot to maintain altitude and heading while referencing the EFB for the amended procedure, would that adequately mitigate the risk? What residual risks remain?
questions.follow_up_answer: Using the autopilot buys critical cognitive bandwidth and reduces the risk of attitude deviation, but residual risks remain: (1) the autopilot must be confirmed engaged and the pilot must monitor that it is maintaining the correct mode — automation complacency is itself an SRM risk; (2) the pilot is still interpreting a new, unbriefed procedure under time pressure in IMC, increasing the chance of misreading altitudes, course, or restrictions; (3) if the autopilot disconnects unexpectedly (common in helicopter operations due to vibration or mode changes), the pilot must immediately transition back to manual flight while potentially mid-task on the EFB. The safest mitigation remains requesting ATC assistance — vectors, time, or a delay — before attempting to brief a new procedure in IMC. Automation management, as covered in FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 SRM, includes understanding automation limitations and not assuming the autopilot eliminates the risk of complex in-flight task changes.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (error chain, SRM, automation management, workload management); FAA AC 120-76D

questions.question: What is the risk of flying an IFR approach using a navigation database that has not been updated within the current 28-day AIRAC cycle?
questions.answer: An outdated navigation database may contain incorrect or superseded procedure information, including wrong waypoint coordinates, outdated frequencies, changed final approach fixes, or approaches that have been amended or decommissioned. Using such data can place the aircraft in the wrong position during an instrument approach, creating a collision or controlled flight into terrain risk. For IFR operations, the database must be current, or the pilot must verify each waypoint against current charts and confirm no NOTAMs affect the procedure.

questions.question: How often are aviation navigation databases updated, and where does that requirement come from?
questions.answer: Navigation databases are updated on a 28-day cycle aligned with the FAA/ICAO Aeronautical Information Regulation and Control (AIRAC) schedule. This cycle ensures that charted procedures, airspace, waypoints, and frequencies remain synchronized between the database and published charts. The FAA requires that GPS/RNAV equipment used for IFR flight have a current database or that pilots verify each waypoint manually, as described in AC 90-100A and the aircraft's AFM/RFMS supplement.

questions.question: What is the difference between a navigation database being 'current' versus 'valid,' and why does that distinction matter for helicopter IFR operations?
questions.answer: A 'current' database is within its active 28-day AIRAC cycle and reflects the latest published aeronautical data. A 'valid' database simply means the equipment will operate — it may be expired but still load and function. The risk is that a valid-but-expired database appears functional to the pilot yet contains outdated procedure data. For helicopter IFR operations, particularly at heliports or on SIAP procedures with tight obstacle clearance criteria, even minor waypoint or altitude discrepancies from an expired database can place the aircraft outside protected airspace.

questions.question: You are preparing for an IFR flight to a remote heliport. During preflight, you discover your FMS navigation database expired four days ago. The approach plate and NOTAMs show no changes to the procedure. How do you manage this risk, and can you legally and safely conduct the flight?
questions.answer: Legally, you may still conduct the flight under 14 CFR 91.103 if you cross-check all database waypoints against current charts and confirm via NOTAMs that no procedure amendments exist. However, the risk management response requires: (1) manually verifying every waypoint, fix, altitude, and frequency in the approach against current published charts; (2) checking applicable NOTAMs for the heliport and any navaids in the procedure; (3) confirming the helicopter's AFM/RFMS supplement does not prohibit IFR use with an expired database; and (4) accepting increased workload in IMC from manual cross-checking. If any discrepancy is found, or if the AFM prohibits it, the flight must be delayed until the database is updated. The safest ADM choice is to update the database before departure.

questions.question: During a GPS/RNAV approach in a helicopter, you notice the FMS-generated waypoint for the final approach fix does not match the fix location shown on your current approach chart. What is the appropriate risk management response, and what are the possible causes?
questions.answer: This is a safety-critical discrepancy that requires an immediate go-around or missed approach if already on approach. Possible causes include: an expired or incorrect database, a database coding error by the provider, the wrong approach procedure loaded, or a chart that has been superseded by a NOTAM the pilot missed. The risk management response is: (1) do not continue the approach past the FAF with a known discrepancy; (2) fly the published missed approach; (3) contact ATC to declare the situation and request vectors or an alternate procedure; (4) verify the correct procedure is loaded and cross-check all waypoints before any second attempt. Continuing with a known waypoint mismatch could place the helicopter below obstacle clearance surfaces.

questions.question: How does the risk of relying on a navigation database change when conducting a helicopter SIAP to a confined or elevated heliport versus a standard runway approach, and how should that influence your preflight database verification habits?
questions.answer: Helicopter SIAPs — particularly point-in-space (PinS) approaches, copter-only RNAV approaches, or approaches to elevated heliports — have tighter obstacle clearance criteria and often include helicopter-specific missed approach segments with unique waypoints not found on fixed-wing approaches. Database coding errors or outdated entries at these specialized procedures carry a higher consequence because there is less obstacle buffer and the final segment may require precision flying to a very specific geographic point. Preflight risk management should include: (1) loading the procedure and visually comparing the map depiction to the approach chart; (2) spot-checking critical waypoints (FAF, MAPt, missed approach holding fix) against published coordinates if available; (3) checking NOTAMs specific to the heliport and any procedure NOTAMs; and (4) confirming the database is within its current cycle. The combination of tight margins and unique waypoints makes database verification more consequential at heliports than at conventional airports.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9; AC 90-100A; 14 CFR 91.103; FAA Order 8260.42

questions.question: A pilot argues that since the GPS is RAIM-capable and the satellite geometry is healthy, a current RAIM prediction eliminates the risk of using an outdated navigation database for an instrument approach. How would you respond to this reasoning, and where exactly does the logic break down?
questions.answer: This reasoning is fundamentally flawed. RAIM (Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring) detects faults in the GPS satellite signal geometry and warns when the position solution is unreliable due to satellite failures or poor geometry. RAIM has absolutely no ability to detect errors in the navigation database itself. It cannot know that a waypoint coordinate in the database is wrong, that an approach procedure has been amended, or that a new obstacle has been identified near the approach path. A healthy RAIM prediction means the GPS receiver is accurately computing the aircraft's position relative to the waypoints stored in its database — but if those waypoints are wrong, the aircraft will be guided accurately to the wrong place. The two systems address entirely separate risk vectors: RAIM addresses signal integrity, while database currency addresses procedural accuracy.
questions.follow_up: If RAIM cannot detect database errors, what system or process is the FAA-approved mechanism for catching database coding mistakes before they affect flight operations?
questions.follow_up_answer: The FAA-approved mechanism is a combination of: (1) the AIRAC quality control process, where database providers such as Jeppesen or Garmin must comply with DO-200A/DO-200B standards for aeronautical data processing and quality assurance; (2) AC 20-153 compliance, which establishes acceptance criteria for database software; and (3) the pilot's own preflight cross-check of loaded procedure against current published charts. Additionally, NOTAM systems serve as the operational safety net when procedure changes occur between AIRAC cycles. No single automated system catches all errors — the pilot's verification remains the last line of defense.

questions.question: During a checkride debrief, an applicant tells you they never check the navigation database expiration date because 'the avionics shop updates it during every annual inspection.' What specific risks does this attitude create, and how would you counsel this pilot to build a proper database risk management habit?
questions.answer: This attitude creates several compounding risks. First, annual inspections occur once every 12 months, but the AIRAC cycle updates every 28 days — meaning the database will be expired for the overwhelming majority of IFR flights between annuals. Second, avionics shops update the database as of the inspection date, not as a standing service — there is no guarantee the shop performed an update or that the update was the most current cycle. Third, this pilot has no personal verification habit, meaning if the avionics shop skipped the update or installed an incorrect file, the pilot has no safety net. The appropriate counseling would address: (1) developing a personal preflight habit of checking the database cycle dates displayed on the avionics before every IFR flight; (2) understanding that database currency is a pilot responsibility under 14 CFR 91.103, not delegable to maintenance; (3) subscribing to a database service with a reminder system; and (4) understanding the specific consequences in helicopter IFR operations where heliport procedures may have been newly added, amended, or decommissioned between annuals. This is also an ADM issue — complacency and over-reliance on others is a documented error chain contributor.
questions.follow_up: If a pilot discovers mid-flight in IMC that their navigation database expired two days ago and no preflight verification was performed, what is the immediate risk management priority and decision-making framework?
questions.follow_up_answer: The immediate priority is to assess whether a safe continuation to destination or alternate is achievable with the available information. The pilot should: (1) check for any NOTAM-filed procedure changes via ATC or datalink if equipped; (2) cross-check the loaded approach procedure against current paper or electronic charts (EFB) to verify no amendments have occurred; (3) if any doubt exists about procedure accuracy, declare the situation to ATC and request radar vectors, a PAR if available, or divert to an alternate where the procedure can be independently verified; (4) apply the ADM principle from the Helicopter Flying Handbook — avoid the word 'probably' and choose the option known to work rather than the option that will probably work. The error chain here began with the preflight omission; the in-flight priority is to stop the chain from progressing to an approach flown to an incorrect waypoint.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.103; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13; AC 90-100A; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9

questions.question: Before an IFR flight, you set the altimeter to the current altimeter setting and it reads 150 feet off from field elevation. What is the maximum allowable altimeter error for IFR flight, and what do you do if it exceeds that limit?
questions.answer: The maximum allowable altimeter error for IFR operations is 75 feet from the known field elevation. If the altimeter reads more than 75 feet off, the helicopter is not airworthy for IFR flight and must be serviced before departure. This is required under 14 CFR 91.411, which mandates that altimeters and static systems be tested and inspected within the preceding 24 calendar months for IFR flight.

questions.question: You are setting up your VOR receiver before an IFR departure. How do you verify the VOR is functioning correctly, and what is the maximum allowable error when checking it using a VOT?
questions.answer: To verify VOR accuracy using a VOT (VOR Test Facility), tune the VOT frequency, center the CDI, and the OBS should indicate 360° with a FROM indication, or 180° with a TO indication. The maximum allowable error for a VOT check is plus or minus 4 degrees. The check must be logged with date, place, bearing error, and pilot signature per 14 CFR 91.171. Other authorized check methods include airborne checks over a designated checkpoint (±6°) and ground checkpoints (±4°).

questions.question: During preflight of your IFR helicopter, you check the heading indicator and find it drifts noticeably even on the ground. What does this indicate, and how does it affect your instrument management during flight?
questions.answer: A heading indicator that drifts excessively suggests a failing gyroscope, inadequate vacuum or pressure supply, or a worn bearing. It indicates the instrument may be unreliable for IFR navigation. If the helicopter uses a traditional vacuum-driven heading indicator, you must verify the suction gauge is within normal range (typically 4.5–5.5 in. Hg). During IFR flight, the heading indicator must be periodically realigned with the magnetic compass — typically every 15 minutes — to correct for precession. Excessive drift may make the aircraft unairworthy for IFR. If an AHRS-based system is installed, the heading is derived electronically and drift is not typically a factor.

questions.question: You are flying IFR in a helicopter equipped with a GPS/WAAS navigator. ATC assigns you a heading, then clears you direct to a waypoint 80 miles ahead. Walk me through how you would manage the navigation equipment from that point through intercepting the new course.
questions.answer: After acknowledging the clearance, I would: (1) enter the destination waypoint directly into the GPS if not already in the flight plan, activating the direct-to function; (2) confirm the GPS is in WAAS-enabled mode and the integrity annunciation shows no flags; (3) cross-check the GPS-derived course on the HSI or CDI against the expected magnetic bearing to the waypoint for reasonableness; (4) fly the assigned heading until ATC confirms I can begin the turn, then engage the GPS course using the selected navigation mode; (5) monitor the CDI for proper course capture, confirming full-scale deflection collapses as I approach centerline; (6) cross-check altitude on the altimeter and verify the GPS groundspeed and track match expectations. Throughout, I maintain a scan that includes attitude, heading, altitude, and navigation source validity.

questions.question: You are shooting an ILS approach in IMC and notice your localizer CDI is showing a full-scale deflection even though you believe you are on centerline. Your VOR receiver on the same nav radio also appears erratic. What is your thought process and how do you manage the situation?
questions.answer: Full-scale localizer deflection combined with erratic VOR behavior on the same receiver strongly suggests a nav radio or antenna failure. My actions: (1) cross-check my position using the GPS overlay or a second nav receiver if installed; (2) check for a valid Morse code identifier on the ILS frequency to confirm I am on the correct frequency and the station is on the air; (3) check if the CDI flag is showing or if the nav receiver annunciates a fault; (4) if the discrepancy is unresolved, execute a missed approach immediately per 14 CFR 91.175 — do not continue below MDA/DA with unreliable navigation; (5) advise ATC of the equipment issue and request an approach using an alternate navigation source such as GPS. I would not attempt to 'split the difference' between two conflicting instruments — I go to a known reliable source or go missed.

questions.question: You are in cruise flight IFR at 6,000 feet MSL and notice the VSI suddenly shows a constant zero while you feel a slight climb. The altimeter is still showing a gradual increase. What instrument failure does this indicate, and how do you manage the remaining instruments?
questions.answer: A VSI stuck at zero while the altimeter is still changing is a classic indicator of a blocked static port. The VSI requires a change in static pressure to show a reading; if the static line is blocked, it shows zero regardless of actual climb or descent. However, if the altimeter is still changing, either the block is partial, or the altimeter has its own static source. I would: (1) activate the alternate static source if equipped — this typically uses cabin static pressure and will cause a slight over-read on the altimeter and slightly high ASI indication; (2) verify the ASI is functioning correctly — a fully blocked static would also cause the ASI to become inaccurate; (3) cross-check attitude and power to maintain altitude using the attitude indicator and tachometer/torque; (4) advise ATC of the malfunction and request any necessary assistance. I would not rely on the VSI for climb/descent rates until the static system is confirmed functional.

questions.question: You are flying an IFR helicopter equipped with an integrated EFIS/glass cockpit including AHRS and ADC. Halfway through the flight you notice the PFD is showing an attitude that doesn't feel right — you sense a slight bank but the PFD shows wings level. Your backup mechanical attitude indicator shows a 10-degree left bank. How do you decide which source to trust, and what is your management strategy going forward?
questions.answer: When there is a conflict between the PFD attitude (driven by AHRS) and the backup attitude indicator, I do not immediately assume either is correct. My strategy: (1) cross-check all available data — if the helicopter is truly in a 10-degree bank, the VSI should show a descent, the altimeter should be unwinding, and the airspeed may be increasing; (2) if the backup AI agrees with the performance instruments (altimeter, VSI, ASI, turn coordinator), trust the backup AI and suspect the AHRS; (3) immediately advise ATC of the equipment problem and request vectors or reduced workload routing; (4) fly the aircraft using the backup AI and cross-check performance instruments continuously; (5) do not attempt to reconcile the two conflicting attitudes — select one source and commit; (6) the AHRS can fail if it loses valid GPS input, experiences magnetic interference, or undergoes a software fault. This is a reason to always brief and verify backup instruments during preflight. Fly the backup, cross-check the primaries, and land at the nearest suitable airport.
questions.follow_up: You commit to the backup AI and are flying to the divert airport. During the descent, the backup AI also starts to tumble. Now what?
questions.follow_up_answer: If the backup AI fails during the same flight, I now have no reliable attitude reference from a gyroscopic source. I must fly using partial panel technique — specifically using the turn coordinator, altimeter, airspeed indicator, and VSI as primary references. For a helicopter, maintaining coordinated flight with the turn coordinator showing wings level, a stable altimeter, and steady ASI gives a reliable wings-level picture. I would immediately declare an emergency with ATC (7700), request radar vectors, and ask for a no-gyro approach if available. The controller will provide turn instructions as 'stop turn / start turn' rather than headings. I will also reduce workload to an absolute minimum — aviate first, communicate second, navigate third. I would request the simplest approach available at the divert airport, ideally an ILS with PAPI, and request ATC to call my turns for me.

questions.question: You are flying an IFR helicopter and notice the GPS navigator has dropped from WAAS to GPS-only navigation mode (no SBAS), and the approach you planned requires LNAV/VNAV minimums. How does this change your approach capability, and what are your options for managing navigation equipment to still complete the flight safely?
questions.answer: LNAV/VNAV approaches require vertical guidance from WAAS (SBAS). If the navigator has dropped to GPS-only (non-WAAS), vertical guidance is no longer available from the GPS, which means LNAV/VNAV minimums are not authorized. My options: (1) Fly the LNAV minimums on the same approach — LNAV is a non-precision approach using lateral GPS guidance only, with a higher MDA and no vertical path guidance; I must evaluate whether the LNAV MDA provides adequate terrain and obstacle clearance at that airport; (2) if the airport has a conventional ILS, VOR, or NDB approach, switch to that procedure using the appropriate navigation source; (3) divert to an alternate where either WAAS has recovered, a precision approach is available, or weather is above alternate minimums for a non-precision approach; (4) advise ATC of the navigation equipment status per 14 CFR 91.187. I must also verify the approach plate's notes for any WAAS NOTAM or GPS RAIM prediction issue that may have caused the downgrade. Do not attempt to fly LNAV/VNAV or LPV minimums without a confirmed WAAS signal and appropriate annunciation.
questions.follow_up: You elect to fly LNAV minimums. As you brief the approach, you realize the LNAV MDA is 1,200 feet AGL and the weather is reported at a 900-foot ceiling. Can you legally and safely continue, and what is your decision?
questions.follow_up_answer: No — if the ceiling is reported at 900 feet AGL and the LNAV MDA is 1,200 feet AGL, the weather is below the applicable minimums for that approach. Under 14 CFR 91.175, I may not descend below MDA unless I have the required flight visibility and can identify one of the visual references required by the rule. A ceiling below MDA means I will almost certainly not acquire the required visual references at or above MDA, making a successful landing from that approach unlikely. The regulation does not prohibit flying the approach, but it prohibits descending below MDA without the required visual references. In practical terms, the weather is below minimums for this approach and I should declare a missed approach before or at MDA, advise ATC, and either hold for improving conditions, divert to the filed alternate (where I confirmed legal alternate minimums apply), or request an ILS at another facility if feasible. Flying into an approach that cannot be completed safely is exactly the type of 'probably will work out' decision-making the FAA warns against in ADM — I need an option I know will work.

questions.question: Before your checkride, you tell me you'll be using an EFB. What is the pilot's responsibility for ensuring that EFB is acceptable for use during the practical test?
questions.answer: The applicant is responsible for providing the EFB and ensuring it is properly configured, charged, and loaded with current, relevant data. The EFB is applicant-supplied, meaning the examiner has no obligation to provide one. The pilot must ensure charts, approach plates, and databases are current and that the device operates as intended. There is no FAA certification requirement for a Class 1 or Class 2 EFB used as a supplemental tool by a private or instrument-rated pilot, but any data used must be current and the device must not create a distraction or safety hazard.

questions.question: What does the term 'electronic flight bag' mean, and what are the three classes of EFB as recognized by the FAA?
questions.answer: An EFB is an electronic device used to perform a variety of flight-related functions traditionally accomplished with paper products. The FAA recognizes three classes: Class 1 EFBs are portable, non-installed devices not connected to aircraft power or data (e.g., a tablet or smartphone). Class 2 EFBs are portable but may be connected to aircraft power or data via approved mounting hardware. Class 3 EFBs are installed avionics subject to full airworthiness certification under the applicable aircraft certification basis. Most pilots use Class 1 devices such as iPads with apps like ForeFlight or Garmin Pilot.

questions.question: You're using an EFB as your sole source of IFR charts during a flight. What is the minimum data currency requirement you must verify before departure?
questions.answer: The pilot must verify that all chart data loaded on the EFB — including enroute charts, approach plates, and terminal procedures — is currently valid and within its effective date range. IFR charts are updated on a 56-day cycle (AIRAC cycle). Approach procedure databases used for navigation purposes must also be current. If the data is expired, the EFB charts may not be used as the primary reference for navigation or instrument approaches; the pilot would need to obtain current charts or update the database before flight.

questions.question: You're established inbound on an ILS approach in IMC and your EFB screen freezes and becomes unresponsive. Walk me through how you manage that situation.
questions.answer: First, do not fixate on the EFB — immediately transition full attention to the aircraft's installed panel instruments, which are the primary reference for the approach. The ILS needles, altimeter, airspeed indicator, and heading indicator on the panel are the authoritative source. Attempt a quick fix only if workload allows — such as pressing the home button or power cycling — but never at the expense of aircraft control or instrument scan. If the EFB is your only approach chart reference, you should have already briefed the approach and know the key altitudes, headings, and missed approach procedure. This underscores why pilots should always brief the approach thoroughly before commencing it, reducing reliance on the EFB during the critical final segment. Declare an issue to ATC if necessary.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA AC 91-78; 14 CFR 91.185 (lost comm contingency awareness); ACS IH.II.B.S2

questions.question: During a cross-country IFR flight in your helicopter, ATC issues an unexpected reroute. How do you manage your EFB to update the flight plan without compromising aircraft control or situational awareness?
questions.answer: The priority is always aviate, navigate, communicate — in that order. If workload and conditions allow, acknowledge the reroute, read it back, and request 'standby' or 'unable to copy immediately' if needed. Once the aircraft is stabilized and heading is confirmed, update the EFB flight plan during a lower-workload phase. Use the EFB's flight plan editing tools to enter the new routing, cross-checking any waypoints ATC provided against known fixes or airways. Verify the new route makes geographic sense before activating it. If the reroute is complex and conditions are demanding, inform ATC you need a moment and manage EFB updates on the ground or at cruise level in VMC, not while executing an approach or transition. Having a co-pilot or second crew member manage the EFB is ideal when available.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA AC 91-78; Helicopter Flying Handbook FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM/workload management)

questions.question: You're using an EFB app that shows GPS-derived traffic and weather overlays. How should you treat that information compared to ATC radar traffic advisories and official weather products?
questions.answer: EFB-displayed traffic (such as ADS-B In traffic shown on apps like ForeFlight) and weather overlays (such as FIS-B NEXRAD) are supplemental tools, not certified primary sources. ATC radar traffic advisories are authoritative and must take priority — 'see and avoid' remains the pilot's responsibility, and EFB traffic displays may have latency or coverage gaps. Similarly, FIS-B NEXRAD displayed on an EFB has a known latency of up to several minutes and lower resolution than NWS radar products. The pilot must treat EFB weather overlays as situational awareness tools, not substitutes for official weather briefings or ATC weather advisories. Over-reliance on EFB overlays has contributed to accidents where pilots penetrated convective weather that appeared to be clear on a delayed NEXRAD image.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA AC 00-45H (Aviation Weather Services); FAA Safety Alert for Operators — ADS-B In; 14 CFR 91.103

questions.question: As an examiner, I've noticed that during the preflight planning portion of your checkride, you used your EFB exclusively to retrieve weather and file your IFR flight plan — but you never accessed an official weather briefing source directly, nor did you obtain a standard weather briefing from a flight service station. Is your preflight weather planning compliant with 14 CFR 91.103, and why or why not?
questions.answer: 14 CFR 91.103 requires the pilot in command to become familiar with all available information concerning the flight, including weather reports and forecasts for IFR operations. The regulation does not mandate that the information come specifically from an FSS briefer — it requires that the pilot obtain all available pertinent information. EFB apps such as ForeFlight, Garmin Pilot, and others that draw from official NWS and FAA data sources (METARs, TAFs, AIRMETs, SIGMETs, NOTAMs, PIREPs) can satisfy the 91.103 requirement if the pilot documents and reviews all relevant products. However, the pilot must demonstrate awareness of all pertinent information — not just a quick glance at a summary screen. If the EFB was used to access official data products and the pilot can articulate what was reviewed, the planning is likely compliant. If the pilot only viewed a graphical overview without reviewing individual METARs, TAFs, AIRMETs, SIGMETs, and NOTAMs, that could represent a deficiency under 91.103.
questions.follow_up: What specific weather products are you required to review for an IFR cross-country, and can you show me where each of those products is accessible on your EFB right now?
questions.follow_up_answer: For an IFR cross-country, the pilot should review at minimum: METARs and SPECIs (current conditions at departure, destination, and alternates), TAFs (terminal forecasts), PIREPs (pilot reports along route), AIRMETs and SIGMETs (significant meteorological information), winds aloft forecasts (FD), NOTAMs (including TFRs), and the area forecast (FA) or graphical forecasts for aviation (GFA). On a modern EFB such as ForeFlight, the pilot should be able to navigate to the weather tab or briefing section and pull up each product individually, demonstrating active review rather than passive consumption of a summary. The examiner is looking for evidence of a thorough, deliberate preflight weather review — not just that the app was opened.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.103; FAA AC 91-78; AIM 7-1-3 (preflight weather briefing)

questions.question: Your EFB is running a moving-map navigation app that is GPS-coupled and displaying your position on an IFR enroute chart. During the flight, the GPS signal drops and the app shows 'GPS Lost.' What are your immediate actions, and what are the implications for your IFR currency and the legality of continuing the flight?
questions.answer: Immediately cross-check position using panel-installed navigation equipment — VOR, DME, ILS, or GPS if a certified panel unit is installed. The EFB moving map is a supplemental situational awareness tool and is not an IFR-approved navigation source unless specifically certified as such (Class 3 EFB). The flight remains legal so long as the aircraft has the required and functioning IFR navigation equipment as approved on the aircraft's equipment list and flight plan. Loss of EFB GPS does not affect legality if panel avionics are operational. However, if the pilot has been relying exclusively on the EFB for navigation without monitoring panel instruments, there is a significant situational awareness gap that must be immediately corrected. The pilot should notify ATC of any uncertainty in position and use installed avionics to re-establish positive position awareness. IFR currency is not affected by EFB failure — it is a personal qualification maintained via 14 CFR 61.57(c).
questions.follow_up: If your installed panel GPS also fails and your only remaining IFR navigation capability is two VORs with no DME, what are the implications for continuing your filed RNAV/GPS IFR flight plan, and what should you do?
questions.follow_up_answer: If the aircraft can no longer navigate via RNAV/GPS, the pilot cannot legally continue an IFR flight plan that requires GPS for the filed routing or approaches. The pilot should immediately inform ATC of the equipment degradation using phraseology such as 'unable RNAV, requesting conventional routing.' ATC will issue a revised clearance using VOR airways or radar vectors as appropriate. The pilot should also consider whether the destination or alternate has a VOR or ILS approach that can be flown with remaining equipment. If no suitable approach is available at the destination without GPS, the pilot must divert to an alternate where conventional approaches are available. This reinforces why pilots should always carry backup navigation capability and brief contingency plans before flight.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.205(d) (IFR equipment requirements); 14 CFR 91.187 (malfunction reports); FAA AC 91-78; AIM 5-3-3 (position reporting); 14 CFR 61.57(c) (IFR currency)

tasks.title: Task C. Instrument Flight Deck Check

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of performing an instrument flight deck check before an IFR flight in a helicopter?
questions.answer: The instrument flight deck check verifies that all required flight instruments are functioning correctly, displaying accurate indications, and free of obvious defects before flight. It ensures the pilot identifies any inoperative or unreliable instruments on the ground — where it is safe to do so — rather than discovering a problem in IMC. The PIC is responsible for ensuring the helicopter is airworthy before flight, which includes confirming instrument serviceability.

questions.question: During your instrument flight deck check, you tap the altimeter and it jumps 200 feet. What does this indicate and why does it matter before an IFR flight?
questions.answer: Tapping the altimeter and seeing a significant needle jump indicates the instrument is sticking internally — the mechanical linkage or aneroid capsule is not responding smoothly to pressure changes. This is a defect that could result in inaccurate altitude readings in flight, which is especially dangerous during IFR operations, approaches, and altitude assignments. A properly functioning altimeter should show little to no movement when lightly tapped. This helicopter should not be dispatched IFR until the altimeter is inspected and found serviceable.

questions.question: What should the VSI read during a normal instrument flight deck check while the helicopter is sitting still on the ground, and why is a non-zero reading a concern?
questions.answer: The vertical speed indicator (VSI) should read exactly zero while the helicopter is stationary on the ground, since no change in altitude is occurring. A non-zero reading while parked indicates the static system may have a leak, the instrument itself has an internal issue, or a partial blockage is causing a false pressure differential. Since the VSI is a static-only instrument, any error at rest suggests the static system — which also feeds the altimeter and airspeed indicator — may be compromised, making the entire pitot-static system suspect for IFR flight.

questions.question: You are preflighting a helicopter for an IFR cross-country. During your instrument flight deck check, you set the Kollsman window to the current altimeter setting and your indicated altitude is 80 feet lower than the field elevation. What are the possible causes and what is the maximum allowable error for IFR flight?
questions.answer: Possible causes include a calibration error within the altimeter itself, a partial static port blockage, a leak in the static system, or an incorrect altimeter setting being used. Per 14 CFR 91.411, an altimeter used for IFR flight must be tested and inspected within the preceding 24 calendar months. However, the regulation does not specify a maximum ground error allowance — that is typically stated in the helicopter's RFM or the altimeter's accuracy standards. As a practical standard, most operators and examiners reference the instrument accuracy tolerance of plus or minus 75 feet when set to the current altimeter setting at a known elevation. An 80-foot error is beyond that tolerance and should be investigated before IFR flight.

questions.question: During your instrument flight deck check, how do you verify that your helicopter's static system is free of blockage, and what instrument indications would alert you to a fully blocked static port?
questions.answer: To check for static system integrity, verify the following during preflight: VSI reads zero, altimeter shows correct field elevation when set to current altimeter setting, and the ASI shows zero (or near-zero for small elevation differences) while parked. A fully blocked static port causes the altimeter to freeze at the altitude it was blocked — it will not update as you taxi or change altitude. The VSI will peg at zero and remain there regardless of actual vertical movement. The ASI will become inaccurate because it cannot sense static pressure changes — it may over-read in a climb and under-read in a descent. These symptoms together during flight indicate a blocked static system, not just a single instrument failure.

questions.question: During rotor engagement on your IFR preflight, you notice your directional gyro (heading indicator) is precessing noticeably within just a few minutes of operation. At what rate is excessive precession typically considered a defect, and why is this critical for helicopter IFR flight specifically?
questions.answer: Excessive precession in a heading indicator is generally considered a defect when the instrument drifts more than approximately 3 degrees in 15 minutes under normal operating conditions, though manufacturer specifications in the RFM may define a tighter tolerance. For helicopter IFR operations, this is especially critical because helicopters frequently operate at lower altitudes, make more frequent heading changes, and may fly in confined or complex airspace where precise heading control is essential for navigation and obstacle clearance. An unreliable heading indicator increases the risk of spatial disorientation and navigational error during IMC, particularly during approaches and missed approach procedures. The pilot must synchronize the heading indicator with the magnetic compass frequently, and excessive precession makes reliable heading information impossible to maintain.

questions.question: During your instrument flight deck check, you activate the alternate static source inside the cabin and notice the altimeter reads 50 feet higher than with the primary static system. A fellow pilot tells you that means the primary static system is probably blocked. Is this pilot correct? Explain why or why not.
questions.answer: No, the pilot is incorrect. This behavior is completely normal and expected. Cabin pressure in a helicopter is typically slightly lower than ambient outside atmospheric pressure due to aerodynamic effects and ventilation. When the alternate static source draws from inside the cabin, the lower cabin pressure causes the altimeter to indicate a slightly higher altitude, the ASI to indicate slightly faster airspeed, and the VSI to momentarily show a climb — even though nothing has actually changed. This is a known characteristic of alternate static systems documented in the Instrument Flying Handbook. The fact that the altimeter reads higher with the alternate source switched on does not indicate a primary static system defect — it confirms the alternate static source is functioning as expected. The pilot should be aware of this when using the alternate static source in flight and apply any correction noted in the helicopter's RFM or supplement.
questions.follow_up: If this helicopter's RFM does not provide an alternate static source correction table, how should the pilot handle the altimeter error in flight if the primary static source becomes blocked in IMC?
questions.follow_up_answer: If the RFM provides no correction factor, the pilot should acknowledge there will be a slight altitude over-indication when using the alternate static source and apply conservative judgment — treating the indicated altitude as slightly optimistic. ATC should be notified of the instrument malfunction if operating in controlled airspace. The pilot should cross-check with any available GPS altitude data as a sanity check, though GPS altitude is not approved as a primary altimeter substitute for IFR. The priority is maintaining aircraft control and safe separation from terrain and other traffic using the best available information while proceeding to land as soon as practicable. The discrepancy should be noted in the aircraft maintenance log after landing.

questions.question: You complete your instrument flight deck check and everything appears normal. Twenty minutes into your IFR flight in IMC, your attitude indicator shows wings level and a slight climb, but your airspeed is decreasing, the altimeter is unwinding, and the VSI shows a descent. What does this instrument conflict tell you, and how do you decide which instruments to trust?
questions.answer: This scenario describes a classic partial panel failure — specifically, a suspected attitude indicator failure or gyroscopic tumble. The three pitot-static instruments (altimeter, VSI, and ASI) are in agreement with each other: the aircraft is descending and slowing, which is consistent with a nose-low, decelerating attitude. The attitude indicator is contradicting all three static and pitot-static instruments. Since the pitot-static instruments are mechanically independent of each other and all agree, they are almost certainly correct. The attitude indicator — being a gyroscopic instrument dependent on either vacuum or electrical power — is the most likely single-point failure. The pilot should immediately declare the attitude indicator unreliable, cover or ignore it to prevent fixation, and transition to partial panel flight using the turn coordinator, altimeter, ASI, and VSI as the primary cross-check. The magnetic compass and heading indicator (if still reliable) provide directional reference. Recovery from the unusual attitude should be initiated immediately using partial panel technique.
questions.follow_up: After recovering from the unusual attitude using partial panel instruments, ATC offers you an immediate instrument approach at your destination. What factors should you consider before accepting, and is there any regulation that requires you to report this malfunction to ATC?
questions.follow_up_answer: Before accepting the approach, the pilot must assess: workload capacity to fly a full approach without an attitude indicator, weather minimums versus the approach minimums, crew resource management factors, fuel state, and whether a more suitable alternate exists for a straightforward approach. Many instrument approaches can be flown partial panel with a turn coordinator, but the margin for error is reduced significantly. Regarding reporting — 14 CFR 91.187 requires the PIC to report any malfunction of a navigational, approach, or communication system to ATC as soon as practical while operating in controlled airspace under IFR. A failed attitude indicator is a flight instrument, not specifically listed in 91.187, but it is best practice to advise ATC of the situation so they can provide additional assistance, extended vectors, or priority handling. The pilot should also note the malfunction in the aircraft maintenance log.

questions.question: What three pitot-static instruments are required for IFR flight in a helicopter, and what pressure source does each use?
questions.answer: The three required pitot-static instruments are: (1) the Airspeed Indicator (ASI), which uses both pitot pressure and static pressure; (2) the Altimeter, which uses static pressure only; and (3) the Vertical Speed Indicator (VSI), which uses static pressure only. All three must be operative for IFR flight.

questions.question: Under 14 CFR 91.409, what inspections are required to maintain a helicopter's airworthiness for IFR flight under Part 91, and how often must they be performed?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.409, a helicopter operated under Part 91 must have an annual inspection every 12 calendar months performed by an appropriately rated FAA-certificated mechanic or repair station. Additionally, for IFR flight, the altimeter system and altitude reporting equipment must be tested and inspected under 14 CFR 91.411 within the preceding 24 calendar months, and the ATC transponder must be tested and inspected under 14 CFR 91.413 within the preceding 24 calendar months.

questions.question: What does the acronym commonly used to remember required IFR equipment cover, and name at least six items required by 14 CFR 91.205(d) for IFR flight?
questions.answer: A common acronym is GRABCARD: Generator or alternator, Radios (communication and navigation equipment), Altimeter (sensitive, adjustable), Ball (slip/skid indicator), Clock (with hours, minutes, and seconds), Attitude indicator, Rate-of-turn indicator (or helicopter equivalent), Directional gyro (heading indicator). Required items under 14 CFR 91.205(d) include: (1) instruments required for VFR flight (91.205(b)), (2) two-way radio communications system, (3) navigation equipment appropriate for the route, (4) sensitive altimeter adjustable for barometric pressure, (5) a clock displaying hours, minutes, and seconds with a sweep-second pointer or digital presentation, (6) attitude indicator, (7) heading indicator, (8) slip/skid indicator, (9) radios meeting 91.205(d) requirements, and (10) DME or RNAV system at or above FL240 if VOR is used.

questions.question: During your preflight instrument check, you discover the helicopter's altimeter was last tested 26 months ago. The weather is IFR. How does this affect your flight, and what are your options?
questions.answer: This helicopter is not airworthy for IFR flight. 14 CFR 91.411 requires that the altimeter system and altitude reporting equipment be tested and inspected within the preceding 24 calendar months by an appropriately rated repair station or mechanic. At 26 months, this requirement is not met. Your options are: (1) ground the aircraft and have the altimeter system tested and inspected before conducting IFR flight, (2) defer the IFR flight and depart VFR if weather and regulations permit, or (3) arrange for maintenance to be performed. You may not dispatch the aircraft on an IFR flight with an out-of-date altimeter check. Under Part 91 there is no MEL provision that would allow deferral of a required IFR inspection.

questions.question: You are conducting a preflight instrument check and notice the VSI is stuck and indicates a 200 fpm climb while the helicopter is sitting on the ground. Under 14 CFR 91.213, walk me through how you would determine if you can legally depart IFR today.
questions.answer: First, check the Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) — if the VSI is listed as required equipment, it cannot be deferred and the flight cannot be conducted IFR. If not listed in the RFM as required, proceed to 14 CFR 91.213(d). Under 91.213(d), an inoperative instrument may be deferred if: (1) it is not required by 14 CFR 91.205 or any other regulation applicable to the flight, (2) it is not required by the RFM or type certificate data sheet, (3) the inoperative instrument is deactivated and placarded INOPERATIVE, and (4) if deactivation requires maintenance (such as pulling a circuit breaker permanently or removing equipment), a certificated maintenance person must perform it. The VSI is listed under 14 CFR 91.205(d) as a required IFR instrument — it is the rate-of-turn indicator reference for some helicopters, but the VSI specifically is not listed as a required IFR instrument under 91.205(d). However, if it is required by the specific helicopter's RFM or TCDS, it cannot be deferred. Assuming it is not required by those documents, it may be deferred per 91.213(d) after being placarded INOPERATIVE.

questions.question: Your helicopter's fuel quantity gauges are reading erratically before an IFR flight. The RFM states fuel gauges are required to be accurate only when reading empty. Can you legally depart IFR, and what practical steps should you take?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 27.1337(b)(1), fuel quantity gauges are only required to be accurate when reading empty — this is a certification standard. Therefore, erratic fuel gauge readings do not necessarily constitute an airworthiness discrepancy that grounds the aircraft, provided the gauges still indicate empty correctly. For the IFR flight, since 14 CFR 91.205(d) does not specifically require fully accurate fuel gauges beyond the regulatory standard, this may not be a legal impediment. However, practically and from a risk management standpoint, you must verify actual fuel quantity using physical measurement (dipping tanks, sumping, or a calibrated stick) before flight. You should document the discrepancy, placard if required by the 91.213 process, and make a go/no-go decision based on known fuel quantity, not gauge indication. Departing IFR without knowing actual fuel on board would be unsafe and potentially violate 14 CFR 91.151 fuel reserve requirements.

questions.question: During your IFR preflight instrument check, you switch to the alternate static source and notice the altimeter reads 60 feet higher than before, the ASI increases slightly, and the VSI briefly shows a climb. Is this helicopter airworthy, and what does this tell you about the static system?
questions.answer: Yes, this behavior is normal and expected — it does not indicate a malfunction. When the alternate static source is selected inside the cabin, the cabin pressure is slightly lower than outside ambient pressure due to airflow over the fuselage creating a slight suction effect. This lower static pressure reference causes: (1) the altimeter to over-read (indicate higher than actual altitude), (2) the ASI to indicate slightly faster than actual airspeed, and (3) the VSI to show a momentary climb indication before settling back to zero. This is consistent with FAA-H-8083-15B guidance on alternate static sources. The pilot should be aware of these errors when using the alternate static source during actual IFR flight and apply appropriate corrections. The fact that the alternate source functions and produces these predictable indications actually confirms both the primary and alternate static systems are intact and the instruments are responsive. The RFM should be checked for any specific correction values when using alternate static.
questions.follow_up: If your primary static port became completely blocked in IMC and you had no alternate static source, what would happen to each of your three pitot-static instruments, and what is your immediate course of action?
questions.follow_up_answer: With a completely blocked primary static port and no alternate source: (1) the Altimeter freezes — it continues to display the altitude at which the blockage occurred regardless of actual altitude changes; (2) the VSI freezes at zero — it shows no vertical trend even during climbs or descents; (3) the ASI becomes inaccurate — it reads high during climbs (lower outside static pressure makes differential appear greater) and low during descents. Immediate actions: declare the situation to ATC, consider breaking the glass face of the VSI if the aircraft does not have an alternate static source — breaking the VSI face vents the static system to cabin air, which acts similarly to using an alternate static source (with the same altitude over-read and ASI errors described above). Consult the RFM for the specific procedure. Maintain last known altitude using power and attitude, cross-check with GPS altitude, and request priority handling from ATC.

questions.question: A pilot tells you the helicopter's RFM specifies a VNE that varies with altitude and gross weight, and there is a placard in the cockpit showing VNE. Before an IFR flight at higher altitude than shown on the placard, how does this affect IFR airworthiness, and what is the pilot's obligation under Part 91?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.9, no person may operate an aircraft above its maximum speed (VNE), and under 14 CFR 91.7, the PIC is responsible for determining the aircraft is airworthy before flight. The RFM is specific to the individual helicopter and the operating limitations within it — including a variable VNE — are FAA-approved and legally binding per 14 CFR 91.9 and Part 27. If the planned IFR altitude would result in a lower VNE than cruise airspeed, the flight profile must be adjusted to remain within limits. The pilot must consult the RFM performance charts or placards to determine the applicable VNE at the planned altitude and gross weight, and ensure that the planned airspeed remains below that value. Departing with a plan to exceed VNE at altitude would render the operation non-airworthy and potentially illegal under 91.9. The aircraft itself is not 'unairworthy' — the pilot is responsible for operating within the documented limitations at all times during the IFR flight.
questions.follow_up: If during an IFR flight you inadvertently exceed VNE due to turbulence or a dive, are you required to have a maintenance inspection before continuing flight, and what should you do?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes — most helicopter RFMs specify that if VNE is exceeded, a maintenance inspection is required before further flight. This is an operating limitation with legal weight under 14 CFR 91.9 and 91.7. Upon exceeding VNE, the PIC should reduce airspeed immediately, note the exceedance (airspeed, duration if known, and circumstances), declare the situation to ATC if assistance is needed, and land as soon as practicable. Upon landing, the aircraft should be grounded pending an inspection by a certificated mechanic in accordance with the manufacturer's maintenance manual. The specific inspection required depends on the RFM — some require a general rotor system and airframe inspection; others require inspection of specific components such as blade retention, pitch links, or rotor hub. The aircraft should not be returned to IFR service until the inspection is complete and documented in the maintenance records.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.9; 14 CFR 91.7; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 5; 14 CFR Part 27

questions.question: Under 14 CFR 91.213(d), what four conditions must be met before you can legally fly a Part 91 helicopter with an inoperative instrument or piece of equipment that is not on an approved MEL?
questions.answer: Under 91.213(d), the four conditions are: (1) The equipment is not required by the VFR-day type certificate instruments list, the aircraft's equipment list, or any applicable AD; (2) The equipment is not required by 14 CFR 91.205 or any other rule for the specific flight being conducted (e.g., IFR, night); (3) The inoperative equipment is removed from the aircraft or deactivated and placarded INOPERATIVE — if deactivation or removal requires maintenance, a certificated mechanic must perform it; and (4) The pilot-in-command determines the inoperative equipment does not constitute a hazard to the flight.

questions.question: What does the FAA require be done to an inoperative piece of equipment before flight when deferring it under 14 CFR 91.213(d), and who is authorized to perform the deactivation if it involves any maintenance action?
questions.answer: The inoperative equipment must be either removed from the aircraft or deactivated, and it must be placarded 'INOPERATIVE' so the crew and passengers are aware it is not functioning. If the deactivation or removal constitutes a maintenance action — such as pulling and collaring a circuit breaker in a way the manufacturer does not approve as a pilot action, or physically removing the unit — a certificated maintenance person must perform that work. The pilot cannot perform unauthorized maintenance to deactivate equipment.

questions.question: According to the Helicopter Flying Handbook, what is the regulatory requirement for fuel quantity gauge accuracy, and why does this matter when assessing inoperative equipment before an IFR flight?
questions.answer: Per 14 CFR 27.1337(b)(1), fuel quantity gauges are only required to be accurate when they read empty — they are not required to be accurate at any other fuel level. This means a fuel quantity gauge that reads incorrectly at mid-tank or full levels is not necessarily airworthy in the way most pilots assume. For IFR preflight purposes, the pilot must cross-check fuel quantity by physically measuring or visually inspecting the tanks rather than relying solely on gauges, and must assess whether a malfunctioning gauge constitutes a hazard before deferring it under 91.213(d).
