questions.question: During your IFR preflight instrument check, you discover the alternate static source selector valve is jammed and will not move. Walk me through how you would determine whether you can legally depart IFR, and what documentation steps you would need to complete.
questions.answer: First, determine if an alternate static source is required equipment for the intended IFR flight. Check: (1) the helicopter's type certificate data sheet and aircraft equipment list to see if it is required equipment; (2) 14 CFR 91.205(d) — the alternate static source is not explicitly listed in 91.205(d) as required IFR equipment, but the static system itself must be functional; (3) the RFM equipment list and any applicable ADs. If not required by any of those sources, you may consider deferral under 91.213(d) provided the equipment can be deactivated/placarded and the PIC determines it does not constitute a hazard. If the primary static system is functioning normally, a stuck alternate static selector (in the 'normal' position) may be deferrable. Document the deferral in the aircraft maintenance record per 91.213(d), placard it INOPERATIVE, and make a PIC hazard determination. If the valve is stuck open on alternate static, the altimeter, VSI, and ASI errors associated with alternate static air would be present and the PIC would likely determine it constitutes a hazard, grounding the aircraft for maintenance.

questions.question: You are IFR en route in a helicopter and your VSI suddenly freezes at zero — it no longer responds to climbs or descents. How does this differ procedurally from discovering the same discrepancy during preflight, and what are your options?
questions.answer: An in-flight discrepancy is handled differently from a preflight deferral. The 91.213(d) deferral procedure applies to pre-departure decisions, not in-flight emergencies. Once airborne, if the VSI fails, the pilot must use the RFM/POH emergency and abnormal procedures as applicable — not the 91.213(d) process. In flight, the pilot relies on the altimeter for vertical rate trend information and on the other pitot-static instruments. A frozen VSI consistent with a blocked static port (altimeter also frozen, ASI inaccurate) would indicate a blocked static system — in that case the pilot should open the alternate static source per the RFM. If only the VSI is affected, it is likely an instrument failure; the pilot continues the flight using remaining instruments, notifies ATC of any equipment issue that affects IFR capability, and documents the discrepancy after landing for maintenance action before the next IFR flight.

questions.question: Your helicopter has an FAA-approved MEL. The MEL lists the encoding altimeter as a CATEGORY B item with a 3-day deferral limit. You find the encoder has failed. What documentation and operational limitations apply before you can depart IFR?
questions.answer: With an FAA-approved MEL, you follow the MEL provisions rather than 91.213(d). For a Category B item, the MEL allows a 3-calendar-day deferral before the aircraft must be grounded for repair. Required steps: (1) The inoperative item must be annotated in the aircraft maintenance log or discrepancy record per MEL procedures, with the date of discovery starting the deferral clock; (2) The item must be placarded INOPERATIVE per the MEL's maintenance and operations procedures (M and O procedures); (3) Any M procedures (maintenance actions required before flight) and O procedures (operational limitations or procedures the crew must follow) specified in the MEL for that item must be complied with. For an encoding altimeter specifically, loss of Mode C altitude reporting may be an operational consideration — ATC will need to be notified, and flight into certain airspace requiring Mode C (e.g., Class B and C airports, 10,000 ft MSL ceiling per 91.215) would not be permitted. IFR flight itself requires a functioning altimeter per 91.205(d), so if the altimeter display is still functional and only the encoder is failed, IFR may be permissible with the noted airspace restrictions.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.213(a); 14 CFR 91.215; 14 CFR 91.205(d); MEL program under MMEL

questions.question: A pilot argues that because VNE varies with altitude and gross weight — and is only shown on a cockpit placard — a placard that is missing or illegible makes the helicopter unairworthy and no deferral is possible under any provision. Is this argument correct? How would you resolve an illegible VNE placard situation before an IFR flight?
questions.answer: The argument has merit but requires nuance. Operating limitations, including VNE, are part of the FAA-approved RFM, which is required to be on board the aircraft per 14 CFR 91.9. The cockpit placard is required by 14 CFR 27.1545 as a means of conveying VNE to the pilot at the point of operation. A missing or illegible required placard is a violation of the aircraft's airworthiness — it cannot be deferred under 91.213(d) because placards are required by the aircraft's type certificate and operating limitations, placing them in the category of equipment that cannot be deferred ('required by the aircraft's equipment list or by an applicable regulation for the specific type of flight'). The correct resolution is: (1) Obtain the VNE information from the RFM for the specific altitude and weight conditions, and (2) Have a new placard fabricated and installed by a certificated maintenance person before flight — this is a minor alteration/repair that does not require an IA, just an A&P and a logbook entry. The pilot cannot simply write the value on a piece of paper and tape it up without proper maintenance authorization.
questions.follow_up: What if the RFM itself is damaged and the VNE table is unreadable — can you call the manufacturer and depart IFR that same day if they give you the value verbally?
questions.follow_up_answer: No. The RFM is an FAA-approved document required to be aboard the aircraft per 91.9 and 91.203. A damaged RFM that renders required operating limitation data unreadable renders the aircraft unairworthy. A verbal manufacturer statement does not constitute FAA-approved documentation. The pilot would need to obtain a replacement RFM — the manufacturer can typically provide one quickly via email or fax as a printed, signed copy — and have it placed aboard the aircraft before IFR departure. Operating on verbal information alone for a type-certificated operating limitation would be a violation of 91.9.

questions.question: During a thorough IFR instrument deck check, you find that the Kollsman window on your altimeter is stuck and will only set to 29.92 — it will not move. The rest of the pitot-static system checks normal. Walk me through your complete airworthiness and regulatory analysis for whether you can depart IFR.
questions.answer: This requires a layered analysis. (1) Equipment requirement: The altimeter is explicitly required for IFR flight under 14 CFR 91.205(d). (2) Functionality test: A functioning altimeter is required, but the question is whether an altimeter with a stuck Kollsman window at 29.92 is 'functioning.' The altimeter will correctly indicate pressure altitude (FL equivalent) but cannot be corrected for local altimeter settings — it will always read as if set to standard pressure. This means: at an altimeter setting other than 29.92, the indicated altitude will be in error by approximately 1,000 feet per 1 inch Hg difference (e.g., at 29.42, the altimeter would read approximately 500 feet too high). (3) IFR implications: IFR altitude assignments are based on true altitude corrections using the local altimeter setting. An altimeter that cannot be set to the current altimeter setting cannot reliably provide the true altitude reference required for IFR separation, terrain clearance, and approach minimums. (4) Conclusion: A stuck Kollsman window constitutes an inoperative altimeter for IFR purposes. It cannot be deferred under 91.213(d) because a functioning altimeter is specifically required by 91.205(d) for IFR. The aircraft is not IFR legal and must be grounded for maintenance.
questions.follow_up: Is there any scenario where an altimeter stuck at 29.92 would produce accurate altitude indications, and could you legally conduct the flight in that scenario?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes — if the current local altimeter setting happened to be exactly 29.92 inHg, the altimeter would produce accurate indicated altitude. However, even in that narrow scenario, the altimeter is still mechanically defective and legally inoperative because its accuracy is coincidental rather than reliable. 14 CFR 91.411 requires the altimeter system to be tested and inspected per the standards of Appendix E to Part 43 within the preceding 24 calendar months for IFR flight, and an altimeter with a stuck adjustment mechanism would fail that inspection standard. A defective instrument does not become airworthy simply because ambient conditions happen to compensate for its defect. The aircraft is still unairworthy and the flight cannot be conducted IFR.

questions.question: Under 14 CFR 91.213(d), what four conditions must be met before you can defer an inoperative instrument or piece of equipment and legally depart on an IFR flight in your helicopter?
questions.answer: Under 91.213(d), all four of these must be satisfied: (1) The helicopter does not have an FAA-approved MEL; (2) the inoperative equipment is not required by the VFR-day type certificate instruments list, the certification rule under which the aircraft was type certificated, or any AD; (3) the inoperative equipment is not required by 14 CFR 91.205 or any other rule for the specific flight being conducted; and (4) the inoperative equipment is either removed and the cockpit control placarded, or deactivated and placarded 'INOPERATIVE.' If deactivation or removal requires maintenance, a certificated maintenance person must perform the work.

questions.question: The Rotorcraft Flight Manual states fuel quantity gauges are only required to be accurate at one specific reading. What is that reading, and what risk does this create during an IFR flight deck check?
questions.answer: Per 14 CFR 27.1337(b)(1), fuel quantity gauges are only required to be accurate when reading empty (zero). This means any reading above empty may be inaccurate. The risk during an IFR preflight check is that a pilot may accept a gauge indication as reliable when it legally is not — leading to fuel mismanagement, unexpected fuel exhaustion, or diversion decisions based on false fuel state. Pilots must cross-check gauge readings by visually inspecting fuel quantity whenever possible and accounting for burn rates carefully.

questions.question: What is the minimum instrument and equipment requirement for a helicopter operating under IFR per 14 CFR 91.205(d), and why does the flight deck check matter before an IFR departure?
questions.answer: 14 CFR 91.205(d) lists the required instruments for IFR flight, including gyroscopic rate-of-turn indicator, slip-skid indicator, sensitive altimeter adjustable for barometric pressure, clock with hours/minutes/seconds, attitude indicator, heading indicator, and the VFR-day instruments (airspeed indicator, altimeter, magnetic compass), plus a generator or alternator and radio communications and navigation equipment suitable for the route. The preflight instrument check matters because discovering an inoperative required instrument on the ground — not in IMC — allows the pilot to make a legal and safe deferral decision or cancel the flight, rather than being caught with failed equipment in instrument conditions where the risk is catastrophic.

questions.question: During your instrument flight deck check before an IFR departure, you discover the VSI is stuck at a constant plus-200 fpm indication. The altimeter and airspeed indicator appear normal. Walk me through your risk assessment and the decision process for whether you can legally and safely depart IFR.
questions.answer: First, check whether the VSI is required for the flight. Under 14 CFR 91.205(d), the VSI is not explicitly listed as a required IFR instrument — the required pitot-static instruments for IFR are the airspeed indicator and sensitive altimeter; the VSI is not mandated. Next, consult the RFM/AFM to confirm the VSI is not required by the type certificate or any AD. If neither source requires it, apply 91.213(d): the equipment must be deactivated or removed and placarded INOPERATIVE (if deactivation requires maintenance, a certificated maintenance person must do it). Risk assessment: losing the VSI in IMC increases workload during climbs and descents — the pilot must rely entirely on altimeter and power settings for vertical rate awareness. This is manageable with solid instrument scan technique but should be weighed against weather complexity, approach type, and pilot proficiency. The decision must be conservative — if the planned IFR environment is demanding (e.g., circling approach, mountainous terrain), consider postponing flight.

questions.question: You complete your IFR instrument check and notice the static system alternate source selector is stuck — you cannot switch to alternate static. The primary static system checks out normal. What is the risk of departing IFR without a functioning alternate static source, and how does this change your go/no-go decision?
questions.answer: The risk is significant: if the primary static system becomes blocked in IMC — due to icing, moisture, or a mechanical fault — you lose accurate altimeter, VSI, and airspeed indications simultaneously with no backup. In IMC, loss of all three pitot-static instruments is an emergency with high accident potential. Check whether the alternate static source is required by the RFM, type certificate, or any applicable rule for the flight (e.g., if flight into known icing is planned, risk increases substantially). If not required by regulation or the RFM, it technically qualifies for 91.213(d) deferral after proper placarding. However, from a risk management standpoint, departing IFR without alternate static — especially into any IMC with icing potential — represents an unacceptable single point of failure for three critical instruments. The prudent decision is to ground the aircraft for maintenance. The FAA Handbook emphasizes that 'probably' is not good enough — if the alternate static may be needed, do not depart without it.

questions.question: You are doing the instrument flight deck check and the attitude indicator is slow to erect — it's still about 15 degrees off after 5 minutes of warm-up. Your departure is time-sensitive. What specific risks does this create for an IFR departure, and what should you do?
questions.answer: The attitude indicator (AI) is a required instrument for IFR flight per 14 CFR 91.205(d). A slow or incomplete erection indicates a possible gyroscopic instrument failure — the instrument may display errors that increase during flight or fail entirely in IMC. Risks include: (1) spatial disorientation if the AI shows false bank or pitch in IMC; (2) no legal alternate required for a single AI in most Part 91 operations; (3) the error chain — time pressure combined with a marginal instrument is a well-documented accident precursor (FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13). Do not depart. The AI must be fully erect and accurate prior to IFR departure. Time pressure is one of the classic hazardous attitudes (anti-authority, invulnerability, impulsivity). The correct action is to delay departure until the instrument performs normally, or ground the aircraft for maintenance. Departing with a known gyroscopic anomaly into IMC violates both the regulatory requirement and basic risk management principles.

questions.question: You are conducting a Part 91 IFR flight in a helicopter that has an FAA-approved MEL. During the instrument flight deck check, you find an inoperative navigation radio. The MEL lists the nav radio as 'Category C — must be repaired within 10 calendar days.' Today is day 9 since the item was deferred. ATC has assigned you a GPS-based IFR routing with no VOR requirement. What are the layered risks and legal considerations you must evaluate before departing?
questions.answer: Several distinct risk layers must be addressed: (1) MEL compliance — Category C items must be repaired within 10 calendar days. Day 9 is still within the window, so the deferral remains legally valid; however, there is no margin left — any delay makes the aircraft unairworthy. Confirm the MEL deferral paperwork is current and properly logged. (2) Regulatory equipment sufficiency — confirm the GPS navigation system is IFR-approved (TSO-C129/C145/C146) and the routing does not require the inoperative nav radio; check NOTAMs for GPS outages along the route. (3) Operational risk — a GPS outage in IMC with no VOR backup creates a high-risk single-point-of-failure scenario; evaluate whether alternate routing with VOR coverage exists and whether your GPS is RAIM-sufficient for the planned route and approaches. (4) ADM — the combination of day-9 MEL status, GPS dependency, and IMC represents an accumulation of risk factors (error chain). The Helicopter Flying Handbook's 'error chain' concept applies: multiple marginal conditions together create disproportionate risk. (5) PIC responsibility — under 14 CFR 91.3, the PIC has final authority and must determine the aircraft is airworthy for the specific operation. Prudent risk management may dictate delaying until repair, even if legally permitted to depart.
questions.follow_up: If you depart on day 9 and the repair is not completed by the end of day 10, what happens to the aircraft's airworthiness status, and what are your options if you are away from your home base?
questions.follow_up_answer: At the end of day 10, the MEL deferral expires and the aircraft is no longer airworthy for flight under the MEL. Flying it would violate 14 CFR 91.7 (operating an unairworthy aircraft) and 91.213. If away from home base, the pilot's options are: (1) contact an FAA-certificated repair station or A&P mechanic at the away-base to complete the repair; (2) request a special flight permit (ferry permit) under 14 CFR 21.197 to reposition the aircraft to a maintenance facility — this requires FAA FSDO coordination and only authorizes flight to a point of repair; (3) do not fly the aircraft until the squawk is corrected. The pilot cannot simply extend the MEL deferral on their own — only the person authorized under the MEL (typically the operator's Director of Maintenance or equivalent) can manage MEL deferrals, and only within the defined category time limits.

questions.question: During your IFR instrument flight deck check, everything appears normal — but you recall that on the previous flight, the altimeter had an intermittent issue where it momentarily froze for a few seconds before correcting itself. The current check shows it functioning normally. The discrepancy was not written up in the maintenance logbook. What are the risk management and legal issues at play here, and what must you do before departing IFR?
questions.answer: This scenario involves multiple intersecting risk management and legal issues: (1) Squawk documentation — under 14 CFR 91.417, maintenance records must include a description of any work performed, but the PIC is also responsible for ensuring the aircraft is airworthy. An unrecorded in-flight discrepancy means no maintenance inspection has addressed the problem. The intermittent nature of the fault makes it especially dangerous in IMC — intermittent failures often precede complete failures. (2) Intermittent instrument failure risk — a frozen altimeter in IMC is a critical safety hazard (FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5 documents that a blocked static system causes the altimeter to freeze at the blockage altitude). An intermittent freeze may indicate a developing static port issue, a failing aneroid capsule, or a loose connection — none of which will be caught by a normal pre-departure check if the fault is not currently active. (3) PIC responsibility — 14 CFR 91.7 requires the PIC to determine airworthiness before flight; 14 CFR 91.3 gives the PIC final authority. Knowingly operating with an unaddressed known discrepancy violates both the letter and spirit of these rules. (4) Required action — the discrepancy must be written up in the aircraft maintenance log immediately; a certificated mechanic must inspect the static system and altimeter before IFR flight is conducted. Do not depart IFR with an uninspected, known intermittent failure of a required instrument — the fact that it 'seems fine now' does not mitigate the risk.
questions.follow_up: What specific test would a mechanic use to check the integrity of the static system on a helicopter, and what standard must the system meet to return to IFR service?
questions.follow_up_answer: Under 14 CFR 91.411, the altimeter system and altitude reporting equipment must be tested and inspected within the preceding 24 calendar months for IFR flight. The static system leak test is performed per 14 CFR Part 43, Appendix E: the system is pressurized (or depressurized) to simulate an altitude of approximately 1,000 feet above the actual test altitude, and then the source is sealed. The system must not lose more than 100 feet of indicated altitude over 1 minute. If the leak exceeds this limit, the static system must be repaired before IFR flight. Additionally, each sensitive altimeter must meet the accuracy requirements of TSO-C10b or equivalent, and must be tested per Appendix E of Part 43 to verify it reads within required tolerances across the altitude range. The aircraft cannot return to IFR flight until a certificated repair station or mechanic with appropriate rating completes and signs off this inspection per 14 CFR 91.411.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3; 14 CFR 91.7; 14 CFR 91.411; 14 CFR 91.417; 14 CFR Part 43 Appendix E; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5

questions.question: How often are en route and terminal procedure charts revised, and how often are electronic navigation databases updated?
questions.answer: En route and terminal procedure charts are revised every 56 days. Electronic navigation databases are updated every 28 days. Using charts or databases beyond their effective dates means the information may not reflect current NOTAMs, procedure changes, airspace modifications, or obstacle data, creating a direct safety risk during IFR operations.

questions.question: Where on an instrument approach chart would you look to determine whether the chart is currently valid for the flight you are about to conduct?
questions.answer: The effective date is printed on the chart itself — typically in the top margin or title block of FAA instrument approach procedure charts. The chart shows the cycle date or the start/end of its effective period. You must verify this date against today's date before using it for IFR flight. If the chart is expired, you must obtain the current chart before proceeding.

questions.question: As PIC, what is your regulatory responsibility regarding the currency of navigation publications and databases before an IFR flight?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.103, the PIC must become familiar with all available information concerning the flight, which includes verifying that navigation publications, charts, and databases in use are current and valid. The PIC is ultimately responsible for airworthiness and proper equipment operation. Flying with outdated navigation data violates the spirit of this regulation and can expose the pilot to enforcement action if the outdated data contributes to a deviation or incident.

questions.question: During your instrument flight deck check, you discover your GPS navigator's database expired 10 days ago. The destination airport has an RNAV (GPS) approach as the only available instrument approach. How do you assess the risk, and what are your options?
questions.answer: An expired GPS database is a significant risk for IFR operations. With an expired database, waypoint positions, approach procedures, and airspace data may no longer be accurate. Many avionics units will still function with an expired database but will display a warning. For a primary GPS approach using an expired database, you cannot legally fly that approach as a standalone RNAV procedure because the database currency is part of the equipment requirement. Options include: updating the database before flight, filing to an alternate with a non-GPS approach, checking if a VOR or ILS approach exists at a nearby airport, or delaying the flight until the database is updated. Flying IFR with an expired database when it is the sole means of navigation is not an acceptable risk.

questions.question: You are planning a helicopter IFR flight to an offshore oil platform using a GPS approach. You confirm your paper approach charts are current, but the FMS database is 35 days old. A colleague says 'it's close enough — nothing ever changes out there.' How do you respond and what risk does this attitude represent?
questions.answer: This attitude is a classic example of hazardous thinking — specifically 'invulnerability' or 'complacency.' The Helicopter Flying Handbook notes that the error chain typically involves multiple poor decisions, and dismissing a known deficiency because 'nothing ever changes' is exactly the kind of link that can lead to an accident. Navigation procedure changes, airspace modifications, obstacle additions, and frequency changes can occur at any time. A 35-day-old database is beyond the 28-day update cycle. The FMS may fly an approach to coordinates or altitudes that are no longer correct. The proper response is to update the database, use a current paper chart as a cross-check only if permitted by the avionics AFM supplement, or delay the flight. You should never pressure yourself to accept a known deficiency in safety-critical navigation equipment.

questions.question: You are conducting a preflight instrument check and notice that your aircraft's RFM supplement for the GPS navigator requires a current database for IFR approaches, but your operator says the database update subscription lapsed. What is the operational and legal status of that GPS for IFR flight, and how does this interact with 14 CFR 91.213?
questions.answer: If the RFM/AFM supplement for the GPS navigator requires a current database as a condition of IFR operation, then operating with an expired database makes that unit non-compliant with its approved operating limitations under 14 CFR 91.9 and 91.213. The unit would be considered inoperative for IFR approach purposes. Under 14 CFR 91.213(d), inoperative equipment may be deferred only if it is not required by the kind of operations being conducted, a VFR day list, or an airworthiness directive. If the GPS is the only approach aid at the destination and it cannot legally be used for the IFR approach, the aircraft may not be dispatched for that IFR flight with that equipment in that condition. The PIC must ensure the helicopter is airworthy before each flight — this is a no-go item unless an alternate approach capability exists.

questions.question: A pilot argues that since they cross-checked their expired GPS database against current paper charts and found no differences, the risk of using the expired database is effectively zero. Critically evaluate this logic from both a safety and regulatory standpoint.
questions.answer: This argument has surface appeal but fails on multiple levels. From a safety standpoint, a comparison of paper charts against the database only verifies the procedure as depicted — it cannot account for changes that affect underlying database parameters such as final approach fix coordinates, vertical path angles, or transition routing that may not be visually obvious on the chart. A mismatch could exist in data the pilot did not specifically check. Additionally, NOTAMs may have modified a procedure after the paper chart was printed, creating a scenario where both are outdated in different ways. From a regulatory standpoint, the AFM/RFM supplement specifying database currency requirements is an operating limitation under 14 CFR 91.9 — pilot judgment about perceived risk does not supersede an approved operating limitation. The FAA establishes database currency requirements based on the integrity standards of the navigation system, not on the likelihood of change at any specific location. Self-certifying compliance through informal cross-checks does not meet the legal standard.
questions.follow_up: If a pilot did fly an RNAV approach with an expired database and successfully completed it without incident, does that retroactively make the flight legal or the decision sound?
questions.follow_up_answer: No on both counts. Outcome does not determine legality or quality of decision-making. The flight was non-compliant with the AFM supplement operating limitations and 14 CFR 91.9 at the time it was conducted — the successful outcome does not change that. From an ADM perspective, the Helicopter Flying Handbook warns that good outcomes from poor decisions can reinforce bad habits, increasing the likelihood of a future mishap. This is sometimes called 'outcome bias.' A real examiner would point out that this is precisely how accident chains begin — repeated departures from standards that went unpunished create false confidence. The correct lesson from a successful outcome under non-compliant conditions is not 'it was fine' but rather 'I was lucky and must not repeat that decision.'

questions.question: You are airborne IFR in a helicopter and ATC assigns an RNAV arrival routing that was added to the national airspace system after your GPS database was last updated. The waypoints for the new arrival do not appear in your database. Walk me through your risk management and communication process in this situation.
questions.answer: This is a serious situational awareness emergency requiring immediate action. First, inform ATC immediately: advise that your navigation database does not contain the assigned arrival and that you are unable to fly the route as assigned. ATC is required to provide alternative routing you can navigate. Second, assess backup navigation: determine if VOR, DME, or radar vectors can be used to navigate to the destination without relying on the unknown waypoints. Many RNAV arrivals can be replicated with conventional navigation if the underlying NAVAIDs are available. Third, consider fuel state and alternate options: if ATC cannot provide workable routing and you cannot safely navigate to the destination, declaring minimum fuel or declaring an emergency may be appropriate to get priority handling. Fourth, document the event: upon landing, report the database deficiency so it can be corrected before next flight. The root cause — departing IFR with an outdated database — was the preventable error. This scenario illustrates why database currency is a hard preflight requirement, not a soft recommendation. The Helicopter Flying Handbook emphasizes that breaking the error chain early is critical; this chain started before engine start.
questions.follow_up: After landing safely, what obligations, if any, do you have to report this event, and could you face certificate action?
questions.follow_up_answer: Reporting obligations depend on the specifics. If you deviated from an ATC clearance, you may have a duty to file a report under 14 CFR 91.123 if ATC requests one. Filing a NASA Aviation Safety Reporting System (ASRS) report within 10 days of the incident provides immunity from certificate action for unintentional violations (except criminal conduct or accidents), per FAA Order 8900.1 and 14 CFR 91.25. Certificate action is possible if the FAA determines you departed IFR flight with a known database deficiency in violation of an AFM operating limitation (14 CFR 91.9) or without proper preflight planning (14 CFR 91.103). The ASRS report is strongly recommended. More broadly, this event should trigger a review of your operator's database update procedures to prevent recurrence.

questions.question: When performing the instrument flight deck check during preflight, what document must you use, and where does that requirement come from?
questions.answer: You must use the checklist specific to that helicopter — the one found in or derived from the approved Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) for that serial number and registration. 14 CFR 91.9 requires compliance with the operating limitations in the approved flight manual, and the Helicopter Flying Handbook states that the PIC is responsible for ensuring airworthiness before flight. The RFM checklist is the authoritative source because the RFM is specific to that individual aircraft.

questions.question: During the instrument preflight check, you verify the altimeter. What is the acceptable range of the Kollsman window setting, and what error is acceptable when you set the current altimeter setting?
questions.answer: The Kollsman window adjustment range is 28.00 to 31.00 inches Hg. When you dial in the current local altimeter setting, the indicated altitude should be within 75 feet of the known field elevation. An error greater than 75 feet is grounds to consider the altimeter unserviceable for IFR flight.

questions.question: During the preflight instrument check, how do you verify that the static system is free of blockage before flight?
questions.answer: Check that the altimeter reads within the acceptable tolerance of field elevation with the current altimeter setting, the VSI reads zero (or within its resting tolerance), and the airspeed indicator reads zero. Any indication that does not match expected values — such as an altimeter frozen at an incorrect altitude or a VSI not reading zero at rest — suggests a blocked or partially blocked static system. Physically inspect all static ports for obstructions such as ice, water, tape, or insect nests.

questions.question: You complete the instrument preflight check and discover the attitude indicator has a slow tumble and does not erect fully within the time specified in the RFM before takeoff. The weather is IMC. Walk me through how you determine whether this helicopter is in a condition for safe instrument flight.
questions.answer: First, consult the RFM for any guidance on attitude indicator erection time — if the instrument hasn't erected within the published timeframe, that is a known discrepancy. Next, check whether your helicopter has an FAA-approved MEL and whether the attitude indicator is listed as deferrable. Under 14 CFR 91.213(d), if no MEL exists, you must determine whether the instrument is required for the kind of operation being conducted — for IFR flight, the attitude indicator is required under 14 CFR 91.205(d). Since IMC is the planned condition and the attitude indicator is required for IFR, the helicopter is not in a condition for safe instrument flight. The flight must be delayed and the discrepancy addressed by a certificated maintenance person before departure.

questions.question: During your preflight instrument check on a cold morning, you notice the airspeed indicator reads zero but you suspect the pitot tube may be frozen. What specific checks do you perform to confirm pitot versus static blockage, and how does each type of blockage affect the instrument indications?
questions.answer: To differentiate: if only the pitot tube is blocked but the drain hole is open, the ASI will slowly drop to zero and remain there because no ram air pressure is entering. If both the pitot tube and drain hole are blocked, the trapped air makes the ASI behave like an altimeter — it rises as you climb and falls as you descend. A blocked static system affects all three static instruments: the altimeter freezes at the altitude of blockage, the VSI reads continuously zero, and the ASI becomes inaccurate. During preflight, physically inspect the pitot tube and all static ports for ice, obstructions, or covers left in place. Confirm the pitot heat is functional by activating it and feeling for warmth. Confirm static port areas are clear and unobstructed.

questions.question: During the preflight instrument check you note the helicopter has an alternate static source selector inside the cabin. How does switching to alternate static affect your instrument readings, and what does that tell you about its use as a backup versus its effect on accuracy?
questions.answer: Cabin static pressure is slightly lower than outside ambient pressure due to the venturi effect of airflow around the fuselage. Switching to alternate static will cause the altimeter to read slightly higher than actual altitude, the airspeed indicator to read slightly faster than actual airspeed, and the VSI to momentarily show a climb before stabilizing. The exact correction values should be published in the RFM or a placard. This confirms the alternate static source is functional during preflight, but pilots must understand that its readings are less accurate than the primary static system. It is a viable backup in IFR if the primary static system becomes blocked in flight, provided the pilot applies the published correction factors.

questions.question: You are doing a preflight instrument check and the fuel quantity gauges show enough fuel for the planned IFR flight. You also physically dipped or visually confirmed the fuel quantity and it matches. However, you recall that the regulations have a specific limitation on fuel gauge accuracy requirements. Explain that regulatory limitation and how it should factor into your preflight determination of whether the helicopter is in a condition for safe instrument flight.
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 27.1337(b)(1), fuel quantity gauges are only required to be accurate when reading empty — they are not required to be accurate at any other quantity. This means a gauge showing a full or partial quantity is not a certified measurement. The preflight determination of adequate fuel must therefore rely on physical verification — visually checking or measuring the actual fuel quantity — not solely on the gauge reading. For IFR flight, you must verify actual usable fuel meets the IFR fuel reserve requirements under 14 CFR 91.167 (fuel to reach destination, plus alternate if required, plus 45-minute reserve at normal cruise). If only the gauges were checked and not physically verified, the helicopter cannot be confidently determined to be in a condition for safe instrument flight.
questions.follow_up: If the fuel gauge reads empty but you physically verified a full tank, can you legally depart IFR under 91.213(d)?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, but it requires careful analysis. A fuel gauge that reads inaccurately (other than at empty) is technically within its certification standard, so it is not a 'malfunction' in the regulatory sense. However, under 91.213(d), if it is an inoperative instrument or piece of equipment, you must determine whether it is required for the operation. Fuel gauges are required by 14 CFR 27.1337 as part of the type design, but since they are only certified to be accurate at empty, a gauge that reads incorrectly at other quantities may not constitute an 'inoperative' item. The key safety point is that the PIC has physically verified fuel quantity and documented this in the logbook or notes. The better practice is to have a mechanic assess whether the gauge is performing within its certified standard before conducting IFR operations.

questions.question: During the preflight instrument check you discover a placard has fallen off the instrument panel — specifically the VNE placard. The helicopter is otherwise airworthy. How does this affect your determination of whether it is in a condition for safe instrument flight, and what is the regulatory basis for your decision?
questions.answer: A missing VNE placard is a significant finding. The Helicopter Flying Handbook notes that VNE varies with altitude and gross weight, and that a placard in the cockpit provides the current VNE for the conditions. Required placards are part of the type certificate data sheet and the approved type design — their presence is required by 14 CFR 27.1541 through 27.1567 (markings and placards). A missing required placard means the helicopter is not in conformance with its type design and is therefore not airworthy. Under 14 CFR 91.9 and 91.7, the PIC cannot operate an aircraft that is not in an airworthy condition. The flight must be grounded until a certificated maintenance person restores the required placard. This is not deferrable under 91.213(d) because a placard is a required marking, not an instrument or piece of equipment with an on/off state.
questions.follow_up: If you found the placard on the floor and it was undamaged, could you simply re-affix it yourself and log it?
questions.follow_up_answer: This is a gray area that requires careful consideration. Re-affixing a placard could be considered preventive maintenance under 14 CFR 43 Appendix A, but placards are not specifically listed as preventive maintenance items a certificated pilot may perform. Since the placard is part of the approved type design and its installation must match the type certificate, it is safest to have a certificated A&P or IA re-affix and inspect it to ensure it is the correct placard in the correct location, and to make a proper maintenance entry in the aircraft records under 14 CFR 43.9. The pilot should not assume this is within their authority as preventive maintenance.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 27.1541-27.1567; 14 CFR 91.7; 14 CFR 91.9; 14 CFR Part 43 Appendix A; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 5 and Chapter 8

areas_of_operation.title: Area of Operation III. Air Traffic Control (ATC) Clearances and Procedures

tasks.title: Task A. Compliance with Air Traffic Control Clearances

questions.question: What are the five elements typically included in a standard IFR ATC clearance, and what memory aid is commonly used to recall them?
questions.answer: The five elements of a standard IFR clearance are: (1) Clearance limit, (2) Route of flight, (3) Altitude, (4) Frequency (departure), and (5) Transponder code. The memory aid is CRAFT: Clearance limit, Route, Altitude, Frequency, Transponder.

questions.question: What is a clearance void time, and what action is the pilot required to take if the helicopter does not depart before that time expires?
questions.answer: A clearance void time is a specific time set by ATC at which an IFR clearance becomes invalid if the aircraft has not departed by that time. If the pilot does not depart before the void time, the clearance is no longer valid and the pilot must contact ATC to obtain a new clearance before departing. Additionally, if the pilot does not depart and does not contact ATC, ATC will initiate search and rescue procedures if they have not heard from the pilot within 30 minutes of the void time.

questions.question: When operating IFR and you receive a route amendment or altitude change from ATC, what is your responsibility as the pilot-in-command before accepting and executing that clearance?
questions.answer: The pilot-in-command must read back all ATC clearances and instructions, especially altitude assignments, runway assignments, and taxi instructions. The PIC must ensure the amended clearance is understood, can be safely complied with, and does not create a hazard to the aircraft. If the clearance is not acceptable or safe, the pilot must advise ATC immediately and request an alternative. The PIC retains final authority for the safe operation of the aircraft under 14 CFR 91.3.

questions.question: You are a helicopter pilot departing a non-towered airport IFR. ATC issues you a clearance with a void time of 15 minutes from now, but your pre-takeoff checks reveal a minor maintenance discrepancy that takes 20 minutes to resolve. Walk me through your decision-making and required actions.
questions.answer: Since the void time will expire before departure is possible, the pilot must not depart under the original clearance. Before the void time expires, the pilot should contact ATC (via radio or phone if radio contact cannot be established) to advise them that departure will not occur before the void time and to request a new or extended clearance. If the pilot cannot reach ATC and the void time passes without departure, the pilot must not depart IFR and should attempt to contact ATC as soon as possible. ATC will initiate search and rescue procedures within 30 minutes of the void time if no communication is received, so notifying them promptly prevents unnecessary SAR activation. A new clearance must be obtained before any IFR departure.

questions.question: While en route IFR at your assigned altitude, ATC instructs you to 'maintain 4,000, expect 6,000 in 10 miles.' You then lose two-way radio communication. What altitudes do you fly and when, and which regulation governs this?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.185, in the event of two-way radio communication failure in IFR conditions, the pilot should fly the highest of three altitudes for the route segment: (1) the assigned altitude, (2) the minimum IFR altitude, or (3) the altitude ATC has advised to expect. In this scenario, ATC assigned 4,000 and advised to expect 6,000 in 10 miles. Before reaching that 10-mile point, the pilot flies 4,000 (the assigned altitude). After the point where ATC said to expect 6,000 (or after 10 minutes if time-based), the pilot climbs to 6,000 because that becomes the highest applicable altitude at that point. The 'expect' altitude is a critical element of a clearance specifically so pilots have guidance for lost communication scenarios.

questions.question: You are a helicopter pilot on an IFR arrival and ATC clears you for an approach but does not give you a specific route from your current position to the IAF. What can you assume, and what are your options?
questions.answer: When cleared for an approach without a specific routing to the IAF, the pilot may proceed via the most direct route to the IAF if already established on a segment of the approach or on a published feeder route. If not on a published route, the pilot should request clarification from ATC to ensure obstacle clearance is maintained. ATC has the responsibility to provide appropriate separation and issue routing to the IAF. The pilot should not assume random routing is acceptable — they should either be on a published route, a radar vector, or should query ATC. During arrival, the pilot must also comply with any published altitude restrictions on the STAR or approach procedure unless otherwise amended by ATC.

questions.question: ATC issues you a clearance that includes the phrase 'cleared as filed.' As an IFR helicopter pilot, what does this mean, and what are the risks of accepting this clearance if your filed route contained an error or outdated information?
questions.answer: 'Cleared as filed' means ATC is authorizing the exact route the pilot filed in the IFR flight plan, without modifications. The risk is that if the filed route contained errors — such as an incorrect airway, a closed or NOTAMed NAVAID, an altitude that violates MEA or TEC requirements, or outdated waypoint identifiers — the pilot is now cleared to fly that incorrect route. ATC may not catch these errors because they may not scrutinize a 'cleared as filed' authorization as carefully as a route they construct. The pilot must verify that the filed route is valid, current, and obstacle-compliant before accepting the clearance. If any doubt exists, the pilot should request confirmation of the full route from ATC. Additionally, the pilot remains responsible for terrain and obstacle clearance during the en route phase.
questions.follow_up: If you accept a 'cleared as filed' clearance and then discover mid-flight that your filed route takes you over a Special Use Airspace (SUA) that is now active, what are your obligations and what should you do?
questions.follow_up_answer: The pilot must immediately advise ATC of the conflict with the active SUA. ATC has the responsibility to provide separation from SUA if they issued the clearance that routes you through it, but the pilot also has the responsibility to avoid prohibited or restricted areas. The pilot should request an amended clearance to route around the active SUA. If the SUA is restricted or prohibited airspace, entering it without authorization is a regulatory violation under 14 CFR 91.133 and 91.137 regardless of ATC clearance. The clearance as filed does not grant permission to enter restricted or prohibited airspace — those require explicit authorization from the controlling agency.

questions.question: You are operating IFR in VMC conditions and ATC issues an altitude change that would place your helicopter below the published MEA for the route segment. You know you are in VMC and believe you can maintain VFR terrain clearance. Can you legally comply with the clearance, and what should you do?
questions.answer: No — a pilot operating on an IFR flight plan cannot simply accept a clearance below the MEA and elect to maintain VFR terrain separation in lieu of IFR obstacle clearance. The MEA guarantees both obstacle clearance and navigation signal reception along that route segment. ATC is not permitted to issue an IFR clearance below the MEA unless a published MOCA or other authorized altitude applies and specific conditions are met. If ATC inadvertently issues such a clearance, the pilot must immediately advise ATC that the assigned altitude is below the MEA for the segment and request a correction. The pilot's responsibility under 14 CFR 91.177 is to fly at or above the minimum IFR altitude applicable to the route. Being in VMC does not relieve an IFR pilot of minimum altitude requirements — those exist for obstacle clearance, not just weather separation.
questions.follow_up: What is the difference between the MEA and the MOCA for this purpose, and under what condition can ATC assign the MOCA altitude instead of the MEA?
questions.follow_up_answer: The MEA (Minimum En Route Altitude) guarantees both obstacle clearance and adequate navigation signal (VOR) reception along the entire route segment. The MOCA (Minimum Obstruction Clearance Altitude) guarantees obstacle clearance for the entire segment, but navigation signal reception is only guaranteed within 22 nautical miles of the VOR. ATC may assign the MOCA altitude in lieu of the MEA when the aircraft is within 22 NM of the applicable NAVAID, which ensures the pilot still has adequate navigation signal. At the MOCA, a pilot farther than 22 NM from the VOR may lose adequate signal quality, so this limitation is critical. The MOCA is depicted on en route charts with an asterisk (*) preceding the altitude.

questions.question: Under what regulation does the PIC have authority to deviate from an ATC clearance during an in-flight emergency, and what is the basic requirement afterward?
questions.answer: 14 CFR 91.3(b) gives the PIC authority to deviate from any rule in 14 CFR Part 91 to the extent necessary to meet an emergency. After the deviation, if requested by ATC, the PIC must submit a written report to the FAA Administrator. There is no automatic requirement to file a report unless ATC requests it.

questions.question: Can the PIC declare an emergency and deviate from an IFR clearance without prior ATC approval? What must the PIC do regarding ATC notification?
questions.answer: Yes. The PIC has the authority under 14 CFR 91.3(b) to deviate from an ATC clearance without prior approval when an emergency exists. The PIC should notify ATC of the emergency and the deviation as soon as practicable. ATC will provide maximum assistance possible once aware of the emergency.

questions.question: What does 14 CFR 91.3(a) establish about PIC responsibility, and how does that relate to PIC emergency authority?
questions.answer: 14 CFR 91.3(a) states the PIC is directly responsible for, and is the final authority as to, the operation of the aircraft. This foundational responsibility is what gives context to 91.3(b) — because the PIC bears final responsibility for the safety of the flight, the regulation correspondingly grants the PIC authority to deviate from rules, including ATC clearances, when necessary to handle an emergency.

questions.question: You are flying a helicopter IFR at 6,000 feet on an assigned clearance when you experience a partial hydraulic failure. ATC clears you to maintain 6,000 feet, but you determine you need to descend to 3,000 feet immediately to reduce airspeed and control forces. Can you deviate from the clearance without waiting for ATC approval, and what should you do next?
questions.answer: Yes. Under 14 CFR 91.3(b), you may deviate from the ATC clearance immediately without waiting for approval because an emergency exists. You should simultaneously declare the emergency on the assigned frequency (or 121.5 MHz if contact is lost), inform ATC of your deviation, state your intentions, and request priority handling. ATC will provide maximum assistance. After landing, if ATC requests it, you must submit a written report of the deviation.

questions.question: You are flying a helicopter IFR in IMC and your co-pilot becomes incapacitated. ATC does not know about the emergency and is issuing you routine traffic advisories and amended routing. How does PIC emergency authority apply here, and what are your priorities?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.3, you as PIC have both the final authority and the responsibility for the safe operation of the flight. Your priority order is Aviate, Navigate, Communicate. You are not required to comply with ATC routing amendments — you may deviate from any ATC clearance to the extent necessary to manage the emergency. Once workload permits, declare the emergency on your assigned frequency, advise ATC of the incapacitation and your intentions, and request priority handling. Document any deviations and submit a written report if ATC requests one after landing.

questions.question: After deviating from an IFR clearance due to an engine fire in your helicopter, you land safely. ATC calls and requests you submit a written report of the deviation. Under what regulation is this required, and to whom is it submitted?
questions.answer: 14 CFR 91.3(b) states that each PIC who deviates from a rule in Part 91 during an emergency shall, upon request of the FAA Administrator, send a written report of that deviation to the Administrator. The report is submitted to the FAA — typically through the Flight Standards District Office (FSDO) responsible for the area where the deviation occurred. The requirement is triggered only by the FAA's request, not automatically.

questions.question: You declare an emergency and deviate from your IFR clearance due to inadvertent IMC deteriorating into spatial disorientation. You land safely at an uncontrolled field. The next day, an FAA inspector contacts you and says your deviation was not justified because the weather was actually VFR at your altitude per radar data. Can the FAA take certificate action against you for the deviation itself under these circumstances?
questions.answer: The FAA has broad enforcement discretion, but 14 CFR 91.3(b) protects PICs who deviate from rules during emergencies. The key legal question is whether the PIC's belief that an emergency existed was reasonable at the time — the regulation does not require the emergency to be objectively verified afterward, only that one existed from the PIC's perspective in the cockpit. Courts and NTSB have generally upheld that a PIC who acts in good faith based on the information available is protected. However, the FAA could still investigate whether the emergency declaration was made in good faith. If the PIC genuinely believed spatial disorientation constituted an emergency requiring immediate deviation, that is a defensible position. The written report (if requested) should accurately document the conditions as the PIC perceived them.
questions.follow_up: Does declaring an emergency automatically trigger a medical review or certificate action by the FAA?
questions.follow_up_answer: Declaring an emergency does not automatically trigger certificate action or a mandatory medical review. However, if the emergency involved a medical issue affecting the PIC (such as hypoxia, cardiac event, or incapacitation), the FAA may investigate whether the PIC is medically qualified to continue holding a certificate. The Aviation Safety Hotline and NASA ASRS report do not grant immunity from enforcement, but they are mitigating factors. The FAA's enforcement philosophy generally discourages punishing honest emergency declarations made in good faith, as it could deter future emergency declarations.

questions.question: During an IFR helicopter flight in Class A airspace, you experience complete communications failure combined with an engine oil pressure emergency. You decide to descend out of Class A and land at the nearest suitable airport, deviating from your clearance altitude and routing. Walk me through every regulatory authority you are operating under simultaneously during this event.
questions.answer: Multiple regulations apply simultaneously: (1) 14 CFR 91.3(b) — PIC emergency authority authorizes deviation from any Part 91 rule including altitude, routing, and airspace requirements; (2) 14 CFR 91.185 — lost communications procedures in IFR apply (squawk 7600, fly last assigned altitude or MEA, proceed to destination via filed route), but these are superseded by 91.3(b) if following them would compromise safety; (3) 14 CFR 91.135 — Class A operations requirements are waived under the emergency authority; (4) Squawk 7700 is appropriate to declare the emergency to ATC via transponder since voice is unavailable. The PIC's obligation is to navigate safely, use the transponder emergency code, land at the nearest suitable airport, and submit a written report of deviations if requested by the FAA. The lost comms procedures of 91.185 would apply as a baseline, but the oil emergency under 91.3(b) takes priority and justifies any departure from those procedures.
questions.follow_up: If you squawk both 7600 and 7700, which takes priority on ATC radar displays, and is that even possible on most transponders?
questions.follow_up_answer: Most transponders can only display one code at a time — you select either 7600 (communications failure) or 7700 (emergency). The generally accepted guidance from the AIM is to squawk 7700 first to alert ATC to the emergency, then switch to 7600 if communications failure is the primary issue and you want ATC to know you cannot communicate. In this scenario with both an emergency and a comms failure, squawking 7700 is the higher priority because it alerts ATC to an active emergency requiring immediate ATC coordination and airspace clearing. ATC can infer communications failure from your non-compliance with instructions. The AIM states that if you have previously been squawking an assigned code, you may retain that code while declaring emergency procedures — but 7700 is preferred for the highest priority alert.

questions.question: If you experience a two-way radio communication failure in IFR conditions, what transponder code should you squawk, and what does it indicate to ATC?
questions.answer: You should squawk 7600. This is the universally recognized lost communications transponder code. ATC radar will see the 7600 indication and know you have lost two-way radio communication. They will then attempt to re-establish contact and begin coordinating your expected route and altitude.

questions.question: Under 14 CFR 91.185, if you lose radio contact in IFR conditions, what route are you required to fly?
questions.answer: You must fly the highest of the following routes in order of priority: (1) the route assigned in the last ATC clearance received; (2) if being radar vectored, the direct route from the point of radio failure to the fix, route, or airway specified in the vector clearance; (3) in the absence of an assigned route, the route ATC has advised may be expected; (4) in the absence of an expected route, the route filed in your flight plan.

questions.question: What altitude must you fly when you experience IFR communications failure, and how do you determine which altitude to use?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.185(c)(2), you must fly the highest of the following altitudes for each route segment: (1) the altitude or flight level assigned in the last ATC clearance received; (2) the minimum IFR altitude for the route segment being flown (as published on charts); or (3) the altitude ATC has advised to expect. The intent is to ensure obstacle clearance and separation while allowing ATC to predict your altitude.

questions.question: You're flying a helicopter IFR in a non-radar environment on an assigned route when you lose radio contact. ATC had previously told you to 'expect 5,000 feet in 15 minutes.' Your last assigned altitude was 4,000 feet, and the MEA for the next segment is 5,500 feet. What altitude do you fly on that segment, and why?
questions.answer: You fly 5,500 feet — the MEA for that segment. Under 14 CFR 91.185(c)(2), you must fly the highest of: last assigned altitude (4,000 ft), expected altitude (5,000 ft), or minimum IFR altitude for the segment (5,500 ft MEA). Since the MEA is highest, it governs. This ensures obstacle clearance is maintained even though ATC told you to expect a lower altitude.

questions.question: You're flying IFR in a non-radar environment and lose communications just after being cleared direct to a fix that is not your destination. You have no further clearance beyond that fix. When should you begin your approach at the destination, and what governs that decision?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.185(c)(3), you leave the clearance limit at the expect-further-clearance (EFC) time if one was given, or if no EFC time was given, you proceed to the destination and begin the approach as close to your ETA as possible — based on the filed or amended flight plan. If the clearance limit is a fix from which an approach begins, start descent and approach as close to the ETA as possible. The goal is to be predictable so ATC can protect your airspace.

questions.question: You lose communications while flying IFR in VFR conditions. How does 14 CFR 91.185 change what you're required to do compared to losing comms in IMC?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.185(b), if communications are lost in VFR conditions, you must continue the flight under VFR and land as soon as practicable. You are not required to follow the IFR lost-comm route and altitude procedures of 91.185(c) — those apply specifically when you are in IMC or when it is not possible or practical to proceed VFR. The regulation recognizes that if you can safely operate VFR, you should do so and get on the ground quickly.

questions.question: A helicopter pilot flying IFR in a non-radar environment loses radio contact while being vectored off the published airway. The last transmitted instruction was a heading of 270° with no fix, route, or airway specified. How does the pilot determine where to go and what altitude to fly?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.185(c)(1), when being radar vectored and communications are lost, the pilot must proceed by direct route from the point of radio failure to the fix, route, or airway specified in the vector clearance. If no specific fix was included in the vector clearance, the pilot should interpret the clearance in context — typically returning direct to the last assigned fix or airway the vector was intended to lead to, as understood from the clearance. For altitude, fly the highest of last assigned altitude, expected altitude, or the MEA for that route segment. The pilot should squawk 7600, document the time and position of failure, and fly as predictably as possible to allow ATC to sequence traffic.
questions.follow_up: What's the danger if a helicopter pilot blindly continues the assigned vector heading of 270° without returning to the published airway or fix?
questions.follow_up_answer: If the pilot continues the assigned vector heading indefinitely, they will deviate from the protected airspace structure. ATC has no way to predict the pilot's position or route, making traffic separation impossible. More critically, the pilot may fly below the minimum IFR altitude for an off-airway area where obstacle clearance is not guaranteed. In mountainous or complex terrain — common in helicopter operations — this could result in CFIT. The published minimum IFR altitude only covers published routes; off-route altitudes must be calculated using 14 CFR 91.177 criteria (1,000 ft above highest obstacle within 4 NM, or 2,000 ft in mountainous terrain).

questions.question: You're flying a helicopter IFR in a remote non-radar environment. Your radio fails completely — including the ability to transmit or receive. You have no datalink. You do have a working transponder. Walk me through every action you would take from the moment of failure through landing.
questions.answer: Immediately squawk 7600 to alert ATC. Confirm failure by checking circuit breakers, switching to backup radio or second comm, trying guard frequency (121.5 MHz), and attempting to receive on nav radios. If no radio can be restored, operate under 14 CFR 91.185. If VFR is possible, proceed VFR and land as soon as practicable per 91.185(b). If in IMC: fly the route per 91.185(c)(1) — last assigned, expected, or filed. Fly altitude per 91.185(c)(2) — highest of last assigned, expected, or minimum IFR altitude. Proceed to destination and begin approach at EFC time or filed ETA per 91.185(c)(3). At destination, if the tower is equipped, watch for light gun signals. When landing, have someone notify ATC immediately. Document time, position, and altitude at failure for the report.
questions.follow_up: At a controlled airport with an operating tower, how do you signal your intent to land after losing all communications, and what light gun signals should you expect during the approach and after landing?
questions.follow_up_answer: Rock the wings (fixed-wing) or flash landing light (helicopter — a commonly accepted visual signal) to indicate you are acknowledging light gun signals. For a helicopter on approach in the pattern: steady green means cleared to land; flashing green means cleared to land (also used when on final); steady red means give way and continue circling; flashing red means airport unsafe, do not land; flashing white means return to starting point on airport; alternating red and green means exercise extreme caution. After landing and clear of the active runway, a flashing white signals to taxi back to parking. These signals are detailed in the AIM and the pilot must acknowledge each signal by rocking wings or flashing lights before proceeding.

questions.question: What should you do if ATC issues you a clearance and you're not completely sure you understood one part of it?
questions.answer: You must request clarification immediately. Never proceed on a clearance you don't fully understand. ATC expects pilots to ask for a readback clarification, a repeat, or a 'say again' for any portion of a clearance that was unclear. Proceeding on a partially understood clearance is a direct violation of 14 CFR 91.123, which requires compliance with ATC clearances, and you cannot comply if you don't fully understand the instruction.

questions.question: What is the purpose of reading back an ATC clearance, and which elements are always required to be read back?
questions.answer: A readback confirms to ATC that you received and correctly understood the clearance. Required readback elements include: hold short instructions, runway assignments (for landing and takeoff), altimeter settings, and any altitude or heading assignments. For IFR clearances, pilots should read back all altitude assignments, heading assignments, altimeter settings, and any holding instructions. This gives the controller an opportunity to catch any misunderstanding before the pilot acts on it.

questions.question: What does 14 CFR 91.123 require of a pilot-in-command when operating under an ATC clearance?
questions.answer: 14 CFR 91.123 requires the PIC to comply with ATC clearances and instructions unless an emergency exists. The pilot may not deviate from a clearance except in an emergency, and if a deviation does occur for emergency reasons, the pilot must notify ATC as soon as possible. This regulation makes it clear that receiving a clearance creates a legal obligation — which is why full understanding before execution is critical.

questions.question: You're flying IFR in a busy terminal environment and receive a complex reroute clearance with multiple waypoints while simultaneously managing a high workload in the cockpit. What is your risk management strategy to ensure full clearance understanding before acting on it?
questions.answer: The first priority is workload management. Ask ATC to 'standby' or request 'unable to copy — ready to copy in 30 seconds' if needed. Write down the clearance using CRAFT (Clearance limit, Route, Altitude, Frequency, Transponder) or your notation system. Read the clearance back in full to ATC and wait for confirmation. Do not begin executing any new routing until you have confirmed understanding. If any element is unclear after readback, ask ATC to 'say again [specific element].' Accepting and executing an incomplete clearance under high workload is a classic link in the error chain — breaking that link by slowing down and confirming is the correct risk mitigation.

questions.question: ATC clears you to 'descend and maintain 3,000, expect 2,000 in 10 miles.' You believe you heard '2,000' as your cleared altitude and begin descending to 2,000 feet. What risk did you introduce, and what should you have done differently?
questions.answer: You introduced a serious altitude deviation risk. 'Expect 2,000 in 10 miles' is an advisory for flight planning purposes only — it is not an altitude clearance. Your cleared altitude is 3,000 feet until ATC issues a new clearance for 2,000. Descending to 2,000 without a clearance violates 14 CFR 91.123 and could result in a loss of separation from traffic or terrain. The correct action was to read back '3,000' as the cleared altitude and, if the phrasing was confusing, ask ATC to clarify before any descent below 3,000. A partial or misunderstood altitude clearance must always be resolved before action.

questions.question: During a helicopter IFR flight, you receive a clearance that includes an unfamiliar intersection name. Rather than ask ATC to repeat it, you decide to 'figure it out once airborne.' How does the ADM principle taught in the Helicopter Flying Handbook apply to this decision?
questions.answer: This is a classic example of poor ADM. The Helicopter Flying Handbook (FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 13) specifically warns against using the word 'probably' — if an action will only 'probably' work out, choose an option that is known to work. Assuming you'll figure out the intersection in flight is 'probably' thinking. The correct ADM approach is to resolve the uncertainty on the ground before departure or immediately on frequency. Additionally, this adds a link to the error chain — once airborne, workload increases and uncertainty compounds. Breaking the chain requires asking for clarification before departure, not hoping to resolve it in flight.

questions.question: ATC issues you an amended clearance while you're heads-down programming the FMS in your helicopter. Your first officer — if you had one — would catch the discrepancy, but you're single-pilot. You catch only part of the new clearance and execute it. Several minutes later, ATC calls with 'verify altitude.' What systemic risk management failures led to this moment, and how should single-pilot IFR helicopter pilots guard against it?
questions.answer: Multiple SRM failures compounded here: first, failure to prioritize aviate/navigate/communicate — FMS programming should have been paused when ATC called. Second, failure to request a 'standby' from ATC to manage workload before receiving an amended clearance. Third, executing a clearance without a complete readback and ATC confirmation. The Helicopter Flying Handbook emphasizes that single-pilot resource management (SRM) requires the pilot to proactively manage workload so that no single task consumes all attention during a critical phase. The correct protocol is: stop FMS input, copy the full amended clearance, read it back completely, receive ATC confirmation, then resume FMS programming using the verified clearance. Automation management and workload sequencing are the specific SRM tools applicable here.
questions.follow_up: If ATC's 'verify altitude' call reveals you're 1,000 feet below your cleared altitude, what are your immediate obligations under 14 CFR 91.123 and what do you tell ATC?
questions.follow_up_answer: Under 14 CFR 91.123, you must immediately return to your cleared altitude and notify ATC. You would say: '[Callsign], verifying altitude, currently [actual altitude], climbing/correcting to [cleared altitude] immediately.' If the deviation constituted an emergency or required you to deviate for safety, you'd invoke 91.123(b) and report it. ATC may issue a pilot deviation report. Honesty and immediate corrective action are required — attempting to conceal the deviation or normalize the wrong altitude compounds both the legal and safety risk.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.123; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (SRM, workload management, automation management)

questions.question: A controller issues a rapid-fire departure clearance that includes an unexpected routing you weren't briefed on. You read it back incorrectly and the controller says 'readback correct' — but you actually copied the wrong altitude. You depart and maintain the wrong altitude. Who bears responsibility, and does the controller's confirmation of an incorrect readback relieve the PIC of accountability?
questions.answer: The PIC retains ultimate responsibility under 14 CFR 91.123. While the controller's confirmation of an incorrect readback is an ATC error and will be documented as such in a safety investigation, it does not legally or operationally absolve the pilot. The FAA's position is that the readback/hearback system is a shared safety net — when both parties fail, it does not eliminate PIC responsibility. The pilot had an obligation to ensure the readback was accurate before executing it. In practice, both a pilot deviation and an ATC incident report may be filed. The risk management lesson is that pilot-side accuracy cannot be delegated to ATC confirmation; the pilot must independently verify what was written/programmed against what was issued.
questions.follow_up: What is the 'hearback' problem in ATC communications, and how does it contribute to altitude busts in IFR helicopter operations?
questions.follow_up_answer: The 'hearback' problem occurs when a controller hears a pilot's incorrect readback but confirms it anyway — either because they missed the error, were distracted by other traffic, or assumed the pilot was correct. This is a recognized human factors issue in ATC. In helicopter IFR operations, it is especially dangerous because helicopters often operate at lower altitudes with less obstacle clearance margin. An altitude bust of even a few hundred feet in mountainous or terminal environments can be catastrophic. The mitigation is for pilots never to rely solely on ATC confirmation of a readback — verify the altitude independently against the filed clearance, expected routing, and any CRAFT notation before executing.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.123; AIM 4-4-9; FAA Human Factors in Aviation Safety (hearback/readback errors)

questions.question: What should you do immediately if ATC issues you a clearance that you believe is unsafe or operationally impossible for your helicopter?
questions.answer: You must not comply with an unsafe clearance. Notify ATC immediately that you are unable to comply and state the reason. ATC has the authority to issue clearances, but pilots have the final authority and responsibility for the safe operation of their aircraft. You are never required to accept a clearance that would compromise safety.

questions.question: What is the correct procedure when you receive an ATC clearance but are unsure whether you copied it correctly?
questions.answer: You must request clarification before executing the clearance. Read back the clearance to ATC and ask for confirmation, or advise ATC you need the clearance repeated. Never execute a clearance you are uncertain about. Compliance with an incorrectly copied clearance can result in airspace violations, controlled flight into terrain, or traffic conflicts.

questions.question: What items in an IFR clearance must always be read back to ATC?
questions.answer: At a minimum, pilots must read back altitude assignments, vectors, runway assignments, taxi instructions that include a runway crossing or hold-short instruction, and any portion of the clearance that is critical to safety. ATC expects a full readback of the ATC route clearance (destination, route, altitude, departure frequency, transponder code) using the CRAFT acronym: Clearance limit, Route, Altitude, Frequency, Transponder. Any discrepancy between what was issued and what is read back should be caught and corrected by the controller.

questions.question: You are flying IFR in your helicopter and ATC clears you to 'descend and maintain 3,000 feet.' Your current position puts 3,000 feet well below the Minimum Enroute Altitude (MEA) for your route segment. How do you handle this clearance?
questions.answer: You should not descend to 3,000 feet if it places you below obstacle clearance limits for your route segment. Advise ATC immediately that 3,000 feet is below the MEA and request a higher altitude. ATC radar may be providing separation from terrain, but the pilot-in-command bears ultimate responsibility for terrain clearance. In mountainous terrain especially, you should be familiar with applicable MEAs and MOCAs and speak up any time a clearance would take you below those values.

questions.question: ATC issues you a heading and altitude that would take your helicopter directly into an area of reported severe icing at an altitude your aircraft is not certified or equipped to handle. You are already IFR. Walk me through your decision-making and communication with ATC.
questions.answer: Declare your inability to comply immediately. Inform ATC that the assigned heading and altitude would route you into severe icing conditions your aircraft cannot safely operate in, and request an alternate routing or altitude. If necessary, declare an emergency under 14 CFR 91.3(b) to deviate from the clearance to avoid the hazard. ATC has weather avoidance assistance responsibilities and will work with you. The key risk management principle here is that the word 'probably' should be avoided — do not accept a clearance that will 'probably' be okay. Choose a course of action known to be safe.

questions.question: You receive an amended IFR clearance from ATC mid-flight that contains five changes simultaneously — new routing, new altitude, new squawk code, a frequency change, and a new departure fix. What risk does this scenario present and how do you manage it?
questions.answer: This scenario presents a high workload and high risk of miscopying one or more elements, which could lead to airspace deviations, traffic conflicts, or CFIT.
