For example, if the DME reads 15 and the OBS is set to the 090 radial with a centered CDI, you are at the intersection of the 090 radial and the 15 DME arc — a precisely defined point in space. As you fly the arc, you should update the OBS frequently (every 10 degrees is a common technique) to keep a lead radial cue for turns, but at any moment the combination of DME = 15 and the current radial shown on the CDI gives you an unambiguous fix. If DME starts increasing, you've drifted outbound; if decreasing, you've cut inside the arc.

questions.question: You're flying an IFR helicopter en route and ATC asks you to report when crossing a specific VOR intersection — defined by two VOR radials from different stations. Your primary navigation radio is tuned to the first VOR and your number two radio to the second. Both CDIs are showing approximately half-scale deflection, but in opposite directions from the expected crossing point. How do you interpret this to accurately assess your position relative to the intersection, and what actions do you take?
questions.answer: Half-scale deflection on a VOR CDI represents approximately 6 degrees of angular error from the selected radial. With both CDIs showing deflection — one from each defining VOR — you are NOT yet at the intersection. You need to assess which radial you have crossed or not yet reached by checking the TO/FROM flags and the direction of deflection on each CDI. For example, if VOR-1 CDI is deflecting right (needle to the right) with a TO flag, you are to the left of the radial and still need to track right to center it. If VOR-2 shows needle to the left, you are to the right of that radial. Together this triangulates your position relative to the intersection. You should continue tracking your assigned route and report the intersection only when BOTH CDIs are simultaneously centered, indicating you are on both defining radials at once. Do not report the fix early, as this could compromise separation.
questions.follow_up: What is the angular sensitivity difference between a VOR CDI and a localizer CDI at full deflection, and why does that matter if one of these 'intersection-defining' signals happened to be a localizer back-course?
questions.follow_up_answer: A VOR CDI at full deflection represents approximately 12 degrees or more off the selected radial. A localizer CDI at full deflection represents only about 2.5 degrees off course — making the localizer approximately 4 to 5 times more sensitive than a VOR. If a localizer back-course were used to define one side of an intersection, even a small angular deviation would produce a large CDI deflection. The pilot must be aware that a half-scale deflection on the localizer represents only about 1.25 degrees off course — a much tighter tolerance than VOR. Additionally, flying a localizer back-course without an approach-specific back-course CDI or HSI reversal means the CDI sensing is reversed: flying toward the needle actually takes you away from the course. Misinterpreting this during intersection identification could cause a significant position error.

questions.question: You're flying a helicopter IFR at night in IMC. Your GPS has failed, your number two VOR receiver just flagged as unreliable, and you're 40 NM from a VOR station flying at the MOCA on the airway. Your single working VOR CDI is centered. Can you confidently determine your position relative to the VOR, and what is the weakest link in your situational picture right now?
questions.answer: A centered CDI confirms you are on the selected radial — it tells you the angular direction from the VOR station, but it does not tell you your distance along that radial. With no GPS and no DME indicated, you cannot determine how far along the radial you are. Additionally, you are at the MOCA — which only guarantees VOR reception within 22 NM of the station. At 40 NM from the VOR, the MOCA does not guarantee navigation signal integrity, meaning the centered CDI may be unreliable or a false indication. The weakest link is the combination of being below MEA (at MOCA) beyond the 22 NM guaranteed reception range and having no independent means (DME, GPS, second VOR cross-radial) to confirm position along the route. You should request an immediate climb to the MEA to restore guaranteed signal reception, advise ATC of your navigation equipment status, and not rely solely on the single VOR CDI for position determination until you are within 22 NM of the station or have climbed to MEA.
questions.follow_up: If you were at the MEA instead of the MOCA, does a centered CDI on a single VOR now give you sufficient positional awareness to identify a required reporting point, and what additional piece of information would make it definitive?
questions.follow_up_answer: At the MEA, VOR signal reception is guaranteed along the entire segment, so the centered CDI is now a reliable angular reference. However, a single centered CDI still only tells you that you are somewhere on that radial — it does not tell you how far from the station you are. To definitively identify a required reporting point defined by that radial alone, you would need to know your distance. DME co-located with the VOR would provide that distance directly. Without DME, you could use elapsed time and groundspeed to estimate position, but this is not as precise. For a charted compulsory reporting point defined by a radial/distance fix, the CDI alone is insufficient — you need the distance component, either from DME or a cross-radial from a second VOR, to make the position fix unambiguous and reportable to ATC with confidence.

questions.question: When setting up to intercept a VOR radial inbound, what is the first thing you do on the CDI after identifying the station?
questions.answer: Center the CDI with a TO indication to identify your current position relative to the desired radial, then twist the OBS to set the inbound course (the reciprocal of the radial) you intend to intercept. This orients the instrument so deflection direction tells you which side of the course you are on and which way to turn.

questions.question: You want to intercept and track inbound on the 270 radial of a VOR. What course do you set in the OBS, and what should the CDI show when you are established on that course?
questions.answer: Set 090° in the OBS — that is the inbound course (reciprocal of the 270 radial). When established on the course inbound, the CDI needle will be centered with a TO indication. The 270 radial extends outbound from the station, so flying inbound on it means flying a magnetic course of 090°.

questions.question: Before you begin an intercept of a VOR course, why is it important to orient yourself by checking which side of the desired course you are on?
questions.answer: Knowing which side of the course you are on determines your intercept direction and prevents turning the wrong way. You check the CDI deflection after setting the desired course in the OBS — a right deflection means the course is to your right, so you turn right to intercept. Turning the wrong direction wastes time, increases workload, and can lead to disorientation under IFR.

questions.question: You are flying a helicopter at 090° and ATC clears you direct to a VOR, then to track outbound on the 180 radial. Walk me through exactly how you set up your instruments to orient and intercept that outbound course.
questions.answer: First, identify and tune the VOR. Set 180° in the OBS — the outbound course on the 180 radial is 180°. Note the CDI deflection: if it shows left deflection with a FROM indication, the course is to your left and you are already northeast of it. Turn to an intercept heading — typically 30° to 45° offset from 180°, so approximately 135° to 150° — to close on the course from the right side. As the CDI centers, turn to 180° and begin tracking outbound. Confirm FROM indication when established.

questions.question: You are flying IFR in a helicopter and ATC instructs you to intercept Localizer 24R. You set the published front course of 240° in the OBS. How is orienting on a localizer different from orienting on a VOR, and what does that mean for how quickly you need to act once the needle starts moving?
questions.answer: The key difference is sensitivity. A VOR CDI at full deflection represents approximately 12° or more off course, while a localizer CDI at full deflection represents only about 2.5° off course — making the localizer roughly 4 to 5 times more sensitive. This means the needle moves much faster as you approach the localizer course. You must be established on your intercept heading, stabilized, and ready to turn to the inbound course promptly once the needle begins deflecting. Waiting too long or using a steep intercept angle will cause you to overshoot.

questions.question: You are in a helicopter at cruise altitude and need to intercept a VOR radial that is 45° away from your current position. ATC has not given you a specific intercept heading. How do you determine a reasonable intercept angle, and what do you consider when choosing it?
questions.answer: A standard intercept angle is 30° to 45° relative to the desired course. Since you are 45° away, a 45° intercept angle is appropriate — you would fly a heading that is 45° offset from the desired course. Factors to consider include distance from the station (farther away gives more time to stabilize before reaching the course), airspeed (helicopters are slower, so needle movement is less abrupt than in fixed-wing), and any ATC altitude or speed restrictions. Avoid angles greater than 90° as they create poor geometry and make it difficult to judge when to turn to the course.

questions.question: You are flying a helicopter on an IFR clearance that requires you to intercept and track inbound on a specific VOR radial, but your RMI has failed. You only have a standard VOR head with a CDI. Describe step by step how you orient yourself and set up the intercept using only the CDI, without the benefit of the RMI needle pointing directly to the station.
questions.answer: Without an RMI, you must use the CDI and your known heading to determine position. First, set the desired inbound course in the OBS. Check the CDI deflection — the direction of deflection tells you which side of the course you are on. Next, rotate the OBS to center the CDI; note whether the indication is TO or FROM. The course shown under the index with a TO indication is your magnetic bearing TO the station, which orients you relative to the station. Compare that bearing to your desired inbound course to determine how far off you are angularly. Then set the desired inbound course back in the OBS and fly an intercept heading offset 30–45° toward the needle. Monitor the CDI: when it begins centering, turn to the inbound course and track it. Without RMI, your situational awareness depends entirely on understanding CDI deflection direction and OBS indications — so methodical instrument cross-check is critical.
questions.follow_up: The CDI is showing a right deflection with your desired course set and a TO flag showing. You are currently heading 090°. Which direction do you turn to intercept, and why?
questions.follow_up_answer: A right deflection with a TO indication means the course is to your right — the station and the course centerline are to the right of your present position. You turn right to an intercept heading. For example, if your desired inbound course is 090°, you might turn to 120° or 135° as an intercept heading. You do not turn left, even though 090° is already your heading, because the deflection tells you the course is still displaced to the right. Turning left would take you further from the course.

questions.question: During a helicopter IFR training flight, your student sets the correct inbound course in the OBS and flies directly toward the VOR rather than intercepting the specific radial at a planned angle. The aircraft arrives overhead the station on course, but the student never actually flew the intercept. Why does this matter from a practical standpoint, and how would you correct this technique?
questions.answer: Flying directly to the station rather than intercepting the assigned radial before reaching it is problematic for several reasons: it does not comply with ATC clearances that specify tracking a particular radial or course segment; it bypasses any stepdown fixes or crossing restrictions on that course; and it creates poor situational awareness because the pilot never confirmed course alignment before reaching the station, where CDI sensitivity is least reliable. The correct technique is to intercept the course at a planned point before the station, establish tracking, then fly along the radial to the station. To correct the student, demonstrate the orientation sequence: set the course, assess CDI deflection to determine position relative to the course, fly an appropriate intercept heading, and turn to track only after the needle is actively centering. Emphasize that arriving on course before the station — not at the station — is the goal.
questions.follow_up: Your student argues that if the OBS is set and the CDI centered at the station, the result is the same. How do you address that argument using IFR regulatory and procedural requirements?
questions.follow_up_answer: The argument fails for several reasons. First, VOR course guidance is least reliable and most erratic directly overhead the station — the cone of confusion makes the CDI unreliable near the NAVAID. Second, many IFR procedures include fixes along the route that require the aircraft to be on the assigned course before reaching the fix; if you bypass those by flying direct, you may miss required altitude restrictions or segment requirements. Third, ATC assigns specific routes and expects route compliance — flying direct to a station instead of tracking the assigned radial is a deviation from your clearance under 14 CFR 91.123. Finally, from a skill standards perspective, the ACS requires the pilot to demonstrate the ability to intercept and track, not just to arrive at the station.

questions.question: When intercepting a VOR radial inbound, what is the general rule for selecting an appropriate intercept angle?
questions.answer: The intercept angle should be greater than the angular difference between your current position and the desired course, but generally between 20° and 90°. A 30° to 45° intercept angle is typical for most situations. The angle should be large enough to intercept promptly but shallow enough to avoid overshooting the course. Once the CDI begins to move, you lead the turn to roll out on the inbound course.

questions.question: What does it mean to intercept a course 'outbound' from a VOR station, and how does the CDI behavior differ from an inbound interception?
questions.answer: Intercepting a course outbound means you are flying away from the VOR on a specified radial. The CDI still indicates displacement from the selected course, but the TO/FROM indicator will show FROM. The needle deflects in the same direction relative to the course centerline regardless of direction of flight — a left deflection still means the course is to the left. However, on an outbound course you must be aware that the CDI is slightly less sensitive at greater distances from the station and that the FROM flag confirms you have passed the station.

questions.question: When ATC tells you to intercept a localizer inbound for an ILS approach, why should you use a shallower intercept angle compared to intercepting a VOR radial?
questions.answer: The localizer CDI is approximately 4 to 5 times more sensitive than a VOR CDI. Full-scale deflection on a localizer represents only about 2.5° off course, compared to 12° or more for a VOR. Because of this sensitivity, a steep intercept angle (greater than 30°) can cause you to overshoot the localizer course before you can complete the rollout. A shallower angle of 20° to 30° or less gives you time to identify needle movement, begin the turn, and establish the inbound course smoothly.

questions.question: You are flying a helicopter at 090° and ATC instructs you to intercept the 180° radial of a VOR inbound. The VOR is off your left nose and you estimate you are about 15 NM from the station. Walk me through how you determine your intercept heading and when you start your turn to track inbound.
questions.answer: The 180° radial inbound means you will be flying TO the station on a course of 360° (reciprocal of the radial). Your current heading is 090°. First, determine the angular relationship: the inbound course is 360° and your current heading is 090°, so the intercept angle is 90°. That is too steep for a smooth intercept, so you would select a 45° intercept angle, giving you a heading of 315° (360° minus 45°). Set the OBS to 360° and fly 315°. The CDI will begin deflecting toward center as you approach the course. Because the VOR CDI has a 10° per dot deflection (roughly 2° per dot), you begin your turn to 360° when the needle is approximately one dot from center — about a 30° lead point — to allow for rollout without overshooting. Once established, track inbound at 360° with corrections for any crosswind.

questions.question: You are established outbound on a published GPS leg departing a waypoint, and the FMS shows you are paralleling the desired track 2 NM right of course. Describe how you would use an appropriate intercept angle to return to the centerline without overshooting.
questions.answer: On a GPS/RNAV system, the course deviation indicator shows lateral displacement from the desired track in a similar fashion to a VOR CDI, though sensitivity may vary by phase of flight (en route, terminal, or approach). With 2 NM of displacement, you are significantly off track. Select an intercept angle proportional to the displacement — typically 20° to 45° for this scenario. Turn left approximately 20° to 30° from your current outbound heading. Monitor the CDI needle moving toward center. As it approaches the half-dot mark, begin a smooth turn back to the original outbound heading to avoid overshooting. The key is to use a lead point based on your groundspeed and the rate of needle movement. In a slower helicopter, a smaller intercept angle may be sufficient; in faster cruise, you need a more generous lead.

questions.question: During an IFR helicopter approach, you are vectored by ATC to intercept the final approach course at a 30° angle, but due to a distraction, you realize you are now 1 NM from the localizer centerline and still at a 30° intercept heading. What should you do, and why is this situation potentially dangerous?
questions.answer: At 1 NM from the localizer with a 30° intercept angle still established, you are very close to overshooting the final approach course. Because the localizer is 4 to 5 times more sensitive than a VOR CDI, the needle will move rapidly as you close on the centerline. You should immediately reduce the intercept angle to 10° to 15° or less, slowing your closure rate. If you are already seeing the needle begin to move, start turning toward the inbound course now and be prepared to be established quickly. The danger is that an overshoot could take you through the localizer, potentially into terrain protection boundaries or conflicting traffic, and re-intercepting on a published approach without a clearance from ATC may be procedurally non-compliant. Inform ATC of the situation if you cannot maintain the approach course.

questions.question: A student consistently overshoots the inbound course during VOR intercepts even when using a 45° intercept angle. You observe they are beginning the rollout only when the CDI reaches full center. What specific technique error are they making, and how would you correct it?
questions.answer: The student is failing to use a lead point — they are waiting until the CDI is fully centered before beginning the rollout, which means the aircraft momentum carries them through the course. At typical helicopter IFR speeds, the rollout to a new heading takes several seconds, during which the aircraft continues closing on and through the desired radial. The correction is to teach lead point selection: for a 45° intercept, begin the rollout when the CDI is approximately one half to one full dot from center (representing roughly 5° to 6° of angular displacement), depending on groundspeed. The faster the groundspeed and the steeper the intercept angle, the earlier the lead point must be. A useful rule of thumb is to divide the intercept angle by 2 and use that number of degrees before centerline as the rollout point. Practice should involve the student verbalizing the expected lead point before the intercept begins.
questions.follow_up: If the helicopter is in a 30-knot headwind component while intercepting inbound, how does that affect the lead point timing?
questions.follow_up_answer: A strong headwind reduces groundspeed, which in turn reduces the rate of CDI needle movement and gives the pilot more time to respond. With a reduced groundspeed, the aircraft covers less distance during the rollout, so the lead point can be slightly later (closer to centerline). However, the pilot must also anticipate that after establishing the inbound course, a headwind will require no wind correction angle on the inbound leg itself, but the slower groundspeed means the station passage and any timing-based segments will take longer than published. The key adjustment is to slightly reduce the lead point from the standard, but not eliminate it — the rollout still requires finite time regardless of groundspeed.

questions.question: You are flying an IFR helicopter flight in IMC and are cleared for an RNAV approach. The FMS is sequencing correctly, but as you attempt to intercept the final approach course inbound to the waypoint, you notice the CDI sensitivity has already transitioned to approach mode (0.3 NM full scale). You are 3 NM from the final approach fix with a 45° intercept angle. Explain the risk and what adjustment you should make immediately.
questions.answer: In approach mode, the RNAV CDI is significantly more sensitive — full-scale deflection represents only 0.3 NM rather than the 2.0 NM in terminal mode or 5.0 NM in en route mode. This means the needle will move extremely rapidly as you close on the final approach course. A 45° intercept angle at 3 NM in approach mode sensitivity is likely to result in an overshoot that takes you well past the course centerline before you can complete the rollout, and may even drive the CDI to full deflection on the opposite side before the aircraft stabilizes. The immediate action is to reduce the intercept angle to 15° to 20° maximum, slow the helicopter to approach speed to reduce groundspeed and closure rate, and begin the rollout earlier than you would for a VOR intercept. If you are unable to intercept the final course in a stabilized manner before the FAF, you should execute the missed approach or request vectors from ATC to set up a longer final. Attempting a non-stabilized intercept in approach mode in IMC is a significant safety risk.
questions.follow_up: At what point does WAAS GPS typically transition from terminal to approach CDI sensitivity, and what triggers that transition?
questions.follow_up_answer: On a WAAS GPS with an RNAV (GPS) approach loaded, the CDI sensitivity transitions from terminal mode (±1.0 NM full scale) to approach mode (±0.3 NM full scale) automatically when the aircraft is within 2 NM of the final approach fix (FAF) and the approach is activated in the FMS. Some systems also require that the aircraft be on a heading consistent with the approach course within a defined angular tolerance. The transition is automatic and does not require pilot input, which is why pilots must be alert to CDI sensitivity changes during the intercept phase — the needle can change behavior abruptly without any warning other than the mode annunciation on the display.

questions.question: What are the ACS tolerances you must maintain for airspeed, altitude, and heading during instrument navigation tasks such as intercepting and tracking a VOR radial or DME arc?
questions.answer: The ACS requires you to maintain airspeed within ±10 knots of the assigned speed, altitude within ±100 feet of the assigned altitude, and selected headings within ±5° of the assigned or calculated heading. These tolerances apply throughout the navigation task, not just at key fix crossings.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Instrument Rating ACS IH.V.A.S5; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 7 (Attitude Instrument Flying)

questions.question: Which three flight instruments are primarily used to verify that you are meeting the ACS airspeed, altitude, and heading tolerances during a VOR intercept?
questions.answer: The airspeed indicator (ASI) is used to monitor airspeed within ±10 knots; the altimeter is used to maintain altitude within ±100 feet; and the heading indicator (directional gyro or HSI compass card) is used to hold headings within ±5°. The VSI is also a supporting instrument for detecting altitude trend deviations before they exceed the ±100-foot limit.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5 (Flight Instruments); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 8 (Helicopter Instrument Flying)

questions.question: Why is maintaining the ±5° heading tolerance especially critical when flying a DME arc in a helicopter?
questions.answer: On a DME arc, the aircraft must constantly adjust heading to maintain a constant distance from the station. A heading error greater than ±5° causes the aircraft to either fly inside or outside the arc, potentially leading to an off-course deviation that compounds quickly at close DME ranges. Because helicopters are highly responsive to control inputs, precise heading control through small cyclic and pedal adjustments is essential to stay on the arc and meet ACS standards.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9 (Navigation Systems, DME Arc procedures); IH.V.A.S5

questions.question: You are tracking inbound on a VOR radial at 3,000 feet MSL and 100 knots. ATC assigns a new heading of 185° to intercept the final approach course. During the turn you notice your altitude has climbed to 3,120 feet and your airspeed has dropped to 87 knots. Are you within ACS tolerances, and what corrections should you make?
questions.answer: You are out of tolerance on both parameters. Altitude at 3,120 feet is 120 feet high, which exceeds the ±100-foot limit. Airspeed at 87 knots is 13 knots slow, exceeding the ±10-knot limit. To correct: lower the collective slightly to arrest the climb and descend back to 3,000 feet while also increasing collective and adjusting throttle (in piston helicopters) to bring airspeed back to 100 knots. Helicopters require coordinated collective, cyclic, and pedal inputs — a common error is chasing altitude with cyclic alone, which changes airspeed. Stabilize on attitude first, then fine-tune with collective.
questions.regulatory_ref: IH.V.A.S5; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 8 (Attitude Instrument Flying in Helicopters)

questions.question: You are flying a 15 DME arc at 110 knots. You notice you need to lead your heading changes every 10° of bearing change to stay on the arc. Midway through the arc, you observe your DME reading is 14.2 NM and your airspeed is 118 knots. What does this tell you about your arc performance and tolerance compliance?
questions.answer: A DME reading of 14.2 NM means you are 0.8 NM inside the arc — this is a navigation tracking error, not directly an ACS tolerance item, but it reflects poor heading management. The airspeed of 118 knots is 8 knots fast, which is within the ±10-knot tolerance. To correct the arc: turn away from the station (increase bearing) to fly back out to 15 DME, then resume arc tracking with smaller, more frequent heading adjustments. To reduce airspeed to 110 knots, smoothly reduce collective while adjusting attitude to maintain altitude. Proper lead point technique is the key to staying on a DME arc without large airspeed or altitude excursions.

questions.question: During a VOR radial intercept at cruise altitude, you have established a 30° intercept heading. You are workload-saturated managing comms with ATC, checking CDI movement, and setting up the approach. Your altitude has drifted 80 feet low and heading is 4° off. What is your priority order for correction, and why?
questions.answer: Both deviations are within ACS tolerances at this moment (altitude within ±100 ft, heading within ±5°), but both are trending toward exceedance. Priority should be: 1) Heading — a 4° heading error during intercept will cause you to overshoot or undershoot the radial, which directly affects navigation accuracy and could cause a missed intercept. 2) Altitude — 80 feet low with a downward trend could breach the ±100-foot limit quickly. Correct heading with a small cyclic input and pedal coordination, then re-establish altitude with a gentle collective increase. This also illustrates the SRM principle of workload management — high task saturation is when deviations most frequently accumulate into ACS failures.

questions.question: A student pilot on a simulated IFR flight consistently holds altitude and airspeed within tolerances in straight-and-level cruise, but repeatedly exceeds the ±5° heading tolerance during VOR intercepts and DME arc turns. As their instructor, what is the most likely root cause and how would you address it technically?
questions.answer: The most likely root cause is over-reliance on the CDI or DME display during intercepts instead of maintaining a disciplined instrument cross-check that includes the heading indicator. The student is likely fixating on the navigation instrument — chasing the needle — rather than establishing a precise intercept heading and holding it while monitoring CDI progression. The correction is to teach the student to: (1) calculate and set a specific intercept heading before the turn, (2) roll out precisely on that heading using the heading indicator as the primary reference, and (3) only then monitor CDI movement as a trend indicator. On DME arcs, they must use a systematic lead-point heading change every 5–10° of bearing change rather than reacting to DME drift. The ±5° heading tolerance requires active instrument cross-check discipline, not reactive steering.
questions.follow_up: If despite technique coaching the student still oscillates ±8° on headings, what underlying instrument flying skill deficiency would you suspect, and how would you isolate it?
questions.follow_up_answer: The underlying deficiency is likely an underdeveloped instrument scan — specifically, the student is not including the heading indicator frequently enough in their cross-check loop, or they are experiencing fixation on the CDI. To isolate it: have the student fly straight-and-level on a constant heading without any navigation task. If they hold heading within ±5° then, the problem is task-induced fixation during navigation workload. If they cannot hold ±5° even in straight-and-level flight, the deficiency is in basic attitude instrument flying and requires remediation back to Chapter 7 fundamentals — establishing attitude, trimming the helicopter, and scanning the heading indicator as part of a disciplined primary-support instrument cross-check.
questions.regulatory_ref: IH.V.A.S5; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 7 (Attitude Instrument Flying); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 8

questions.question: You are flying an IFR helicopter with a blocked static port. You activated the alternate static source from inside the cabin. How does this affect your ability to meet the ±100-foot altitude tolerance and ±10-knot airspeed tolerance during a subsequent VOR radial intercept, and what must you account for?
questions.answer: With alternate static source selected from the unpressurized cabin, cabin static pressure is slightly lower than outside ambient pressure. This causes the altimeter to read slightly higher than actual altitude, the ASI to read slightly fast, and the VSI to show a momentary false climb indication when first selected. For the ±100-foot altitude tolerance: you must apply the correction factor found in the AFM/POH for the specific helicopter (if provided), or accept that your indicated altitude is higher than actual and adjust your target accordingly. For the ±10-knot airspeed tolerance: the ASI will read slightly fast — again, use the POH correction. If no correction is published, you must note the error and cross-check with GPS groundspeed where available. Failing to account for these errors could cause you to fly below MDA/DA during an approach or mismanage energy on the arc. This is also a situation requiring enhanced instrument cross-check discipline.
questions.follow_up: If the alternate static source in your helicopter is placarded with a specific correction (e.g., 'add 50 feet to altimeter when alternate static is in use'), and you are flying a VOR approach with a published MDA of 1,200 feet MSL, what indicated altitude should you fly to ensure you are at or above the true MDA?
questions.follow_up_answer: If the altimeter reads 50 feet high when the alternate static is in use, your indicated altitude is higher than actual. To be at or above the true MDA of 1,200 feet MSL, you must fly an indicated altitude of 1,250 feet (1,200 + 50). This keeps your actual altitude at 1,200 feet true. Flying the indicated MDA of 1,200 feet while alternate static is active would place your actual altitude at 1,150 feet — 50 feet below the true MDA — which violates 14 CFR 91.175 and creates a terrain/obstacle clearance hazard.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5 (Alternate Static Source); 14 CFR 91.175; IH.V.A.S5

questions.question: What is the maximum allowable CDI deflection when tracking a course during an instrument flight, according to the Instrument Helicopter ACS standards?
questions.answer: The ACS requires you to maintain no more than ¾-scale deflection of the CDI at all times when tracking a navigational course. Full-scale deflection on a VOR CDI represents approximately 12° off course, so ¾-scale is roughly 9° off course. On a localizer, full-scale is about 2.5°, making ¾-scale approximately 1.9° — a much tighter tolerance.

questions.question: When flying a DME arc, what is the tolerance you must maintain from the published arc distance?
questions.answer: When flying a DME arc, you must maintain the arc within ±1 nautical mile of the published arc distance. For example, if flying a 15 DME arc, your DME readout must stay between 14 and 16 NM from the station at all times.

questions.question: When the CDI begins to deflect off center while tracking inbound on a VOR radial, what is the correct initial correction technique to bring the needle back within limits?
questions.answer: When the CDI deflects off center, you should turn toward the needle by doubling the number of degrees the needle has moved off center as your initial correction heading. For example, if the CDI has drifted approximately ¼ scale (about 3° on a VOR), turn 6° toward the needle. Once the CDI begins returning to center, turn back to a bracketed heading — one that bisects your original heading and correction heading — to compensate for the crosswind component.

questions.question: You are flying a 12 DME arc around a VOR and your DME reads 13.4 NM. Describe exactly what you should do next and why.
questions.answer: At 13.4 NM you are still within the ±1 NM tolerance (limit is 13 to 15 NM on a 14-mile arc — or in this case, 11 to 13 NM on a 12 DME arc, so 13.4 NM means you are already 1.4 NM outside the arc and beyond the tolerance). You must immediately turn toward the station — increase your arc-inbound lead — to reduce the DME distance back toward 12 NM. Lead the turn so you don't overshoot inward. You should use a turn of roughly 20–30° toward the station and monitor the DME closely to roll out as you approach the 12 NM point, anticipating the need to resume the arc heading. If you delay, the deviation will worsen and you risk busting the standard.

questions.question: You are tracking inbound on a VOR approach and notice the CDI has been slowly drifting to the right, consistently reaching about ½-scale deflection before your corrections bring it back. What does this pattern tell you, and how should you adjust your technique?
questions.answer: A persistent drift to the right with the CDI consistently deflecting before each correction tells you there is a crosswind from the left pushing you to the right of course. Your current wind correction angle is insufficient. You should establish a wind correction angle to the left (into the wind) by adding crab to your inbound heading. Start with a correction of approximately 5–10° left of the inbound course, hold it until the CDI centers, then reduce to a smaller wind correction angle to maintain center. Bracket the heading until you find the angle that keeps the CDI steady. The goal is to keep the CDI centered continuously, not to chase it back and forth.

questions.question: You are flying a localizer approach and your CDI deflects to ¾ scale. How does this compare in physical distance off course versus the same ¾-scale deflection on a VOR, and why does it matter to your correction technique?
questions.answer: On a VOR, full-scale CDI deflection represents approximately 12°, so ¾ scale is about 9° off the radial — a relatively wide margin. On a localizer, full-scale is only about 2.5°, so ¾ scale is roughly 1.9° off the localizer centerline. While the ACS maximum tolerance is the same (¾ scale) for both, physically you are much closer to the runway centerline in linear distance on a localizer — but the tolerance for error is dramatically tighter. This means corrections on a localizer must be small and precise. Aggressive corrections that work on a VOR will cause overshooting and oscillation on a localizer. Use small heading changes of 2–5° maximum when correcting on a localizer.

questions.question: During an IPC with you, a candidate is flying a DME arc and consistently allows the DME to fluctuate between 10.2 and 13.8 NM on a 12 DME arc. They insist they are correcting every time it moves. What is the root cause of this pattern, and what specific skill deficiency are you identifying?
questions.answer: The candidate is reacting to CDI or DME movement rather than anticipating it — this is a reactive rather than proactive scan and correction technique. The oscillation between 10.2 and 13.8 NM (a 3.6 NM swing) indicates they are allowing the deviation to develop fully before correcting, then over-correcting, causing the opposite deviation. The root cause is likely a combination of: (1) scan rate too slow — not checking DME frequently enough to catch small deviations early, (2) corrections too large — turning too aggressively toward the station and then overcorrecting away, and (3) lack of lead point awareness — not anticipating when to stop the correction turn before reaching the arc. The fix is to check DME every 10–15 seconds, make small corrections of 10–20° maximum, and lead the roll-out before the DME reaches the desired distance.
questions.follow_up: The candidate tells you they were making corrections every time the DME moved more than 0.5 NM. Is that the right trigger for a correction, and if not, what is?
questions.follow_up_answer: Waiting for a 0.5 NM deviation before correcting is too late — by the time you complete the correction maneuver at helicopter speeds, the arc error will have grown further. The correct technique is to correct continuously and proactively. On a DME arc, you should be making small heading adjustments as soon as the DME begins trending away from the arc value — even 0.1 to 0.2 NM of movement is an early indicator to begin a shallow turn toward the station. The goal is to never let the error accumulate; constant small adjustments yield far better arc tracking than large reactive corrections.

questions.question: A helicopter pilot is flying a GPS RNAV approach in terminal (LNAV) mode and believes the ¾-scale CDI tolerance still applies, but argues the CDI sensitivity is the same as a VOR. Do you agree, and how does GPS CDI scaling in approach mode affect what ¾-scale actually represents?
questions.answer: This is a critical misunderstanding. GPS CDI scaling changes depending on the phase of flight. In en route mode, full-scale CDI deflection represents ±5 NM. In terminal mode (within 30 NM of destination), it transitions to ±1 NM. Once the approach is activated and within 2 NM of the FAF, it transitions to approach mode at ±0.3 NM (LNAV) full scale. So ¾-scale in approach mode represents approximately 0.225 NM — a much tighter physical tolerance than either VOR or en route GPS. The ACS standard of ¾ scale still applies, but the pilot must understand that the CDI is far more sensitive in approach mode, and the same visual deflection represents much less physical distance off course. Overcorrecting aggressively like a VOR will cause the same oscillation problem seen on localizers.
questions.follow_up: If the GPS transitions from terminal to approach mode and the CDI suddenly appears to peg nearly full scale even though you haven't changed heading, what likely happened and what should you do?
questions.follow_up_answer: The sudden full-scale CDI deflection after the scaling transition means the system rescaled from ±1 NM to ±0.3 NM. If you were, for example, 0.4 NM off the approach centerline — which would have shown as less than ½ scale in terminal mode — you are now well beyond full scale in approach mode. You need to immediately correct back toward the course centerline using small, smooth corrections. If you are too far off course to re-intercept before the FAF, you should consider flying the missed approach or requesting vectors from ATC rather than attempting to salvage a badly positioned approach, as continuing below MDA while significantly off course could pose a CFIT risk.

questions.question: You are tracking a VOR radial inbound and notice the CDI needle swings from full deflection to the other side and back repeatedly, and the TO/FROM flag flickers. What does this indicate, and what is your immediate action?
questions.answer: This indicates a VOR facility or receiver failure — erratic or unreliable signal. The flag flickering between TO, FROM, and OFF indicates the signal is unusable. You should immediately stop using that VOR for navigation, cross-check with another navigation source, and if you are operating IFR and the VOR was required for your route or approach, report the failure to ATC as soon as practical so they can provide alternate routing or vectors.

questions.question: Under 14 CFR 91.187, when are you required to report a navigation system malfunction to ATC during IFR flight?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.187, the pilot in command of an aircraft operating IFR is required to report to ATC as soon as possible any malfunction of navigational, approach, or communication equipment that occurs in flight. This includes any equipment that is required for the operation or that ATC is relying upon for your clearance.

questions.question: What indications on your ADF receiver would tell you the NDB station has failed or the signal is unreliable, and what should you do with that information?
questions.answer: Indications of NDB station failure or unreliable signal include the ADF needle spinning aimlessly or pointing erratically rather than consistently toward the station, the bearing pointer oscillating wildly, or the signal strength indicator dropping significantly. On some receivers, a warning flag may appear. If you suspect the station has failed, you should stop relying on the ADF for navigation, cross-check position with another available navaid, and report the suspected facility failure to ATC so they can verify the station status and provide alternate guidance.

questions.question: You are flying a helicopter on an IFR clearance direct to a GPS waypoint when your GPS suddenly displays 'RAIM NOT AVAILABLE' and your moving map freezes. You still have a functioning VOR receiver. Walk me through your decision-making and what you say to ATC.
questions.answer: First, immediately transition to your backup navigation — in this case the VOR. Identify the VOR by its Morse code identifier, establish the current radial, and begin tracking to maintain situational awareness. Do not continue relying on the GPS for primary navigation. Then contact ATC promptly and report: identify yourself, state your position, report that you have lost GPS navigation capability due to RAIM unavailability, and advise what backup navigation you have available. Request amended routing if needed, especially if the assigned routing requires GPS navigation you can no longer provide. ATC may issue radar vectors or an alternate clearance. Document the failure. Under 14 CFR 91.187, this report is required because GPS was the navigation equipment being relied upon for the IFR clearance.

questions.question: During a VOR-DME arc approach in your helicopter, you lose DME while still on the arc segment. The VOR needle is still functional. What are the signs of DME failure, and can you legally continue the approach?
questions.answer: Signs of DME failure include the DME display going blank, showing dashes, or producing an unreliable or frozen distance readout. If DME fails during a VOR-DME arc, you can no longer maintain the arc precisely since distance from the station is required to fly the arc. Legally, you may not continue an approach that requires DME as a primary component if that equipment has failed, unless there is an alternate procedure published that does not require DME. You must report the DME failure to ATC under 14 CFR 91.187, declare your inability to continue the arc, and request an alternate clearance — which may be radar vectors to the final approach course, an alternate approach, or a hold while you troubleshoot. Do not attempt to estimate the arc position by timing or guess — that is not an approved substitute for DME on a DME arc procedure.

questions.question: You are IFR in a helicopter and your COM radio fails, but your navigation equipment — VOR, GPS — is still fully functional. Does 14 CFR 91.187 require you to report the navigation equipment status, and how do you handle ATC communication with a failed COM?
questions.answer: 14 CFR 91.187 requires reporting malfunctions of navigational, approach, OR communication equipment. So yes, a COM radio failure is a reportable malfunction. However, by definition, if your COM has failed, you cannot make a radio report directly. In this situation, you should follow two-way radio communication failure procedures under 14 CFR 91.185: squawk 7600, continue the flight according to your last ATC clearance, then by the expected approach clearance time or ETA, proceed to the destination and execute the published approach. If a partial COM failure exists (receive only), you can advise ATC by squawking as instructed or using light signals. If you later regain communication, report the failure as soon as possible. Your navigation equipment being functional is a positive factor to report to ATC once communication is restored.

questions.question: You are flying IFR in a helicopter and your GPS receiver fails entirely. You have a VOR receiver, but the VOR station you were using to navigate a low-altitude T-route is now showing an OFF flag. You suspect the VOR facility itself may be out of service. What specific information do you include when you report this situation to ATC, and what is the relevance of whether this is a receiver failure versus a ground station failure?
questions.answer: When reporting to ATC, you should provide: your aircraft call sign, current position (using whatever reference is available — last known GPS position, radar returns, etc.), altitude, the specific equipment that has failed (GPS and now VOR), the VOR identifier that is showing an OFF flag, and your current navigation capability — which at this point may be limited to pilotage or DR if both GPS and VOR are unavailable. The distinction between a receiver failure and a ground station failure matters significantly: if it is YOUR receiver that failed, only you are affected and ATC may continue routing other aircraft via that VOR. If the VOR ground station itself is out of service, ATC needs to know so they can issue a NOTAM, reroute all affected IFR traffic off the T-route, and notify other pilots. ATC will typically confirm ground station status with their facility or check NOTAMs. You should clearly state 'I am receiving an OFF flag on [VOR identifier] — I am unable to determine if this is my receiver or the station' so ATC can investigate from their end. Under 14 CFR 91.187, both types of failures require reporting.
questions.follow_up: If ATC confirms the VOR ground station is normal and other aircraft are receiving it fine, but your VOR still shows an OFF flag, what does that tell you and how does it affect your decision to continue IFR?
questions.follow_up_answer: If ATC confirms the VOR ground station is operational and other aircraft are receiving it normally, the failure is isolated to your airborne VOR receiver. This means you have a receiver malfunction, not a facility failure. At this point, you have lost both GPS and your VOR receiver — you must evaluate whether you have any remaining navigation capability required for the IFR operation. If you are below MEA with no functioning navigation equipment, you cannot maintain the IFR route safely. You must advise ATC of your situation and request radar vectors, declare an emergency if safety is at risk, and plan to land at the nearest suitable airport. Continuing IFR with no functioning navigation equipment when the route requires it is not legally or operationally acceptable.

questions.question: You are flying a helicopter on an IFR clearance and you notice your GPS is tracking normally by all indications on the display, but your position appears to be inconsistent with your VOR cross-check — the GPS says you are on course but your VOR CDI shows a full-scale deflection. There are no failure flags on either system. How do you determine which system to trust, and what do you report to ATC?
questions.answer: This is a silent GPS error scenario — one of the most dangerous navigation failures because neither system is flagging a failure. Your process: First, do not discard either system immediately. Cross-check with a third source if available — DME, ADF, radar position from ATC, or a visual fix if VMC is present. Ask ATC for a position confirmation using radar. If ATC radar confirms a position consistent with one of your instruments, that is your answer. If the VOR is cross-checked with another VOR and both agree against the GPS, the GPS signal is suspect — possibly due to signal interference, spoofing, or a software fault. Report to ATC: state that you are receiving conflicting navigation indications between GPS and VOR with no failure flags displayed, provide your best estimated position, and request radar identification and vectors. This is a reportable malfunction under 14 CFR 91.187 — 'malfunction' includes unreliable or conflicting indications, not just flagged failures. Until resolved, navigate using the cross-checked VOR and ATC radar vectors rather than the GPS, since RAIM does not catch all GPS errors and a silent failure can lead to significant course deviation.
questions.follow_up: What is RAIM and why does it not guarantee that a GPS error like this will be detected?
questions.follow_up_answer: RAIM stands for Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring. It is a GPS receiver function that uses redundant satellite geometry to verify that the satellite signals being received are consistent with each other. If one satellite is transmitting an erroneous signal, RAIM can detect the inconsistency and alert the pilot. However, RAIM does not guarantee detection of all errors because it requires a sufficient number of satellites with adequate geometry to perform the comparison. If GPS spoofing is occurring — where false signals are being broadcast — all signals may appear consistent to RAIM even though they are all wrong. Additionally, RAIM has horizontal protection limits, meaning small errors below the alert threshold will not trigger a warning even if they are large enough to cause a course deviation on a precision approach. This is why cross-checking GPS against other navigation sources, especially on approaches, is a critical discipline in IFR operations.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a Multi-Function Display (MFD) during IFR navigation in a helicopter?
questions.answer: The MFD provides a graphical moving map display that allows the pilot to monitor the helicopter's current position relative to waypoints, airways, terrain, and airspace. It supplements the primary flight instruments by giving a big-picture situational awareness view, helping the pilot identify track deviations, wind drift, and proximity to obstacles or controlled airspace boundaries.

questions.question: How can you identify wind drift from a graphical navigation display or MFD during IFR flight?
questions.answer: On an MFD with GPS-based moving map capability, wind drift is visible when the aircraft's ground track line (the direction of actual movement across the map) differs from the aircraft's heading symbol or desired course line. A wind vector arrow, if displayed, directly shows wind direction and magnitude. Some MFDs also display a wind correction angle caret or show estimated wind speed and direction in a data block. The pilot uses this information to apply the appropriate wind correction angle to maintain the desired track.

questions.question: When an MFD is installed and operational, should it replace your primary instrument scan during IFR flight? Why or why not?
questions.answer: No. The MFD is a supplemental situational awareness tool and must never replace the primary instrument scan of the attitude indicator, altimeter, airspeed indicator, and other flight instruments. The MFD helps with big-picture navigation awareness — position monitoring, traffic, terrain, weather — but aircraft control is maintained through the primary flight instruments. Over-reliance on the MFD at the expense of the primary scan is a common cause of spatial disorientation and controlled flight into terrain (CFIT).

questions.question: You are flying a DME arc approach in IMC. Your MFD shows your helicopter's position consistently drifting inside the arc. What is this telling you about your wind situation, and how do you correct it?
questions.answer: Drifting inside the arc means your ground track is curving toward the station — the wind is pushing you inward (toward the NAVAID). On the MFD, you can confirm this by observing that your actual ground track line is angling inward relative to the desired arc path. To correct, you need to turn away from the station to increase your arc radius, then reintercept the arc. Once back on arc, apply a wind correction angle that keeps the nose pointed slightly away from the station to compensate for the inbound drift. Monitoring the MFD continuously allows you to fine-tune these corrections in real time rather than relying solely on DME distance crosschecks.

questions.question: During an IFR flight in a helicopter equipped with an MFD, you notice the map display is showing your position approximately 1.5 miles off your filed airway, yet your CDI is centered and the OBS is correctly set. What are two possible explanations, and how do you resolve this?
questions.answer: Two possible explanations are: (1) The MFD's GPS database or the GPS position source may have an integrity issue or the GPS is in a degraded mode with RAIM reduced, causing the displayed position to be inaccurate. (2) There could be a database discrepancy — the MFD may be using an outdated or incorrect nav database that has the airway charted in a slightly different position than the actual VOR radial you're tracking. To resolve, cross-check your CDI, DME, and any available raw data from the underlying NAVAID against the MFD display. Verify the MFD database currency (updated every 28 days per FAA standard) and check GPS RAIM/integrity status. Trust the raw navigation data (CDI on the correct radial) and treat the MFD as advisory until the discrepancy is resolved.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 1 (database update cycles)

questions.question: As a helicopter IFR pilot, describe how you would use an MFD moving map to maintain situational awareness while intercepting a VOR radial in IMC. Walk me through your scan and MFD usage during the intercept.
questions.answer: During the intercept, my primary instrument scan remains on the attitude indicator, HSI/CDI, heading indicator, altimeter, and airspeed. I glance at the MFD periodically — roughly every 10–15 seconds during a stable intercept — to confirm: (1) my position relative to the desired radial and the station, (2) that my ground track on the moving map is converging on the radial at the appropriate intercept angle, and (3) that I'm not drifting into adjacent airspace or controlled airspace boundaries. As the CDI begins to center, I check the MFD to visually confirm my position is approaching the radial, then transition to bracketing corrections. The MFD helps me anticipate lead points and verify I am on the correct side of the station. I also monitor the wind vector data if displayed to anticipate the wind correction angle needed once established on the radial.

questions.question: Your MFD fails completely during an IFR flight in IMC while tracking a VOR airway at the MEA. You have a functioning CDI, HSI, and DME but no moving map. What impact does this have on your situational awareness, and what techniques do you use to compensate for the loss of the graphical display?
questions.answer: Loss of the MFD removes your primary big-picture situational awareness tool — you no longer have a real-time visual depiction of position relative to terrain, airspace, traffic targets (if TIS/ADS-B was feeding the MFD), and weather overlay. To compensate: (1) Increase frequency of position cross-checks using raw nav data — cross-radials from nearby VORs, DME distance fixes, and ATC position confirmation. (2) Use your paper or iPad en route chart more actively, mentally tracking position along the airway using DME and time. (3) Brief terrain and airspace more carefully before reaching critical areas — heightened awareness since you can no longer glance at a map. (4) Request ATC radar advisories or position confirmation if uncertain. (5) Consider declaring to ATC that you've lost your moving map capability if operating near terrain or complex airspace, so they can provide additional advisory service. You must continue to fly the primary instruments — but workload management and proactive position awareness become critical.
questions.follow_up: If the MFD failure also took out your GPS position source, and your only remaining navigation is a VOR-only airway at the MEA, how does that change your obstacle clearance confidence — specifically, what does the MEA guarantee versus what it does NOT guarantee?
questions.follow_up_answer: The MEA (Minimum Enroute Altitude) guarantees two things: (1) obstacle clearance — typically 1,000 feet above the highest obstacle within the protected airspace of the airway (2,000 feet in mountainous terrain), and (2) adequate VOR navigation signal reception from the defining NAVAIDs along the route. However, the MEA does NOT guarantee coverage of all terrain directly below the aircraft if you deviate from the airway centerline — obstacle clearance only applies within the defined airway protected area. It also does not guarantee GPS signal availability or GPS RAIM. With VOR-only navigation and no moving map, the pilot must stay precisely on the VOR radial defining the airway; any course deviation reduces obstacle clearance margin. The MOCA (Minimum Obstruction Clearance Altitude) can be used as an alternative but only guarantees navaid reception within 22 NM of the NAVAID, not the full airway segment.

questions.question: On your MFD, the wind vector shows a 35-knot direct crosswind from the left while you're established on a VOR radial at cruise airspeed. Your CDI is centered, but your heading is significantly right of course. A student watching you says 'that can't be right — you're not flying toward the station.' How do you explain what the MFD is showing, and what does this scenario reveal about the difference between heading, course, and ground track?
questions.answer: This is a classic wind correction angle scenario. With a 35-knot crosswind from the left, I must point the nose significantly into the wind — to the right — to maintain the desired ground track along the VOR radial. The CDI being centered confirms I am on the radial and tracking it correctly. My heading (where the nose points) is to the right of the radial direction because I'm crabbing into the wind. My ground track (actual path over the ground, shown on the MFD) aligns with the VOR radial because the wind is being compensated. The MFD moving map will show the aircraft symbol pointed to the right of the course line while the actual movement vector or ground track line is aligned with the course — this visually confirms a proper wind correction is being held. The student's confusion stems from conflating heading with ground track; the MFD graphically separates these concepts, which is one of its key training and situational awareness values.
questions.follow_up: If that same 35-knot crosswind is present while flying a DME arc, how does the required heading correction change throughout the arc, and how would you use the MFD to anticipate heading changes needed to stay on arc?
questions.follow_up_answer: On a DME arc, the required wind correction angle changes continuously because the arc curves around the station, meaning the crosswind component relative to your direction of flight changes as you proceed around the arc. At some points the wind will push you toward the station (requiring a heading away from the station), at other points it will push you outward. Using the MFD, you can monitor whether your actual position track is drifting inside or outside the arc in real time — the moving map will show your ground track curving more sharply inward or outward than the arc itself. This allows you to anticipate lead turns: instead of waiting for the CDI or DME to show deviation, the MFD lets you see the drift developing and make proactive heading adjustments. For a 35-knot crosswind, you may need to vary your heading by 5–15 degrees throughout the arc depending on the arc radius and your airspeed, and the MFD's ground track vector is the clearest indicator of when and how much to correct.

questions.question: When using the autopilot to intercept a VOR radial, which autopilot mode do you select, and what does the autopilot need from you before it can capture the course?
questions.answer: You select NAV mode (or HEADING mode to position the aircraft on an intercept angle first, then arm NAV for capture). Before the autopilot can capture the course, you must have the correct OBS course set in the CDI/HSI, the navaid tuned and identified, and the autopilot armed for course capture. The autopilot will fly the selected heading until the CDI begins to center, then transition to track the radial.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5 (Autopilot systems); aircraft AFM/POH autopilot supplement

questions.question: What is the significance of the phrase 'at the discretion of the evaluator' in ACS element IH.V.A.S9, and under what condition does this element apply at all?
questions.answer: The phrase means the evaluator chooses whether or not to task the applicant with using the autopilot — it is not required to be demonstrated unless the evaluator requests it. The second condition is that an autopilot must actually be installed in the helicopter. If the aircraft is not equipped with an autopilot, this element does not apply. When the evaluator does elect to test this skill, the applicant must demonstrate competency in selecting the correct autopilot modes to execute a course intercept.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Instrument Rating – Helicopter ACS (FAA-S-ACS-9); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5

questions.question: After engaging the autopilot in NAV mode to intercept a radial, what is your primary responsibility as the pilot in command?
questions.answer: Even with the autopilot engaged, the pilot remains fully responsible for the safe conduct of the flight. Primary responsibilities include monitoring the autopilot's performance to ensure it is capturing the intended course correctly, verifying navaid identification, cross-checking the CDI/HSI for proper course tracking, maintaining situational awareness, managing workload, and being ready to immediately take manual control if the autopilot deviates, disconnects, or malfunctions. The autopilot is a tool — PIC authority and responsibility never transfer to the automation.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (automation management)

questions.question: You are being vectored to intercept the 090 radial inbound (flying westbound on a 270° course) to a VOR. You engage the autopilot in HEADING mode at 030° intercept angle. At what point do you arm NAV mode, and what do you watch for to confirm the autopilot is transitioning correctly to track the radial?
questions.answer: ARM the NAV mode as soon as you are established on the intercept heading and the navaid is tuned, identified, and the OBS is set to 270° (the inbound course). Some systems require NAV to be armed before the CDI begins moving — check the AFM/POH for the specific autopilot's arm-and-capture sequence. You confirm correct transition by observing: (1) the CDI begins to move from full deflection toward center as the aircraft approaches the radial, (2) the autopilot begins a smooth turn toward the course as the CDI centers, and (3) the mode annunciator transitions from HDG/NAV ARM to NAV TRACK or equivalent. The aircraft should roll out wings-level on the 270° course with the CDI centered.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9 (VOR tracking); aircraft-specific autopilot AFM supplement

questions.question: While using the autopilot to track a localizer inbound, you notice the CDI is showing a half-dot deflection to the left and the autopilot is not correcting. What are the possible causes, and what is your immediate action?
questions.answer: Possible causes include: (1) the autopilot is in NAV mode using VOR sensitivity rather than LOC/APPR mode — localizer CDI is 4-5 times more sensitive than VOR CDI, so a small physical deviation appears larger; (2) the autopilot mode is not correctly set to LOC or APPR mode; (3) a wind correction angle has not been established and the autopilot is lagging; (4) autopilot malfunction or disconnect. Immediate action: verify the autopilot mode annunciation matches what you expect (APPR or LOC mode, not NAV/VOR), check that the localizer frequency is correctly tuned and identified, and assess whether the deviation is growing or stable. If the autopilot is not correcting and you are inside the FAF, take manual control immediately to maintain course. Remember localizer full deflection is only 2.5° — do not allow drift to continue.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9 (localizer sensitivity); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5 (autopilot systems)

questions.question: You are flying a helicopter equipped with a coupled autopilot and are cleared direct to a GPS waypoint on an RNAV route. Describe the step-by-step process you would use to engage the autopilot for the course intercept from a heading that is 45 degrees offset from the direct-to track.
questions.answer: Step 1: Ensure the GPS is in the active navigation leg with the correct waypoint selected and the flight plan or direct-to course is active in the FMS/GPS. Step 2: Verify the CDI source is set to GPS (not VOR/LOC). Step 3: Set the autopilot to HEADING mode and fly the current heading or a heading that provides a reasonable intercept angle toward the active GPS track. Step 4: ARM the NAV or GPS mode on the autopilot — the system will begin searching for the course to capture. Step 5: Monitor the course deviation indicator; as the aircraft approaches the GPS track, the autopilot should begin a turn to align with the direct-to course. Step 6: Confirm the mode annunciation transitions to NAV TRACK or GPS TRACK and the CDI centers. Step 7: Monitor for proper tracking, wind correction, and waypoint sequencing throughout the leg.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9 (RNAV/GPS); aircraft AFM autopilot supplement; 14 CFR 91.3

questions.question: You are demonstrating an autopilot-coupled VOR intercept for the evaluator. The autopilot captures the radial and begins tracking, but after 2 minutes you notice the heading has drifted 8 degrees from the inbound course and the CDI is now showing 3/4 deflection — yet the autopilot NAV mode is still annunciated as active. What does this pattern tell you, and how do you respond?
questions.answer: This pattern is consistent with the autopilot's NAV mode being active but failing to apply wind correction — the aircraft is being blown off course and the autopilot is not compensating, or there is a navaid tracking error (e.g., VOR signal degradation, scalloping, or a CDI source/mode mismatch). It could also indicate the autopilot's course datum is set to the wrong radial, causing it to 'track' toward the wrong course. Immediate response: (1) cross-check the OBS/HSI course setting against the clearance, (2) verify the navaid is properly tuned and identified, (3) assess whether the deviation is stable or growing (growing = autopilot not correcting = likely system problem), (4) if inside any approach fix, disconnect the autopilot and take manual control immediately. Do not allow continued autopilot-coupled flight when the system is not correcting a known deviation — PIC authority requires intervention when automation is not performing as expected.
questions.follow_up: If you disconnect the autopilot and take manual control, what is your immediate instrument scan priority to re-establish on the VOR radial?
questions.follow_up_answer: After disconnecting, immediately establish the correct intercept heading using the heading indicator and HSI/CDI. Priority scan: (1) heading indicator — confirm you are turning toward the correct intercept angle, (2) CDI — monitor whether the needle is moving back toward center, (3) VSI and altimeter — ensure you haven't deviated from assigned altitude during the transition (a common distraction error), (4) airspeed — confirm no unintended speed change. Re-intercept using a standard angle (typically 30°) toward the radial, then re-establish tracking once CDI begins centering. This is also a high-workload moment — verbalize your actions and maintain situational awareness for any ATC calls.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9 (VOR tracking errors); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5 (autopilot monitoring); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (automation management, SRM)

questions.question: As a helicopter instrument pilot, how does your reliance on autopilot-coupled intercepts during an IFR flight in IMC introduce a specific human factors risk, and what practical technique do you use to mitigate it?
questions.answer: The primary human factors risk is automation complacency — a well-documented phenomenon where pilots reduce their active monitoring of flight parameters when automation is engaged. In IMC, this is especially dangerous because spatial disorientation can develop rapidly if the pilot is not actively cross-checking instruments, and a subtle autopilot deviation or disconnect can go unnoticed until it becomes a serious situation. A secondary risk is mode confusion: not knowing which autopilot mode is active, what the mode is expected to do, and when it will sequence to the next mode. Practical mitigation techniques include: (1) maintaining a disciplined instrument scan even when coupled — never stop cross-checking, (2) verbalizing mode changes as you make them ('NAV armed, expect capture in approximately 2 miles'), (3) setting altitude pre-selects and cross-checking the mode annunciator panel frequently, (4) mentally staying one step ahead of the automation rather than reacting to it, and (5) applying the SRM principle from FAA-H-8083-21B that automation management is an active, continuous skill — not passive monitoring. Remember: 80% of aviation accidents involve human factors; automation does not eliminate that risk, it shifts where the risk lives.
questions.follow_up: The Helicopter Flying Handbook notes that accident rates correlate more strongly with hours in a specific aircraft type than total flight hours. How does this apply specifically to autopilot proficiency in the helicopter IFR environment?
questions.follow_up_answer: This principle means that a pilot with 2,000 total hours but only 50 hours in a specific helicopter with a coupled autopilot is more accident-prone with that automation system than a 500-hour pilot with 400 hours in type. Autopilot systems are not generic — each has unique mode logic, arm-and-capture sequencing, and failure behaviors. A pilot unfamiliar with the specific autopilot in their helicopter may misidentify mode annunciations, misuse the arm/engage sequence for course intercepts, or be slow to recognize an autopilot malfunction. This reinforces why recurrency in the specific aircraft with the specific autopilot is critical, not just overall IFR currency. Practical implication: before any IFR flight with a coupled autopilot, review the AFM autopilot supplement, brief the expected modes for each phase of flight, and do not rely on muscle memory from a different aircraft's system.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (automation management, SRM, human factors, accident statistics); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5 (autopilot systems)

areas_of_operation.title: Area of Operation V. Navigation Systems

tasks.title: Task B. Departure, En Route, and Arrival Operations

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of a Departure Procedure (DP), and what are the two types of DPs published by the FAA?
questions.answer: A Departure Procedure (DP) is a preplanned instrument flight rule (IFR) departure route that provides obstacle clearance and a transition from the terminal environment to the en route structure. The two types are: (1) Obstacle Departure Procedures (ODPs), which provide obstacle clearance only and may be textual or charted; and (2) Standard Instrument Departures (SIDs), which are ATC-assigned procedures that also provide obstacle clearance but are primarily designed to simplify clearance delivery and reduce pilot/controller workload.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Instrument Flying Handbook FAA-H-8083-15B; AIM 5-2-8

questions.question: What standard climb gradient is assumed when flying a Departure Procedure, and what does that gradient translate to in terms of feet per nautical mile?
questions.answer: The standard climb gradient assumed for Departure Procedures is 200 feet per nautical mile (ft/NM). This gradient is the minimum required to ensure obstacle clearance during the departure. If a greater climb gradient is required due to obstacles, it will be published on the procedure. If the aircraft cannot meet a published climb gradient, the pilot must use an alternate means of terrain/obstacle avoidance or not depart under IFR.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Instrument Flying Handbook FAA-H-8083-15B; AIM 5-2-8; 14 CFR 91.175

questions.question: What is a Standard Terminal Arrival Route (STAR), and who is it primarily designed to benefit?
questions.answer: A Standard Terminal Arrival Route (STAR) is a preplanned ATC arrival procedure published for IFR aircraft transitioning from the en route environment to a terminal environment near an airport. STARs are primarily designed to benefit ATC by simplifying clearance delivery and reducing frequency congestion, while also helping pilots by providing a standardized, charted routing from the en route structure to the initial approach fix (IAF) or a meter fix. Pilots must have the STAR in their possession and accept it in their clearance to fly it.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Instrument Flying Handbook FAA-H-8083-15B; AIM 5-4-1

questions.question: You are planning a helicopter IFR departure from a mountainous airport and notice the published SID requires a climb gradient of 340 ft/NM to 8,500 feet MSL. Your helicopter's performance charts show you can only achieve 280 ft/NM at maximum gross weight with current conditions. What are your options, and what is your responsibility as PIC?
questions.answer: As PIC, you cannot legally accept a clearance for that SID if your aircraft cannot meet the published climb gradient, as the gradient exists specifically to ensure obstacle clearance. Your options include: (1) Reduce weight (burn fuel, reduce payload) until performance charts show you can meet 340 ft/NM; (2) Wait for more favorable conditions (cooler temperatures, lower density altitude); (3) Request the ODP instead, if it has a lower gradient requirement; (4) Request an alternate departure routing from ATC that your aircraft can meet; (5) Delay departure until visual conditions allow a VFR departure. You must not accept the SID and then attempt to fly it knowing you cannot meet the gradient — that would place the aircraft and occupants at risk and violates your PIC responsibility under 14 CFR 91.13 (careless or reckless operation).

questions.question: You receive an IFR clearance that includes a STAR for your destination. While reviewing the STAR plate during cruise, you notice it lists a published speed constraint of 250 KIAS at a specific fix, and a crossing altitude restriction of 'AT OR ABOVE 8,000 feet' at another fix. As a helicopter pilot, how do these constraints apply to you, and what happens if ATC does not amend them?
questions.answer: Published speed and altitude constraints on a STAR are mandatory unless ATC amends them or the pilot receives an 'Expect' altitude/speed. The 'AT OR ABOVE 8,000 feet' crossing restriction means you must cross that fix at or above 8,000 feet MSL — you are free to be higher, but not lower. The 250 KIAS speed restriction means you must be at or below 250 KIAS at that fix. For most helicopters, which cruise well below 250 KIAS, the speed restriction is inherently met. Altitude constraints, however, require active planning — particularly for helicopters on STAR procedures, since helicopter cruise altitudes may make some STAR crossing restrictions difficult to meet in a descent profile. If you cannot meet a published constraint, you must advise ATC and request an amended clearance. Flying a STAR and busting a published constraint without ATC authorization is a pilot deviation.

questions.question: While departing IFR from an uncontrolled airport, you find there is no SID published, but there is a charted ODP. Your IFR clearance says 'Cleared to [destination] via filed route, maintain 5,000, squawk 4521.' No specific departure routing was given. Are you required to fly the ODP, and what should you do?
