questions.answer: At the MAP, the pilot must immediately initiate the published missed approach procedure by simultaneously increasing collective to add power, transitioning to a climbing attitude via aft cyclic as needed, and reconfiguring navigation sources to follow the missed approach routing. The pilot should also set the appropriate missed approach airspeed, retract any external equipment if applicable, and notify ATC. Delaying or mismanaging this configuration change risks descent below the MDA/DA and terrain clearance loss.

questions.question: You are flying a VOR non-precision approach to a remote helipad in IMC. During the final approach segment, you realize you set the wrong altimeter setting and your indicated altitude is 200 feet higher than actual. How does this configuration error affect your approach, and what immediate action do you take?
questions.answer: An altimeter set 200 feet high means you are actually 200 feet lower than your instruments indicate. If you descend to your indicated MDA, you may actually be 200 feet below the actual MDA, placing you dangerously close to obstacles or terrain that the procedure was designed to clear. Immediate action: cross-check the current ATIS or AWOS for the correct altimeter setting, reset the Kollsman window, note the corrected altitude, and if you cannot verify terrain clearance is maintained, execute an immediate missed approach. This is a critical safety-of-flight error requiring no hesitation.

questions.question: A helicopter pilot is flying a GPS non-precision approach and forgets to select the correct CDI source before the final approach fix (FAF). The pilot is navigating via moving map only. What are the specific configuration-related risks in this scenario?
questions.answer: Without the CDI properly sourced to the GPS approach, the pilot loses lateral course deviation guidance calibrated to the approach. Moving maps provide situational awareness but do not replace CDI sensitivity needed for precise lateral tracking — on an approach, the CDI should be in terminal or approach mode (approximately ±1 NM and ±0.3 NM sensitivity respectively). The risks include: flying off course without CDI deviation feedback, potential incursion into obstacle or terrain clearance zones, failure to satisfy approach requirements for course tracking, and increased workload while trying to correct the configuration in IMC at a critical phase. This configuration error should trigger an immediate go-around and restart.

questions.question: During a single-pilot helicopter IFR non-precision approach, at what point should configuration changes be completed, and why does delaying them into the final approach segment significantly increase risk?
questions.answer: All configuration changes — including airspeed stabilization, power setting, avionics source selection, missed approach altitude preselected, and briefing reviewed — should be completed before or at the FAF, not after. Delaying configuration into the final approach segment increases risk because: (1) workload spikes precisely when the pilot must devote maximum attention to course tracking and altitude management; (2) IMC provides no visual cues to compensate for instrument deviations caused by distraction; (3) single-pilot operations leave no redundancy for task saturation; and (4) SRM principles require tasks to be completed at the lowest-workload point possible. The FAF is a hard boundary — after it, the pilot should be executing, not configuring.

questions.question: A helicopter crew is flying an NDB non-precision approach. During the procedure turn inbound, the pilot flying (PF) reconfigures the helicopter while the pilot monitoring (PM) calls out passing the FAF altitude. Due to a miscommunication about who is managing the descent rate after the FAF, the helicopter descends through MDA without visual contact. Identify the specific configuration and crew coordination failures that created this risk, and what should have been done differently.
questions.answer: Several compounding failures occurred here: (1) Configuration was not completed before the FAF — the PF was still reconfiguring during a critical navigation phase; (2) Crew duties were not clearly divided — neither pilot had unambiguous ownership of altitude management through MDA; (3) The PM's altitude callout was not acknowledged or actioned, meaning the error chain was not broken despite a verbal cue being present; (4) No stabilized approach criteria were enforced — the approach should have been abandoned if not configured and stabilized at or before the FAF. Proper risk mitigation requires: completing all configuration prior to FAF, clearly briefed crew duties (PF flies, PM monitors altitude/course and calls deviations), a firm callout-and-response protocol at MDA ('Minimums — no contact — go missed'), and pre-briefed stabilized approach criteria. Per ADM principles, the word 'probably' should never be used — if not configured and stabilized, go missed.
questions.follow_up: If both pilots heard the MDA callout but neither initiated the missed approach, what FAR were they potentially in violation of, and does the presence of two pilots reduce or eliminate that violation?
questions.follow_up_answer: They were potentially in violation of 14 CFR 91.175(c), which requires that descent below MDA (or DA) not occur unless the aircraft is continuously in a position from which a normal approach to landing can be made and the required visual references are clearly visible. The presence of two pilots does not reduce or eliminate the violation — 14 CFR 91.3 places responsibility on the PIC regardless of crew size, and both crewmembers share operational responsibility during an IFR operation. The PIC bears primary legal accountability, but the PM also has a professional and safety obligation to call for a go-around if MDA is breached without visual contact.

questions.question: A helicopter flying a non-precision approach reaches the MAP with no visual contact, initiates the missed approach, and during the climbing transition the pilot notices rotor RPM has decayed into the caution range due to a delayed power application. How does improper configuration at the missed approach transition create this specific helicopter hazard, and what makes it more dangerous in IMC than VMC?
questions.answer: During the missed approach transition, the pilot must rapidly increase collective to arrest descent and establish a climb. If the pilot is slow on collective due to attention divided by navigation reconfiguration tasks — such as re-engaging the missed approach routing on the GPS, entering a hold, or switching radio frequencies — the power addition is delayed. In a helicopter, delayed collective at low altitude during a climbing transition can cause rotor RPM decay as the blades are loaded without sufficient engine response or anticipation. Low rotor RPM in IMC is especially dangerous because: (1) the pilot has no visual horizon to detect an unusual attitude that may accompany RPM decay; (2) recovery inputs (lowering collective, coordinating throttle) require instrument reference and deliberate action without instinctive visual cues; (3) rotor stall in a helicopter is unrecoverable per the FAA; and (4) the aircraft is at its lowest energy state at the MAP — any further energy loss is critical. Proper configuration risk mitigation requires the missed approach be fully briefed and pre-configured (missed approach altitude set, routing loaded) BEFORE the FAF, so the only required action at the MAP is immediate, undivided execution of the power and attitude change.
questions.follow_up: If you observe rotor RPM in the caution range during the missed approach climb in IMC, what is the correct recovery sequence, and is there a point at which the recovery is no longer possible?
questions.follow_up_answer: The correct recovery sequence for low rotor RPM is: (1) immediately lower collective to unload the rotor disk and allow RPM to recover; (2) ensure throttle is fully open (or governor is functioning); (3) adjust airspeed as needed — in a climb, slowing slightly may reduce rotor demand; (4) once RPM is restored to normal range, gradually re-apply collective for the desired climb. This must all be accomplished via instrument reference in IMC. The point of no return is rotor stall — the FAA states explicitly that rotor stalls are unrecoverable. The pilot must act at the first indication of RPM decay; by the time a full stall develops, aerodynamic forces cannot be reversed regardless of control inputs. This is why early recognition and pre-emptive configuration are essential — waiting until the needle is buried is too late.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (Low Rotor RPM/Rotor Stall); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13; 14 CFR 91.175

questions.question: What does the term 'unstabilized approach' mean in the context of a helicopter non-precision instrument approach?
questions.answer: An unstabilized approach is one where the helicopter fails to meet established stabilization criteria by a defined gate — typically the final approach fix (FAF) or a specified altitude. Stabilization criteria generally include: being on the correct track/course centerline, established at the appropriate descent rate, at the correct airspeed (within ±10 knots), with power set appropriately, and configured for landing. Any significant deviation from these parameters — including excessive descent rate, off-course deviation, or improper airspeed — constitutes an unstabilized approach and requires an immediate go-around.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Flying Handbook, Chapter 9; AC 120-71B (Stabilized Approach Criteria)

questions.question: On a non-precision approach in a helicopter, what is considered an excessive descent rate, and why is it particularly hazardous?
questions.answer: An excessive descent rate on a non-precision approach is generally considered to be greater than 1,000 feet per minute in the final approach segment, though some operators set lower limits (e.g., 800 fpm). It is particularly hazardous because: (1) it may prevent the pilot from leveling off at the MDA in time to avoid terrain or obstacles; (2) helicopters have less inertia than fixed-wing aircraft, so corrections must come more quickly; (3) a high sink rate close to the ground dramatically increases the risk of controlled flight into terrain (CFIT); and (4) the pilot may become task-saturated trying to arrest the descent and simultaneously identify the runway environment, increasing the likelihood of a missed approach being executed too late.

questions.question: At what point on a non-precision approach must a pilot decide to execute a missed approach if the approach is not stabilized?
questions.answer: If the approach is not stabilized by the final approach fix (FAF), or if stabilization is lost at any point on the final approach segment, a missed approach must be initiated immediately — the pilot should not continue hoping it will correct itself. Additionally, if the required visual references have not been acquired by the time the helicopter reaches the MDA (or DA/DH on precision approaches), a missed approach is mandatory. The key principle is: an unstabilized approach should never be 'flown through' to the MDA — a go-around is the only safe option.

questions.question: You are flying a VOR non-precision approach in your helicopter. After crossing the FAF, you realize your descent rate has increased to 1,200 fpm to try to get back on the step-down fix altitude. You are now on course but high, and the MDA is only 400 feet below your current altitude. What risk factors are compounding here, and what is the correct decision?
questions.answer: Multiple risk factors are compounding: (1) The excessive descent rate (1,200 fpm) means you could blow through the MDA without adequate time to level off, risking CFIT; (2) Being high means you are already behind the vertical profile — trying to 'dive' to MDA is a classic unstabilized condition; (3) With only 400 feet to MDA at 1,200 fpm, you have approximately 20 seconds to level off — an extremely tight window; (4) The fixation on re-capturing the profile creates task saturation and degrades situational awareness. The correct decision is to immediately execute the missed approach. The approach is unstabilized by definition, and continuing in this condition is a high-risk, unacceptable practice regardless of weather conditions or pressure to complete the approach. The missed approach is always the safe option.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM/error chain)

questions.question: How does the higher sensitivity of a localizer CDI compared to a VOR CDI affect the risk of an unstabilized approach on a non-precision localizer (LOC) approach in a helicopter?
questions.answer: A localizer CDI is approximately 4–5 times more sensitive than a VOR CDI — a full deflection on a localizer represents only about 2.5° off course, versus approximately 12° for a VOR. This means that small lateral deviations produce large needle movements on a localizer. For helicopter pilots, this creates a risk of over-controlling laterally while simultaneously managing the vertical profile on a non-precision approach. If a pilot is chasing the localizer needle with large cyclic inputs, this degrades vertical profile management, potentially leading to an excessive descent rate or altitude bust. The risk is compounded by the fact that the localizer provides no vertical guidance — the pilot must manage descent independently. Smooth, anticipatory control inputs and a pre-briefed, stabilized approach profile are critical to avoiding an unstabilized condition on a LOC approach.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9 (VOR vs. localizer CDI sensitivity); 14 CFR 91.175

questions.question: You are conducting a non-precision GPS approach to a remote heliport. The weather is right at minimums, your passenger is a medical crew waiting to pick up a critical patient, and your company dispatcher is asking for status. You arrive at MDA slightly fast and slightly high. How do the psychological pressures present here affect your risk of continuing an unstabilized approach, and what risk management tool applies?
questions.answer: This scenario illustrates the classic 'get-there-itis' or 'press-on-itis' hazardous attitude compounded by external pressures (critical patient, dispatcher, crew expectation). The psychological pressures create a strong bias toward continuing the approach despite being unstabilized — arriving fast and high at MDA violates stabilization criteria. The risks include: (1) descending below MDA without adequate visual reference to land safely; (2) misjudging the flare due to excessive airspeed; (3) CFIT risk if terrain is near the heliport. The applicable risk management tools include: the IMSAFE checklist for pre-flight self-assessment; the PAVE model (Pilot, Aircraft, enVironment, External pressures) — specifically the 'E' (external pressure) component; and recognizing the hazardous attitude of 'invulnerability' or 'resignation.' The correct action is to execute the missed approach immediately. Per ADM principles from the Helicopter Flying Handbook, if an action will only 'probably' work out, choose the option known to work — in this case, the missed approach.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM, SRM, PAVE, hazardous attitudes); 14 CFR 91.175

questions.question: A helicopter pilot executes what appears to be a normal non-precision approach but continuously makes small adjustments — varying airspeed by 15–20 knots, chasing the CDI, and adjusting collective frequently — yet never technically exceeds any single parameter threshold before reaching MDA. Is this approach stabilized? What is the deeper safety concern with this type of approach behavior?
questions.answer: No — this approach is not stabilized despite no single parameter exceeding a threshold in isolation. Stabilization is not simply a binary check of individual parameters; it requires a consistently controlled, predictable flight path with minimal corrections. Continuous large adjustments indicate the pilot is reacting rather than anticipating — a reactive control technique that signals loss of situational awareness and degraded automation management. The deeper safety concern is workload saturation: the pilot is spending cognitive resources chasing deviations rather than monitoring the approach environment, identifying required visual references, and preparing for the missed approach or landing. Near MDA, this reactive state dramatically increases the risk of descending below MDA unintentionally or failing to recognize the need for a go-around in time. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook notes that accidents correlate with loss of situational awareness — and this type of approach behavior is a precursor indicator of that loss.
questions.follow_up: If this pilot makes it to MDA and the runway environment is in sight, is it now safe to continue the landing given the unstabilized approach?
questions.follow_up_answer: Not necessarily. Under 14 CFR 91.175, even when the required visual references are acquired at MDA, the pilot must be in a position to make a normal approach and landing using normal maneuvers. An unstabilized approach — even with the runway in sight — does not guarantee the pilot can safely transition to a landing. The excessive speed variations and reactive control technique mean the approach geometry may be unsuitable: the helicopter could be too fast, too high, or improperly configured to complete a safe landing from that point. The pilot must assess whether a normal landing is achievable from the current position and energy state. If there is any doubt, the missed approach must be executed. Continuing a bad approach because the runway is visible is a well-documented accident cause chain in helicopter operations.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175(c); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (situational awareness, SRM); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9

questions.question: On a non-precision approach with step-down fixes, explain how the structure of the approach itself — with multiple required altitude changes in a short distance — creates an inherent risk of excessive descent rates, and what specific technique mitigates this risk in a helicopter.
questions.answer: Non-precision approaches with step-down fixes require the pilot to descend to progressively lower altitudes at designated fixes before reaching MDA. This creates an inherent risk because: (1) if a pilot is late crossing a step-down fix at the required altitude, they must descend more steeply in a shorter remaining distance to reach the next fix altitude or MDA — producing an excessive descent rate; (2) the pilot may fixate on reaching the next step-down altitude while simultaneously tracking course, managing airspeed, and cross-checking navigation — increasing error chain risk; (3) helicopters, with their lower approach airspeeds compared to fixed-wing aircraft, cover less ground per unit of time, which can create a false sense of having more time between fixes than actually exists if mental math is not done precisely. The primary mitigation technique is pre-computing required vertical descent rates between each fix using the known groundspeed and altitude difference, and configuring the helicopter to achieve those rates before reaching each fix rather than reacting after. Using a published vertical descent angle (if available on the approach chart) and a continuous descent final approach (CDFA) technique — descending smoothly from the FAF to MDA as if flying a precision approach — eliminates the step-dive-level cycle entirely and produces a more stabilized approach profile.
questions.follow_up: If you use a Continuous Descent Final Approach (CDFA) technique on a non-precision approach and descend below MDA before acquiring the required visual references, what are the legal and safety implications?
questions.follow_up_answer: Descending below MDA without the required visual references is a violation of 14 CFR 91.175(c), which prohibits descending below MDA unless the aircraft is continuously in a position to make a normal landing and the required visual references are clearly visible. In the CDFA technique, the pilot must treat MDA as a decision altitude — if visual references are not acquired by MDA, an immediate missed approach is executed by applying go-around power rather than leveling off at MDA. The safety implication is critical: if a pilot using CDFA mentally commits to a 'constant glide' mindset and does not have a firm pre-briefed decision point at MDA, the momentum of the descent can carry the helicopter below MDA and into obstacle/terrain clearance areas — exactly the CFIT scenario the MDA is designed to prevent. The pre-briefing of the missed approach point and the 'go-around at MDA if no visual reference' decision must be absolute and non-negotiable.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175(c); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9 (step-down fixes, CDFA); TERPS criteria for step-down fixes

questions.question: What is the published missed approach point (MAP) on a non-precision approach, and what must the pilot have in sight to continue below MDA?
questions.answer: The MAP is the point at which a missed approach must be initiated if the required visual references have not been established. To descend below MDA and continue to a landing, the pilot must have the runway environment in sight, be in a position to land using normal maneuvers, and have flight visibility at or above the published minimum. These three conditions must all be met simultaneously. If any one is absent at or before the MAP, a missed approach is mandatory.

questions.question: If the weather is reported above minimums when you start the approach but drops below minimums by the time you reach MDA, are you required to execute a missed approach?
questions.answer: Yes. Regardless of what the weather was at approach initiation, if you arrive at or before the MAP and do not have the required flight visibility and runway environment in sight, you must execute a missed approach. 14 CFR 91.175(c) prohibits operating below MDA unless those conditions are met at that moment. The weather report at the start of the approach does not authorize you to continue if conditions have since deteriorated.

questions.question: What weather sources should an IFR helicopter pilot monitor for potential deterioration when conducting a non-precision approach in dynamic weather conditions?
questions.answer: The pilot should monitor the ATIS or D-ATIS for current field conditions, request PIREPs from ATC if available, and monitor any applicable METARs or Special METARs (SPECIs) issued for rapidly changing conditions. If ASOS or AWOS is available on a discrete frequency, it can be monitored throughout the approach. ATC can also be asked for the latest weather observation. On approach, any trend of decreasing RVR or lowering ceilings is a strong indicator to consider the missed approach early rather than pressing to the MAP.

questions.question: You are 4 miles from the runway on a VOR/DME approach in a helicopter, descending to MDA. The ATIS you copied 20 minutes ago showed ceiling 800 overcast and 3 miles visibility — above your approach minimums. ATC now calls you and says a SPECI has been issued showing 300 overcast and 1/2 mile in fog. What should you do, and does 14 CFR 91.175 require you to do anything specific at this point?
questions.answer: At this point the weather has dropped well below approach minimums. While 14 CFR 91.175 does not technically prohibit continuing inbound to the MAP — it restricts descent *below* MDA — the smart and safe decision is to immediately advise ATC and execute a missed approach or hold to reassess. Continuing to MDA with weather already confirmed below minimums serves no purpose: you will not acquire the required visual references, and delaying the missed approach only increases workload and exposure to CFIT risk. This is also a textbook application of the ADM principle of avoiding the 'pressing' trap. Declare intentions to ATC, fly the missed approach, and seek an alternate.

questions.question: You are flying a helicopter IFR to a remote mountain helipad. The destination has no weather reporting, but the nearest weather station 15 miles away shows 1,200 broken and 5 miles visibility — fine for your approach. You start the GPS approach and notice fog beginning to fill the valley below you on the inbound segment. How does the absence of official weather reporting at the destination change your risk calculus, and what actions should you take?
questions.answer: Without official weather reporting at the destination, there is no guarantee the conditions at the helipad match the nearby station. Mountain terrain creates localized weather phenomena — valley fog, orographic lift, and rapid ceiling changes — that can be completely independent of stations just miles away. The developing fog you observe visually is a real-time PIREP that the approach environment is deteriorating. Risk management here requires deciding early: if you cannot confirm an acceptable environment at the MAP, a missed approach to an alternate must be executed. You should brief the missed approach thoroughly before beginning, confirm alternate minimums and fuel, and establish a personal decision point (e.g., a specific fix or altitude) beyond which you will not continue unless conditions clearly allow a safe landing. Waiting until the MAP in these circumstances significantly compresses decision time and increases CFIT risk.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175(c); 14 CFR 91.169 (alternate requirements); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 1

questions.question: During a non-precision approach in a helicopter, you break out of the clouds briefly at MDA and identify the runway environment. You begin transitioning to land, but the visibility suddenly drops and you lose visual contact with the runway. What are your immediate obligations and actions?
questions.answer: Once visual contact with the runway environment is lost below MDA, you must immediately execute a missed approach. 14 CFR 91.175(c) requires that the flight visibility and required visual references be maintained continuously from MDA to touchdown. If they are lost at any point during that segment, remaining below MDA is no longer authorized. Immediately apply go-around/missed approach power, climb to the published missed approach altitude, and follow the published missed approach procedure. This is not a judgment call — it is a regulatory requirement. Attempting to 'feel around' below MDA without visual references in a helicopter creates extreme CFIT exposure, especially at low altitudes and low airspeeds.

questions.question: A helicopter pilot flying a non-precision approach argues that since helicopters can operate at lower speeds and hover, it's acceptable to slow to a near-hover just above MDA to 'wait out' a momentary patch of fog obscuring the runway before the MAP. Evaluate this argument from a regulatory, aerodynamic, and risk management standpoint.
questions.answer: This argument fails on all three grounds. Regulatory: 14 CFR 91.175(c) does not permit extended maneuvering below MDA or at MDA without continuous visual references regardless of aircraft type. The regulation applies equally to helicopters. There is no provision to loiter at MDA awaiting improving visibility. Aerodynamic: At very low airspeeds near a hover in IMC or marginal VMC, a helicopter is in an extremely vulnerable flight regime — potential loss of translational lift, increased susceptibility to settling with power (vortex ring state), reduced tail rotor effectiveness, and greatly reduced ability to climb away quickly if the situation worsens. Risk Management: This behavior is a textbook example of 'pressing' — continuing toward an outcome that will 'probably' work rather than taking the known safe option (missed approach). The FAA's ADM framework and the Trescott principle specifically warn against this. Any tactic that extends time near terrain in degraded visibility multiplies CFIT risk. The correct action is always a timely missed approach.
questions.follow_up: Suppose the pilot claims the helicopter POH specifically authorizes slow flight at MDA for instrument approaches — does that change the regulatory picture?
questions.follow_up_answer: No. An aircraft flight manual or POH can define aircraft performance and limitations, but it cannot supersede 14 CFR 91.175. The FARs are minimum standards; an operating limitation in a POH cannot authorize flight below those regulatory standards. If the POH described a slow-flight technique for transitioning from instruments to visual at MDA, it would still be predicated on having the required visual references as mandated by 91.175(c). The regulation controls — not the POH.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175(c); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM/Trescott); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (vortex ring state, LTE)

questions.question: You are conducting a non-precision approach to an airport that has a published alternate minimum of 800-2. Your fuel state allows one missed approach before you must divert. At the initial approach fix, the ATIS shows 900 overcast and 3 miles. By the time you reach the FAF, ATC reports the ceiling has dropped to 700 and visibility to 1-1/2 miles. Your approach minimums are 660-1. Describe the complete risk management decision framework you should apply at that moment.
questions.answer: At this moment, conditions are below alternate minimums (800-2) and trending downward, approaching your approach minimums (660-1). The risk management analysis must include: (1) Fuel: You have fuel for one missed approach only — if you fly this approach and miss, you must immediately divert, possibly into further deteriorating conditions without margin. (2) Trend: The ceiling dropped 200 feet and visibility dropped more than 1 mile just during your approach — a rapid deterioration trend that argues conditions will likely be worse, not better, at the MAP. (3) Approach minimums: At 700/1.5, you are technically above your approach minimums of 660-1, but with very little margin and a downward trend. (4) Alternate status: Your alternate may no longer be legal if its weather has also changed, and you have not confirmed that. The sound decision under this risk picture is to not commence or to discontinue the approach and divert NOW while fuel allows a safe diversion. This applies the ADM principle of acting on known threats rather than hoping conditions stabilize. Continuing the approach consumes precious fuel and time, and a missed approach from MDA in these conditions leaves you with minimal options. Declare intentions to ATC, request vectors or routing to your alternate, and confirm alternate weather before committing.
questions.follow_up: 14 CFR 91.175(l) describes when a pilot may not begin an instrument approach procedure. How does that regulation apply to this scenario, and is the pilot already in violation by reaching the FAF?
questions.follow_up_answer: 14 CFR 91.175(l) states that a pilot operating under Part 91 may not begin an instrument approach procedure if the latest weather report for the destination airport shows conditions below the authorized minimums. However, this regulation references conditions at the *beginning* of the approach, typically interpreted as the IAF. In this scenario, weather was above minimums at the IAF, so the pilot was legal to begin. By the FAF, ATC has provided updated weather showing conditions very close to minimums with a downward trend. While 91.175(l) technically may not be violated at the FAF, 91.175(c) still controls whether the pilot may descend below MDA, and sound ADM strongly argues against continuing. There is no regulatory obligation to continue an approach once started — a pilot may always execute a missed approach at any point for any reason. The prudent and professionally correct action is to discontinue and divert, and this is entirely consistent with both the regulations and the ADM framework.

questions.question: What is the Minimum Descent Altitude (MDA), and what is the pilot required to have in sight before descending below it on a non-precision approach?
questions.answer: The MDA is the lowest altitude, expressed in feet MSL, to which descent is authorized on a non-precision approach unless the required visual references have been established. Before descending below the MDA, the pilot must have the runway environment in sight — this includes the runway, runway markings, runway lighting, the approach light system, or other visual references specified in 14 CFR 91.175(c). The flight visibility must also meet or exceed the visibility prescribed for the approach.

questions.question: If you reach the MDA on a non-precision approach and the runway is not in sight, what must you do?
questions.answer: If the required visual references are not established upon reaching the MDA, you must execute a missed approach immediately. You are not permitted to descend below the MDA and must fly the published missed approach procedure. Continuing the descent below MDA without the required visual references is a serious violation of 14 CFR 91.175 and constitutes an unsafe and illegal act.

questions.question: What specific visual references does the FAA consider acceptable for a pilot to continue descent below the MDA on a non-precision approach?
questions.answer: Per 14 CFR 91.175(c), acceptable visual references include: the approach light system (ALS), the runway threshold, threshold markings, threshold lights, runway end identifier lights (REIL), visual approach slope indicator (VASI), touchdown zone or touchdown zone markings, touchdown zone lights, runway or runway markings, or runway lights. Simply seeing the glow of lights through fog is not sufficient — the pilot must clearly identify one of these specific elements. For helicopters, the helipad or heliport lighting may substitute where applicable.

questions.question: You're flying a VOR approach to a remote helipad in your helicopter. You break out just above MDA and catch a brief glimpse of what you think is the helipad lighting through a thin layer of scud, but you're not certain. Is it safe and legal to descend below the MDA?
questions.answer: No. Descending below the MDA requires that the required visual references be clearly established and that reported flight visibility meets the published minimum. A glimpse of what might be the helipad through scud does not constitute having the required visual references 'distinctly visible and identifiable.' The risk here is significant — if you descend based on uncertain references, you may lose visual contact entirely at low altitude with no margin for obstacle clearance. The correct action is to hold at MDA, reassess briefly, and if the references cannot be positively established, execute the missed approach. Wishful thinking is a known contributor to CFIT accidents.

questions.question: You are conducting an NDB approach in a helicopter. You level off at MDA and start to drift slightly below it while maneuvering to align with the runway. You can see the approach lights but have not yet acquired the runway. What risk does this create, and how should it be managed?
questions.answer: Drifting even slightly below the MDA — even with approach lights in sight — is potentially illegal and dangerous. Under 14 CFR 91.175(c)(1), seeing only the approach light system (ALS) permits descent to 100 feet above the touchdown zone elevation (TDZE), but not lower unless additional runway environment elements are acquired. The risk is loss of obstacle clearance, as the MDA is set to provide a specific buffer above the highest obstacle in the final approach area. In a helicopter, which may be maneuvering at slower airspeeds with greater attitude changes, precise altitude control at MDA is critical. The pilot should proactively use vertical speed and power management to hold the exact MDA altitude and not permit creep-down during maneuvering.

questions.question: A pilot reports 'field in sight' when calling the tower on a non-precision approach at MDA. Does this satisfy the requirement to descend below the MDA? What is the actual risk if the pilot then descends?
questions.answer: 'Field in sight' is not a legally sufficient declaration to descend below the MDA. The requirement under 14 CFR 91.175(c) is that the pilot has the specific runway environment elements in sight and that flight visibility meets the approach minimums — not simply that the general airport area is visible. The risk of descending based on a generic 'field in sight' call is that the pilot may have spotted a taxiway, ramp lighting, or airport beacon that does not provide adequate guidance to safely complete the landing. Descending without confirmed runway environment identification removes the obstacle clearance protection provided by the MDA and increases CFIT risk significantly, particularly during off-airport or remote helicopter operations where terrain may be adjacent to the landing area.

questions.question: A helicopter pilot flying a GPS LNAV approach acquires the approach lights at MDA but immediately loses sight of them due to patchy ground fog while maneuvering. The pilot is now below MDA and no longer has visual references. What is the correct course of action, and what factors made this scenario especially dangerous for a helicopter?
questions.answer: The pilot must immediately execute a missed approach. Once visual references are lost after descending below MDA, the pilot is in an illegal and highly dangerous situation — they have lost the visual cues required to continue and are below the obstacle clearance altitude. The correct response is to apply the missed approach procedure immediately, transitioning to instrument flight. For helicopters, this scenario is especially dangerous because: (1) helicopters often operate to confined or off-airport landing areas with adjacent terrain/obstacles at or below MDA; (2) the slow airspeeds used in helicopter approaches can make transitions back to instruments more demanding; (3) patchy fog creates an illusion that conditions are 'good enough,' triggering continuation bias — a well-documented ADM hazard. Pilots must resist the impulse to press forward hoping conditions will improve and must commit to the missed approach the moment visual references are lost.
questions.follow_up: Let's say the pilot recognized the situation and initiated the missed approach correctly, but in doing so momentarily descended an additional 50 feet while transitioning to instruments. Is this a violation, and what regulatory or safety implications arise?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, this could constitute a violation of 14 CFR 91.175(c) if the descent below MDA was not due to a normal landing maneuver and visual references were not maintained. However, the FAA generally recognizes that there can be a brief transition period when executing a missed approach — the pilot's obligation is to initiate the missed approach as promptly as possible. The safety implication is significant: 50 feet at low altitude near terrain or obstacles may be the difference between survival and a CFIT accident. This underscores why maintaining strict MDA discipline and not allowing any altitude creep during the approach is critical. Examiners look for proactive altitude management, not reactive corrections at minimum altitude.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175(c)(3); 14 CFR 91.175(e); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9

questions.question: A highly experienced helicopter EMS pilot flying an NDB approach at night tells you: 'I've flown this approach a hundred times. I know exactly where the hospital helipad is, so if I don't have it in sight at MDA I'll just descend slowly and I know I'll pick it up before I get too low.' What specific risks and regulatory issues do you identify with this mindset?
questions.answer: This statement reveals multiple serious risk factors and regulatory misunderstandings. First, it is a direct violation of 14 CFR 91.175(c) — descent below MDA without required visual references is prohibited regardless of pilot experience or familiarity with the area. Second, 'familiarity bias' is one of the most dangerous traps in aviation ADM; familiarity breeds overconfidence and reduces situational awareness. Third, night conditions dramatically reduce peripheral visual cues and spatial awareness, making a slow uncontrolled descent toward terrain or obstacles far more hazardous. Fourth, NDB approaches have the least precision of all instrument approaches, with potential bearing errors — the pilot cannot be certain of their actual lateral position based on NDB guidance alone. Fifth, EMS operations are time-pressured environments known to contribute to ADM errors and get-there-itis. The FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 specifically identifies that breaking the error chain requires recognizing the accumulation of bad decisions — this pilot has already made multiple poor decisions before even executing the approach.
questions.follow_up: If this pilot were flying under Part 135 EMS operations, what additional regulatory layer would apply regarding descending below MDA without visual references, and would a company operations spec override the minimums in this scenario?
questions.follow_up_answer: Under 14 CFR Part 135, operators must comply with instrument approach minimums established in 14 CFR 135.225, which prohibit beginning or continuing an approach below MDA unless the runway environment is clearly in sight and reported visibility meets approach minimums. Operations Specifications (OpSpecs) issued by the FAA to Part 135 certificate holders may authorize special approaches or reduced minimums (e.g., Copter approaches or HAA-specific procedures), but OpSpecs can never authorize operations that fall below the legal requirements of 14 CFR 91.175 or 135.225 — they operate within those bounds, not outside them. No OpSpec can permit a pilot to descend below MDA without visual references. Furthermore, a company SOP that encourages or condones such behavior would itself be a regulatory violation and subject the certificate holder to enforcement action.

questions.question: When flying a VOR non-precision approach in a helicopter, what is the significance of the Minimum Descent Altitude (MDA), and what must you do if you reach it before acquiring the required visual references?
questions.answer: The MDA is the lowest altitude you may descend to on a non-precision approach without having the required visual references (runway environment, approach lights, etc.) in sight. If you reach the MDA and do not have the required visual references, you must execute an immediate missed approach — you cannot descend below the MDA in hopes of acquiring the runway. The MDA is not a floor you level off at and cruise along indefinitely; helicopter pilots must execute the missed approach if visual contact is not established in time to make a normal descent to landing.

questions.question: On an NDB/ADF non-precision approach, where does the ADF needle point, and how do you use that information to track inbound on the final approach course?
questions.answer: The ADF needle always points TO the station regardless of aircraft heading. To track inbound on the final approach course, you must apply wind correction to maintain the needle at a fixed relative bearing that accounts for wind drift — this is called tracking, not homing. Homing (keeping the needle at 0° relative bearing) will result in a curved, crabbed path into the station in a crosswind. For approach purposes, you establish a wind correction angle on the inbound course and hold the needle at the corresponding relative bearing offset to maintain the desired track over the ground.

questions.question: What are the required visual references a helicopter pilot must identify before descending below the MDA on a non-precision approach?
questions.answer: Per 14 CFR 91.175(c), to descend below MDA the flight visibility must be at or above the visibility prescribed for the approach, and the pilot must have at least one of the following: the approach light system (unless only REIL or ODALS), runway threshold, threshold markings, threshold lights, REIL, VASI/PAPI, touchdown zone or markings, touchdown zone lights, runway or runway markings, runway lights, or a helicopter landing pad or markings. The pilot must also be in a position to make a normal descent to landing using a normal rate of descent.

questions.question: You are flying a GPS LNAV non-precision approach to a remote hospital helipad. During the final approach segment you notice your CDI sensitivity changes from 0.3 NM full-scale to 0.6 NM full-scale. What likely caused this and how does it affect your ability to complete the approach?
questions.answer: GPS approaches use RAIM (Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring) and automatic CDI scaling. On the final approach segment of an LNAV approach, the CDI should scale to 0.3 NM full-scale deflection. If it reverts to 0.6 NM (en route sensitivity) or fails to scale down, this likely indicates a loss of approach-mode activation, a RAIM integrity failure, or the GPS has reverted from approach mode to terminal mode. If approach mode is not annunciated and RAIM is not available, you cannot continue below the MDA using GPS guidance. You should fly the published missed approach immediately unless the approach can be completed using an alternate approved means. This is a critical skill item — flying an LNAV approach with degraded CDI sensitivity significantly reduces your ability to stay on course.

questions.question: You are established on a VOR final approach course in a helicopter at the appropriate descent rate but you realize you are going to be significantly high at the FAF inbound. ATC has not issued a speed restriction. What technique can you use to correct your altitude without abandoning course tracking, and what is the risk of being high at or inside the FAF?
questions.answer: If you are high at the FAF inbound, you can increase your rate of descent by using a steeper descent angle (more collective reduction), provided you remain within the approach airspeed range and do not exceed the descent profile that allows you to level at or before the MDA with adequate visibility checks. A helicopter's ability to make steeper and slower approaches is an advantage here. The risk of being high inside the FAF is that you may not have sufficient distance to descend to the MDA before reaching the MAP (missed approach point), forcing either a rushed, unstabilized final or an inadvertent descent below MDA while trying to 'make it work.' An unstabilized approach that puts you at the MAP still high and without visual contact requires an immediate missed approach.

questions.question: During a non-precision NDB approach in IMC, you cross the FAF inbound and begin your final descent. The ADF needle begins drifting left. Without an RMI, how do you determine whether this indicates you are drifting right of course, left of course, or simply experiencing station passage?
questions.answer: You must mentally compute the relationship between your magnetic heading and the relative bearing shown on the ADF. If you are tracking inbound on a 270° bearing TO the station with a 10° right wind correction (heading 260°), the ADF needle should be at 10° left of the nose (350° relative bearing). If the needle drifts further left, you are likely drifting right of course (downwind); if it moves right toward the nose, you may be drifting left of course or approaching station passage. Without an RMI you must apply the formula: Magnetic Heading + Relative Bearing = Magnetic Bearing TO the station. Track corrections must be made based on logical analysis of needle movement relative to your heading. At or near the station, needle oscillation and erratic behavior signal station passage — this is your FAF or MAP timing cue.

questions.question: You are flying a VOR non-precision approach and reach the MDA with the runway environment barely in sight — you can see the approach lights but not the runway itself. You are at the MAP. Visibility is right at minimums. Can you continue the descent, and what is the limiting factor for a helicopter versus a fixed-wing aircraft at this point?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.175(c), approach lights alone (without seeing at least the red terminating bars or red side row bars of the ALSF) allow descent to 100 feet above the touchdown zone elevation, not all the way to the surface. Seeing only approach lights does not authorize descent to touchdown. For a helicopter, the published HAA (height above airport) or HAT (height above touchdown) applies to the helipad or runway threshold. A key helicopter advantage is that unlike a fixed-wing aircraft requiring forward momentum to land, a helicopter can legally slow to a hover over a helipad at MDA if visual contact is maintained and the approach is conducted under Part 91 in accordance with the published minimums. However, the descent below MDA is still only authorized when the required visual references are clearly identified. If visibility is fluctuating at minimums, the safe and legal choice is a missed approach — the word 'probably' should never drive the decision to continue.
questions.follow_up: You decide to execute the missed approach. As you apply power and begin climbing, you notice your heading is drifting 20 degrees off the published missed approach course. What is the correct priority of actions and why does heading deviation matter on a helicopter missed approach?
questions.follow_up_answer: Aviate first — establish a positive climb attitude and ensure adequate rotor RPM and power application. Then navigate — intercept the published missed approach course. Heading deviation on a missed approach matters because the published procedure is obstacle-protected only along the specified track. Deviating off course during the climb can expose you to terrain or obstacles that are not protected by the missed approach design, particularly in mountainous or confined areas common to helicopter operations. A 20-degree drift in IMC during a missed approach climb is a high-risk scenario — once a safe climb is established, immediately correct to the published course and advise ATC of your position.

questions.question: You are flying a RNAV (GPS) LNAV non-precision approach and your avionics display an LNAV/VNAV minimums line on the chart. Your GPS is WAAS-capable and shows 'LPV' as the approach mode annunciation. Are you flying a non-precision approach, and how should you fly to the minimums published on the LNAV/VNAV line versus the LPV line?
questions.answer: If your GPS annunciates 'LPV,' you are flying an approach with vertical guidance (APV) equivalent to a precision approach in terms of decision altitude use — not a non-precision approach. The LPV minimums line uses a DA (decision altitude), not an MDA. The LNAV/VNAV minimums line is also flown to a DA (barometric VNAV using Baro-VNAV), not an MDA, but only LPV uses WAAS-generated glidepath guidance. If your unit annunciates LPV, you must fly to the LPV DA — flying to the higher LNAV/VNAV DA when LPV is available is legal but unnecessarily conservative. If WAAS integrity is not available and the unit downgrades to LNAV, the approach reverts to a non-precision approach with an MDA. Understanding which minimums line applies to the annunciated mode is a critical skill — using the wrong minimums line (e.g., flying to LNAV MDA when LPV DA is available, or vice versa when degraded) can result in either unnecessary missed approaches or descending below authorized minimums.
questions.follow_up: During the approach your WAAS GPS downgrades from LPV to LNAV mid-final at 800 feet AGL. What actions should you take and what minimums now apply?
questions.follow_up_answer: Immediately transition to LNAV non-precision approach procedures: level off at or above the LNAV MDA rather than continuing to descend on the glidepath cue. The LNAV MDA is typically significantly higher than the LPV DA, so if you were below the LNAV MDA when the downgrade occurred, you must immediately climb back to the LNAV MDA and treat the approach as a standard non-precision approach from that point forward. You must advise ATC of the navigation degradation. If already past the FAF and unable to safely level at the LNAV MDA with sufficient distance to reach the MAP, the safest action is to execute the missed approach. Never continue descending on the now-invalid LPV glidepath after a mode downgrade.

questions.question: When you're inbound on a non-precision approach and ATC has already cleared you for the approach, do you need to check in again when switching to the tower frequency?
questions.answer: Yes. When ATC instructs you to contact tower, you must establish two-way communication with tower before entering tower-controlled airspace or at the point specified by ATC. You check in with your callsign, aircraft type, position (e.g., 'inbound on the VOR-A approach'), and any relevant information such as information code received from ATIS. Two-way communication means the controller has acknowledged your callsign — a one-way broadcast is not sufficient.

questions.question: What information should you include in your initial call-up when checking in with approach control prior to beginning a non-precision instrument approach?
questions.answer: Your initial call-up to approach control should include: (1) the facility name you are calling, (2) your full aircraft callsign, (3) aircraft type, (4) your current position or assigned fix, (5) altitude, (6) the ATIS information code you have received, and (7) your request or intentions (e.g., requesting the VOR-A approach). This gives the controller the situational awareness needed to sequence and clear you efficiently.

questions.question: After ATC clears you for a non-precision approach with the phrase 'cleared VOR-A approach,' what is the correct readback?
questions.answer: You must read back the clearance to confirm understanding. A correct readback would be: '[Callsign], cleared VOR-A approach.' You must also read back any altitude restrictions, heading assignments, or frequency changes included in the clearance. The AIM requires pilots to read back all ATC clearances and instructions, and controllers are required to listen for and verify the readback. Omitting or incorrectly reading back a clearance is a communication error that could have safety consequences.

questions.question: You're flying a helicopter on an IFR flight plan and are vectored for the NDB approach to a non-towered airport. ATC says 'radar service terminated, squawk VFR, contact traffic advisory frequency.' You still have 10 miles to the FAF in IMC. What communications steps do you take from this point forward?
questions.answer: First, acknowledge the ATC transmission and readback: '[Callsign], wilco, squawking 1200.' Then tune to the traffic advisory frequency (CTAF) for that airport. Since the airport is non-towered, you should broadcast your position and intentions on CTAF at appropriate points — typically when 10 miles out, entering the final approach, and on the missed approach if applicable. You are no longer in two-way communication with ATC, so you must self-announce position calls. You should also confirm you have all approach briefing items complete (minimums, MDA, timing, MAP) before passing the FAF, since you no longer have a controller available to assist with sequencing. Monitor CTAF throughout.

questions.question: On a RNAV (GPS) approach in your helicopter, ATC issues a last-minute instruction: 'turn left heading 250, maintain 3,000 until established, cleared RNAV runway 18 approach.' You are currently heading 310 and descending through 3,500. Walk me through your exact readback and how you immediately manage the communication and cockpit workload.
questions.answer: Readback: '[Callsign], left heading 250, maintain 3,000 until established, cleared RNAV runway 18 approach.' Immediately after the readback, initiate the left turn to 250 and level off at 3,000. In the cockpit, use SRM principles to manage workload: aviate first (turn and altitude), then communicate (readback already done), then navigate (verify GPS is sequenced to the correct approach and that 'LNAV' or appropriate mode is displayed). You should have already briefed the approach, so confirm the final approach course, DA/MDA, and missed approach procedure as you become established. Do not allow the communication event to distract from the altitude and heading control that are now safety-critical on the approach.

questions.question: You are flying a helicopter IFR approach into a Class D airport. You switch to tower and check in, but the controller does not respond for over a minute and you are now 3 miles from the FAF. What actions do you take, and how does communication requirement factor into your decision?
questions.answer: Attempt contact again on the tower frequency, then try the approach control or CTAF for that airport to confirm you have the correct frequency. If contact still cannot be established after reasonable attempts, 14 CFR 91.129 requires two-way radio communication prior to entering Class D airspace — if you cannot establish it, you should not enter. However, if you were already cleared into Class D by approach control before frequency change and are actively trying to reach tower, you should broadcast your position and intentions in the blind, squawk 7600 (lost communications), and follow the lost communication procedures under 14 CFR 91.185. Document the event after landing and notify ATC as soon as possible.

questions.question: A student pilot you are evaluating checks in with approach control using only their callsign and altitude, omitting aircraft type, ATIS, and position. The controller responds with a full clearance. The student reads it back and proceeds. As the examiner, what specific communication deficiencies are present, and under what circumstances could this incomplete initial call-up actually create a safety issue on a non-precision helicopter approach?
questions.answer: The deficiencies are: (1) no aircraft type — the controller cannot apply appropriate wake turbulence separation, assign correct approach speeds, or anticipate a helicopter's need for a non-standard arrival path; (2) no ATIS information — the controller does not know if the pilot has current weather, altimeter setting, or NOTAM information, which could affect the approach minimums decision; (3) no position report — the controller must spend additional time with radar identification and may issue an inefficient vector. The safety issue arises specifically for helicopters because approach controllers may assume fixed-wing performance (speed, descent rate) without aircraft type confirmation. On a non-precision approach, if the controller issues a speed restriction or expect-further-clearance altitude based on assumed aircraft type, the helicopter pilot may be unaware it does not apply or may comply unnecessarily, potentially creating a collision hazard or a stabilized approach problem.
questions.follow_up: The student argues that since the controller responded and gave a clearance, communication was 'established' and the content didn't matter. How do you explain to the student why proper initial call-up information is still required even when the controller responds?
questions.follow_up_answer: Two-way communication being 'established' only means the controller acknowledged your callsign — it does not mean the quality or completeness of the communication was acceptable. The AIM 4-2-3 outlines what a proper initial call-up should contain specifically because the controller needs that data to provide safe separation and sequencing. In a busy terminal environment, a controller who must ask for missing information ties up frequency time, delays other traffic, and increases pilot workload at a high-workload phase of flight. Furthermore, if the controller issues instructions based on an incorrect assumption (e.g., treating your helicopter like a fixed-wing aircraft), an incomplete callup was the root cause. Proper phraseology is not a formality — it's a safety tool.

questions.question: During the practical test, you observe the applicant fly an entire non-precision approach with correct navigation and accurate MDA control, but they only transmitted when required by ATC and never voluntarily provided position reports or condition updates. At a towered airport in IMC, was anything missing from a communication standards standpoint?
questions.answer: At a towered airport under IFR in a radar environment, ATC is responsible for separation and sequencing — the pilot is not required to provide unsolicited position reports as long as two-way communication is maintained with the appropriate ATC facility for each phase. However, there are specific required transmissions: reporting leaving assigned altitudes, reporting established on a published segment if required by ATC, reporting the FAF inbound if requested, and reporting a missed approach. If none of these situations arose and ATC never requested additional reports, the applicant may have been technically within standards. The examiner would need to assess whether the applicant was actively monitoring and ready to communicate, or simply passive. A fully competent IFR pilot also understands when voluntary communication adds safety value — such as calling the missed approach promptly — and would do so without prompting.
questions.follow_up: What if this same approach was flown into a non-towered airport where an FSS was not available and no CTAF calls were made? Would that change your evaluation?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, significantly. At a non-towered airport without ATC radar service, self-announce CTAF calls are the primary mechanism for traffic awareness and collision avoidance. The AIM 4-1-9 recommends broadcasting position and intentions at approximately 10 miles out, on each leg of the traffic pattern or approach segment, on final, and when clear of the runway. Failure to make any CTAF broadcasts during an IMC approach into a non-towered airport is a meaningful safety deficiency, even if no regulatory violation occurred in the absence of other traffic. On the practical test, this would reflect a gap in the applicant's understanding of communication as a collision avoidance tool, not just a regulatory obligation, and would likely result in additional questioning or a task failure determination depending on the severity.

questions.question: When setting up a VOR for a non-precision approach in a helicopter, how do you confirm the VOR station is operational and correctly identified?
questions.answer: Tune the VOR receiver to the published frequency for that approach, then listen to the Morse code identifier broadcast by the station and compare it to the identifier printed on the approach chart. If the station is undergoing maintenance, it will broadcast the identifier with a TEST or TST signal, or the identifier may be removed entirely — in either case, the VOR should not be used for navigation. You must hear the correct Morse code identifier match before relying on that VOR for an approach.

questions.question: What does it mean when a VOR ground station transmits the Morse code identifier at a slower-than-normal rate or preceded by 'T-E-S-T'?
questions.answer: A slow or TEST Morse code transmission indicates the VOR is operating in a test or unreliable status and should not be used for IFR navigation. When a VOR is out of service or undergoing flight checks, the FAA may remove the identifier entirely or broadcast a test signal. If no identifier is heard, or a TEST signal is present, the station is not authorized for instrument navigation and the pilot must not use it for an approach.

questions.question: On an NDB/ADF approach, after you tune the ADF receiver to the NDB frequency, what must you do before using that bearing for guidance on the approach?
questions.answer: After tuning the frequency, you must confirm station identification by listening to the Morse code or voice identifier broadcast by the NDB and matching it to the identifier shown on the approach chart. You should also verify the ADF needle deflects consistently toward the station and is not pointing erratically, which could indicate interference or a weak signal. Only after positive identification and a stable needle indication should you use the ADF for approach guidance.

questions.question: You're flying a helicopter IFR and are cleared for a VOR approach. While setting up, you tune the frequency and get needle movement on the CDI, but when you press the identifier button you hear nothing — just static. What do you do and why?
questions.answer: If you cannot positively identify the VOR by its Morse code identifier, you must not use it for the approach, regardless of CDI needle activity. CDI movement without a confirmed identifier could mean you've tuned the wrong frequency, the station is temporarily off the air, or you're receiving an unreliable signal. You should notify ATC immediately that you are unable to identify the VOR, request an alternate approach if available, or hold while troubleshooting. Never begin a final approach descent on an unidentified NAVAID — it is a violation of IFR procedure and a significant safety risk.

questions.question: Your helicopter is equipped with a GPS/WAAS navigator and you've been cleared for an LNAV approach. Walk me through how you confirm the GPS is appropriate and operationally ready before beginning the approach.
questions.answer: First, verify the approach is loaded correctly in the FMS/GPS by cross-checking the approach name, airport, runway, and waypoints against the paper or electronic chart. Confirm RAIM or WAAS integrity is available — for WAAS-equipped units, look for the WAAS status annunciation and check that approach mode will activate at the FAF. Confirm there are no active NOTAMs disabling GPS or WAAS in the area. Verify the GPS database is current (updated within the last 28 days). As you approach the FAF, confirm the navigator transitions from terminal to approach sensitivity (CDI narrows to ±0.3 NM for LNAV). If WAAS is providing vertical guidance (LNAV+V or LPV), confirm the appropriate minimums are being used. The unit should annunciate 'APPROACH' or 'LPV/LNAV' active before the FAF.

questions.question: You're inbound on a VOR approach and notice your CDI has a red OFF flag showing. You still have 8 miles to the VOR. What are your options, and what does that flag tell you about the signal?
questions.answer: A red OFF flag on the VOR CDI indicates the receiver is not receiving a usable signal from the station — this could be due to line-of-sight obstruction at low altitude, terrain shadowing, receiver failure, or the station being off the air. VOR is a VHF line-of-sight system, so signal reception depends on altitude and distance from the station. At 8 miles out, you should be within range if terrain is not a factor. Your options are: (1) cross-check against a backup VOR if available, (2) advise ATC of the issue and request radar vectors or an alternate approach, or (3) if the flag clears and identification is confirmed, you may continue. You must never descend below MDA without a reliable, identified navigation signal.

questions.question: A pilot flies an NDB approach and says, 'I identified the station at initial setup, so I didn't re-check the identifier during the approach.' As an examiner, what concern does this raise, and what is the correct standard?
questions.answer: This is a significant procedural gap. NDB stations can shift frequencies, experience interference, or fail mid-flight. Additionally, at low altitudes near terrain, ADF needles can be deflected by electrical storms, other transmitters, or static buildup — sometimes called 'false bearing' errors. The correct standard is to periodically re-confirm the identifier during the approach, not just at initial setup. While the AIM does not specify an exact re-check interval, best practice and instrument training doctrine call for confirming the identifier at each key gate: the IAF, the FAF, and when established on final. A single identification at setup does not guarantee the station remained reliable throughout the approach.
questions.follow_up: What specific environmental factor unique to helicopters flying low-and-slow approaches could further degrade ADF accuracy compared to a fixed-wing aircraft on the same approach?
questions.follow_up_answer: Helicopters often fly non-precision approaches at lower airspeeds and altitudes than fixed-wing aircraft, placing them closer to terrain, power lines, and structures that can induce ADF bearing errors. Additionally, rotor wash and the metallic rotor system itself can create interference with the ADF antenna, particularly on older airframes where antenna placement is not optimally separated from rotor components. At very low altitudes on final, the helicopter may also encounter static discharge and precipitation static more significantly, causing needle oscillation. These factors mean a helicopter pilot must be especially vigilant in monitoring ADF reliability throughout the approach, not just at the outset.

questions.question: Your helicopter has a certified IFR GPS with an expired navigation database, but the actual approach waypoints you've manually verified are unchanged from the current chart. A fellow pilot says it's fine to fly the GPS approach since nothing has changed. What is the regulatory and practical problem with this?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.175 and the AIM, IFR use of GPS for instrument approaches requires a current, FAA-approved navigation database. Flying an approach with an expired database is not authorized for IFR operations, even if the pilot believes the data is unchanged. The database also contains RAIM/WAAS integrity predictions, frequency assignments, obstacle clearance data, and procedural constraints — any of which may have changed without a corresponding chart revision. Additionally, many GPS units will not activate approach mode or will generate a warning when the database is expired, which itself compromises the operational status confirmation required before beginning an approach. The correct action is to either obtain a current database, use an alternate approach with approved equipment, or declare the GPS unavailable for IFR use and request a different approach.
questions.follow_up: If the GPS database has expired but the unit is functioning normally with no warnings, is there any scenario where using it for situational awareness — but not primary guidance — on an approach would be acceptable?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes — an expired GPS database may be used for situational awareness only, provided the pilot uses a properly identified and operational primary NAVAID (such as a current VOR or NDB) as the sole navigation source for the approach. In this case, the GPS serves as a supplemental cross-check, not the primary means of navigation. The pilot must make clear to ATC which NAVAID is being used for the approach and must not use the GPS CDI or course guidance as the basis for descent decisions. This is consistent with the AIM guidance that GPS with an expired database is not approved for IFR navigation but does not prohibit its use as a situational awareness tool.

questions.question: During a non-precision approach, ATC issues you a clearance to 'cross MAPCO intersection at or above 3,000 feet.' What does compliance with that clearance require of you as the pilot?
questions.answer: Compliance requires that you reach MAPCO intersection at an altitude of 3,000 feet MSL or higher — not below it. You must plan your descent profile so that you arrive at the fix at or above the assigned altitude. If you cannot comply, you must notify ATC immediately and request an amended clearance.

questions.question: ATC clears you for the VOR approach and instructs you to 'report procedure turn inbound.' What are the two distinct obligations embedded in that single clearance?
questions.answer: First, you are authorized to execute the VOR approach procedure, including the procedure turn. Second, you have a specific reporting requirement — you must contact ATC when you are established inbound on the final approach course after completing the procedure turn. Failing to report is a clearance compliance failure.

questions.question: During a non-precision approach, if you receive an amended clearance from ATC that changes your assigned altitude while you are already established on final, what is the correct immediate action?
questions.answer: Read back the amended clearance in full to confirm you received it correctly, then comply with it. If you cannot safely comply — for example, if executing the change would cause you to violate a step-down fix altitude or compromise obstacle clearance — you must advise ATC immediately of your inability to comply and request an alternative instruction. You may not simply ignore or delay an ATC clearance.

questions.question: You are flying a helicopter on the LOC/DME-E approach. ATC clears you for the approach and adds 'maintain 2,500 until established.' You reach the final approach fix (FAF) before you are fully established on the localizer. How do you handle the conflict between the published FAF crossing altitude and ATC's altitude restriction?
questions.answer: ATC's instruction to 'maintain 2,500 until established' supersedes the published FAF crossing altitude until you are established on the final approach course. You must comply with the ATC restriction first. Once you are established — meaning you are on the localizer course within the normal full-scale deflection limits and tracking it — you may then descend in accordance with the published approach procedure. If this creates a geometry problem where you cannot make a stabilized approach, advise ATC and request a revised clearance or a side-step if appropriate.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.123; AIM 5-4-6; Instrument Flying Handbook FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9

questions.question: During your non-precision approach briefing, you note the published missed approach procedure. Shortly after passing the FAF, ATC issues: 'Helicopter 5ZX, go around, turn left heading 270, climb and maintain 3,000.' How does this differ from the published missed approach, and which do you follow?
questions.answer: ATC's issued missed approach instruction overrides the published missed approach procedure. The published procedure is a default to be used when no ATC missed approach instructions have been issued. Since ATC has issued specific vectors and an altitude — heading 270, climb to 3,000 — you must comply with those instructions rather than turning to the published missed approach fix or following the charted climb gradient. Execute the go-around immediately, apply collective for maximum power, establish a positive climb, then comply with the heading and altitude as assigned.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.123; AIM 5-4-21; Instrument Flying Handbook FAA-H-8083-15B

questions.question: You are flying an NDB approach in a helicopter. ATC clears you for the approach and then issues a speed restriction: 'Maintain 90 knots until 5 DME.' You are currently flying at 110 knots. Describe specifically how you comply with this clearance while managing the helicopter on approach.
questions.answer: You must slow to 90 knots and maintain that speed until reaching 5 DME from the referenced NAVAID. In a helicopter, you would reduce collective slightly to reduce power and bleed off airspeed, adjusting cyclic to maintain approach attitude. You must reach 90 knots before passing 5 DME — not at 5 DME. Once past 5 DME, the speed restriction is lifted and you may adjust to your normal final approach speed. Throughout this, you must also continue to comply with all altitude restrictions on the approach and maintain ADF needle tracking.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.123; AIM 4-4-11; Instrument Flying Handbook FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9

questions.question: Halfway down the VOR final approach course, ATC issues a clearance you partially hear due to radio interference. You catch your callsign and the words 'climb maintain' but miss the assigned altitude. What is the correct procedure, and what must you NOT do while awaiting clarification?
questions.answer: Immediately request a full repeat of the clearance: 'Center, Helicopter 5ZX, say again clearance, missed altitude.' Do not guess at the altitude or begin climbing to an assumed figure. While awaiting the response, continue complying with the last clearance you received and understood — in this case, continue the approach as cleared. If you cannot reach ATC and the instruction sounded like an emergency or immediate climb instruction (e.g., traffic conflict), declare NORDO procedures may apply, but absent that urgency, hold position in the last known clearance until confirmed. Flying an assumed altitude that was not actually issued is a clearance deviation.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.123; AIM 4-4-4; 14 CFR 91.185 (two-way radio failure guidance)
questions.follow_up: If you cannot re-establish communication and you are already past the FAF, what do you do?
questions.follow_up_answer: If two-way radio communication fails after passing the FAF, 14 CFR 91.185 governs. You are considered NORDO. Since you received your approach clearance before the failure, you may continue the approach and land — radio failure after the FAF does not require you to abandon an approach already in progress. Complete the approach, land, and then contact ATC by any available means (phone, UNICOM relay, squawk 7600) as soon as practicable.

questions.question: During the practical test, the evaluator — acting as ATC — issues you a clearance to descend to an altitude that is below the published MDA for the VOR approach you are executing, and you are not yet at the MAP. How do you handle compliance with this clearance?
questions.answer: You must not descend below the MDA unless you meet all three conditions of 14 CFR 91.175(c): the aircraft is continuously in a position from which a normal landing can be made, the flight visibility meets the published minimum, and you have one of the required visual references in sight. Even if an ATC or evaluator instruction directs you lower, you cannot legally descend below MDA without those conditions being met. The correct response is to advise: 'Unable, below MDA, do not have required visual references' and request an amended clearance or initiate the missed approach. An evaluator issuing such a clearance is testing whether you will prioritize regulatory compliance over ATC instruction.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175(c); 14 CFR 91.123; Instrument Flying Handbook FAA-H-8083-15B
questions.follow_up: If you are at the MDA in level flight and the evaluator says 'continue descent, runway in sight,' but you personally cannot see the runway, what do you do?
questions.follow_up_answer: You must not descend. The visual reference requirement of 14 CFR 91.175(c) is personal to the pilot-in-command — it is YOUR flight visibility and YOUR visual contact that matters.
