questions.question: You are established on the final approach segment of an LNAV approach and leveled at MDA. You have flown past the VDP but the MAP is still 30 seconds away. You have no visual contact with the runway environment. Describe your altitude management obligations and what you do at the MAP.
questions.answer: Once you reach MDA and level off, you must maintain altitude at MDA — the ACS allows +100 feet above but 0 feet below. You are not permitted to descend further without the required visual references regardless of how close the MAP is. Because you passed the VDP without visual contact, a normal descent to the runway is no longer possible even if you acquire visual references before the MAP — initiating a descent from MDA beyond the VDP typically results in an unstabilized approach. At the MAP, if the required visual references (as defined in 14 CFR 91.175(c)) are not clearly established, you must immediately execute the published missed approach procedure. Continuing past the MAP without visual contact is a regulatory violation.

questions.question: On a non-precision approach in a helicopter, why is airspeed control within ±10 knots particularly important during the final approach segment, and how does an airspeed deviation affect your ability to manage the other ACS tolerances?
questions.answer: In a helicopter, airspeed directly affects rotor system efficiency, translational lift, and the rate of descent. If airspeed drops more than 10 knots below target on final, rotor efficiency decreases and the power required increases — the pilot may need to add collective to maintain altitude, which can lead to MDA busts or an unstable approach. If airspeed exceeds target by more than 10 knots, the aircraft will cover ground faster than planned, compressing the time available to identify visual references before the MAP, and will require more collective reduction to avoid climbing above MDA. Either deviation creates a cascade effect: the pilot must simultaneously correct airspeed while managing CDI deflection and altitude, increasing cognitive workload and the likelihood of exceeding one of the other tolerances. Stabilized approach technique — established on course, airspeed, and altitude before the final approach fix — is the most effective way to manage all three parameters simultaneously.
questions.regulatory_ref: ACS IH.VII.A.S12; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9

questions.question: During your checkride, you fly a VOR non-precision approach and maintain ¾ scale or less CDI deflection the entire time, but your altitude at level-off is 80 feet above MDA and you hold it there precisely all the way to the MAP without ever going below. I observe a steady ¾ scale CDI deflection for the last mile of the approach. Have you met the ACS standards? Explain your reasoning.
questions.answer: The altitude standard is technically met — you are within the +100/-0 foot tolerance above MDA. However, the CDI deflection standard is marginally met only if the deflection did not exceed ¾ scale at any point. A steady ¾ scale deflection held for a full mile is at the absolute limit of the standard and raises a real-world concern: you are at the edge of the protected obstacle clearance area for the final approach course, and any further drift would result in a failure. From an examiner's perspective, a sustained ¾ scale deflection with no trend toward centerline suggests a lack of effective course tracking technique rather than precise flying. The ACS standard is 'no more than ¾ scale' — technically you passed — but the quality of the performance would invite a follow-up discussion about whether you were truly in command of the approach or simply lucky not to exceed the limit.
questions.follow_up: If that same ¾ scale deflection had been on a localizer rather than a VOR, would the significance of the deviation be different, and why?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, significantly. A localizer CDI is approximately 4–5 times more sensitive than a VOR CDI. Full-scale localizer deflection represents about 2.5° of course deviation, compared to approximately 12° for a VOR. This means ¾ scale on a localizer equals roughly 1.875° off course, while ¾ scale on a VOR equals approximately 9° off course. Although the ACS uses the same '¾ scale' language for both, the actual lateral displacement from centerline is dramatically larger on a VOR approach. On a localizer-based approach (which is technically a precision or precision-like approach), sustaining ¾ scale deflection would represent a much tighter and more critical deviation relative to the runway centerline and the ILS protected area. This distinction highlights why pilots must understand the underlying sensitivity of the navigation system they are using, not just the raw needle position.

questions.question: A helicopter pilot flying a GPS LNAV approach descends to MDA and levels off, holding altitude within ACS tolerance. As the aircraft approaches the VDP, the pilot notices the CDI begin to deflect slowly right, reaching ½ scale by the time the VDP is reached. The pilot has not yet acquired visual references. What is the correct immediate action, and what does this scenario reveal about the pilot's scan and workload prioritization during the final approach segment?
questions.answer: The correct immediate action at the VDP without required visual references is to execute the missed approach — the VDP is the last point from which a normal descent to the runway is possible, and without visual contact the approach cannot be continued safely. The slow CDI drift to ½ scale before the VDP reveals a breakdown in the instrument cross-check: the pilot was likely focused on altitude management at level-off and did not detect or correct the gradual course deviation early enough. In helicopter IFR flying, the final approach segment demands a continuous, disciplined scan cycling through CDI, altimeter, airspeed indicator, and vertical speed indicator. A drift to ½ scale that goes uncorrected to the VDP indicates the scan slowed or fixated — a classic symptom of high workload or task saturation near MDA. A well-managed approach would catch and correct a CDI deviation well before it reaches ½ scale, maintaining a steady trend toward centerline throughout. This scenario also illustrates the 'error chain' concept: altitude preoccupation leads to course deviation, which leads to an unstabilized approach at the VDP — multiple small failures compounding into a missed approach or worse.
questions.follow_up: If this same pilot, rather than executing the missed approach at the VDP, instead descended below MDA because they thought they saw the runway environment, what regulatory standard governs whether that descent was legal, and what are the specific visual references required?
questions.follow_up_answer: The descent below MDA is governed by 14 CFR 91.175(c), which states that no pilot may operate an aircraft below MDA or continue an approach below DH unless three conditions are simultaneously met: (1) the aircraft is continuously in a position from which a descent to a landing on the intended runway can be made at a normal rate of descent using normal maneuvers, (2) the flight visibility is not less than the visibility prescribed in the IAP being used, and (3) at least one of the following visual references for the intended runway is distinctly visible and identifiable — the approach light system, threshold, threshold markings, threshold lights, REIL, VASI/PAPI, touchdown zone or markings or lights, runway or runway markings, runway lights, or ILS touchdown zone lights. Simply 'thinking' the runway environment is visible is insufficient — the reference must be distinctly visible and identifiable. A glow of lights or a vague outline does not meet this standard. Descending below MDA without meeting all three conditions simultaneously is a regulatory violation regardless of the outcome.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175(c); ACS IH.VII.A.S12; AIM 5-4-19; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13

questions.question: At the MDA on a non-precision approach, what specific visual references must you have before you can descend below MDA and continue for landing?
questions.answer: Per 14 CFR 91.175(c), you must have the flight visibility at or above the published minimum AND at least one of the following in sight: the approach light system, threshold, threshold markings, threshold lights, runway end identifier lights (REIL), visual approach slope indicator (VASI/PAPI), touchdown zone or markings, runway or runway markings, or runway lights. You must also be in a position to make a normal descent to landing.

questions.question: What is the difference between decision altitude (DA) and MDA, and why does that distinction matter when you're assessing visual references on a non-precision approach?
questions.answer: A DA is used on precision approaches — you must initiate the missed approach at or before reaching DA. An MDA is used on non-precision approaches — you may not descend below MDA unless you have the required visual references AND are in a position to land using normal maneuvers. The difference matters because at an MDA you can legally circle at that altitude awaiting visual contact, whereas at a DA the missed approach must be initiated at that point if you don't have the required references.

questions.question: When must you initiate the missed approach procedure on a non-precision approach if you have not acquired the required visual references?
questions.answer: You must initiate the missed approach at or before reaching the missed approach point (MAP). You may not continue past the MAP without the required visual references and flight visibility. Additionally, even if you have the runway in sight at MDA, if at any point those references are lost before landing, you must execute the missed approach immediately.

questions.question: You're flying an LNAV approach in your helicopter at night. At MDA you can see the approach light system (ALS) but nothing else. The published flight visibility minimum is 1 mile and you estimate your flight visibility is about 1 mile. Can you descend below MDA and continue to land? Walk me through your decision-making.
questions.answer: Seeing only the approach lights does not authorize descent below 100 feet above the touchdown zone elevation (TDZE) unless you also see the red terminating bars or the red side row bars — per 14 CFR 91.175(c)(1). If you can see those red ALS components in addition to the forward ALS, you may continue to 100 feet above TDZE, but you still cannot continue to landing without additional runway environment references (threshold, markings, touchdown zone, etc.). At night, this assessment is more difficult. If the red ALS bars are visible and estimated flight visibility meets the published minimum, you may descend to 100 feet AGL above TDZE; otherwise, execute the missed approach. Also critical: your position must allow a normal rate of descent to landing — as a helicopter pilot you have more flexibility here, but you cannot deviate from stabilized approach criteria.

questions.question: You reach MDA on a VOR approach in your helicopter and spot the runway — but you're significantly high and fast due to a tailwind that was stronger than forecast. You have the required visual references. Are you required to continue to land, or can you execute a missed approach? What factors should drive that decision?
questions.answer: You are never required to land — 14 CFR 91.175 permits a missed approach at any time. Having the required visual references only means you are legally allowed to continue, not obligated to. In this scenario, if you cannot make a stabilized, normal approach to landing from your current position using normal helicopter maneuvering, you must execute the missed approach. A high, fast approach significantly increases the risk of loss of control, landing long, or dynamic rollover on touchdown. ADM and SRM principles support choosing a known good option over one that will 'probably' work out — executing the missed approach and setting up for another attempt is the sound decision.

questions.question: During a non-precision approach in IMC, you briefly acquire the runway at MDA but then lose sight of it in patchy fog as you continue inbound. What are your obligations at that point, and how should you respond as a helicopter pilot?
questions.answer: Once the required visual references are lost, you must immediately execute the missed approach — 14 CFR 91.175(c) requires that the required visual references be maintained continuously from the point of descent below MDA through landing. You cannot continue descending and 'hope' to reacquire the runway. As a helicopter pilot, you should immediately apply the published missed approach procedure: climb to the published missed approach altitude, follow the lateral course, and contact ATC. Do not delay the missed approach — continuing into deteriorating visibility below MDA without visual references is a serious regulatory violation and extremely hazardous.

questions.question: On a non-precision approach at night, you acquire the runway at MDA and begin descent. At 200 feet AGL you realize you have the wrong runway in sight — you're lined up on a parallel taxiway with lights that looked like runway edge lights. What should you do and why is this scenario particularly relevant to helicopters?
questions.answer: Immediately execute the missed approach. The 'runway' you're aligned with is not an approved landing area — the visual references you have no longer qualify under 14 CFR 91.175(c) because a taxiway is not a runway. Continuing descent toward a taxiway creates serious collision hazard with ground vehicles and personnel. This is particularly relevant to helicopters because pilots sometimes rationalize that a taxiway or open area is 'good enough' for a helicopter landing — it is not on an instrument approach where 14 CFR 91.175 applies. Additionally, from an ADM standpoint, this is a classic error chain scenario: misidentification of runway at night, confirmation bias, and continuation of an unstable approach. Breaking the chain with an immediate missed approach is the only correct response.
questions.follow_up: Once you're established on the missed approach, what would you tell ATC, and what are your options for a second attempt?
questions.follow_up_answer: Immediately advise ATC you are executing the missed approach and state the reason — something like 'Executing missed approach, misidentified runway.' ATC needs to know so they can separate you from other traffic and reassign a clearance. For a second attempt, ATC will provide vectors or clearance back to the IAF. You should also assess why the misidentification occurred: ATIS for current conditions, brief the approach again, use all available cues (PAPI/VASI if available, ILS if available, GPS moving map) to confirm alignment before descending below MDA on the next attempt. You should also consider whether crew workload, fatigue, or environmental factors contributed to the error.

questions.question: As a helicopter pilot flying a non-precision approach to a helipad at an offshore oil platform, the reported visibility is right at minimums. You reach MDA and can see the helipad lights but the deck appears to be moving and you can't clearly determine the vessel's heading. Are the required visual references met, and what factors should influence your go/no-go decision here?
questions.answer: Technically, the helipad lights may qualify as a visual reference under 14 CFR 91.175(c) if they correspond to the threshold or landing area lighting. However, 91.175(c) also requires that you be in a position to make the landing using normal maneuvers — and if the vessel is moving, pitching, or its heading is indeterminate, this condition may not be met. An unclear deck heading is operationally significant because landing direction relative to relative wind on a moving vessel directly affects rotor control and landing safety. The regulatory minimum is the floor, not the standard for operational go/no-go. ADM applies: if you cannot positively determine the platform's orientation and confirm a safe approach direction, you do not have the situational awareness required to land safely. Executing a missed approach and reassessing — getting updated platform status from the vessel operator or ATC — is the correct decision. The Trescott principle from FAA-H-8083-21B applies: if it will only 'probably' work out, choose an option you know will work.
questions.follow_up: If you execute the missed approach and hold while waiting for conditions to improve, what fuel and regulatory considerations apply specifically to IFR helicopter operations?
questions.follow_up_answer: Under 14 CFR 91.167, IFR flight fuel requirements require enough fuel to complete the flight to the first airport of intended landing, fly from there to the alternate airport (if one is required), and fly after that for 45 minutes at normal cruise speed. If you are now holding and burning through reserves, you must assess whether you can still reach your alternate with required reserves. As a helicopter operating under 91.167, the 45-minute reserve applies. If your fuel state no longer supports reaching the alternate plus 45 minutes, you must declare minimum fuel or emergency fuel as appropriate and advise ATC — this changes your priority handling. Additionally, if the destination is deteriorating below alternates minimums, you must legally divert rather than continue to hold indefinitely.

questions.question: What is the primary purpose of using the MFD moving map during a non-precision approach in a helicopter?
questions.answer: The MFD moving map provides continuous situational awareness by showing the helicopter's current position relative to the approach path, nearby terrain, airspace boundaries, and the destination. During a non-precision approach, it allows the pilot to monitor track, identify any lateral deviation from the intended course, and confirm position relative to step-down fixes and the missed approach point — especially useful in confined or mountainous areas common to helicopter operations.

questions.question: How can you use the MFD to identify wind drift during a non-precision approach?
questions.answer: Most MFDs display both the aircraft's heading and its GPS-derived ground track. When those two values differ, the angular difference indicates the wind correction angle (crab) required to maintain the desired course. If the ground track vector shown on the moving map is drifting left or right of the extended centerline, the pilot can see the drift visually in real time and adjust heading accordingly to regain and maintain the desired track.

questions.question: On the MFD moving map during an approach, what is the difference between the heading bug vector and the ground track line, and why does it matter?
questions.answer: The heading bug vector shows the direction the nose of the helicopter is pointed (magnetic heading), while the ground track line shows the actual path being traveled over the ground as computed by GPS. The difference between the two is the wind correction angle. If you are flying a heading of 090° but your ground track shows 085°, you have 5° of wind drift pushing you north of course. Recognizing this difference allows the pilot to proactively correct crab angle rather than waiting for CDI deflection to grow.

questions.question: You are flying a VOR/DME non-precision approach and notice your CDI is centered, but the MFD moving map shows your position track gradually diverging left of the final approach course extended. How do you reconcile this and what action do you take?
questions.answer: A centered CDI with an off-track MFD depiction can result from several things: the VOR CDI has relatively coarse sensitivity (full-scale deflection at 10° off-course near the NAVAID), so small deviations may not register on the needle while being clearly visible on the GPS-driven moving map. Trust both instruments together — the MFD provides higher resolution positional data. Immediately apply a wind correction to the right to regain the correct track, and monitor whether the CDI begins to show a corresponding deflection as the deviation grows. Do not dismiss the MFD; use it to catch drift early before it becomes an un-briefed CDI deflection.

questions.question: During an RNAV (GPS) non-precision approach in IMC, how would you use the MFD terrain depiction or obstacle layer to improve situational awareness in a mountainous operating area common to helicopter EMS operations?
questions.answer: In mountainous terrain, the MFD terrain awareness display (color-coded terrain relative to aircraft altitude) allows the pilot to visually confirm adequate terrain clearance throughout the approach, not just at published step-down altitudes. The pilot should: (1) verify the terrain database is current; (2) keep the terrain overlay active alongside the approach course; (3) watch for amber or red terrain depictions that could indicate an obstacle proximity issue near the final approach segment; and (4) cross-check MFD terrain warnings with published MEA/MOCA values and the approach plate obstacle notes. This is especially critical for helicopter point-in-space approaches where the missed approach procedure may route through mountainous terrain.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B, Chapter 9; FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 11 (CFIT awareness); 14 CFR 91.175

questions.question: You are at the FAF inbound on a non-precision approach. Your workload spikes due to a passenger medical situation in back. Describe how you would manage the MFD to maintain situational awareness without over-scanning or neglecting primary flight instruments.
questions.answer: This is a workload management and SRM challenge. The correct technique is to reduce MFD interaction to brief, intentional glances — not continuous staring. Before the FAF, set the MFD range to show the full approach segment so minimal manipulation is needed inbound. Use the MFD as a cross-check, not a primary instrument. Prioritize: (1) attitude and power on primary flight instruments; (2) brief MFD scan to confirm on-track and no terrain anomalies; (3) timers and altimeter for step-down compliance. Declare a passenger emergency to ATC if needed to request priority handling, reducing the mental divide between flying and managing the situation. As the FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook notes, SRM integrates workload management — assign cognitive resources deliberately, and never let a secondary task degrade aircraft control.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 13 (SRM, workload management); FAA-H-8083-15B, Chapter 9

questions.question: Your MFD shows your position clearly on the correct final approach course, but your VOR CDI is deflecting full-scale to the left. You are 8 miles from the station. Which display do you trust, and what are the possible causes of this discrepancy?
questions.answer: At 8 miles from a VOR station, a full-scale CDI deflection represents being approximately 10° off the selected radial, which would be roughly 1.4 NM laterally — that is a significant deviation. If the GPS-driven MFD clearly shows you on course, the most likely causes are: (1) incorrect OBS setting on the VOR receiver; (2) VOR receiver malfunction or loss of signal; (3) the MFD is referencing a different navigation source (e.g., GPS overlay) while the CDI is slaved to the raw VOR; (4) the VOR NAVAID is experiencing a course bent or signal anomaly. The correct response is to verify the OBS setting matches the published inbound course, check the CDI source selector (VLOC vs GPS), and verify the VOR identifier by listening to the Morse code. Do not descend below MDA if primary navigation (VOR) is unreliable. The MFD is a supplemental tool — it does not replace certified navigation equipment for IFR approaches unless flying an RNAV approach with GPS as the primary source.
questions.follow_up: If this is an RNAV (GPS) approach and your GPS is driving both the MFD and the CDI — but they disagree — what does that most likely indicate and what immediate action is required?
questions.follow_up_answer: If both the MFD and the CDI are sourced from the same GPS receiver and they disagree with each other, this most likely indicates a display or avionics integration fault — not a navigation error. Possible causes include a partial avionics failure, a display rendering error, or database corruption. Immediate actions: (1) check for any RAIM, INTEG, or GPS status annunciations; (2) cross-check position against any other available navigation source (VOR, DME, or a second GPS if installed); (3) if integrity cannot be confirmed, execute the missed approach immediately — you cannot rely on either display; (4) declare a problem to ATC and request radar vectors. You must have RAIM confirmed and no GPS failure flags to continue an RNAV approach. A disagreement between co-sourced displays is a clear indication the system is not airworthy for approach guidance.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175; FAA-H-8083-15B, Chapter 9 (VOR CDI sensitivity, GPS RAIM); AIM 1-1-17

questions.question: A helicopter pilot flying a non-precision approach becomes so focused on the MFD moving map to track a complex curved path to a helipad that they fail to notice their altitude has dropped 200 feet below the published MDA. What ADM principle does this represent, and as the examiner, what would you expect to see a competent instrument helicopter pilot do differently?
questions.answer: This represents channelized attention — a form of fixation where the pilot over-focuses on one instrument or task to the exclusion of critical flight parameters. It is a classic human factors error chain link. According to the FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook, approximately 80% of aviation accidents involve pilot error, and fixation is a well-documented contributor. A competent instrument helicopter pilot should: (1) never use the MFD as a primary altitude reference — the altimeter and vertical speed indicator are primary; (2) set MDA in the altitude alerter or bug before the FAF so an aural/visual alert triggers if altitude deviates; (3) use a disciplined instrument scan that always includes altitude on each circuit, even when monitoring the MFD; (4) brief the approach thoroughly beforehand so the MFD requires only confirmation glances, not problem-solving attention; (5) apply crew resource management principles (even single-pilot) by verbalizing key altitudes at step-down fixes. The MFD is an excellent situational awareness tool, but it must never displace the primary scan.
questions.follow_up: If during this approach the pilot also had an audible MDA altitude alert and ignored it, what does that tell you about their aeronautical decision-making, and how does the 'error chain' concept apply?
questions.follow_up_answer: Ignoring an audible MDA alert while simultaneously fixating on the MFD represents multiple links in the error chain: (1) fixation on the MFD (first link); (2) failure to respond to a designed safety alert (second link); (3) busting MDA in IMC (third link — now in CFIT territory). The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook explicitly states that breaking just one link in the error chain can change the outcome. Any one of those three points was an opportunity to stop the sequence. As an examiner, this would represent an unsatisfactory performance not just for MFD use but for fundamental ADM, situational awareness, and altitude discipline — all of which are separate ACS elements. This scenario also illustrates the Trescott Tip from the Helicopter Flying Handbook: if the safe outcome only 'probably' will happen, choose the option you know will work — in this case, executing a go-around when alert triggers rather than assuming the approach will still work out.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 13 (ADM, error chain, fixation); 14 CFR 91.175(c) (MDA compliance); FAA-H-8083-15B, Chapter 9

questions.question: What does SRM stand for, and what are the core components it integrates during a non-precision instrument approach in a helicopter?
questions.answer: SRM stands for Single-Pilot Resource Management. It integrates risk management, situational awareness, workload management, controlled flight into terrain (CFIT) awareness, and automation management. During a non-precision approach, a single-pilot helicopter operator must manage all of these simultaneously — briefing the approach, monitoring altitude, maintaining awareness of terrain, and managing any automation or navigation equipment — without a second crewmember to cross-check.

questions.question: During an IFR non-precision approach, at what point in the sequence should you complete your approach briefing, and why does timing matter for SRM?
questions.answer: The approach briefing should be completed before beginning the descent or entering the terminal environment — ideally during cruise or while being vectored, before workload increases. Timing matters because SRM principles emphasize workload management: completing the briefing early keeps mental capacity available for flying, monitoring instruments, and communicating with ATC during the high-workload final approach segment. Attempting to brief while actively descending on final degrades situational awareness and increases risk.

questions.question: What is the 'error chain,' and how does it apply specifically to flying a non-precision helicopter approach single-pilot?
questions.answer: The error chain is a sequence of multiple poor decisions or errors that, when linked together, lead to an accident. No single link typically causes the accident — it is the accumulation. On a non-precision approach single-pilot, a typical error chain might start with a rushed approach briefing, followed by failing to set the MDA correctly, then becoming distracted by ATC communications, leading to descending below MDA without visual contact. Breaking any one of those links — such as executing a missed approach when visual contact is not established — changes the outcome. The FAA notes that approximately 80% of aviation accidents involve human factors.

questions.question: You are single-pilot in a helicopter flying a VOR non-precision approach in IMC. ATC issues a last-minute frequency change and a traffic advisory simultaneously as you pass the final approach fix. Walk me through how you apply SRM principles to manage this situation.
questions.answer: This is a classic workload spike at the highest-risk segment of the approach. Using SRM: First, prioritize aviate — maintain the approach profile, track the course, and hold altitude/descent rate. Do not allow the radio task to distract from flying. Acknowledge ATC briefly and professionally, then defer the full frequency change until workload permits — if necessary, say 'standby' to ATC. For the traffic advisory, assess whether it presents an immediate threat; if not, continue the approach while maintaining awareness. Use any available automation (GPS, autopilot) to reduce manual workload so cognitive capacity is available for the radio tasks. After stabilizing, complete the frequency change. Throughout, continuously cross-check that you remain on course and above the step-down fixes and MDA. The SRM principle here is workload management: sequence tasks, delegate to automation where possible, and never sacrifice aircraft control for a secondary task.

questions.question: You are flying a two-pilot helicopter IFR operation on an NDB non-precision approach. The flying pilot becomes fixated on the ADF needle and is drifting below the published step-down altitude. As the monitoring pilot, how does CRM require you to respond, and what specific language would you use?
questions.answer: CRM requires the non-flying/monitoring pilot to assertively call out deviations — this is a crew duty, not optional. The correct CRM response is a clear, direct callout: 'Altitude — we're below step-down, [altitude] is the minimum.' If the flying pilot does not correct immediately, escalate: 'My controls — go-around' and execute the missed approach. CRM principles stress that crew members must speak up regardless of experience differential or cockpit authority gradient. Waiting or hinting is not acceptable when safety is compromised. Afterward, debrief the event to understand why fixation occurred and how to prevent recurrence. The NDB approach is particularly susceptible to this because the ADF needle requires mental processing to determine track, increasing cognitive load and the risk of altitude neglect.

questions.question: You briefed the non-precision approach for Runway 18, but during vectors ATC offers a visual approach. The weather is reported at 1,200 broken and 5 miles visibility — technically VFR. Applying SRM risk management, what factors should influence your decision to accept or decline?
questions.answer: SRM risk management requires evaluating the full picture, not just the minimum legal standard. Factors to consider: (1) Is the ceiling and visibility stable, improving, or deteriorating? Reported conditions can change before you reach the runway. (2) Do you have a current, complete approach brief for the instrument approach already loaded as a backup? (3) What is terrain like in the area — a visual approach in marginal VFR conditions near rising terrain is a significant CFIT risk, which SRM specifically flags. (4) What is your personal currency and proficiency for visual vs. instrument approaches? (5) What is your fatigue and overall workload state? The FAA cautions against choosing options that will only 'probably' work out — if accepting the visual means losing the instrument backup plan and conditions are marginal, the instrument approach may be the lower-risk choice. Declining a visual approach is always acceptable and demonstrates sound SRM.

questions.question: During a single-pilot RNAV non-precision approach, your GPS displays a 'RAIM not available' message just after the final approach fix. You are in IMC at 500 feet above MDA with the runway environment not yet in sight. Using SRM, walk me through your decision-making process and the exact actions you take.
questions.answer: RAIM loss after the final approach fix means GPS integrity cannot be guaranteed — the approach is no longer valid. SRM demands immediate, decisive action: (1) Aviate — maintain current altitude, do not continue descending. (2) Communicate — advise ATC: 'RAIM lost, executing missed approach.' (3) Execute the published missed approach immediately, regardless of how close you feel you are to minimums. SRM's risk management principle is clear: if you cannot confirm the system providing navigation is reliable, you cannot safely continue. The temptation to 'press on' because the runway is probably close is exactly the 'probably' trap the FAA warns against. After initiating the missed approach, advise ATC, request alternate approach options or hold while troubleshooting, and assess whether a non-GPS approach (VOR, ILS, NDB) is available and your navigation equipment supports it. Document the RAIM failure for maintenance.
questions.follow_up: If RAIM was predicted to be unavailable for your arrival window during preflight planning, what should you have done, and what regulatory requirement addresses GPS approach availability?
questions.follow_up_answer: If RAIM was predicted unavailable during preflight, you should have selected an alternate navigation method — either a different approach type (ILS, VOR) or delayed the flight until RAIM availability was confirmed. Under 14 CFR 91.185 and the GPS approach NOTAMs, pilots must check RAIM availability via the FAA RAIM prediction tool or equivalent service before relying on GPS for an instrument approach. If WAAS is installed and operational, RAIM is automatically provided by the WAAS system and this concern is largely mitigated — but the pilot must verify WAAS operational status as part of the preflight. Flying a GPS approach without confirming RAIM/WAAS availability is a significant SRM failure at the preflight planning stage.

questions.question: You are the more experienced pilot in a two-pilot helicopter on a non-precision approach. You are the pilot monitoring. The flying pilot — a newer instrument pilot — is clearly behind the aircraft: slow to configure, has not called the FAF inbound, and you notice the MDA is not set. You recognize the scenario is deteriorating. How do you apply CRM without simply taking control, and at what point does CRM require you to take control?
questions.answer: CRM first calls for graduated intervention, not immediate takeover — because building the less-experienced pilot's decision-making is also a crew resource goal. Start with an inquiry: 'What's your plan at the FAF?' This prompts self-correction without undermining confidence. If no correction follows, escalate to a directive: 'Set MDA now — [altitude].' Simultaneously, call out any configuration items that are behind. If the aircraft is approaching a safety threshold — descending through a step-down fix without proper altitude set, or getting close to MDA in IMC without visual contact — you must escalate immediately: 'My controls — go-around.' CRM does not require you to watch a controlled flight into terrain to preserve a crew dynamic. The threshold for takeover is any condition where continued flight by the current pilot-in-control presents an imminent safety risk that verbal correction cannot fix in time. After landing, a thorough, non-punitive debrief is a CRM obligation — identify what broke down, what environmental or human factors contributed, and build a plan to prevent recurrence.
questions.follow_up: If you take control during the approach and execute a missed approach, who is the legal PIC for the flight, and what documentation responsibilities exist?
questions.follow_up_answer: The designated PIC under 14 CFR 91.3 remains the PIC for the flight — that legal designation does not transfer simply because the other pilot physically took the controls. However, if the originally designated PIC was not actually flying when the critical event occurred and you made all safety-of-flight decisions, there may be a practical question about who exercised PIC authority in the moment. Under 14 CFR 61.51, each pilot must log the flight time they acted as PIC or SIC. If both pilots are required crewmembers, both may log the appropriate time. The key regulatory point is 14 CFR 91.3(b): in an emergency, the PIC may deviate from any rule to the extent necessary to meet that emergency, and must submit a written report to the FAA if requested. If the situation required an emergency declaration, that should be documented.

tasks.title: Task B. Precision Approach

questions.question: What makes an ILS approach a 'precision approach,' and how does it differ from a non-precision approach?
questions.answer: A precision approach provides both lateral and vertical electronic guidance to the runway. The ILS provides a localizer for lateral guidance and a glideslope for vertical guidance, allowing the pilot to fly a precise glidepath to decision altitude (DA). A non-precision approach provides only lateral guidance — the pilot must use a published step-down profile or CDFA technique to descend to MDA. The key distinction is the presence of approved vertical guidance, which allows lower minima and a DA rather than an MDA.

questions.question: On an ILS approach, what is the standard glideslope angle, and what does a full-scale CDI deflection on the localizer represent in degrees?
questions.answer: The standard ILS glideslope angle is 3 degrees, though it may vary from approximately 2.5 to 4 degrees on some approaches. A full-scale localizer CDI deflection represents approximately 2.5 degrees off centerline — making the localizer 4 to 5 times more sensitive than a VOR, where full deflection represents 12 degrees or more. This high sensitivity requires smooth, precise control inputs especially in helicopters at slower airspeeds.

questions.question: What is Decision Altitude (DA) on a precision approach, and what must a pilot do if the required visual references are not established at DA?
questions.answer: Decision Altitude (DA) is the altitude (referenced to MSL) at which a decision must be made to either continue the approach or execute a missed approach. At DA, the pilot must have the runway environment in sight — specifically, the required visual references listed in 14 CFR 91.175(c) — to continue below DA. If those references are not clearly visible and identifiable at DA, the pilot must immediately execute the published missed approach procedure. Unlike MDA, the pilot cannot hover at DA waiting for conditions to improve.

questions.question: You are flying an ILS approach in a helicopter at 70 knots groundspeed on a 3-degree glideslope. What is the approximate required descent rate to stay on glidepath, and how would you calculate it?
questions.answer: A simple rule of thumb: multiply groundspeed by 5 to get the approximate feet-per-minute descent rate required for a 3-degree glideslope. At 70 knots, that gives 70 × 5 = 350 feet per minute. A more precise calculation uses the formula: descent rate = (groundspeed in knots × glideslope angle × 101.3). For a standard 3-degree slope, the simplified '×5' rule is accurate enough for practical use. Helicopters often fly ILS approaches slower than fixed-wing aircraft, so the required VSI reading will be lower — but the pilot must be careful not to let groundspeed decay further without adjusting the descent rate, or the aircraft will go above glidepath.

questions.question: The ILS approach chart for your destination shows a note: 'Inoperative glideslope: increase minimums to 700-2.' You arrive at the FAF and your glideslope flag comes into view. Can you continue the approach, and what procedure do you now fly?
questions.answer: Yes, you can continue, but you must convert to non-precision approach procedures. With the glideslope inoperative, you lose the vertical guidance that makes the ILS a precision approach — the approach now becomes a localizer (LOC) approach. You must use the higher minimums specified on the chart (700-2 in this case), fly the published step-down altitudes or use a constant descent angle technique to the localizer MDA, and apply the same missed approach criteria used for non-precision approaches. You may not descend below MDA unless the required visual references are in sight. Note that an inoperative glideslope flag appearing airborne does not necessarily mean it failed on the ground — verify the ATIS and NOTAM information.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175; Aeronautical Chart User's Guide; FAA-H-8083-15B

questions.question: Your helicopter is not equipped with an operating marker beacon receiver. The ILS approach you intend to fly shows the outer marker as the FAF. How does this affect your approach, and what alternatives do you have?
questions.answer: With an inoperative marker beacon receiver, you must check the approach chart and applicable NOTAMs for an alternative means of identifying the FAF. Most modern ILS approach charts provide a DME fix, a crossing radial from a nearby VOR, or a GPS waypoint to identify the FAF as an alternative to the outer marker. If one of these alternatives is available and you have the appropriate equipment, you may use it to identify the FAF and continue the approach legally. If no alternative FAF identification is available and you cannot determine the FAF, you must increase minimums as required by the inoperative components table in the front of the approach chart booklet (e.g., TPP), which may raise the ceiling/visibility requirements. The pilot must also check if ATC can provide a precision radar fix at the FAF as a substitute.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175; FAA Instrument Approach Procedure charts inoperative components table; FAA-H-8083-15B

questions.question: A pilot flies an ILS approach to DA and acquires the approach lights only — no runway environment is visible. They continue descending below DA because they can see the approach lights. At what point, if any, may they continue descending below 100 feet above TDZE, and what is the regulatory basis?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.175(c)(3), a pilot may descend below DA using approach lights as the sole visual reference, but only to 100 feet above the touchdown zone elevation (TDZE). To descend below 100 feet above TDZE, the pilot must have at least one of the following runway environment references in sight: the runway threshold, threshold markings, threshold lights, runway end identifier lights (REIL), visual approach slope indicator (VASI/PAPI), touchdown zone or markings, touchdown zone lights, runway or runway markings, or runway lights. If at 100 feet above TDZE only approach lights remain visible with no red terminating bars or red side row bars visible, descent may continue to 100 feet AGL but not lower. This rule applies equally to helicopter pilots and is a common source of confusion on checkrides.
questions.follow_up: What is the significance of seeing the red terminating bars or red side row bars on the approach lighting system in this scenario?
questions.follow_up_answer: Under 14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i), if the pilot can see the red terminating bars or red side row bars of the approach lighting system, those are considered part of the approach light system and the pilot may still only descend to 100 feet above TDZE — they do not grant authority to go lower on lights alone. However, the red bars provide spatial orientation cues that help the pilot determine if the runway threshold is close enough to transition to a landing. If neither the red bars nor any runway environment reference is visible below 100 feet AGL, a missed approach is mandatory.

questions.question: You are flying a helicopter ILS to a helipad using special instrument approach procedures. The approach has a DA of 300 feet MSL. Your alternator fails during the approach, and your glideslope indicator begins fluctuating. You have battery power remaining. Walk me through your decision-making regarding whether to continue the approach and what limitations now apply.
questions.answer: This is a compounding equipment failure scenario. First, with an alternator failure, you must assess remaining battery life and which systems are critical — the ILS receivers, flight instruments, and communications all draw power. If battery life is uncertain, the workload of managing a partial-panel ILS in IMC significantly increases risk. Regarding the fluctuating glideslope: if the glideslope is unreliable, you must treat it as inoperative and apply the inoperative component minimums from the approach chart — the approach reverts to a localizer approach with higher DA/MDA and visibility minimums. You must also consider whether the special instrument approach procedure (SIAP) to the helipad has published inoperative component tables, as not all SIAPs do. If no adjusted minimums are available for glideslope out, you may not be legally authorized to continue below the LOC MDA. Given the combination of electrical failure and glideslope unreliability, SRM principles from the Helicopter Flying Handbook suggest that continuing this approach likely places you in the 'improbable success' category — and the FAA guidance is clear: if an action will only 'probably' work, choose an option known to work. A missed approach to a better-equipped alternate is the safest decision.
questions.follow_up: If you declare an emergency due to the alternator failure, does that change the minimum equipment requirements or the legal authority to continue the ILS below the adjusted minimums?
questions.follow_up_answer: Declaring an emergency under 14 CFR 91.3(b) grants the pilot-in-command the authority to deviate from any rule to the extent necessary to meet the emergency. This means the PIC could legally continue below the adjusted LOC minimums if they determine it is necessary for the safety of the flight. However, this is not a blank check — the pilot must still be able to comply with 14 CFR 91.175(c) visual reference requirements before descending below DA/MDA, because those requirements exist for physical safety, not just regulatory compliance. After landing, the pilot must submit a written report to ATC upon request per 14 CFR 91.3(c). The emergency declaration changes legal authority but does not change the physical limitations of flying without a reliable glideslope in low IMC.

questions.question: On a CDI during an ILS approach, what does a full-scale deflection of the localizer needle represent in degrees off course, and how does that compare to a VOR CDI full-scale deflection?
questions.answer: A full-scale localizer CDI deflection represents approximately 2.5° off course. By comparison, a VOR CDI full-scale deflection represents 12° or more off course. This makes the localizer CDI roughly 4 to 5 times more sensitive than a VOR CDI, which is why small corrections are required when tracking the localizer on an ILS approach.

questions.question: What does a WAAS-enabled GPS receiver display on the CDI annunciation panel to indicate it is providing LPV (Localizer Performance with Vertical Guidance) approach guidance, and what does LPV mean operationally?
questions.answer: When a WAAS GPS receiver is providing LPV guidance, the annunciator will display 'LPV' in the approach mode field. Operationally, LPV is a type of RNAV approach that uses WAAS to provide lateral and vertical guidance with performance similar to an ILS, including glidepath guidance. It allows pilots to fly to decision altitudes as low as 200 feet AGL at qualifying airports, comparable to a CAT I ILS, but does not require ground-based ILS equipment.

questions.question: During an ILS approach, what is the purpose of the glideslope indicator on the CDI or EHSI, and what does it mean when the glideslope needle is positioned above center?
questions.answer: The glideslope indicator shows the aircraft's vertical position relative to the ILS glidepath signal transmitted from the ground. A needle positioned above center means the aircraft is below the glidepath — the needle always points toward the glidepath, so 'fly up' corrections are required. Conversely, a needle below center means the aircraft is above the glidepath and must descend. Standard glideslope angle for an ILS is typically 3°.

questions.question: You are flying a helicopter on an ILS approach and notice the HSI shows the localizer needle alive and centered, but the glideslope flag is showing. What does the glideslope flag indicate, and how should you proceed?
questions.answer: A glideslope flag (often a red 'GS' flag or a warning flag over the glideslope pointer) indicates that the glideslope receiver is not receiving a valid or reliable signal from the ground-based glideslope transmitter. This means vertical guidance is unreliable and should not be used. You should declare the approach a localizer-only approach, apply the localizer minimums (which are higher than ILS minimums), and use the published step-down fixes and MDA rather than the DH. ATC should be notified if the change affects your ability to complete the approach as cleared.

questions.question: You are briefing an RNAV (GPS) approach and note the chart shows both LNAV and LPV minimums. Your GPS navigator is WAAS-capable and the RAIM/WAAS integrity check passes before departure. During the approach, the unit annunciates 'LNAV' instead of 'LPV.' What are two possible reasons for this downgrade, and what operational change must you make?
questions.answer: Two possible reasons the system annunciated LNAV instead of LPV are: (1) WAAS signal integrity or accuracy has degraded below the threshold required to support LPV vertical guidance, and the receiver automatically stepped down to the next available mode; or (2) satellite geometry (VDOP — Vertical Dilution of Precision) is insufficient to support vertical navigation to LPV standards at that time and location. Operationally, you must use the LNAV minimums (MDA, not DH), treat the approach as a non-precision approach with no electronic vertical guidance, and plan your missed approach from the MAP rather than a decision altitude. You cannot use the lower LPV decision altitude.

questions.question: A helicopter pilot flying an ILS approach in IMC notices the localizer CDI is showing a slow, continuous full-scale deflection even though the aircraft is on the published centerline heading. What navigation display anomaly might explain this, and what action is appropriate?
questions.answer: A slow, continuous full-scale localizer deflection while tracking the correct inbound course could indicate: (1) the aircraft is flying the back course of the ILS rather than the front course (back course signal causes reverse sensing unless a back-course switch or HSI course pointer corrects for it); (2) the course selector on the CDI is not set to the inbound localizer course; or (3) there is a receiver or antenna malfunction. The appropriate action is to cross-check the published inbound course against the course set in the navigation instrument, verify you are receiving the correct ILS frequency, confirm the Morse code identifier, and if the anomaly persists and cannot be resolved, execute the missed approach and notify ATC of a possible navigation system or facility anomaly.

questions.question: During a coupled ILS approach in a helicopter equipped with an autopilot and FMS, the FMS mode annunciator shows 'APP' active and the autopilot is tracking both localizer and glideslope. Passing the FAF, the autopilot suddenly reverts from 'APP' to 'HDG' mode and the glideslope needle begins moving upward. Walk me through what has likely occurred, what the flight instruments will show, and exactly what pilot action is required in the next few seconds.
questions.answer: The transition from APP to HDG mode indicates the autopilot has disengaged from coupled approach mode and reverted to heading hold — likely due to a glideslope signal loss, localizer deviation exceeding coupled limits, an avionics fault, or inadvertent mode change. Simultaneously, the glideslope needle moving upward means the aircraft is sinking below the glidepath. With the autopilot now in HDG mode, it will maintain the current heading but will not correct for localizer or glideslope deviations — the aircraft will continue to descend below glidepath without automated correction. Immediate pilot action: (1) announce 'going missed' or take manual control immediately if below a safe altitude; (2) if sufficient altitude exists, manually fly to re-intercept the glidepath using pitch and power while monitoring both needles; (3) advise ATC of the autopilot reversion and declare intentions; (4) do not allow the aircraft to continue below MDA/DH without the required visual references. Given that this is a precision approach with potentially low ceilings, the safest action is almost always to execute the published missed approach immediately upon losing coupled guidance near or below the FAF.
questions.follow_up: If the glideslope flag had not appeared but the needle still moved above center, how would you determine whether the aircraft actually drifted below glidepath versus the glideslope signal bending due to interference or a false glideslope?
questions.follow_up_answer: You cross-check multiple independent data sources: (1) compare your altimeter reading against the published altitude at your DME fix or step-down fix — if you are at or above the charted altitude, the aircraft has not actually descended below the correct glidepath, suggesting signal anomaly; (2) check the VSI — if it shows a steady normal descent rate consistent with glidepath geometry (approximately 300–500 FPM for a helicopter on a 3° glideslope at typical approach speeds), the aircraft is likely tracking correctly; (3) use GPWS/TAWS terrain proximity alerts as a cross-check; (4) if DME is available, compare actual altitude to the glidepath altitude table printed on the approach chart at each DME fix. False glideslopes typically exist at angles steeper than the published glidepath (often 9° or 15°) and the aircraft's descent rate would be abnormally high if captured on one. If any doubt exists, execute the missed approach — the cost of a go-around is always lower than the cost of a CFIT accident.

questions.question: A helicopter crew is flying an RNAV (GPS) approach using a certified WAAS navigator. The unit annunciates 'LP' mode rather than 'LPV' or 'LNAV/VNAV.' The crew has never seen this annunciation before. What does LP mean, how does it differ from LPV and LNAV, and why is it significant for helicopter operations specifically?
questions.answer: LP stands for Localizer Performance — it is a lateral-only RNAV approach mode that provides lateral guidance with precision comparable to a localizer but no vertical guidance. It is generated when the WAAS system has enough integrity to support precision lateral guidance but cannot support the WAAS vertical component required for LPV. LP is more accurate than standard LNAV (which uses terminal RNAV tolerances of ±0.3 NM) because LP lateral sensitivity scales similarly to a localizer CDI as the aircraft approaches the runway threshold. However, LP provides no electronic glidepath — the crew must use the published LP MDA and step-down fixes just as with any non-precision approach. For helicopter operations specifically, LP is significant because helicopters are authorized to use published helicopter-specific approach minimums, and some heliport RNAV approaches are designed only with LP or LNAV minimums rather than LPV due to the unique obstacle environment near heliports. Additionally, because helicopters can use Point-in-Space (PinS) approaches, the crew must recognize that LP guidance only applies to the instrument portion of the PinS approach — the 'proceed visually' or 'proceed VFR' segment after the MAP is not guided by the navigation system at all.
questions.follow_up: If the approach plate shows LP minimums of 400-1 and the crew elects to fly it, at what point must they have the required visual references, and what is the missed approach point for an LP approach?
questions.follow_up_answer: For an LP approach, which is a non-precision approach, the crew must have the required visual references (runway environment, approach lights, etc. as defined in 14 CFR 91.175(c)) upon reaching the MDA and must maintain them throughout the descent to landing. The MDA is 400 feet AGL in this example. The missed approach point for an LP approach is defined on the chart — typically a specific distance from the threshold (often the runway threshold itself or a stated distance/time from the FAF) rather than a decision height. Unlike a precision approach where the missed approach is initiated at DH regardless of where the aircraft is physically, on an LP non-precision approach the crew must not descend below MDA unless visual references are established, and must execute the missed approach at or before the MAP even if still above MDA. If visual references are lost after descending below MDA, an immediate missed approach is required per 14 CFR 91.175(e).
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B, Chapter 9; 14 CFR 91.175; AC 90-107; FAA PinS Approach Design Criteria

questions.question: When flying a VOR-based instrument approach, your CDI shows a full-scale deflection. What does that represent in terms of degrees off course, and how does that compare to a full-scale localizer deflection?
questions.answer: A full-scale VOR CDI deflection represents 12 or more degrees off the selected radial. A full-scale localizer CDI deflection represents approximately 2.5 degrees off the localizer centerline. This makes the localizer roughly 4 to 5 times more sensitive than a VOR, which is why localizer approaches have significantly tighter lateral guidance and require smaller corrections.

questions.question: What is the difference between an MEA and a MOCA on an IFR en route chart, specifically regarding VOR navigation signal coverage?
questions.answer: Both the MEA (Minimum En Route Altitude) and the MOCA (Minimum Obstruction Clearance Altitude) guarantee obstacle clearance along the route. However, only the MEA guarantees adequate VOR navigation signal reception along the entire segment. The MOCA only guarantees VOR signal reception within 22 nautical miles of the NAVAID. Flying at the MOCA beyond 22 NM from the station means you have obstacle clearance but may not have reliable navigation signal.

questions.question: You are about to fly a GPS approach and notice a NOTAM indicating GPS signal testing in your area. What does this mean for your approach, and what regulation governs GPS equipment requirements for flying instrument approaches?
questions.answer: GPS signal testing or jamming NOTAMs indicate that GPS signal integrity may be unreliable or unavailable in a specific area and time window. If the NOTAM covers your approach time and location, you should not plan to use GPS as your primary navigation source for that approach. You must have an alternate means of navigation or divert. For IFR GPS use, the equipment must meet TSO-C129, TSO-C196, or TSO-C145/C146 (WAAS) standards, and the database must be current. Operations under 14 CFR 91.205 require IFR-approved avionics, and AIM Chapter 1 and 5 provide GPS RAIM and signal integrity requirements.

questions.question: You are flying a helicopter ILS approach in IMC when your ADF needle begins swinging erratically. ATC has not reported any NOTAMs about NDB outages. What are the possible causes, and how should you manage your navigation data integrity for the remainder of the approach?
questions.answer: Erratic ADF needle behavior can be caused by several factors: thunderstorm electrical activity (precipitation static), the ADF being tuned to a station below its usable reception range, station transmission interference, or a malfunctioning ADF receiver. ADF uses ground wave propagation and is susceptible to atmospheric interference and sky wave contamination at night. For this ILS approach, the ADF may be used as a non-required supplemental aid (such as identifying a fix), but the ILS localizer and glideslope are your primary navigation sources. You should cross-check the ILS indications against DME or GPS if available, report the anomaly to ATC, and not rely on the ADF for critical fix identification until the source of interference is resolved. Prioritize the ILS as the primary precision guidance.

questions.question: During a RNAV (GPS) approach in your helicopter, you receive a GPS RAIM alert just after the final approach fix. Walk me through your decision-making process regarding signal integrity and what options you have.
questions.answer: A RAIM (Receiver Autonomous Integrity Monitoring) alert after the FAF is a serious situation. RAIM checks that the GPS signal geometry is sufficient to detect errors that could affect navigation accuracy. If RAIM is lost on final approach, the GPS system cannot guarantee the accuracy of the position data. You should immediately execute the published missed approach using the best available navigation — whether from another GPS receiver, VOR, or DME if applicable. You should not continue below the FAF without verified RAIM integrity on a GPS approach. ATC should be notified of the situation. If WAAS (SBAS) is being used, check whether the annunciation indicates loss of LPV or LNAV/VNAV capability, as WAAS provides its own integrity monitoring separate from RAIM. Document the event for maintenance review.

questions.question: You are briefing a VOR approach and notice the chart indicates 'GPS or DME required.' Your helicopter has a VOR receiver, GPS, and no DME. Can you fly this approach? Explain how you determine orientation and course on a VOR approach versus a GPS approach.
questions.answer: Yes, you can fly this approach using your IFR-certified GPS in lieu of DME to identify fixes. FAA AC 90-108 allows GPS to substitute for DME on conventional approaches, provided the GPS meets the applicable equipment standards and the database is current. On a VOR approach, orientation is established by selecting the inbound course on the OBS and using CDI needle deflection — VOR radials are oriented FROM the station, so you center the needle with a TO indication on the inbound course. Course determination on a GPS approach uses the flight management system or GPS navigator to fly a defined lateral path to a waypoint sequence. The GPS provides along-track and cross-track guidance rather than the radial-based geometry of a VOR. Both systems require the pilot to understand that CDI sensitivity differs, and on an RNAV approach the scaling changes progressively from ±1 NM en route to ±0.3 NM at the FAF.

questions.question: A pilot argues that because their WAAS GPS is TSO-C146 certified, they never need to check RAIM availability during preflight for any approach. Is this accurate? Explain the specific integrity monitoring differences between WAAS and non-WAAS GPS, and under what conditions even a WAAS receiver could lose LPV approach capability.
questions.answer: This is not entirely accurate. WAAS (Wide Area Augmentation System) does provide its own continuous integrity monitoring through the SBAS network, which is more robust than standalone RAIM. Unlike conventional GPS where the pilot must verify RAIM availability via a prediction tool (especially within 1 hour of ETA), WAAS provides real-time integrity alerts through the ground network. However, WAAS LPV availability is not guaranteed — it depends on WAAS signal availability from SBAS geostationary satellites, which can be affected by satellite outages, high ionospheric activity (particularly during solar events), signal blockage, or WAAS system maintenance. If WAAS integrity is insufficient, the receiver will automatically downgrade from LPV to LNAV/VNAV or LNAV minimums, or even annunciate GPS not available. The pilot must check NOTAMs for WAAS outages and should understand that even a certified WAAS receiver can lose LPV capability in flight without warning due to real-time signal conditions. Preflight planning should always include a WAAS NOTAM check.
questions.follow_up: If your WAAS GPS downgrades from LPV to LNAV minimums automatically during an approach, and you are already inside the FAF, are you required to immediately execute a missed approach?
questions.follow_up_answer: Not necessarily immediately, but you must reassess your situation against the new applicable minimums. If you were flying to LPV DA and the system downgrades to LNAV, the MDA is now your applicable minimum, and you must evaluate whether you are still above that MDA and in a position to continue safely. If you have already descended below the LNAV MDA and cannot acquire the required visual references, you must execute an immediate missed approach. If you are above the LNAV MDA, you may continue the approach using LNAV minimums. The key issue is that the approach is no longer a precision or APV operation — you must fly a step-down profile to the MDA and comply with LNAV visibility requirements. Always cross-check with ATC and declare the situation if needed.

questions.question: A helicopter pilot is planning to fly an ILS approach at night into a remote hospital helipad. The ILS LOC and GS appear functional on a check, but the pilot notices the VOR collocated at the outer marker site has a flagged NOTAM about potential harmonic interference on localizer frequencies. How should the pilot assess localizer signal integrity, and what specific VOR/LOC interaction could cause false course guidance?
questions.answer: The pilot must treat this NOTAM seriously. ILS localizer signals operate in the 108–111.95 MHz frequency range, and VOR stations operate in the 108–117.95 MHz range — the lower end of both bands overlap. A VOR transmitter experiencing harmonic distortion can generate spurious signals that interfere with localizer receivers tuned to an adjacent or harmonically related frequency. This can produce false CDI deflections, erratic flag behavior, or a false course indication that mimics a valid signal. To assess integrity, the pilot should: (1) verify the localizer identifier is being received correctly (Morse code ID), since a false signal may not carry the correct identifier or may produce a continuous tone; (2) cross-check lateral position using GPS, if available, against the ILS centerline; (3) check whether the CDI behavior is consistent with expected aircraft position during approach; (4) brief the approach assuming the ILS may be unreliable and identify an alternate approach or diversion airport. At a hospital helipad, there may be no alternate instrument approach, making this risk management decision critical. The pilot should notify ATC of the NOTAM concern and request a PIREPs from preceding traffic if any.
questions.follow_up: If you are flying the ILS and the localizer CDI suddenly reverses — showing a fly-left deflection when you are clearly left of centerline — what is your immediate action and what is the most likely cause?
questions.follow_up_answer: Immediate action is to execute the published missed approach. A reversed CDI is a classic sign of a false localizer course or a back-course signal, and continuing the approach with reversed guidance is dangerous and could result in CFIT. The most likely cause in this scenario is localizer backcourse signal capture — the aircraft may have intercepted the back lobe of the localizer, which transmits a mirror-image signal behind the antenna array. On a standard ILS, the back course produces reversed CDI deflections unless a back course approach is published and the HSI/CDI is set up to compensate. Other causes include receiver malfunction or signal interference as discussed. The pilot should report the anomaly to ATC and file an ASRS report. This type of event should also be flagged to the facility for a signal integrity check.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9; AIM 1-1-9; FAA Order 8200.1 (Flight Inspection)

questions.question: What does the term 'stabilized approach' mean in the context of a precision instrument approach in a helicopter?
questions.answer: A stabilized approach means the helicopter is established on the correct glidepath and localizer course with a consistent descent rate, airspeed within limits, correct power setting, and the aircraft configured for landing — all maintained continuously from a defined gate (typically by FAF or 500 feet AGL in IMC) through the landing or missed approach. There should be no large deviations in heading, pitch, airspeed, or vertical speed during this phase.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM/SRM stabilized approach criteria)

questions.question: What are the key parameters a helicopter pilot should be monitoring to confirm a stabilized approach is being maintained during an ILS?
questions.answer: The pilot should be monitoring: (1) localizer needle — centered with no sustained full deflection; (2) glideslope needle — centered with no sustained full deflection; (3) airspeed — at or near the target approach speed for the aircraft; (4) vertical speed — consistent with the glidepath angle (typically around 500–700 fpm for a 3° ILS in a helicopter); (5) power setting — stable and appropriate; (6) aircraft configuration — landing checklist complete. Any parameter that drifts significantly and is not immediately corrected indicates an unstabilized approach.

questions.question: In the context of a helicopter precision approach, what is 'energy management' and why is it particularly important for helicopters compared to fixed-wing aircraft?
questions.answer: Energy management refers to the pilot's ability to control the helicopter's total energy state — the balance between airspeed (kinetic energy) and altitude (potential energy) — throughout the approach to arrive at the decision height with the correct speed, power, and configuration to either land or execute a missed approach. It is especially important in helicopters because of the high power-to-drag relationship, the sensitivity of rotor RPM to power changes, and the relatively short transition from approach speed to hover or landing. Unlike fixed-wing aircraft, helicopters can decelerate very rapidly; if the pilot allows airspeed to decay too much before reaching DH, there may be insufficient energy to execute a safe missed approach or landing transition.

questions.question: You are flying an ILS approach in a helicopter and notice at 800 feet AGL that your airspeed is 15 knots above your target approach speed, your glideslope needle is one dot low, and you are slightly right of the localizer. Using energy management concepts, how would you prioritize and manage your corrections?
questions.answer: This is an energy-high, off-course situation. The priority is to re-intercept the glideslope from below (since you are below it — one dot low means you are below the glideslope), correct the localizer deviation, and bleed off excess airspeed in a coordinated way. Reduce collective slightly to arrest the descent rate and allow the glideslope needle to center from below, simultaneously apply left cyclic to correct the localizer deviation. The excess airspeed (high kinetic energy) can be used carefully — it provides a buffer, but it must be reduced to target speed by the gate altitude. Avoid the trap of pitching up aggressively to lose altitude, which could cause rotor RPM fluctuation. Use small, deliberate control inputs. If by 500 feet AGL the approach is not stabilized on glideslope, localizer, and at target airspeed, execute a missed approach — do not attempt to salvage a significantly unstabilized approach below minimums.

questions.question: During an ILS approach, a helicopter pilot allows airspeed to decay well below the target approach speed while still on the glideslope. What are the specific energy management risks this creates, and how does it differ from the same scenario in a fixed-wing aircraft?
questions.answer: When a helicopter's airspeed decays below target on the glideslope, the pilot is flying in a low-energy state. The risks include: (1) Entering the 'avoid curve' of the height-velocity diagram — the combination of low airspeed and low altitude may not allow a safe autorotation if the engine fails; (2) Increased susceptibility to vortex ring state if the pilot applies large power corrections to maintain glidepath while at low airspeed and high power descent; (3) Reduced ability to execute a go-around — a missed approach from low airspeed at low altitude requires significant power application and nose-low attitude to accelerate, which takes altitude and time the pilot may not have. In a fixed-wing aircraft, low airspeed below the glideslope is correctable with pitch and throttle, and the aircraft can accelerate along the runway if needed; a helicopter must complete its energy recovery entirely in the air, with no runway acceleration phase available in a hover-to-hover scenario.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapters 11 (autorotation, height-velocity diagram), 13; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9

questions.question: A student pilot asks why the concept of a 'stabilized approach gate' exists — why not simply require the approach to be stabilized at Decision Height? How would you explain the purpose and logic of the gate altitude?
questions.answer: The stabilized approach gate (typically 500 feet AGL in IMC or 300 feet AGL in VMC for many operators) exists because it takes time and altitude to make corrections. If you wait until Decision Height to evaluate whether the approach is stabilized, you have no remaining altitude to fix the problem or safely execute a missed approach. The gate is the point at which the pilot commits to a fully stabilized state — if the approach is not stabilized by the gate, the only safe action is a missed approach while there is still sufficient altitude, airspeed, and time to do so safely. Requiring stabilization only at DH would mean a pilot might be making large corrections in the last few hundred feet in IMC, which dramatically increases the risk of controlled flight into terrain (CFIT) or losing aircraft control at a critical phase. The gate altitude gives the pilot a clear, earlier decision point consistent with good aeronautical decision-making principles.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM, CFIT awareness); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 2

questions.question: A helicopter pilot flying an ILS to a helipad consistently arrives at DH with the glideslope and localizer centered but reports feeling 'rushed' and needing large power changes in the last 200 feet. The approach looks stabilized on the needles but something is wrong. What underlying energy management issue might explain this, and how would you identify it?
questions.answer: The pilot is likely experiencing a symptom of being energy-high or energy-low in a way the CDI needles don't reveal. If the pilot has excess airspeed (kinetic energy) at DH, the needles can be centered while the aircraft is not truly stabilized — the pilot must then rapidly decelerate and convert that energy to either a hover or landing in a very short altitude window, which creates the rushed feeling. Alternatively, the pilot may be managing glideslope with power instead of pitch, causing the power setting to be unstable even when the needles look good. The key diagnostic is to look at the airspeed at DH versus the target, and evaluate whether power changes are reactive (chasing the glideslope) or proactive (set for stable descent). A properly energy-managed approach has the power set for a stable descent rate at the target airspeed well before DH, so the transition to hover or landing is smooth and predictable. The examiner should ask the pilot to verbalize airspeed and power targets before beginning the approach.
questions.follow_up: If this pilot is consistently high energy at DH on every approach, what would you investigate about their technique during the segment between the FAF and DH?
questions.follow_up_answer: Between the FAF and DH, the pilot is likely not reducing to the target approach airspeed promptly after the FAF, allowing excess kinetic energy to carry into the final segment. The pilot may be flying the approach at cruise or transit speed and delaying the deceleration too long, or using a pitch-up attitude to intercept/maintain the glideslope rather than using collective, which temporarily inflates airspeed. The correct technique is to configure and slow to the target approach airspeed at or before the FAF, establish the power setting appropriate for the target airspeed and descent rate, and then manage glideslope primarily with small collective adjustments and localizer with cyclic — arriving at DH already at landing airspeed with power set for a stable deceleration to hover.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9 (ILS approach technique); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13

questions.question: A pilot argues that helicopter precision approaches are inherently more dangerous than fixed-wing precision approaches because of the unique energy management challenges involved. Do you agree or disagree, and what specific helicopter aerodynamic characteristics make energy management more complex on a precision approach than for a comparable fixed-wing aircraft?
