questions.answer: The argument has merit from a physics standpoint, though 'more dangerous' is operationally dependent on training and proficiency. The helicopter-specific factors that complicate energy management on a precision approach include: (1) Height-velocity diagram — at low altitudes and low airspeed, the helicopter may be in a region where safe autorotation is not possible, meaning the margin for engine failure is reduced during the critical final approach segment; (2) Vortex ring state susceptibility — if the pilot descends steeply at low airspeed with high power, the rotor can enter vortex ring state, which is most likely in exactly the speed/power conditions a precision approach demands; (3) Translational lift loss — as the helicopter decelerates below approximately 16–24 knots, it loses translational lift, requiring a significant power increase at the worst possible time (near the ground in IMC); (4) Inertia and control response — helicopters have less aerodynamic damping than fixed-wing aircraft, making precise airspeed and vertical speed control harder to maintain without active pilot input; (5) Rotor RPM management — large, rapid power changes required to salvage an unstabilized approach can cause rotor RPM fluctuations, especially in turbine helicopters at the low end of the power curve. These factors together mean a helicopter pilot has a much narrower acceptable energy corridor on a precision approach, making a well-planned stabilized approach not just preferred but essential.
questions.follow_up: Given the vortex ring state risk you mentioned, at what approximate airspeed and descent rate combination during an ILS approach would a helicopter be most vulnerable, and what is the correct recovery action if it is encountered at low altitude in IMC?
questions.follow_up_answer: Vortex ring state (also called power settling) is most likely when airspeed is below approximately 30 knots (especially below translational lift speed of ~16–24 knots), rate of descent is above approximately 300 fpm, and the pilot is applying significant power — conditions that can easily occur during a slow, power-on descent on an ILS final. The warning signs are increasing vibration, loss of altitude despite increasing collective, and reduced control effectiveness. Recovery requires simultaneously increasing forward airspeed (cyclic forward) to fly out of the vortex, reducing collective, and potentially adding power — though on a precision approach at low altitude in IMC, altitude and time may not permit full recovery. This is why maintaining translational airspeed above ~30 knots and a controlled, stabilized descent rate throughout the approach is critical, and why any developing vortex ring state condition at or below DH may necessitate immediate missed approach execution.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapters 11 (vortex ring state, height-velocity diagram, translational lift), 13; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9

questions.question: When ATC clears you for a specific precision approach — say, the ILS RWY 24 — and you decide on your own to fly a different approach to an adjacent runway because you think conditions favor it, what regulatory problem have you created?
questions.answer: You have deviated from an ATC clearance, which is a violation of 14 CFR 91.123. ATC clearances have the force of regulatory authority, and the assigned approach procedure is part of that clearance. You must comply unless an emergency exists under 91.3, in which case you must notify ATC as soon as possible. Deviating without authorization also creates potential traffic conflict and destroys ATC's sequencing and separation plan.

questions.question: What is the correct procedure if, while being vectored for an ILS approach, you realize you cannot comply with the approach clearance as issued — for example, you're too high and too close to capture the glideslope properly?
questions.answer: You must immediately advise ATC that you cannot comply, state your intentions, and request amended clearance or a go-around/re-sequence. ATC needs this information to maintain separation. Simply continuing and hoping you can salvage the approach creates serious safety risk — an unstabilized approach in IMC is one of the most common accident precursors. Under 14 CFR 91.123, if unable to comply, you must notify ATC as soon as possible.

questions.question: A pilot flying an ILS approach decides to skip a published hold-in-lieu-of-procedure-turn because it seems unnecessary and they want to save time. Why is this a risk, even if visibility is good?
questions.answer: Skipping a mandatory procedure turn or hold-in-lieu-of-PT without ATC authorization is a deviation from the assigned approach procedure and violates the clearance. The hold or PT exists to establish the aircraft on the proper inbound course, at the correct altitude, and stabilized before the final approach fix. Bypassing it in IMC risks intercepting the localizer or glideslope from an improper position, leading to an unstabilized approach, CFIT risk, and a potential airspace conflict with other IFR traffic. ATC must explicitly state 'procedure turn not authorized' or 'cleared straight-in' to omit it.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.123; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 1; Instrument Approach Procedure notes

questions.question: You're flying a helicopter ILS approach in marginal IMC. At the FAF, you're 200 feet above the glideslope. Your instinct is to descend aggressively to intercept the GS from above and continue the approach. Walk me through the risks of that decision versus the proper course of action.
questions.answer: Intercepting the glideslope from above is dangerous for several reasons: you risk flying through the GS and continuing below it, possibly below the decision altitude, without proper stabilization. The localizer CDI is much more sensitive than a VOR (full deflection = 2.5° vs. 12°), and an unstabilized approach in IMC significantly increases CFIT risk. The proper course of action is to execute a missed approach immediately, advise ATC, and request re-sequencing. This is a deviation risk scenario — continuing an unstabilized approach deviates from the spirit and safety intent of the assigned procedure. Aggressive maneuvering in IMC also risks spatial disorientation, which is especially acute in helicopters due to the flight envelope and vibration environment.

questions.question: ATC clears you for the ILS RWY 18, but during the approach briefing you notice the chart shows a non-standard missed approach that requires climbing to 3,000 feet and turning to a specific heading before contacting departure. You forget to brief this and fly a straight-ahead missed approach instead. What risks did your deviation from the assigned procedure create, and what should you have done?
questions.answer: Flying a non-standard missed approach procedure incorrectly is a deviation from the assigned approach clearance and creates serious risk. Non-standard missed approach procedures often exist because of terrain, obstacles, or airspace conflicts — flying straight ahead may take you directly into an obstruction or restricted area. The risk is amplified in IMC because you cannot see terrain. Proper risk management requires thoroughly briefing the entire approach including the missed approach segment before beginning the approach — not just the final approach course and minimums. If you fly an incorrect missed approach, advise ATC immediately, declare your position and intentions, and comply with their guidance. The error chain here starts with inadequate approach briefing — a classic single link that, had it been caught, would have prevented the deviation.

questions.question: You are flying a helicopter EMS mission at night in IMC. The medical crew is pressuring you to get into the hospital helipad quickly, and you consider deviating from the published ILS approach minimums by descending below DA to look for the pad. Applying ADM and SRM, how do you evaluate and manage this pressure?
questions.answer: This is a classic hazardous attitude scenario involving 'get-there-itis' and external pressure — both identified human factors in ADM. The correct risk management approach is to recognize that descending below DA without the required visual references is illegal under 14 CFR 91.175 and could be fatal. SRM principles require managing workload, maintaining situational awareness, and using all available resources — but medical crew urgency is NOT a valid resource for overriding regulatory minimums. The proper response is to execute the missed approach if visual contact with the required references is not established at DA, and communicate clearly with the crew that safety is non-negotiable. The FAA-H-8083-21B notes that 'probably' is not good enough — if descending below DA will 'probably' be okay, that means it might not be. Accidents correlate with accumulated bad decisions; the pressure is one link in the error chain that must be broken.

questions.question: During an ILS approach in solid IMC, you receive a TCAS resolution advisory commanding a climb just as you reach DA with the runway environment in sight. Complying with the RA means you deviate from the approach procedure and lose visual contact. What is the correct action, and what regulatory priority governs this conflict between the RA and your clearance?
questions.answer: You must comply with the TCAS Resolution Advisory immediately, even if it means deviating from the assigned approach procedure and losing visual contact with the runway. FAA guidance and ICAO standards are clear: TCAS RAs take priority over ATC instructions and approach clearances. The system exists specifically to prevent mid-air collisions, and the RA is generated because ATC radar may not have detected the conflict in time. Once you comply with the RA, you must advise ATC immediately of the deviation and the RA. If you lose visual contact with the runway while executing the RA climb, you are in IMC below published minimums and must fly the full missed approach procedure. The RA compliance is a legally recognized deviation justification — it is not a violation of 14 CFR 91.123 because the deviation is required for safety.
questions.follow_up: After complying with the RA and notifying ATC, the RA clears and ATC gives you a new heading and altitude to re-sequence. At what point are you legally back under ATC authority, and what happens if the RA re-triggers immediately after the 'clear of conflict' annunciation?
questions.follow_up_answer: You are back under ATC authority as soon as the RA clears and you acknowledge ATC's new instructions — at that point, the RA is no longer active and ATC's clearance governs. If the RA re-triggers immediately, you must comply with the new RA again, advise ATC again, and the same priority applies: TCAS RA overrides ATC. Each RA is evaluated independently. This scenario illustrates why TCAS compliance must be automatic and unconditional — hesitation or prioritizing ATC over an active RA has been a causal factor in mid-air collisions. The FAA guidance in AC 120-55 reinforces mandatory RA compliance.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.123; 14 CFR 91.175; FAA AC 120-55C; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5

questions.question: A helicopter pilot flying an ILS approach in IMC loses the glideslope indication at the FAF due to a suspected avionics anomaly. The localizer is still functioning. The pilot decides to continue the approach using localizer-only minimums without informing ATC or formally amending the approach type. What are the layered risks of this silent deviation, and what is the correct procedure?
questions.answer: This silent deviation creates multiple layered risks. First, the pilot is now flying a localizer-only approach but is still mentally framed as flying an ILS — the higher ILS DA may still be active in their mind, meaning they could descend to ILS minimums (lower) rather than the higher LOC-only minimums, creating CFIT risk. Second, ATC believes an ILS is being flown and may have sequenced other traffic or issued altitudes based on ILS performance assumptions. Third, the pilot has not declared a failure or amended the clearance, so there is no safety net — if an incident occurs, the deviation is undocumented. The correct procedure is to immediately advise ATC of the glideslope failure, request a new clearance for the localizer approach if desired, comply with LOC-only minimums from the instrument approach plate, and verify the aircraft is still legal to continue under 14 CFR 91.213 (inoperative equipment). Flying an approach with a failed component without notifying ATC is a deviation from the assigned approach procedure with compounded risk.
questions.follow_up: If the MEA on the route guarantees navigation signal coverage, but the pilot is now flying a localizer — which is a different type of navigation — what coverage guarantee does the pilot actually have for obstacle clearance below the ILS glideslope path?
questions.follow_up_answer: The MEA guarantees obstacle clearance and navigation signal for en route navigation, but it does not apply inside the terminal instrument approach environment. For the localizer approach, obstacle clearance is only guaranteed when the pilot adheres to the published LOC-only minimums — which are higher than ILS minimums precisely because without glideslope guidance, the pilot must maintain a higher DA/MDA to ensure obstacle clearance on the final segment. The glideslope provides continuous vertical guidance that keeps the aircraft above obstacles on the approach path. Flying to ILS DA without glideslope removes that protection. The published LOC minimums account for this and must be used — this is why silently switching from ILS to LOC without updating the target minimums is so dangerous.

questions.question: Before beginning an ILS approach, you tune the localizer frequency. How do you confirm you have the correct frequency selected for your intended runway?
questions.answer: You must identify the station by listening to or verifying the Morse code identifier broadcast on the ILS frequency. The identifier is printed on the approach chart and must match what you hear or see displayed. Never rely solely on tuning the correct frequency — always verify the identifier before using the navigation signal for guidance.

questions.question: What is the VHF frequency range used for ILS localizers, and why does selecting the wrong frequency in that range matter on a precision approach?
questions.answer: ILS localizer frequencies are in the VHF band between 108.10 and 111.95 MHz (odd tenths only). Selecting the wrong frequency in this range could cause you to follow a different localizer — possibly one serving a different runway or airport — without realizing it, especially if the CDI shows deflection that appears plausible. This risk is highest at airports with multiple ILS approaches or nearby facilities on adjacent frequencies.

questions.question: On an ILS approach, what is the relationship between the localizer frequency and the glideslope frequency, and what happens if you tune only the glideslope frequency manually?
questions.answer: The glideslope frequency (UHF, 329.15–335.00 MHz) is paired with the localizer VHF frequency and is automatically selected when you tune the localizer frequency on most avionics. You cannot manually tune the glideslope independently on standard ILS receivers. If your localizer frequency is wrong or not tuned, you will have no glideslope signal, or you may receive a false glideslope from an adjacent paired frequency.

questions.question: You are flying a helicopter ILS approach into a towered airport and ATC clears you for the ILS Runway 27L approach. You tune what you believe is the correct frequency, but the CDI centers unusually early and you notice the Morse code identifier does not match the chart. What should you do, and what risk does continuing present?
questions.answer: You should immediately stop the approach, advise ATC you need to verify your navigation frequency, retune to the correct ILS frequency, and re-identify the station before continuing. Continuing with an unverified or misidentified navigation signal creates the risk of flying a false or wrong course — potentially toward terrain, obstacles, or conflicting traffic. In a helicopter operating at lower altitudes and slower speeds, there may be less reaction time if course deviation is discovered late. Declaring the situation to ATC also allows them to provide vectors and keep traffic separated.

questions.question: During preflight planning for an ILS approach, you notice the approach plate shows a NOTAM that the glideslope is out of service. How does frequency selection risk change, and what approach type can you now fly?
questions.answer: With the glideslope out of service, you can still tune the localizer frequency and fly a Localizer (LOC) approach, which is a non-precision approach. The risk changes because the localizer itself is still usable, but you no longer have vertical guidance from the glideslope — you must use the published LOC minimums, which are higher than ILS minimums. The frequency selection risk remains the same: you must still tune and positively identify the localizer. Additionally, you must not mistake any residual glideslope needle movement for valid guidance, as the signal may be unreliable or absent.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9; 14 CFR 91.175; Aeronautical Information Manual 1-1-9

questions.question: You are single-pilot in a helicopter flying an ILS in IMC at night. Workload is high and you realize you tuned the navigation frequency during taxi but never re-verified it after receiving the amended approach clearance to a different runway. At what point in the approach does this error become most dangerous, and how should workload management principles from SRM address this risk?
questions.answer: The error is most dangerous when you intercept what appears to be the localizer course and begin descending toward minimums — if the wrong frequency is tuned, you could be tracking a false or entirely different course while believing you are established. In a helicopter operating at low altitude in IMC at night, terrain or obstacle contact could occur quickly. SRM workload management requires completing navigation frequency verification as part of a structured approach briefing and descent checklist — not during high-workload intercept phases. The SRM principle of managing tasks early (pre-loading the frequency and verifying the identifier well before the FAF) directly mitigates this risk. Announcing or mentally confirming 'frequency tuned and identified' as a checklist item prevents late-stage discovery of an error.

questions.question: A helicopter pilot flying an ILS approach with a glass cockpit notes the nav frequency auto-populates from the FMS flight plan. The identifier checks out on the display. Is there any remaining risk associated with frequency selection that the automation does not eliminate, and how would you address it?
questions.answer: Yes. Even with automation populating the frequency and displaying the identifier, several risks remain: (1) the FMS database could be outdated — ILS frequencies or identifiers may have changed if the database is beyond its 28-day update cycle; (2) a database error could populate the correct identifier label with the wrong frequency; (3) the pilot may not catch a subtle discrepancy if they accept the automated selection without cross-checking the paper or EFB chart; and (4) on some avionics, the identifier shown is pulled from the database, not decoded from the actual received signal — meaning the display shows what should be received, not necessarily what is being received. Best practice is to always cross-check the auto-populated frequency against the approach chart and, where possible, confirm the audible or decoded identifier from the actual received signal rather than relying solely on the FMS label.
questions.follow_up: How often is the instrument approach procedure chart cycle updated versus the avionics navigation database, and what does that difference mean for a pilot using an EFB?
questions.follow_up_answer: Instrument approach procedure charts (en route and terminal) are revised on a 56-day cycle, while electronic navigation databases are updated every 28 days. For an EFB, if the chart application and the avionics database are on different update cycles — or if either is not current — a discrepancy could exist between what the chart shows and what the avionics have stored. The pilot must confirm both the avionics database and the chart are current before the flight. Using an expired chart or database independently introduces risk; using them together without confirming they reflect the same cycle compounds that risk.

questions.question: During an ILS approach in a twin-engine helicopter with two NAV radios, you have the ILS tuned and identified on NAV 1 and a VOR approach on a nearby field tuned and identified on NAV 2 as a divert option. Both radios are correctly set. What specific risk exists from having both NAV radios active simultaneously, and how do you manage it during a precision approach?
questions.answer: The primary risk is inadvertent switching of the active navigation source — either manually by the pilot during high workload, or through an autopilot mode change — from NAV 1 (ILS) to NAV 2 (VOR). If the CDI source switches to NAV 2 without the pilot noticing, the displayed course guidance changes and the glideslope signal disappears (since VOR does not provide vertical guidance), but the aircraft may continue descending on the autopilot's last vertical mode. In a helicopter at low altitude in IMC, this can result in controlled flight into terrain. Additionally, some older avionics can experience inter-radio interference or squelch interaction with two active VHF NAV receivers on close frequencies. Management practices include: confirming NAV source selection before and during the approach, briefing which radio is active for the approach, monitoring CDI source throughout the approach, and being deliberate about any radio switching after the FAF.
questions.follow_up: If you are hand-flying the ILS and accidentally switch the CDI source from the localizer to the VOR at 500 feet AGL in IMC, what is the immediate correct response?
questions.follow_up_answer: Immediately execute the published missed approach. At 500 feet AGL in IMC you do not have sufficient altitude or time to diagnose the instrument discrepancy, reselect the correct source, re-establish on the localizer, and verify you are configured correctly before reaching minimums. The missed approach is the only safe option. After climbing to a safe altitude, you can troubleshoot, reselect the ILS on the correct NAV source, re-identify the frequency, and request another approach from ATC. The Trescott Tip from ADM applies here: if the situation will only 'probably' work out by attempting to continue, choose the option you know works — the missed approach.

questions.question: When flying a precision approach with the autopilot coupled to the ILS, what is the pilot's primary responsibility with respect to the automated system?
questions.answer: The pilot remains the pilot-in-command at all times and is responsible for the safe outcome of the flight. Even with the autopilot coupled, the pilot must continuously monitor the automated system's performance, cross-check flight instruments, and be prepared to immediately take manual control if the automation deviates from the intended flight path or fails. Automation does not transfer PIC responsibility.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5 (Autopilots and FMS); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM/SRM)

questions.question: What does the term 'automation complacency' mean, and why is it a specific risk during a coupled precision approach in a helicopter?
questions.answer: Automation complacency is the tendency for a pilot to become passive and reduce active monitoring of systems and instruments because the automated system appears to be working correctly. During a coupled precision approach, this is particularly dangerous because the helicopter is close to terrain, in IMC, at low altitude and airspeed, and any undetected deviation or autopilot disconnect can leave very little time for recovery. The pilot must remain mentally engaged and actively cross-check instruments throughout the approach.

questions.question: Before beginning a coupled ILS approach, what should a helicopter pilot verify about the FMS or navigation system database to ensure the automation is being used safely?
questions.answer: The pilot should verify that the navigation database is current and within its effective date cycle. Instrument procedure databases are updated every 28 days. An expired database may contain outdated procedure data — including incorrect final approach courses, frequencies, or waypoints — which could cause the automation to fly an incorrect or non-current procedure. The pilot should also confirm the correct procedure is loaded and matches the ATC clearance and the published approach plate.

questions.question: You are flying a helicopter ILS approach at night in IMC with the autopilot coupled. Passing through 600 feet AGL on final, the autopilot suddenly disconnects with an aural warning. What immediate actions do you take, and what risks must you manage in the next few seconds?
questions.answer: Immediately take positive manual control of the cyclic, collective, and pedals to maintain the ILS flight path. Cross-check the attitude indicator, altimeter, airspeed, and both ILS needles simultaneously. The risks to manage include: startle/surprise effect causing over-control; spatial disorientation from the sudden transition to manual flight in IMC at low altitude; task saturation from simultaneously hand-flying the approach, monitoring instruments, and troubleshooting the autopilot; and the proximity to terrain and minimums. Unless the approach cannot be safely continued manually and stabilized, continue to DA/DH, then execute the missed approach or land. Do not attempt to re-engage the autopilot during the critical final approach segment without positively diagnosing the cause of the disconnect.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5 (autopilots); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM, workload management); 14 CFR 91.175

questions.question: A pilot is cleared for the ILS approach and programs the FMS, which will couple to the autopilot for the approach. The FMS shows the final approach course as 092°, but the published ILS course on the approach plate is 087°. How should the pilot handle this discrepancy, and what are the risks of ignoring it?
questions.answer: The pilot must not proceed with the approach using the FMS data without resolving the discrepancy. The published approach plate is the authoritative source. The pilot should verify the correct procedure is selected in the FMS, check that the correct ILS frequency is tuned, confirm the localizer course is properly identified, and cross-check the raw ILS CDI against the FMS path. A 5-degree error on final approach could place the aircraft significantly off the protected airspace centerline, potentially leading to terrain or obstacle contact, especially in IMC. If the discrepancy cannot be resolved, the pilot should either fly the approach using raw ILS data without FMS coupling or request a delay/alternate approach.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9 (VOR/ILS, CDI sensitivity); 14 CFR 91.103; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13

questions.question: During a coupled ILS approach, you notice the autopilot is flying a slightly high glideslope — the glideslope needle is consistently showing one dot low (aircraft above glideslope). You are at 1,500 feet MSL with the DA at 800 feet MSL. What is your risk management decision process?
questions.answer: One dot high on the glideslope means the aircraft is above the published glidepath but still within normal operational tolerance for the ILS glideslope. However, being consistently above glideslope during a precision approach means the aircraft will be higher than normal at DA, requiring more aggressive descent to land, and could result in a long landing or go-around. The risk management process: (1) Verify the glideslope indicator is functioning by cross-checking the raw needle against any FMS vertical guidance. (2) Determine whether the deviation is stable, worsening, or trending toward correction. (3) With sufficient altitude remaining, consider manually overriding or adjusting autopilot pitch mode if permitted by the aircraft's procedures, or disconnecting and hand-flying. (4) If the deviation does not correct before DA, execute the missed approach rather than attempting a salvage landing from an unstabilized position. Continuing an unstabilized approach is a leading cause of CFIT accidents.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9 (ILS glideslope); 14 CFR 91.175; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (CFIT awareness)

questions.question: A helicopter pilot who regularly flies coupled ILS approaches has become so reliant on the autopilot that they have not hand-flown an ILS to minimums in over eight months. Beyond regulatory currency requirements, what operational and human factors risks does this practice create, and how should the pilot address them?
questions.answer: This practice creates the risk of significant skill degradation — a well-documented human factors phenomenon where manual flying proficiency deteriorates when a task is consistently delegated to automation. The risks include: (1) Loss of manual instrument scan proficiency, meaning that in an autopilot failure at low altitude in IMC the pilot may be unable to maintain precise flight path control during the most critical phase of flight. (2) Reduced situational awareness of what 'normal' ILS needle behavior looks and feels like, making it harder to detect when the automation is performing abnormally. (3) Increased startle response and workload if forced to revert to manual flight. (4) Overconfidence in automation reliability. To mitigate: the pilot should regularly practice hand-flown ILS approaches to minimums, both in the aircraft and in an approved simulator; establish a personal currency standard for manual ILS approaches; and treat manual reversion as a core skill. FAA human factors research consistently shows accident rates decrease significantly after 100 hours in type, but automation dependency can artificially mask true proficiency.
questions.follow_up: If this pilot is flying under Part 135, is there a regulatory requirement for instrument proficiency checks that would specifically address manual flying skills?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes. Under 14 CFR 135.297, pilots operating under Part 135 in IFR conditions must complete an instrument proficiency check every six months (or 12 months with certain conditions). The check must be given by an authorized check airman or the FAA and must include actual or simulated instrument flight tasks, including approaches. Additionally, 14 CFR 135.293 requires recurrent training and competency checks. However, regulations do not specifically mandate that approaches during the IPC be hand-flown rather than autopilot-coupled — this is a gap that operators and pilots should address through company policy, training programs, and personal standards to ensure genuine manual proficiency is maintained.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 135.297; 14 CFR 135.293; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (automation management, SRM); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5

questions.question: During a briefing for a coupled ILS approach into a mountainous airport, you realize that although the FMS will fly the localizer correctly, the vertical navigation computed by the FMS diverges slightly from the published glideslope angle beginning at the FAF because the FMS is using a baro-VNAV computed path rather than the ILS glideslope signal. What is the specific risk here, and how must the pilot manage the autoflight system to mitigate it?
questions.answer: The specific risk is mode confusion — the pilot may believe the autopilot is tracking the ILS glideslope (a precision approach with protected obstacle clearance) when it is actually flying a baro-VNAV computed path, which has different and generally less precise obstacle clearance guarantees. Baro-VNAV is affected by non-standard temperature (particularly significant in mountainous/cold weather environments) and does not provide the same integrity as an ILS glideslope signal. In mountainous terrain, even small deviations below the published glidepath can result in CFIT. To mitigate: (1) Before the FAF, verify exactly which mode the autoflight system is using — confirm the autopilot is capturing and tracking the ILS glideslope signal, not a computed VNAV path, by checking the mode annunciator. (2) Cross-check the raw ILS glideslope needle against the FMS vertical path throughout the approach. (3) If the FMS VNAV and ILS glideslope diverge, the ILS raw data is authoritative for a precision approach — the pilot should fly the ILS glideslope signal. (4) If the aircraft is only capable of flying baro-VNAV on this procedure, the approach should be treated as a non-precision approach and flown to LNAV/VNAV minimums, not ILS DA, with appropriate obstacle clearance expectations. Mode awareness is a critical component of autoflight system management.
questions.follow_up: In cold temperature conditions, how does temperature affect a baro-VNAV computed glidepath, and what correction is available to the pilot?
questions.follow_up_answer: In cold temperatures, the air is denser and the altimeter — which is calibrated to the standard atmosphere — will read higher than the actual altitude. This means the aircraft is actually lower than the altimeter indicates. A baro-VNAV computed path uses baro-altimeter data to compute the vertical path, so in cold weather the aircraft will be physically lower than the computed path suggests — the actual glidepath will be shallower and lower than intended, increasing terrain clearance risk. The FAA provides cold temperature altitude correction tables in the AIM (Chapter 7) and on some approach plates. Pilots can apply a cold temperature correction to add altitude to their minimums and step-down fixes. Some approach plates have a note indicating cold temperature restrictions or corrections. At locations where cold temperature corrections are published, the pilot must apply the correction unless the aircraft has a certified cold temperature compensation system.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9 (RNAV, GPS, WAAS, baro-VNAV); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5 (autopilots, FMS); AIM Chapter 7 (cold temperature corrections); 14 CFR 91.175

questions.question: Why is it important to establish and maintain a stabilized configuration early on a precision instrument approach in a helicopter?
questions.answer: Establishing a stabilized configuration early reduces cockpit workload and allows the pilot to focus on tracking the glideslope and localizer. A destabilized or changing configuration — such as hunting for the correct power setting or adjusting airspeed — diverts attention from instrument cross-check, increasing the risk of deviation or CFIT. The FAA recommends that helicopters be configured and stabilized no later than the final approach fix (FAF) to ensure a consistent, predictable flightpath to minimums.

questions.question: What does 'helicopter configuration' refer to during an ILS approach, and what are the key items a pilot must manage?
questions.answer: Helicopter configuration during an ILS approach refers to the combination of airspeed, power setting, flight attitude, and any applicable checklist items (such as landing light, anti-ice, fuel selector, and rotor RPM) that produce a stabilized descent on glideslope. Key items to manage include: holding a target approach airspeed (often 60–80 KIAS depending on aircraft), setting power for the appropriate rate of descent, trimming the aircraft to reduce control pressures, and completing before-landing checklist items. Improper configuration leads to unstable approaches, excessive workload, and increased risk of deviating below minimums or being unprepared for a missed approach.

questions.question: During a missed approach from a precision approach, what is the primary risk if the helicopter pilot delays reconfiguring from approach to climb configuration?
questions.answer: The primary risk is terrain or obstacle contact. A delayed transition to climb configuration means the helicopter may continue descending or fail to achieve the required climb gradient to clear obstacles and terrain in the missed approach segment. On an ILS, the missed approach point is at or near the runway threshold, leaving very little margin. Immediately applying climb power, transitioning to the published missed approach climb attitude and airspeed, and following the published missed approach procedure is critical. Hesitation or fumbling with configuration changes at low altitude in IMC is a significant contributor to controlled flight into terrain (CFIT).
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 1 (NAS/IFR procedures); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (CFIT awareness)

questions.question: You are shooting an ILS to minimums in a single-pilot helicopter. At 500 feet AGL you notice you are high on the glideslope and fast by 15 knots. How does this configuration risk affect your decision-making at decision altitude?
questions.answer: Being high and fast at 500 feet AGL on an ILS is a significant red flag. The localizer CDI is approximately 4–5 times more sensitive than a VOR CDI, and the glideslope is similarly precise — so being high and fast means the aircraft is out of the normal touchdown zone energy envelope. At decision altitude (DA), if you are not stabilized and configured for landing, the risk of a hard landing, runway overrun, or loss of directional control is elevated. Per sound ADM principles, you should initiate a missed approach well before DA if the approach cannot be salvaged — not attempt to 'save' an unstabilized approach at minimums. The error chain here includes accepting the unstabilized condition rather than going around earlier when altitude and options existed.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9 (localizer sensitivity); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (error chain, ADM)

questions.question: A helicopter crew is flying an ILS approach and the pilot flying calls for the before-landing checklist at the outer marker. The pilot monitoring is also handling a radio frequency change to tower at the same time. What risk does this workload scenario introduce regarding helicopter configuration?
questions.answer: This scenario creates a workload spike at a high-task phase of flight, increasing the risk that configuration items are missed, rushed, or done out of sequence. In single-pilot operations, or when crew coordination is poor, the pilot flying may become task-saturated managing the approach while also completing checklist items. Items critical to safe landing — such as fuel selector, rotor RPM confirmation, anti-torque check, and landing light — could be skipped or verified without proper attention. SRM/CRM principles require workload management: ideally, the before-landing checklist is completed prior to the final approach fix so that inside the FAF the crew focus is exclusively on flying the approach and monitoring for a missed approach. Dividing attention between ATC communications, checklists, and precision tracking simultaneously is a setup for configuration errors.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (SRM, workload management); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 2 (ATC communications)

questions.question: You execute a missed approach from an ILS but do not immediately transition to the published climb airspeed — instead you accelerate slowly while trying to maintain visual contact with the runway environment. What specific risks does this introduce?
questions.answer: Delaying the transition to climb airspeed and configuration while attempting to maintain visual contact introduces multiple risks: (1) CFIT — the aircraft may not achieve the obstacle clearance gradient required by the missed approach procedure; (2) spatial disorientation — trying to look outside while transitioning from approach to climb in IMC conditions breaks the instrument scan and increases disorientation risk; (3) vortex ring state — if the helicopter decelerates or enters a low-airspeed, high-power, descending flight regime during the transition, vortex ring state becomes possible; (4) loss of situational awareness — fixating on visual contact breaks the scan and allows deviations in heading and altitude to go unnoticed. The correct action is to immediately execute the published missed approach: apply climb power, establish climb attitude and airspeed, and fly the published course — visual contact is irrelevant once the missed approach is initiated.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (CFIT, ADM); FAA-H-8083-21B Glossary (vortex ring state); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 1 (missed approach procedures)

questions.question: A student tells you: 'On the missed approach I'll just climb straight ahead at whatever airspeed I have and sort out the configuration once I'm above 1,000 feet AGL — that keeps it simple.' As an examiner, what is wrong with this reasoning, and what specific risks does it introduce during the configuration transition phase?
questions.answer: This reasoning is fundamentally flawed because it separates aircraft configuration from the safety-critical missed approach segment, where obstacle clearance is only guaranteed if the published procedure is followed precisely — including at the correct airspeed. Specific risks include: (1) Climb gradient — the published missed approach obstacle clearance is predicated on a specific climb gradient (typically 200 ft/NM unless otherwise published). An unknown or incorrect airspeed may produce a climb rate that fails to meet this gradient, placing the aircraft below obstacle clearance altitude during the early missed approach. (2) Vortex ring state — if the helicopter is slow and descending while applying climb power with a tailwind or during the deceleration phase, vortex ring state conditions can occur before reaching 1,000 feet AGL. (3) Autopilot/avionics mode confusion — on equipped aircraft, transitioning to a climb without properly configuring the flight management system or autopilot modes can result in the avionics flying the wrong profile. (4) The FAA's ADM guidance warns against 'probably' logic — assuming the aircraft will probably clear obstacles at an unknown airspeed is exactly the type of reasoning that leads to accident chains. Configuration must be deliberate and immediate, not deferred.
questions.follow_up: If the missed approach procedure requires a climb to 3,000 feet before turning, but the pilot is uncertain whether the aircraft can achieve the required climb gradient due to a heavy fuel load and hot/high conditions, what should have been evaluated before the approach even began?
questions.follow_up_answer: Before beginning the approach, the pilot should have evaluated whether the aircraft could meet the published missed approach climb gradient under current conditions (weight, density altitude, wind). This is part of pre-approach planning and risk management. The required climb gradient is published on the approach plate — if performance charts show the helicopter cannot meet it, the crew must either divert to an alternate with a more achievable procedure, reduce weight, or wait for conditions to change. Discovering this limitation during the missed approach itself — at low altitude in IMC — removes all options. This is a classic example of failing to manage risks before they become emergencies, which is at the core of SRM and ADM principles.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 1 (missed approach obstacle clearance); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM, SRM, 'probably' warning); FAA-H-8083-21B Glossary (vortex ring state)

questions.question: During an ILS approach in actual IMC, you break out at 300 feet AGL and immediately recognize the VASI/PAPI shows two red over two white — you are exactly on glidepath. However, your airspeed is 20 knots above your target approach speed. You have 800 feet of runway remaining to your intended touchdown point. Walk me through the risk factors and the correct decision.
questions.answer: This scenario presents a classic unstabilized-at-minimums situation with compounding risks. Being 20 knots fast at 300 feet AGL means: (1) the kinetic energy of the helicopter is significantly higher than planned — stopping distance, rotor flare effectiveness, and LTE susceptibility are all affected; (2) the before-landing checklist may have been rushed or incomplete if airspeed was not managed on final; (3) with only 800 feet to the intended touchdown point, there is insufficient margin to bleed off 20 knots and establish a proper hover or run-on landing; (4) attempting to force the landing introduces risk of a hard landing, runway excursion, or dynamic rollover if the touchdown is rushed. The correct decision is to execute an immediate missed approach. Breaking out of the clouds does not eliminate the obligation to go around if the approach is not stabilized — it only means the missed approach is flown in VMC. The 'probably' trap here is assuming you can probably get it stopped in time — if it only 'probably' works, the FAA's ADM guidance is clear: choose the option known to work, which is the missed approach. After going around, request vectors for another approach and establish the correct configuration and airspeed no later than the FAF.
questions.follow_up: If you chose to continue and landed, the aircraft ran off the end of the runway with minor damage. During the NTSB investigation, would your decision to continue from a destabilized approach constitute pilot error, and how does the 'error chain' concept apply here?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, continuing an unstabilized approach past the decision point — knowing the aircraft was 20 knots fast with limited runway — would constitute pilot error and likely be cited as the proximate cause of the accident. The error chain, however, almost certainly began much earlier: failing to manage airspeed on final, possibly accepting a rushed or late checklist, perhaps failing to confirm the approach was achievable given winds or conditions. The FAA's error chain concept (FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13) teaches that accidents rarely result from a single bad decision — they result from a series of smaller compromises, each of which could have broken the chain. Breaking the chain at the point of recognizing the unstabilized condition — by going around — would have prevented the outcome entirely. The NTSB and FAA both emphasize that pilots who continue unstabilized approaches to accidents bear responsibility for each link in that chain they chose not to break.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (error chain, ADM, 'probably' guidance); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9 (ILS glideslope sensitivity)

questions.question: What is the definition of an unstabilized approach, and at what point during a precision instrument approach should you be fully stabilized in a helicopter?
questions.answer: An unstabilized approach is one where the aircraft is not on the correct glidepath, on the correct airspeed, in the correct configuration, and with a controlled descent rate at the designated stabilization gate. For helicopters conducting precision instrument approaches (such as an ILS), the aircraft should be stabilized no later than reaching the final approach fix (FAF) or by 500 feet AGL in IMC conditions, whichever comes first. Key parameters include: on glideslope and localizer centerline, at target approach airspeed, with correct power and flight attitude, and with a normal descent rate — typically 400–800 FPM for most precision approaches. Any deviation outside these parameters constitutes an unstabilized condition and a go-around should be initiated.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 13; FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Flying Handbook, Chapter 7

questions.question: What does an excessive descent rate mean in the context of a precision approach in a helicopter, and why is it particularly dangerous near the decision altitude?
questions.answer: An excessive descent rate on a precision approach is a descent rate significantly above the normal profile required to track the glideslope — typically anything well above 800–1,000 FPM in a standard helicopter precision approach. It is particularly dangerous near decision altitude (DA) because the helicopter is close to terrain and obstacles, and the time available to arrest the descent is extremely limited. A high sink rate at DA can result in ground contact before the pilot can recover, especially if combined with being below glideslope. Additionally, in a helicopter, a high descent rate with low power risks entering vortex ring state if the pilot attempts an abrupt power reduction or if the descent rate is not controlled during the approach-to-hover transition.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9; FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Flying Handbook, Chapter 9

questions.question: On an ILS approach in a helicopter, the CDI shows a full fly-up deflection and your VSI reads 1,200 FPM down. What two specific indications tell you this approach is unstabilized?
questions.answer: Two specific indications of an unstabilized approach are: (1) The full fly-up deflection on the CDI indicates the aircraft is significantly below the glideslope — for a localizer, full deflection is approximately 2.5°, meaning a full deflection on the glideslope represents a substantial displacement below the required glidepath; and (2) A descent rate of 1,200 FPM is well above the normal range for a typical ILS glideslope approach in a helicopter (approximately 400–800 FPM depending on aircraft speed and glideslope angle). Both conditions together indicate the aircraft is not on the required profile and a go-around must be executed immediately.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Flying Handbook, Chapter 9; FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9

questions.question: You are flying a helicopter ILS approach in IMC at night. At 600 feet AGL you are on localizer centerline but half a dot below glideslope, 8 knots fast, and your VSI shows 900 FPM down. You believe you can correct everything before DA. What is the correct risk management decision, and why?
questions.answer: The correct risk management decision is to execute a go-around immediately. At 600 feet AGL in IMC at night, the approach is already unstabilized — the aircraft is below glideslope, above target airspeed, and has an elevated descent rate. The pilot's belief that they 'can probably correct' the errors before DA is exactly the type of optimism bias that leads to accidents. The Helicopter Flying Handbook emphasizes that the word 'probably' is a warning sign: if an action will only 'probably' work out, choose an option that is known to work. Attempting to simultaneously correct glideslope, airspeed, and descent rate in close proximity to terrain with limited visual cues at night in IMC significantly compresses decision time and increases workload. A go-around restores known safety margins and allows for another fully stabilized approach.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 13 (ADM/SRM); FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Flying Handbook, Chapter 7

questions.question: A helicopter pilot is flying an ILS approach with a strong tailwind component that developed after departure from the final approach fix. How does this tailwind affect the risk of an unstabilized approach and excessive descent rate, and what actions should the pilot take?
questions.answer: A tailwind on final approach creates several compounding risks: (1) Groundspeed increases significantly above the planned approach speed, meaning the aircraft covers distance to the runway much faster — this compresses the time available to correct any deviations; (2) The increased groundspeed means the vertical speed required to maintain the glideslope increases proportionally, pushing the descent rate higher than expected and potentially into excessive territory; (3) If the airspeed indicator shows a normal approach speed but groundspeed is high due to tailwind, the pilot may be deceived about the true energy state of the aircraft. Actions: The pilot should recognize the tailwind's effect, expect a higher-than-normal descent rate, increase approach airspeed reference as appropriate per the aircraft POH/RFM to maintain adequate rotor efficiency, and seriously consider whether a circling approach or a different runway is more appropriate. If the approach becomes unstabilized, a go-around is mandatory.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 9; FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Flying Handbook, Chapter 7

questions.question: During a helicopter ILS approach to a helipad at a hospital rooftop, the pilot notices the VASI/PAPI is not available and the approach lighting is minimal. At 300 feet AGL the glideslope needle shows one dot below and the airspeed is 5 knots low. What human factors risks does this scenario present, and how should the pilot manage them?
questions.answer: This scenario presents several compounding human factors risks: (1) Somatogravic illusion and spatial disorientation risk — without robust visual references from VASI/PAPI or approach lighting, the pilot is more susceptible to visual illusions, particularly the black hole effect at night over a dark area leading to a rooftop; (2) Confirmation bias — the pilot may rationalize that one dot low and 5 knots slow are 'minor' deviations and continue rather than go around; (3) Fatigue or mission pressure (especially in EMS operations) can lower the pilot's threshold for accepting an unstabilized approach; (4) Increased workload — managing instruments, communications, and environmental scanning simultaneously; (5) Being one dot below glideslope at 300 feet AGL puts the helicopter dangerously close to obstacles around a hospital structure. Risk management actions: Maintain strict instrument scan, adhere to a pre-briefed stabilization criteria, initiate go-around immediately for any criteria not met, and use SRM to manage the high-workload environment. Any approach that is not known to be stable should result in a go-around.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 13 (ADM, human factors); FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Flying Handbook, Chapter 5

questions.question: A student pilot continues an ILS approach past DA after going below glideslope with a 1,400 FPM descent rate, stating they 'saw the lights' and thought they could make it. As the examiner, how would you characterize the chain of errors that led to this point, and what systemic risk management failure does this represent?
questions.answer: This scenario represents a classic error chain with multiple compounding failures: (1) The approach was already unstabilized prior to DA — excessive descent rate and glideslope deviation should have triggered a go-around earlier; (2) The pilot violated the fundamental DA rule — at DA, if the required visual references are not clearly identified and the approach is not in a position to complete a normal landing, a missed approach is mandatory (14 CFR 91.175); (3) The 'I saw the lights' statement reflects get-there-itis and scud running mentality even in an instrument environment; (4) The pilot used 'probably' reasoning — believing they 'could make it' rather than choosing the known-safe option of a go-around; (5) Situational awareness failed — the pilot was not maintaining an accurate mental picture of energy state, position relative to terrain, and proximity to the missed approach point. The systemic failure is a breakdown of ADM and SRM: the pilot's decision-making process was not systematic, risk was not continuously assessed, and the pre-established 'go-around triggers' were ignored. The error chain likely began well before DA — possibly in the approach briefing where stabilization criteria were not explicitly defined.
questions.follow_up: What does 14 CFR 91.175 specifically require at decision altitude, and would there be any circumstance where a helicopter pilot could legally continue below DA without having the required visual references?
questions.follow_up_answer: 14 CFR 91.175(c) states that no pilot may operate an aircraft below DA/DH or MDA unless: the aircraft is continuously in a position from which a descent to a landing on the intended runway can be made at a normal rate of descent using normal maneuvers, the flight visibility is not less than the visibility prescribed in the procedure, and at least one of the specified visual references for the intended runway is distinctly visible and identifiable to the pilot. For helicopters, the required visual references include the approach light system, threshold, threshold markings, threshold lights, REIL, VASI, PAPI, or the runway/helipad itself. There is no circumstance under 14 CFR Part 91 that allows a pilot to continue below DA without the required visual references. The only exception-adjacent scenario would be a contact approach (14 CFR 91.175(j)), but that requires ATC authorization, at least 1 SM flight visibility, and must be specifically requested — it does not apply mid-ILS approach without prior coordination.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175(c); FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 13; FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Flying Handbook, Chapter 7

questions.question: A highly experienced helicopter pilot with 5,000 total hours but only 40 hours in a new glass-cockpit IFR helicopter tells you they feel comfortable flying ILS approaches in IMC. Based on accident data and ADM principles, what specific risk does this pilot's experience profile present regarding unstabilized approaches, and how would you evaluate this risk as an examiner?
questions.answer: This pilot presents a high-risk profile despite impressive total hours. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook explicitly states that accident rates correlate more strongly with hours in the specific aircraft model than with total flight hours, and accident rates decrease significantly only after approximately 100 hours in type. With only 40 hours in type, this pilot has insufficient time to develop true automation of glass-cockpit scan patterns, EFIS/FMS integration under workload, and helicopter-specific precision approach techniques in this aircraft. Specific risks regarding unstabilized approaches: (1) High total hours may create overconfidence — the pilot may underestimate how different glass-cockpit automation management is during a precision approach; (2) Automation bias — trusting the FMS/autopilot without verifying its outputs can mask developing glideslope/localizer deviations until they are severe; (3) Mode confusion on an EFIS platform can lead to unexpected automation behavior during critical phases near DA; (4) The pilot may default to older aircraft habits that are inappropriate for the new avionics suite, causing delayed recognition of an unstabilized condition. As an examiner, I would probe this pilot's understanding of their specific aircraft's automation modes during the oral, and during the practical test, I would observe whether they maintain a proper instrument scan independent of automation and whether they demonstrate clear, pre-briefed go-around criteria.
questions.follow_up: If this same pilot is flying under BasicMed and the IFR helicopter is a turbine aircraft with a 12,000 lb MTOW, is BasicMed valid for this operation? What are the key limitations?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, BasicMed under 14 CFR Part 68 and 14 CFR 61.113(i) is valid for this operation. BasicMed now authorizes operations in aircraft with a maximum certificated takeoff weight up to 12,500 lbs, which covers this 12,000 lb turbine helicopter. There is no restriction on turbine-powered aircraft under BasicMed. The key limitations that still apply are: the pilot must remain within the United States; the aircraft must carry no more than 6 occupants (pilot plus 5 passengers); the operation must not be for compensation or hire; maximum altitude is 18,000 feet MSL; maximum airspeed is 250 KIAS; the pilot must have held a valid medical certificate at some point after July 14, 2006; a medical education course must be completed every 24 months; and a physical examination from a state-licensed physician must be completed every 48 months. Assuming all these conditions are met and the flight is a private IFR flight within U.S. airspace, BasicMed is valid.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 13; 14 CFR Part 68; 14 CFR 61.113(i)

questions.question: What are the published weather minimums that must exist at the time of arrival for you to legally begin a precision instrument approach in a helicopter?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.175, a pilot may begin an instrument approach if the latest weather report indicates that the ceiling and visibility are at or above the published minimums for that approach. If the weather is below minimums, the approach may not be commenced. For Part 91 operations, there is no specific 'ceiling' requirement to begin the approach — only that the pilot must have the runway environment in sight before descending below DA/DH. However, dispatching or initiating an approach when weather is clearly below minimums presents serious safety risk and is operationally unsound.

questions.question: What is the difference between Decision Altitude (DA) and Decision Height (DH), and why does that distinction matter on a precision approach in deteriorating weather?
questions.answer: Decision Altitude (DA) is expressed in MSL and is used for approaches with a glideslope referenced to MSL, such as GPS LPV approaches. Decision Height (DH) is expressed as a height above touchdown zone elevation (AGL) and is used for ILS approaches. The distinction matters in deteriorating weather because the pilot must determine whether they have the required visual references at that specific point — if not, an immediate missed approach must be executed. In deteriorating conditions, confusing the two could cause a pilot to descend below the correct go/no-go point.

questions.question: If you receive an updated ATIS during your ILS approach showing the visibility has dropped below the published minimum, what is the required action under Part 91?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.175, a Part 91 pilot is not legally prohibited from continuing an approach that has already been started, even if weather drops below minimums. However, if the required visual references are not in sight at or before DA/DH, the pilot must execute an immediate missed approach. Landing when visual references are not acquired by DA/DH is prohibited regardless of weather updates received en route. Good risk management would include beginning to plan the alternate and alerting ATC of the situation prior to reaching DA/DH.

questions.question: You are established on the glideslope inbound on an ILS. At approximately 1,500 feet AGL, ATC advises that the latest special observation shows RVR has dropped to 1,200 feet — below your published minimums. You have your alternate filed and sufficient fuel. Walk me through your risk management process for the rest of this approach.
questions.answer: First, acknowledge the weather update and confirm the alternate is legal and within fuel range. Under Part 91, you may continue the approach since it was already commenced — the regulation does not require you to break off an approach in progress due to weather updates. However, sound risk management requires mentally committing to the missed approach NOW rather than waiting to see at DA/DH. Brief yourself on the missed approach procedure, ensure full attention is on flying the ILS precisely, and confirm autopilot or hand-flying technique is maintaining full instrument accuracy. At DA/DH, unless all required visual references are clearly in sight and you can maintain them, execute the missed approach immediately without hesitation. Delay at DA/DH in low RVR conditions increases the risk of controlled flight into terrain or runway incursion. After the missed approach, proceed to the alternate.

questions.question: How does the higher sensitivity of a localizer CDI compared to a VOR CDI affect your risk exposure when weather is deteriorating and you are hand-flying an ILS approach in a helicopter?
questions.answer: A localizer CDI full deflection represents approximately 2.5° off course, while a VOR CDI full deflection represents 12° or more. This makes the localizer roughly 4–5 times more sensitive. In deteriorating weather — especially with reduced visibility and low ceilings — any course deviation becomes more consequential because there is less time and altitude to correct before reaching DA/DH. In a helicopter, workload increases significantly as weather deteriorates because the pilot may also be managing icing, turbulence, or changing winds. The high sensitivity of the localizer means that even small control inputs or distractions can produce significant CDI deflection, potentially placing the aircraft outside the protected area. Maintaining instrument scan discipline and minimizing heads-down time is critical during deteriorating approach conditions.

questions.question: A helicopter EMS pilot is conducting a Part 135 ILS approach to a hospital helipad. Weather was at minimums when the approach began but is now deteriorating. The patient is critical. How does 14 CFR Part 135 change the legal and ethical risk management equation compared to Part 91?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 135.225, a Part 135 pilot may not begin an instrument approach unless the latest weather report indicates the ceiling and visibility are at or above the minimums for that approach. More critically, if weather drops below minimums after the approach begins, the pilot must execute a missed approach at DA/DH if visual references are not established — same as Part 91. However, Part 135 imposes stricter dispatch and operational control obligations, and no mission urgency — including a critical patient — overrides the pilot's authority and responsibility to execute the missed approach. FAA ADM principles and the Helicopter Flying Handbook reinforce that the 'press-on' impulse driven by external pressure (patient urgency) is a classic hazardous attitude known as 'invulnerability' or 'get-there-itis.' The pilot-in-command must make the go/no-go decision based solely on safety, not mission pressure.

questions.question: You are on an ILS approach and break out of the clouds at exactly DA/DH with 800 RVR — right at minimums. You see the approach lighting system but not the runway. As you begin transitioning to visual, you notice the fog is patchy and you momentarily lose sight of the approach lights. What is the correct action, and what common decision-making error could trap a pilot here?
questions.answer: The correct action is to immediately execute the missed approach. Under 14 CFR 91.175(c), a pilot may not descend below DA/DH unless the required visual references are continuously in sight. A momentary loss of visual references below DA/DH — even if you had them at DA/DH — requires an immediate missed approach. The common decision-making trap here is 'continuation bias' combined with 'scud running instinct' — the pilot has invested effort in the approach, is close to the runway, and subconsciously expects visibility to improve. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook describes this as the 'error chain' — multiple small rationalizations that chain together, leading the pilot to press on when the objective evidence says go missed. In patchy fog near the surface, the pilot may also be at risk for spatial disorientation and CFIT, making immediate execution of the missed approach the only safe choice.
questions.follow_up: If you execute the missed approach and climb back into IMC, but your alternate is now reporting below minimums due to the same frontal system, what are your options and what regulatory obligation exists?
questions.follow_up_answer: Under 14 CFR 91.169, the alternate airport must have weather forecast at or above alternate minimums at the ETA. If the alternate is now below minimums, the pilot should immediately declare an emergency if fuel or options are critically limited, and work with ATC to identify any airport within range that has acceptable weather. ATC is required under FAA Order 7110.65 to provide the best available assistance to aircraft in distress. The pilot may also consider holding if fuel permits and waiting for improving conditions at the destination or another airport. Declaring an emergency removes regulatory constraints and allows the pilot to deviate from any rule to the extent necessary to meet the emergency — this is both a legal tool and the right ADM choice. Fuel awareness and alternate selection during preflight planning is the upstream fix to this scenario.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175(c); 14 CFR 91.169; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13; FAA Order 7110.65

questions.question: During a precision approach in deteriorating IMC, your alternator fails at approximately 2,000 feet AGL on the glideslope. Your avionics are temporarily still powered by the battery. How does this compound the risk of deteriorating weather, and what is your priority order for managing this situation?
questions.answer: An alternator failure during an ILS approach in deteriorating weather creates compounding risks: battery-only power has a finite duration (typically 30 minutes or less depending on aircraft and electrical load), avionics may begin to fail sequentially, and the distraction of managing the electrical failure increases cockpit workload at the most critical phase of flight. Priority order: (1) Fly the aircraft — maintain glideslope and localizer tracking; an unstabilized approach in IMC with a distraction kills pilots. (2) Reduce electrical load immediately — shed all non-essential equipment to extend battery life for the ILS, communications, and transponder. (3) Communicate — advise ATC of the electrical failure so they can provide priority handling and have emergency equipment standing by. (4) Decide — if the approach can be completed before battery depletion and weather permits, continue with commitment to go missed at DA/DH if visual is not acquired. If battery life is uncertain, executing the missed approach now and declaring an emergency may be the lower-risk option. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook emphasizes that the word 'probably' should be avoided in decision-making — if battery life will 'probably' last, that is not a safe standard. Choose the option known to work.
questions.follow_up: If you lose your primary attitude indicator during this same approach due to the electrical failure, but your backup vacuum-driven AI is still functional, how does the loss of your primary flight display change your approach to the ILS and what currency requirement is relevant?
questions.follow_up_answer: With the loss of the primary EFIS/PFD, the pilot transitions to the backup vacuum AI and raw data instruments. This significantly increases workload because EFIS displays integrate attitude, altitude, airspeed, and navigation on one screen — the pilot must now scan multiple individual instruments. The pilot must be proficient at partial panel flying under 14 CFR 61.57(c), which requires instrument experience, but there is no specific 'partial panel' currency event required. However, 14 CFR 91.205(d) requires that all instruments required for IFR flight be operative — if the primary flight instruments are inoperative and the aircraft is not equipped with a legal alternative, the aircraft may not be flown IFR. In an emergency, 14 CFR 91.3(b) permits deviation from any rule to the extent necessary. Practically, the pilot should declare an emergency and fly the approach carefully using the backup instruments, accepting a higher workload and potentially higher risk, while prioritizing aircraft control above all else.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3; 14 CFR 91.205(d); 14 CFR 61.57(c); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5

questions.question: What is the Decision Altitude (DA) on a precision instrument approach, and what action is required when the aircraft reaches that altitude?
questions.answer: The Decision Altitude (DA) is a specified altitude, expressed in MSL, on a precision instrument approach at which the pilot must decide whether to continue the approach or execute a missed approach. At DA, if the required visual references — such as the runway environment, approach lighting system, or threshold markings — are not distinctly visible and identifiable, the pilot must immediately initiate a missed approach. Descending below DA without the required visual references is prohibited.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175(c); Instrument Flying Handbook FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5 and Chapter 9

questions.question: What are the specific visual references required by regulation before a pilot may continue descending below DA on a precision instrument approach?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.175(c), the pilot must have at least one of the following elements of the runway environment in sight and be able to maintain it throughout the approach to landing: the approach light system (ALS), threshold, threshold markings, threshold lights, runway end identifier lights (REIL), visual approach slope indicator (VASI), touchdown zone or touchdown zone markings, touchdown zone lights, runway or runway markings, or runway lights. Simply seeing the glow of lights through clouds or fog does not satisfy this requirement — the reference must be distinctly visible.

questions.question: What is the difference between Decision Altitude (DA) and Decision Height (DH), and which one is typically used on an ILS approach?
questions.answer: Decision Altitude (DA) is referenced to Mean Sea Level (MSL) and is used on approaches where barometric altimetry is the primary reference. Decision Height (DH) is referenced to the Height Above Threshold (HAT) or Height Above Airport (HAA) and is expressed in feet AGL. ILS approaches use Decision Height (DH) because the aircraft's position relative to the runway threshold is what matters at that critical decision point. Both serve the same function — defining the lowest altitude at which a pilot may continue descent without the required visual references — but DH is measured from the runway elevation, making it directly relevant to how high the aircraft is above the ground at the threshold.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175; Instrument Flying Handbook FAA-H-8083-15B; Aeronautical Information Manual (AIM) 5-4-5

questions.question: You are flying an ILS approach to minimums in a helicopter. At DA, you see the approach lighting system but nothing else — no runway, no threshold, no lights beyond the ALS. Are you legal to continue descending below DA?
questions.answer: It depends on whether you can make out the red terminating bars or the red side row bars of the ALS. Under 14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i), if the approach light system is the only element visible, a pilot may descend to 100 feet above the touchdown zone elevation — but no lower — unless other runway environment elements come into view. In a helicopter context, if you can only see the ALS and not any of the runway environment elements listed in 91.175(c)(3)(ii) through (x), you are limited to no lower than 100 feet above TDZE. If the visibility further deteriorates or the runway never comes into view before that point, a missed approach must be executed immediately. Continuing below that 100-foot buffer without additional visual references is a regulatory violation and an extreme safety risk.

questions.question: During an ILS approach in a helicopter, you reach DA and momentarily glimpse what appears to be runway lights, but then you fly back into IMC. Your copilot says 'I think I saw it — keep going.' What is the correct decision and why?
questions.answer: You must execute a missed approach immediately. 14 CFR 91.175(c) requires that the required visual references be distinctly visible and identifiable at the DA, not just momentarily glimpsed. The regulation also implies that the pilot must be in a position from which a normal landing can be made. If you re-enter IMC after DA, you have lost the visual contact required to continue legally and safely. The copilot's suggestion represents a classic 'get-there-itis' or 'continuation bias' hazard — a well-documented ADM trap where pilots press on despite deteriorating cues. The Helicopter Flying Handbook emphasizes that 80% of accidents involve human factors, and continuing below DA without solid visual references is precisely the error chain link that leads to CFIT. Initiate the missed approach without hesitation.

questions.question: How does the higher sensitivity of the localizer CDI compared to a VOR CDI specifically increase the risk of spatial disorientation and controlled flight into terrain (CFIT) if a helicopter pilot descends below DA without visual references?
questions.answer: The localizer CDI has a full-scale deflection of approximately 2.5°, compared to 12° for a VOR — making it roughly 4 to 5 times more sensitive. At low altitude near DA, this extreme sensitivity means small course deviations produce large needle deflections, demanding intensive instrument scan and precise control inputs. If the pilot simultaneously tries to peer outside looking for the runway environment, the instrument scan degrades rapidly. If visual references are not clearly established at DA and the pilot continues descending while distracted by the sensitive localizer, a momentary diversion of attention can result in an undetected deviation — and at 200 feet AGL, there is essentially no recovery margin. Descending below DA without clear visual references in this environment is one of the highest-risk scenarios in IFR helicopter operations, directly linked to CFIT accidents.
questions.regulatory_ref: Instrument Flying Handbook FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9 (localizer sensitivity); 14 CFR 91.175(c); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13

questions.question: A helicopter pilot is conducting a CAT I ILS approach with a reported RVR of 2,400 feet — right at minimums. The aircraft breaks out briefly at DA with a fleeting glimpse of the ALS, and the pilot continues descending. At 50 feet AGL the runway environment disappears again. The pilot lands anyway. Aside from the safety implications, what specific regulatory violations may have occurred?
questions.answer: Multiple violations are possible. First, under 14 CFR 91.175(c), the pilot may only continue below DA if the required visual references are distinctly visible and identifiable — a fleeting glimpse at DA likely does not satisfy 'distinctly visible.' Second, if the runway environment was lost again after DA and before landing, the pilot was legally required to execute a missed approach — continuing to land is a violation of 91.175(c).
