Third, if the RVR dropped below the published minimum at any point during the final approach segment, operating below published minimums is a violation under 91.175(a) and (b). Depending on the outcome and certificate type, enforcement actions could range from a Letter of Correction to certificate suspension or revocation. If operating under Part 135, additional operator-specific minimums under 14 CFR 135.225 may also have been violated.
questions.follow_up: You said 'distinctly visible' is the standard. How would the FAA or an NTSB investigator attempt to determine after the fact whether the pilot actually had the required visual references at DA, given there is no recording of what the pilot saw?
questions.follow_up_answer: Investigators would rely on a combination of objective and circumstantial evidence: ATC radar data to verify the aircraft's altitude profile and whether descent continued below DA; cockpit voice recorder (CVR) or communications recordings for any crew comments about visual contact; ATIS or official weather observations (METARs, SPECI, or tower RVR readings) at the time of the approach; witness statements from ATC controllers or ground personnel; and any available FDR or GPS track data showing altitude vs. distance from threshold. They would also evaluate whether the landing rollout was consistent with a stabilized visual approach or whether it showed deviations suggesting the pilot never had clear visual contact. The absence of a go-around itself becomes evidence of the pilot's decision-making. In Part 135 operations, flight following records and dispatch weather releases would also be examined.

questions.question: Given that helicopters can hover and maneuver at very low speeds, some pilots rationalize that they can 'feel their way' below DA to find the runway if they almost have visual contact. What is wrong with this reasoning both operationally and from an ADM standpoint?
questions.answer: This rationalization is fundamentally flawed on multiple levels. Operationally, the DA is established based on obstacle clearance surfaces, terrain, and the visual segment required for a stabilized approach — not the aircraft's maneuverability. Below DA without visual references, even a helicopter has no guarantee of obstacle clearance; towers, wires, terrain, and structures are not avoidable by slow flight if they cannot be seen. Hovering or slow flight in IMC at very low altitude creates extreme spatial disorientation risk, as vestibular illusions are more dangerous at slow speeds with subtle attitude changes. From an ADM perspective, this thinking is a textbook example of 'plan continuation bias' and 'invulnerability' hazardous attitude — the pilot overestimates their ability to handle a deteriorating situation and underestimates the consequences of being wrong. The Helicopter Flying Handbook notes that the word 'probably' in a pilot's reasoning — 'I can probably see it if I get lower' — is a red flag that the safer known option (missed approach) should be chosen instead. The unique hover capability of helicopters does not create a legal or safety exception to DA requirements under 14 CFR 91.175.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175; FAA Order 8260.42 (Helicopter Instrument Procedures); AIM 10-1-2; FAA-H-8083-21B
questions.follow_up: Are there any published instrument approach procedures specifically designed for helicopters that do allow lower minima or special descent profiles that take helicopter maneuverability into account?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes. The FAA publishes Helicopter Instrument Approaches (COPTER procedures) that are specifically designed for helicopters. These may include: (1) Copter ILS or Copter LPV approaches with lower minima than the fixed-wing equivalent, down to 100-foot DH in some cases, because helicopters can use a steeper approach angle (typically 6–9° vs. 3° for fixed-wing) and shorter visual segment; (2) Copter SIAP procedures using GPS/RNAV that take advantage of the helicopter's ability to approach at lower speeds; and (3) some procedures may authorize use of a point-in-space (PinS) approach that terminates at a point above an off-airport helipad, with a visual segment from the missed approach point. However, even on these helicopter-specific procedures, the DA/DH still applies — if the required visual references are not in sight at the published minima, a missed approach is required. The lower minima reflect obstacle clearance standards specific to helicopter approach geometry, not an allowance to descend through IMC by feel.

questions.question: When flying an ILS approach in a helicopter, what is the significance of the localizer CDI sensitivity compared to a VOR, and how does that affect your control inputs on final?
questions.answer: The localizer CDI is approximately 4–5 times more sensitive than a VOR CDI. Full-scale deflection on a localizer represents only about 2.5° off course, versus 12° or more for a VOR. In a helicopter, this means even small heading deviations produce noticeable needle movement. Control inputs must be smaller and more precise — chase the needle with large corrections and you will overcontrol and oscillate through centerline. Make small heading adjustments, cross-check frequently, and lead your corrections to keep the needle centered.

questions.question: What are the three indications you are monitoring simultaneously to fly a full ILS approach to minimums in a helicopter?
questions.answer: You are simultaneously monitoring: (1) the localizer needle for lateral course guidance — keep it centered left/right; (2) the glideslope needle for vertical path guidance — keep it centered up/down; and (3) airspeed/altitude/VSI to confirm you are descending at the appropriate rate consistent with the glideslope. In a helicopter you also scan for any required altitude constraints or step-down fixes on the profile view of the approach plate, and monitor the altimeter to identify the Decision Altitude (DA) when a missed approach must be initiated if the runway environment is not in sight.

questions.question: At Decision Altitude on an ILS approach, what specific elements of the 'runway environment' must you have in sight before you can continue descending below DA in a helicopter?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.175(c), at least one of the following runway environment elements must be distinctly visible and identifiable: the approach light system; threshold; threshold markings; threshold lights; runway end identifier lights (REIL); visual approach slope indicator (VASI/PAPI); touchdown zone or touchdown zone markings; touchdown zone lights; runway or runway markings; runway lights. Seeing only the approach lights does not authorize you to descend below 100 feet above the touchdown zone elevation unless the red terminating bars or red side row bars are also visible, or another runway environment item is visible. In a helicopter, if the required visual reference is not established at DA, an immediate missed approach must be executed.

questions.question: You are flying an ILS approach in IMC and notice the glideslope needle is full-scale high as you cross the final approach fix. You are at the correct glideslope intercept altitude per the approach plate. What do you do, and what could explain this situation?
questions.answer: Full-scale high glideslope at the FAF when you are at the correct published altitude is a red flag — do not chase the glideslope downward. Possible causes include: (1) a false glideslope lobe — the ILS glideslope transmits multiple lobes, and the false upper lobe can appear at roughly twice the normal glideslope angle (e.g., ~6° instead of 3°); intercepting it would cause a dangerously steep descent; (2) receiver or antenna malfunction; (3) the glideslope transmitter is flagged or unreliable. The correct action is to cross-check your altitude against the published FAF crossing altitude and the step-down profile on the plate. If the needle is off but your altitude is correct, treat it as a glideslope-out situation and either fly a localizer-only approach to the appropriate higher minimums, or execute a missed approach. Never track a glideslope indication that conflicts with your published altitudes.

questions.question: During an ILS approach in your helicopter, you break out of the clouds at 400 feet AGL and have the approach lights in sight, but the runway itself is obscured. Your DA is 200 feet HAT. Can you continue descending, and if so, to what altitude?
questions.answer: Yes, you may continue descending below DA because you have a required visual reference — the approach lights. However, under 14 CFR 91.175(c)(1), when approach lights alone are in sight (without the red terminating bars or red side row bars), you may not descend below 100 feet above the touchdown zone elevation. To descend below that 100-foot threshold, you must have in sight an additional runway environment element beyond just the approach lights. Since you are in a helicopter with more flexibility in transitioning to a landing, you must still comply with this regulation — if you reach 100 feet AGL over the TDZ and have only approach lights without the additional required elements, you must execute a missed approach.

questions.question: You are assigned an ILS approach in your helicopter and the ATIS reports a 15-knot crosswind from the left. Describe how you would manage drift correction on the localizer from the time you intercept final approach course to touchdown.
questions.answer: After intercepting the localizer, establish a wind correction angle (crab) to the left sufficient to track the course — start with an estimated correction based on wind and your approach speed. Monitor the localizer needle: if it begins drifting right (wind is pushing you right of course), increase the crab left; if left, reduce it. Helicopter advantage: unlike a fixed-wing aircraft committed to a runway heading at flare, a helicopter can maintain a stabilized crab all the way to the hover or touchdown point and then pedal-turn into the wind just before touchdown, or transition to a sideslip. Do not use excessive sideslip on a stabilized ILS approach in IMC — maintain the crab. The key is making small, early corrections to prevent full-scale deflection. If the localizer needle goes full-scale, the indication is unreliable and the approach must be abandoned.

questions.question: Your helicopter is equipped with a functioning autopilot coupled to the ILS. Halfway down final approach, the autopilot suddenly disconnects. Walk me through your immediate actions and how your scan and workload management must adapt instantly.
questions.answer: Immediately take positive control of the cyclic, collective, and pedals — the aircraft may have begun deviating during the disconnect transient. Simultaneously verbalize 'autopilot off' if flying with a crew, or note it mentally if single-pilot. Your scan priority shifts: cross-check attitude indicator to verify wings-level and correct pitch, then immediately re-center localizer and glideslope needles with manual corrections. Workload jumps significantly — you are now hand-flying a coupled approach profile that the automation was managing. Apply SRM principles: slow down your thought process, resist the urge to chase needles aggressively, and make small coordinated corrections. If workload becomes unmanageable or situational awareness is degraded, execute a missed approach — there is no requirement to complete the approach. Do not attempt to re-engage the autopilot in IMC during a critical phase of flight unless the cause of the disconnect is known and the system is confirmed serviceable. After go-around, brief yourself or your crew on the failure and declare the autopilot inoperative per MEL procedures before the next approach attempt.
questions.follow_up: If you continued the approach manually and reached DA but were not stabilized — say the localizer was half-scale deflection and airspeed was 15 knots fast — what does the ACS require you to do, and is there any discretion?
questions.follow_up_answer: The ACS for precision approaches (IH.VII.B) requires that the approach be stabilized and conducted within specific tolerances — for a helicopter ILS approach, the pilot should maintain the localizer and glideslope within 3/4 scale deflection throughout the approach, and the aircraft must be in a position and condition from which a normal landing can be made. At DA with half-scale localizer deflection and 15 knots fast, the approach is not stabilized. There is no discretion — a missed approach is required. 14 CFR 91.175(c) requires the aircraft to be in a position from which a normal approach to landing can be made before continuing below DA. An unstabilized condition at DA does not meet that standard. The ACS is explicit that deviations beyond these parameters require the pilot to initiate a go-around/missed approach. Pressing a non-stabilized approach to landing is a leading contributor to approach and landing accidents.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175(c); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (SRM/workload management); ACS IH.VII.B

questions.question: You are flying an ILS approach and your static system becomes blocked during the final approach segment. Describe exactly how each of your pitot-static instruments will be affected and how you will manage the approach.
questions.answer: With a completely blocked static system: (1) The altimeter freezes at the altitude it was reading when the blockage occurred — it will not update as you descend, so you will not know your true altitude; (2) the VSI will drop to zero and remain there regardless of actual climb or descent — it is unreliable; (3) the ASI will become inaccurate — as you descend and static pressure should increase, the trapped static pressure will cause the ASI to over-read (indicating faster than actual). The pitot tube is unaffected, so dynamic pressure input to the ASI is still accurate; the error is on the static side. Management: If the aircraft has an alternate static source, select it immediately. The alternate static source (typically inside the cabin, which is slightly lower pressure than outside) will produce a slightly higher altitude indication, a slightly faster airspeed indication, and a momentary climb indication on the VSI due to the lower cabin pressure — these errors are small and charted in the POH/AFM. If no alternate static source is available, you may break the VSI glass as a last resort to vent the system to cockpit air (check POH authorization first). With the altimeter frozen, you must immediately inform ATC, request vectors or radar altimetry assistance, cross-reference GPS altitude if available, and seriously consider executing a missed approach — continuing an ILS to DA with an unserviceable altimeter is extremely hazardous.
questions.follow_up: If you select the alternate static source and your altimeter now reads 50 feet higher than it was reading, does that mean you are actually 50 feet higher than you thought, and how does that affect your DA call?
questions.follow_up_answer: No — the higher altimeter reading with alternate static does not mean you are physically higher. The alternate static source (cabin air) has slightly lower pressure than outside ambient static, so the altimeter interprets it as being at a slightly higher altitude than actual. This is a known instrument error when using alternate static. The FAA-H-8083-15B states the altimeter will read slightly higher with alternate static selected. Practically, this means your actual altitude is slightly lower than the altimeter now shows — which is a safety concern on an approach. The POH/AFM for your specific aircraft will have a correction table for alternate static errors. You must apply that correction. For your DA call: if the plate shows DA as 200 feet and alternate static adds a +50 foot error, you must initiate the missed approach when the altimeter reads 250 feet (DA + correction) to ensure you are not actually below DA. Always know your aircraft's alternate static correction values before flight.

questions.question: When you check in with approach control for an instrument approach, what information must you include in your initial call?
questions.answer: Your initial check-in with approach control should include: aircraft callsign (tail number or flight number), aircraft type, current position or fix, altitude, and the ATIS information code received. For example: 'Approach, Helicopter N123AB, Robinson R44, 15 miles northeast at 3,000, information Delta.' This gives the controller immediate situational awareness without requiring additional transmissions.

questions.question: What does it mean to establish 'two-way communications' with ATC, and why is simply transmitting on a frequency not sufficient?
questions.answer: Two-way communications means you have transmitted to ATC and received a response that acknowledges your callsign. Simply transmitting on a frequency does not establish two-way communications — you must receive a reply from ATC specifically addressing your aircraft. This is critical for airspace entry requirements (Class C and D) and for IFR operations, because until ATC confirms contact, you have no assurance they are aware of your position or intentions.

questions.question: As a helicopter on an ILS approach, ATC issues: 'N456AB, cleared ILS Runway 28 approach, maintain 2,500 until established, contact tower 120.3.' What is the correct readback?
questions.answer: The correct readback is: 'Cleared ILS Runway 28 approach, maintain 2,500 until established, tower 120.3, N456AB.' You must read back the clearance limit (the approach cleared for), the altitude restriction, the tower frequency, and your callsign. Altitude assignments, frequency changes, and clearances are all items that require a full readback per AIM guidance on hearback/readback procedures.

questions.question: You are flying a helicopter IFR and are handed off from TRACON to tower just as you reach the final approach fix (FAF) inbound. The tower frequency is congested and your first call goes unanswered. How do you handle communications and continue the approach safely?
questions.answer: Make one or two additional attempts on the tower frequency, spacing them several seconds apart. If still no response, attempt to raise the previous TRACON frequency to advise them of the communication difficulty. You may continue the approach — an unanswered call does not require you to abandon an IFR approach already in progress. However, you must not land or enter the movement area without tower clearance (at a controlled airport). If you reach the missed approach point with no contact established, execute the published missed approach and continue attempting to reach ATC. Squawk 7600 (radio failure) if all frequencies fail. Document the attempt and time of lost contact.

questions.question: During a helicopter precision approach in IMC, ATC gives you a speed restriction of 'maintain 90 knots until 5-mile final' but your helicopter's Vne is 100 knots and the approach requires slowing to 60 knots by the FAF. How do you communicate your inability to comply and what do you say to ATC?
questions.answer: You must immediately advise ATC that you are unable to comply and provide the reason and what you can do instead. A proper response would be: 'Approach, N123AB, unable 90 knots to 5-mile final, we'll need to slow to 70 knots by 7 miles for our approach speed requirements, request amended restriction.' ATC cannot require you to fly at a speed that compromises aircraft safety. You have the authority and responsibility to notify ATC of the limitation. Never simply ignore an ATC instruction — always communicate and coordinate an alternative.

questions.question: You are established on a precision approach in a helicopter when approach control calls: 'N789CD, traffic alert, unknown traffic 12 o'clock, 2 miles, altitude unknown, advise if you have the traffic.' You are IMC. What is your proper response, and what are your responsibilities at this point?
questions.answer: Your proper response is: 'N789CD, negative contact, IMC.' This informs ATC you cannot visually acquire the traffic because you are in instrument meteorological conditions. ATC should then issue a vector or other instruction to resolve the conflict. You are not required to maneuver based solely on a traffic advisory — it is advisory information only. However, if ATC issues a Traffic Alert and Collision Avoidance System (TCAS) resolution advisory (RA), you must follow the RA immediately and notify ATC of the deviation. Maintain your assigned altitude and heading unless ATC provides further instructions or safety of flight requires immediate action.

questions.question: During a precision approach evaluation, I notice you switched to tower frequency before ATC issued the frequency change. You said you 'always do it that way at that airport.' What is wrong with this practice from both a regulatory and operational standpoint, and what is the correct procedure?
questions.answer: Switching frequencies without authorization is improper and potentially hazardous. You must remain on the approach control frequency until instructed to contact tower. TRACON may need to issue last-minute instructions — a go-around clearance, traffic information, or a wind shear alert — and if you have self-initiated a frequency change, you will miss that call. From a regulatory standpoint, 14 CFR 91.123 requires compliance with ATC clearances and instructions; departing the frequency without authorization violates this requirement. The correct procedure is to remain on the assigned frequency, acknowledge all instructions, and only change frequencies when ATC explicitly directs you to do so.
questions.follow_up: If you reach the missed approach point and still have not been told to contact tower, and you are breaking out of the clouds and can see the runway, what do you do?
questions.follow_up_answer: You remain on the approach control frequency and advise them: 'N123AB, runway in sight, request frequency change to tower.' Do not self-initiate the switch. Approach control may have a reason for keeping you — traffic conflicts, coordination in progress, or other factors. At a towered airport you need a landing clearance from tower before touching down, so timely communication is important, but it must be ATC-directed, not pilot-initiated without authorization.

questions.question: You are conducting a precision approach checkride in a helicopter. The candidate receives a clearance that includes an altitude restriction they read back incorrectly — they say '2,000' when ATC said '3,000' — and ATC does not catch it. The candidate then descends to 2,000. As the examiner, how do I evaluate this, and what is the pilot's underlying responsibility regarding readback errors?
questions.answer: This is a serious error that reflects a failure of the hearback/readback safety system. The pilot holds sole responsibility for the accuracy of their readback — ATC's failure to catch the error does not transfer responsibility. If ATC does not respond to an incorrect readback with a correction, the pilot should not assume the readback was accepted as correct; the pilot must verify any uncertainty before executing a clearance that could compromise safety. Under 14 CFR 91.123, the pilot in command is responsible for compliance with ATC clearances. Descending to the wrong altitude could constitute an altitude deviation, which may result in a pilot deviation report. On the checkride, this could be grounds for unsatisfactory performance if it creates a safety issue or demonstrates a lack of understanding of communication responsibilities.
questions.follow_up: If you realized mid-descent that you may have read back the wrong altitude, what is the correct immediate action?
questions.follow_up_answer: Stop the descent immediately, return to the last assigned altitude you are confident about, and immediately contact ATC: 'Approach, N123AB, request confirmation of assigned altitude, we may have had a readback error.' ATC will clarify, and you comply with the corrected clearance. Proactive self-correction and immediate communication with ATC is the correct response — it demonstrates ADM and situational awareness, and it is far better than continuing a potentially wrong clearance and hoping it works out.

questions.question: When setting up for an ILS approach in a helicopter, what is the correct sequence for confirming your navigation equipment is properly tuned and identified before the final approach fix?
questions.answer: The correct sequence is: Select the correct ILS frequency from the approach chart and tune the NAV receiver to that frequency. Then identify the station by listening to the Morse code identifier and comparing it to the identifier printed on the approach chart. Finally, confirm the CDI needle and glideslope indicator are alive and responding correctly. You must positively identify the station — an unidentified or flagged NAV receiver should never be used for an approach.

questions.question: What does a NAV flag or OFF flag on your CDI indicator tell you about the operational status of the navigation equipment, and how should you respond?
questions.answer: A NAV flag or OFF flag indicates the received signal is too weak, unreliable, or outside usable range — the equipment cannot be considered operational for navigation. You should not use that receiver for the approach. You must treat the navigation equipment as unreliable, declare the approach unavailable with that equipment, notify ATC, and either hold until the issue is resolved or divert to an alternate. Never attempt a precision approach with a flagged NAV receiver.

questions.question: How do you positively identify a VOR or ILS station, and why is listening to the audio identifier not enough if the station is in a TEST or maintenance condition?
questions.answer: You positively identify a VOR or ILS by tuning the correct frequency, enabling the audio, and decoding the Morse code identifier, then matching it to the identifier printed on the approach chart. A station under maintenance or in test mode may transmit an identifier with the letter 'T' inserted (e.g., 'T-ILS'), or it may transmit no identifier at all. A station transmitting only 'T' in its identifier is not approved for operational use. Always verify the identifier matches exactly — any discrepancy means you cannot use that facility for the approach.

questions.question: You are being vectored for an ILS approach in IMC. ATC gives you a heading and tells you to expect the ILS. As you tune and identify the localizer, you notice the CDI needle is pegged hard left and not centering as you get closer to the final approach course. What do you do, and what could cause this?
questions.answer: A CDI pegged hard left while being vectored toward the final approach course is not necessarily abnormal — it may simply mean you are well left of the localizer centerline and the needle will center as you intercept. However, if the needle never moves or responds abnormally as you approach the course, suspect a tuning error (wrong frequency), a failed or flagged receiver, or a back-course situation. You should: verify the frequency against the approach chart, check the Morse code identifier is correct, confirm no NAV flag is present, and cross-check with any other available navigation. If the equipment status cannot be confirmed as operational, do not continue the approach — advise ATC and request an alternate course of action.

questions.question: You are flying a GPS/ILS approach in a helicopter using an RNAV-capable FMS. Explain how you would select and confirm the operational status of navigation equipment for this approach differently than you would for a traditional ILS-only aircraft.
questions.answer: For an FMS/RNAV-capable helicopter shooting a GPS overlay or ILS: First, load the correct approach from the FMS database and verify the approach plate identifier and transition match what ATC has cleared you for. Confirm the GPS receiver has RAIM availability (or WAAS integrity) for the approach segment — the system should annunciate 'APCH' mode when within approximately 30 NM and then 'LPV' or 'LP' as appropriate. Additionally, if the ILS is being used as a cross-check or primary, tune and identify the ILS frequency on the NAV radio as you would normally. Confirm no GPS integrity flags are present and that the CDI source is correctly set. Do not assume the FMS has auto-loaded the correct approach without verifying frequency, identifier, and transition.

questions.question: During your approach briefing in the helicopter, you notice the NOTAM states the ILS glideslope is out of service. The localizer is operational. How does this affect your equipment selection and setup, and what minimums apply?
questions.answer: If the glideslope is out of service, you cannot fly a full ILS precision approach. You may still fly the localizer-only approach if that procedure is published, using localizer-only minimums — which are higher than ILS minimums (typically a higher MDA instead of a DA). You set up the NAV receiver the same way (tune and identify the localizer frequency), but you should verify your glideslope needle is flagged or disregarded since it is not operational. Confirm you are using the correct minimums column on the approach chart for 'LOC only.' Advise ATC that you are flying the localizer approach if required. This is a non-precision approach and helicopter operators should also confirm any helicopter-specific minimums published on the chart.

questions.question: You are flying a single-pilot IFR helicopter in high workload conditions, and ATC clears you for the ILS approach with a very short vector — leaving you only about 90 seconds before the final approach fix. Walk me through your exact prioritization for selecting, tuning, identifying, and confirming navigation equipment under time pressure, and what gets dropped or deferred if you cannot complete everything?
questions.answer: Under time pressure, prioritize in this order: (1) Fly the aircraft — maintain assigned heading and altitude first, never sacrifice aircraft control for setup. (2) Tune the correct ILS frequency immediately — this is the single most critical step because without the correct frequency you have no guidance. (3) Confirm the Morse code identifier — even a quick listen to catch obvious errors is better than nothing; if you cannot positively identify the station, do not continue the approach. (4) Confirm CDI and glideslope needles are alive and not flagged. (5) Brief minimums — at minimum, know your DA and missed approach heading. If you cannot accomplish all of this in the available time, ask ATC for a longer vector or a 360-degree turn for sequencing. SRM principles apply here: if the situation is deteriorating, take action early — not at the FAF. Never rush a setup to the point where you cannot confirm equipment status. A 'probable' correct setup is not an acceptable standard.
questions.follow_up: If you identify the ILS frequency and hear the correct identifier, but the CDI needle is not responding at all — it is centered and perfectly still as you are crossing the FAF — what is your decision and why?
questions.follow_up_answer: A perfectly centered, motionless CDI needle at the FAF is a red flag, not a green light. This could indicate a failed NAV receiver, a stuck CDI, or a flagged signal that is not displaying the flag properly. You should not continue the approach using that CDI as your primary guidance. Cross-check all available sources: check for a NAV flag, verify the frequency one more time, monitor the audio identifier again, and if possible cross-check with GPS or DME. If you cannot confirm the equipment is functioning and responding correctly, execute the missed approach. A needle that never moves provides no useful guidance and creates false confidence — continuing the approach would be a serious safety error.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (SRM/ADM); AIM 5-4-5; 14 CFR 91.175

questions.question: A student pilot tells you: 'I tuned the ILS, the needle is centered, and the glideslope is alive — I'm good to go.' What critical step did they skip, and why can a centered CDI needle actually be the most dangerous indication you can have when setting up for an ILS?
questions.answer: The student skipped positive station identification — they never confirmed the Morse code identifier. Tuning a frequency and getting a live needle does not prove you are on the correct ILS. A centered CDI when you are on the extended centerline may be correct, but if you have accidentally tuned the wrong frequency or a nearby VOR, the needle could appear centered for completely wrong reasons. More dangerously, a centered CDI can occur when: (1) you are on the back course of a different ILS, (2) you are accidentally tuned to an adjacent localizer frequency, or (3) the receiver is failed in a centered position with no flag. The FAA requires positive identification before using any NAV facility for an instrument approach. If the identifier is not confirmed, the approach must not be commenced. The hazard is that a 'good-looking' instrument can create false situational awareness — which is exactly how CFIT accidents occur.
questions.follow_up: Imagine both of your NAV radios can receive the localizer frequency, but only one has audio capability. How do you confirm station identification if your audio NAV is inoperative on the primary NAV receiver you intend to use for the approach?
questions.follow_up_answer: If the primary NAV receiver lacks audio capability and you cannot hear the Morse code identifier, you cannot positively identify the station using that receiver alone. Your options are: (1) Use the secondary NAV radio (if it has audio) tuned to the same frequency to confirm the identifier, then use the primary for guidance — as long as you have confirmed both are receiving the same valid station. (2) If GPS is available and the approach is a GPS overlay, you may be able to confirm station identity through the FMS database. (3) If no method of positive identification is available, you cannot legally or safely use that facility for the approach — you must declare the equipment issue to ATC and request an alternate approach or divert. The inability to identify the station is a no-go condition, not a workaround.
questions.regulatory_ref: AIM 1-1-7; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9; 14 CFR 91.187; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13

questions.question: During an ILS approach, ATC issues you a new altimeter setting of 29.85. At what point are you required to set that altimeter, and what happens to your indicated altitude when you do?
questions.answer: You must set the new altimeter setting as soon as it is received. If your previous setting was higher than 29.85, your indicated altitude will decrease slightly. Each 0.01 Hg change equals approximately 10 feet of indicated altitude change. Failing to update the altimeter means your indicated altitude will not accurately reflect your true pressure altitude correction, which is critical during a precision approach where you must cross fixes and the decision altitude at precise heights.

questions.question: ATC clears you for the ILS approach and instructs you to maintain 3,000 feet until established on the localizer. What does 'established on the localizer' mean, and how does that instruction affect when you can descend on the glideslope?
questions.answer: 'Established on the localizer' means the aircraft is tracking the localizer course within the normal full-scale deflection limits — generally within about one dot or less of center — and is stable on course. The instruction to maintain 3,000 feet until established means you cannot begin glideslope descent until you have first intercepted and are tracking the localizer. This is a common ATC technique to ensure sequencing and obstacle clearance. Descending on the glideslope before being established on the localizer would violate the ATC clearance.

questions.question: You are on an ILS approach and ATC issues a missed approach instruction before you reach your DA. Are you required to comply immediately, and what are your general obligations when ATC issues an instruction mid-approach?
questions.answer: Yes, you are required to comply immediately with ATC instructions unless doing so would compromise safety. Under 14 CFR 91.123, a pilot in command must comply with ATC clearances and instructions unless an emergency exists. If ATC tells you to execute a missed approach at any point, you must begin the published or assigned missed approach procedure immediately. You must also read back any holding instructions, altitude assignments, or frequency changes as required. If you are unable to comply, you must advise ATC immediately.

questions.question: You are on final on an ILS approach in a helicopter at 800 feet AGL when ATC instructs you to side-step to a parallel taxiway for landing due to a disabled aircraft on the runway. How do you handle this clearance, and what are the key considerations specific to a helicopter performing this maneuver under IFR?
questions.answer: You should acknowledge and read back the instruction immediately. For a helicopter, a side-step to a parallel surface is more operationally feasible than for a fixed-wing aircraft, but under IFR you must ensure you maintain positive visual reference to the new landing surface before maneuvering laterally. You should not abandon the ILS guidance until you have visual contact sufficient to safely transition to the side-step surface. Key considerations include: confirming the taxiway is clear and usable, ensuring obstacle clearance during the lateral transition, and verifying the maneuver is within your helicopter's performance capability. If unable, you must advise ATC and execute the missed approach.

questions.question: During a practice ILS approach, the evaluator acts as ATC and instructs you to fly a 360-degree turn for spacing while on the final approach course at 2,500 feet. Walk me through how you comply with this clearance while maintaining instrument proficiency and not losing your position relative to the approach course.
questions.answer: Acknowledge and read back the clearance. Begin the turn using standard rate or as appropriate for the helicopter, maintaining 2,500 feet throughout. Use the HSI or CDI to track where the localizer course is during the turn so you can re-intercept it properly. Monitor your distance from the FAF using DME if available so you know where to re-intercept the localizer at the correct angle. When ATC clears you to resume the approach, re-intercept the localizer at an appropriate angle (typically 30 degrees or less on final), confirm glideslope capture, and continue the approach. Throughout the maneuver, maintain altitude precisely, and manage workload with good scan technique to avoid spatial disorientation during the turn.

questions.question: You are shooting an ILS to minimums in actual IMC. At DA, you do not have the required visual references to land and begin the missed approach. During the missed approach climb, ATC issues a heading of 180 degrees and an altitude of 4,000 feet, which differs from the published missed approach procedure. What do you do?
questions.answer: Comply with the ATC-issued heading and altitude. Once you have initiated the missed approach and are flying clear of obstacles per the published procedure, ATC radar vectors supersede the published missed approach procedure and you must follow them. The key is to first execute the published missed approach climbing turn or course to ensure obstacle clearance, and then as soon as safely able, comply with ATC's heading and altitude instructions. ATC issues radar vectors during missed approaches to provide traffic separation and sequencing. You must read back the altitude assignment and heading. If there is any conflict with obstacle clearance, advise ATC immediately.

questions.question: You are on an ILS approach in a helicopter and ATC issues a speed restriction of 'maintain 90 knots to the FAF.' After the FAF, you slow to approach speed without a further clearance. Did you violate the ATC instruction, and how should speed restrictions on ILS approaches be managed by helicopter pilots?
questions.answer: No, this was not a violation. Speed restrictions issued by ATC apply up to the point specified — in this case the FAF. After the FAF, you are no longer bound by that restriction and may adjust speed as appropriate for the approach. This is consistent with AIM guidance that ATC-issued speed adjustments on approach are normally cancelled or become inapplicable at the FAF or when cleared for the approach. For helicopter pilots, it is especially important to understand this because helicopters often need to slow significantly after the FAF to maintain a stabilized approach and safe airspeed for DA/DH decision-making. If ATC wants a speed restriction past the FAF, they must issue a new specific instruction.
questions.follow_up: What if ATC says 'maintain best forward speed on the ILS' — does that instruction continue past the FAF, and is there a minimum speed you must fly?
questions.follow_up_answer: An instruction to maintain best forward speed is a general spacing instruction and, like other speed restrictions, technically applies to the segment for which it was issued. Past the FAF, you have operational flexibility to slow to a safe approach speed. There is no regulatory minimum approach speed for helicopters on an ILS beyond aircraft performance requirements — you must stay above effective translational lift or ETL airspeed if needed to maintain controllability and must not descend below DA without the required visual references. The helicopter's flight manual and stabilized approach criteria should guide your speed management. If ATC is pressing for speed that compromises safety, you must advise ATC you are unable and state your intentions.

questions.question: You are flying an ILS approach and ATC issues a clearance you believe contains an error — they clear you to descend to 1,800 feet, but the glideslope intercept altitude on the plate is 2,500 feet and the terrain in the area is mountainous. How do you handle this situation, and what are your legal obligations versus your safety obligations?
questions.answer: You must query ATC immediately. Under 14 CFR 91.123 you are required to comply with ATC clearances, but you also have the authority and responsibility under 14 CFR 91.3 as PIC to deviate from any rule or clearance to the extent necessary to meet an emergency or ensure safety. If you believe a clearance will result in controlled flight into terrain or violates obstacle clearance requirements, you must advise ATC that you are unable to comply and state the reason. You should request clarification or an amended clearance. If ATC confirms the clearance and you still believe it is unsafe, you have the right and duty to refuse it, citing safety of flight. After the flight, if you deviated from an ATC clearance, you must submit a written report to ATC if requested under 91.123(b). This scenario also illustrates the importance of the error chain concept — a single misheard or misissued clearance combined with distraction and high workload can lead to CFIT.
questions.follow_up: If you comply with the erroneous clearance and strike terrain, who bears responsibility — you as PIC or ATC?
questions.follow_up_answer: As PIC, you bear ultimate responsibility for the safety of the flight under 14 CFR 91.3. ATC may share administrative or legal liability, but the FAA's position is clear that PIC authority and responsibility cannot be delegated. Courts and NTSB findings have consistently held that the pilot cannot blindly follow an ATC clearance that a reasonable pilot would recognize as unsafe. ATC services are provided to assist pilots, not to relieve them of their responsibilities. If a pilot follows an obviously erroneous clearance without question, they will likely be found at fault. This is why IFR pilots must maintain situational awareness independently of ATC, verify altitudes against published minimums, and never hesitate to question a clearance that appears to conflict with terrain, obstacles, or published procedure altitudes.

questions.question: During a precision approach in IMC, you notice your altimeter needle is frozen and not moving as you descend. What does this tell you, and what is the most likely cause?
questions.answer: A frozen altimeter that does not respond to altitude changes indicates a blocked static port. The altimeter operates solely on static pressure; if that source is blocked, the instrument will display the altitude at which the blockage occurred and remain there regardless of actual altitude changes. The VSI will also show zero, and the ASI will be inaccurate.

questions.question: On final approach, you activate the alternate static source inside the helicopter cabin. How will this affect your altimeter and airspeed indicator readings, and why?
questions.answer: Cabin static pressure is slightly lower than outside ambient pressure due to airflow around the fuselage. Selecting the alternate static source will cause the altimeter to read slightly higher than actual altitude, the ASI to read slightly faster than actual airspeed, and the VSI to momentarily indicate a climb before stabilizing. You must be aware of these errors and account for them during the approach.

questions.question: What are the three instruments driven by the pitot-static system, and which of them would still provide usable data if only the pitot tube became blocked with the drain hole remaining open?
questions.answer: The three pitot-static instruments are the airspeed indicator (ASI), altimeter, and vertical speed indicator (VSI). The ASI uses both pitot and static pressure; if the pitot tube is blocked but the drain hole is open, ram pressure bleeds off and the ASI will slowly drop toward zero. The altimeter and VSI rely only on static pressure and would remain fully functional since the static system is unaffected.

questions.question: You are established on an ILS final in a helicopter at 1,500 feet MSL. Your pitot heat fails and you suspect ice ingestion. The ASI begins rising steadily even though you have not changed power or attitude. What is happening and what immediate actions do you take?
questions.answer: A blocked pitot tube with a blocked drain hole causes the ASI to act like an altimeter — as you descend, static pressure increases relative to the trapped pitot pressure, causing the ASI to show a decreasing reading, or if climbing, an increasing reading. If the ASI is rising while descending on final, this is consistent with both holes being blocked — the trapped pressure makes the ASI respond inversely. Immediate actions: activate pitot heat if available and not already failed, cross-check attitude indicator and VSI to verify actual flight path, do not chase the erroneous ASI, fly attitude and power, advise ATC of the malfunction, and consider executing a missed approach to troubleshoot in a controlled environment rather than continuing to a precision approach minimums environment with an unreliable airspeed indication.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B, Chapter 5; 14 CFR 91.187 (malfunction reports in controlled airspace)

questions.question: Descending through 800 feet AGL on a precision approach, you notice your attitude indicator is tumbling and showing erratic bank indications. Your autopilot, which is coupled to the approach, is beginning to make aggressive roll inputs. What do you do?
questions.answer: An erratic attitude indicator (AI) during a coupled approach is a serious situation. Immediately disconnect the autopilot to prevent it from acting on faulty gyro data and driving the helicopter into an unusual attitude. Revert to partial panel flying using the turn coordinator for bank information, the altimeter and VSI for pitch reference, and the GPS or ILS raw data for course guidance. Cross-check the standby AI if equipped. Since you are below 1,000 feet AGL in IMC with a failed primary attitude reference, the safest action is to execute a missed approach immediately — do not attempt to hand-fly a precision approach to minimums on partial panel without a verified backup attitude source. Declare the malfunction to ATC as required under 14 CFR 91.187.

questions.question: On an ILS approach, you are fully established on the localizer but the glideslope indicator is pegged full-scale down and never moves throughout the approach. ATC reports your altitude readouts are normal on radar. What are the possible causes and how do you handle it?
questions.answer: A glideslope needle pegged full-scale down and unresponsive could indicate: (1) a failed glideslope receiver or antenna, (2) an avionics circuit fault or pulled CB, (3) the glideslope transmitter is out of service (NOTAM), or (4) you are below the glideslope capture range when intercepting from above. Check NOTAMs for a glideslope NOTAM, check the avionics/circuit breakers, and confirm the correct ILS frequency is tuned and identified. If the glideslope is confirmed inoperative, the approach cannot be flown as a precision approach. You must treat it as a localizer-only (non-precision) approach using the LOC minimums from the approach plate, which are higher than ILS DH. Advise ATC of the situation.

questions.question: You are flying a coupled ILS in a helicopter at night in IMC. At 400 feet AGL, your primary EFIS display fails to black screen. You have a standby ASI, altimeter, and attitude indicator, but your autopilot disconnects automatically. Walk me through your exact thought process and actions for the next 60 seconds.
questions.answer: This is a high-workload, time-critical scenario at a very low altitude in IMC. Immediately: (1) Aviate — hands on controls, transition to the standby instruments (attitude, altimeter, ASI). Maintain wings level and a safe attitude. (2) Do NOT fixate on the failed display — transfer scan entirely to standby instruments. (3) Assess altitude: at 400 feet AGL you are near or below DA/DH for most ILS approaches. The safest action is to execute a missed approach immediately, as you no longer have the full instrument suite needed to safely continue to minimums. (4) Apply missed approach power and attitude, climb straight ahead per the published missed approach procedure. (5) Communicate: advise ATC of the EFIS failure and missed approach. (6) Once at a safe altitude and established on the missed approach, troubleshoot — check circuit breakers for the EFIS, attempt a reboot if the AFM permits. (7) Declare the malfunction per 14 CFR 91.187 if in controlled airspace. Do not attempt another approach without either restoring the primary display or being certain the standby instrument suite is legally and practically sufficient for the approach being attempted.
questions.follow_up: You manage to restore the EFIS display on the missed approach. ATC asks if you want to attempt the ILS again. Before you say yes, what do you need to verify about your instrument system to legally and safely attempt another precision approach?
questions.follow_up_answer: Before accepting another approach, verify: (1) the EFIS is displaying correctly and cross-checks with the standby instruments — a display that rebooted once may fail again; (2) the root cause of the failure is understood (e.g., loose connector vs. systemic avionics fault); (3) confirm all instruments required for the approach are functional and agree — altimeter, ASI, attitude, CDI/glideslope, and any required navigation equipment; (4) check the AFM for any limitations on operating following an avionics reset; (5) ensure the autopilot is functional if you intend a coupled approach; (6) consider whether crew/pilot workload and psychological state are appropriate for another approach after a significant distraction event. Per 14 CFR 91.175, you must be able to operate under IFR, and you are PIC — if you are not fully confident in the avionics reliability, declaring the emergency landing or diverting to VMC conditions is the correct decision.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175; 14 CFR 91.187; FAA-H-8083-15B, Chapter 5; FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 13

questions.question: During an ILS approach, your altimeter reads 200 feet higher than what ATC radar shows your actual altitude to be, and the discrepancy has been consistent for the last 2,000 feet of descent. Your static system appears normal. What are the possible explanations, and how does this affect your decision to continue to the published decision height?
questions.answer: A consistent 200-foot high altimeter error compared to ATC Mode C readout could result from: (1) an incorrect altimeter setting (Kollsman window) — each 0.10 Hg error equals approximately 100 feet, so a 0.20 Hg error would produce this discrepancy; (2) a faulty encoding altimeter sending incorrect Mode C data to ATC while your primary altimeter is actually correct; (3) an actual altimeter instrument error. First, verify your altimeter setting is the current local altimeter received from ATIS or ATC. Cross-check with the tower-reported field elevation when over the threshold or with GPS altitude as a sanity check. If the altimeter setting is correct and the discrepancy is real, you may be 200 feet lower than indicated when the altimeter reads DH — meaning you could break out of clouds 200 feet lower than expected or descend below DH unknowingly. This is a serious safety-of-flight concern. The correct action is to add 200 feet to your published DH and treat that as your effective DH, or execute a missed approach and resolve the discrepancy before attempting another approach. Notify ATC of the potential altimeter error.
questions.follow_up: The altimeter setting is confirmed correct. You suspect the encoding altimeter is sending wrong Mode C data. Does an incorrect Mode C output affect your primary altimeter reading, and what is the regulatory requirement for Mode C accuracy?
questions.follow_up_answer: No — the encoding altimeter and primary altimeter are separate systems. The encoder converts pressure altitude to a digital code sent to the transponder; it does not affect the primary altimeter display. The primary altimeter reads from its own aneroid capsule and is independent of the encoder. Per 14 CFR 91.217, Mode C altitude information must be within 125 feet of the aircraft's actual pressure altitude. If the encoder is out of tolerance, it must be corrected before the aircraft is operated in Mode C-required airspace. ATC can identify discrepancies and may ask you to stop squawking altitude. In this scenario, the implication is your actual altitude matches your primary altimeter — the ATC radar picture is what is incorrect — which changes the risk calculus significantly from the initial concern.

questions.question: You receive an ATC clearance during a precision approach that you cannot comply with. What is your immediate obligation as pilot in command?
questions.answer: You must advise ATC immediately that you are unable to comply with the clearance. You are never required to accept a clearance you cannot safely execute. The PIC has the authority and responsibility under 14 CFR 91.3 to reject or request an amended clearance, and must communicate this to ATC without delay so they can issue an alternative.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3; FAA Instrument Flying Handbook FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 2

questions.question: What is the correct phraseology a helicopter pilot should use when advising ATC that they cannot comply with a clearance during an ILS approach?
questions.answer: The pilot should state their callsign followed by 'UNABLE' and briefly state the reason or request an alternative. For example: 'Approach, Helicopter N123AB, UNABLE that clearance, request [alternative, e.g., heading 180, vectors to final].' The word UNABLE is the standard ICAO and FAA phraseology that immediately signals non-compliance to ATC.
questions.regulatory_ref: AIM 4-2-3; FAA Instrument Flying Handbook FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 2

questions.question: Does readback of an ATC clearance obligate you to comply with it, even if you realize shortly after reading it back that you cannot safely execute it?
questions.answer: No. Readback confirms receipt and understanding of a clearance, but it does not legally obligate you to comply if you determine you cannot do so safely. Under 14 CFR 91.3, the PIC is the final authority for safe operation. You must immediately advise ATC using 'UNABLE' and request an amended clearance if circumstances change or you recognize a conflict after the readback.

questions.question: You are flying a helicopter ILS approach in IMC and ATC clears you to cross a fix at an altitude that is below the published minimum crossing altitude for that fix. What should you do?
questions.answer: You should immediately advise ATC using 'UNABLE' and state you are unable to cross the fix at the assigned altitude, then request a clearance consistent with the published minimums. The published minimum crossing altitude exists for obstacle clearance and navigation signal requirements — descending below it could compromise both safety and legal IFR compliance. The PIC must not accept a clearance that violates published minimums without a specific reason and full understanding of the situation.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.177; 14 CFR 91.3; FAA Instrument Flying Handbook FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 1

questions.question: During a precision approach in the helicopter, ATC issues a speed restriction that would require you to fly below your helicopter's published minimum airspeed for IMC operations. Walk me through how you handle this.
questions.answer: First, recognize the conflict — the ATC-assigned speed would place you below the aircraft's safe IMC operating envelope. Immediately respond with your callsign and state 'UNABLE [assigned speed], minimum IFR speed is [X] knots, request amended clearance.' Do not attempt to comply and then manage the unsafe condition silently. Advising ATC promptly allows them to adjust spacing, issue a different clearance, or accommodate you with a different sequence. Flying below minimum airspeed in IMC is a safety-critical hazard unique to helicopters and must be communicated immediately.

questions.question: You are on an ILS final approach in actual IMC and ATC issues a frequency change that you believe would require you to break off the approach to reset avionics. How do you handle this?
questions.answer: Advise ATC immediately: '[Callsign] UNABLE frequency change at this time, on final in IMC.' ATC generally does not intend to disrupt a stabilized final approach, and the controller may not have been aware of your exact position on the approach. Your priority is maintaining the approach safely. Once you are in a position to safely make the change — or after landing — you can comply. If the frequency change is safety-critical and required, declare your situation clearly so ATC can assist. Never silently non-comply; always communicate.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3; AIM 4-2-3; FAA Instrument Flying Handbook FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 2

questions.question: During this checkride, I issue you a simulated ATC clearance to fly an ILS approach to a runway that has a ceiling reported at 100 feet — well below the published decision altitude. You know the approach is not operationally legal to complete to a landing. How do you respond to me as your evaluator, and how does that mirror how you would handle a real ATC situation?
questions.answer: On the checkride, I would advise you directly: 'Unable to conduct that approach to landing — reported ceiling is below the published DA and approach minimums. I would not continue below DA without the required visual references per 14 CFR 91.175. I can fly the approach to DA and execute the missed approach.' In a real IFR environment, I would advise ATC the same way using 'UNABLE,' explain that conditions are below minimums, and request either holding, an alternate, or a different approach if available. The key principle is that neither ATC nor an evaluator can compel a pilot to continue an approach below minimums — the PIC must clearly communicate their inability to comply and the reason.
questions.follow_up: What if I told you this is a simulated approach, the airport is VFR, and I just want to see if you'll fly it — does your answer change?
questions.follow_up_answer: In a training or checkride simulation context where actual minimums don't apply because the airport is VFR, I can fly the simulated approach and execute the missed approach procedure at DA as required by the ACS. However, I should still verbalize: 'In actual IMC this approach would be below minimums — I would be unable to continue below DA without required visual references.' The evaluator is testing whether I recognize the scenario and know the rule, not whether I refuse to fly the procedure. Understanding the distinction between simulated and actual IMC operations is itself a knowledge and judgment requirement.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175(c); 14 CFR 91.3; FAA Instrument Flying Handbook FAA-H-8083-15B

questions.question: You are shooting a precision approach and ATC issues a clearance that is technically legal but conflicts with a TCAS resolution advisory that simultaneously commands a climb. You have two conflicting instructions. Which do you follow, and how do you communicate it?
questions.answer: You follow the TCAS Resolution Advisory (RA) immediately and without deviation, even if it conflicts with the ATC clearance. TCAS RA takes priority over ATC instructions per FAA and ICAO guidance. Simultaneously or as soon as workload permits, you advise ATC: '[Callsign] TCAS RA, UNABLE clearance, [state your deviation, e.g., climbing to X altitude].' After the conflict is resolved and TCAS issues a clear-of-conflict advisory, you return to the ATC clearance and advise ATC you are returning to assigned altitude. Never ignore a TCAS RA to comply with ATC — the whole system depends on pilots following RAs.
questions.follow_up: After you comply with the TCAS RA and the conflict is resolved, ATC asks why you deviated. What do you tell them, and is there any subsequent reporting requirement?
questions.follow_up_answer: I would advise ATC that I received a TCAS Resolution Advisory and complied with it as required. Regarding reporting: under 14 CFR 91.187, if operating under IFR and the deviation was from an ATC clearance, I must report the deviation to ATC as soon as possible — which I already did. Additionally, if the RA was triggered, operators and pilots are strongly encouraged (and in some cases required under air carrier rules) to file a voluntary ASAP or ASRS report. For Part 91 helicopter operations, filing an ASRS report is not mandatory but is best practice to document the event and protect against enforcement action.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.187; AIM 4-4-15; FAA Instrument Flying Handbook FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5

questions.question: During a precision instrument approach in a helicopter, at what general points in the procedure should you be running checklists?
questions.answer: Checklists should be completed at logical, low-workload phases: typically before beginning the approach (approach checklist), upon intercepting the final approach course (before descending below the FAF), and after landing or executing a missed approach. The exact checklist titles and timing depend on the specific helicopter's POH/RFM, but the principle is to complete them before entering high-workload phases, not during them.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (workload management); individual helicopter POH/RFM

questions.question: What is the difference between a 'do-list' and a challenge-response checklist, and which is more common in helicopter instrument operations?
questions.answer: A 'do-list' is completed flow by flow — the pilot performs actions from memory and then uses the checklist to verify nothing was missed. A challenge-response checklist requires reading each item aloud and confirming each action before moving on. Both are valid; helicopters in single-pilot IFR often use a do-list/flow method followed by a verification checklist to manage workload without eyes off instruments for extended periods. The key is that the checklist is actually completed, not skipped.

questions.question: What items are typically addressed in an approach checklist for a helicopter flying a precision ILS approach?
questions.answer: While exact items depend on the specific aircraft's POH/RFM, a typical helicopter approach checklist includes: ATIS/weather obtained, altimeter set, navigation radios tuned and identified (ILS frequency, Morse code ID confirmed), course/heading bug set, approach briefing completed, decision altitude (DA) set or noted, fuel state checked, landing light as required, any system-specific items (hydraulics, anti-ice), and passengers briefed if applicable. The goal is to complete all setup before intercepting the final approach course.
questions.regulatory_ref: Individual helicopter POH/RFM; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9 (ILS operations)

questions.question: You're being vectored for an ILS approach and ATC gives you a tight vector — you're only 4 miles from the final approach fix and still need to complete your approach checklist. How do you handle checklist completion without compromising aircraft control or situational awareness?
questions.answer: This is a workload management scenario. The correct technique is to advise ATC you need additional maneuvering time — 'Request extended vector, need time to configure' — or to use a flow-and-verify method: run the critical items from memory (altimeter, nav radios tuned and identified, DA noted, heading bug set) and verify with the checklist during brief stable periods. Checklists must never be rushed to the point of skipping items or becoming a distraction during a critical phase of flight. If truly unable to complete the checklist properly, it is appropriate to request a delay vector or even a missed approach. Situational awareness and aircraft control always come before checklist completion.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (workload management, SRM); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 2 (ATC communications)

questions.question: You execute a missed approach from a precision approach. Walk me through what checklist actions you take and when you take them during the missed approach sequence.
questions.answer: Immediately upon executing the missed approach: apply go-around power and establish climb attitude — aircraft control first. Once a positive rate of climb is established and the aircraft is stabilized, complete the missed approach checklist (typically: power set, attitude established, gear up if applicable, nav radios reset for published hold or next approach, missed approach altitude set on altimeter/altitude bug, ATC notified). Do not attempt to run a checklist while simultaneously initiating the climb and reconfiguring — prioritize aircraft control, then communicate, then checklist. The missed approach checklist should be completed before reaching the published holding fix or first assigned altitude.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5 (instrument procedures); individual helicopter POH/RFM; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13

questions.question: You've just broken out of the clouds at decision altitude on an ILS and acquired the runway environment. As you transition to a visual landing, your co-pilot says 'don't forget the before-landing checklist.' How do you respond, and when do you run it?
questions.answer: Ideally the before-landing checklist should have been completed before reaching DA, not after. If it was not completed, the safest response is to acknowledge the reminder, quickly assess whether any critical items (gear down/locked if applicable, fuel on correct tank, etc.) can be verified without losing visual reference or aircraft control. If there is any doubt about aircraft configuration, execute a missed approach, complete the checklist properly, and make another approach. Attempting to run a full checklist after breaking out at DA while transitioning to a visual landing in IMC-adjacent conditions is a high-risk, high-workload moment — this is exactly why approach checklists are completed before the FAF.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (SRM, workload management); individual helicopter POH/RFM

questions.question: On a single-pilot helicopter IFR flight, you notice that completing checklists during the approach causes you to lose track of your position relative to the final approach course. What does this tell you about your instrument proficiency, and what are two specific SRM strategies you can use to address it?
questions.answer: This is a significant red flag — it indicates that checklist management is consuming too much attentional bandwidth, which should prompt honest self-assessment of currency and proficiency. Per the FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook, accidents in helicopters are correlated more with hours in a specific aircraft model than total flight hours, and proficiency in a specific aircraft reduces cognitive workload. Two SRM strategies: (1) Internalize a memory flow for the approach checklist so it can be run quickly without reference to a paper checklist, using the printed checklist only for verification — this frees visual attention for instruments; (2) Use automation management — set the autopilot to maintain heading/altitude during the checklist flow where equipped, or use the heading bug and altitude alerter to reduce manual tracking workload. If neither resolves the issue, the pilot should consider whether the flight is safe to continue or whether more dual instrument training in this specific aircraft is needed.
questions.follow_up: If you're flying a helicopter with no autopilot and find yourself consistently losing positional awareness during checklist completion on approaches, at what point does this become a go/no-go consideration under ADM principles?
questions.follow_up_answer: Under ADM principles, if a pilot cannot safely manage checklists and maintain instrument scan simultaneously in a single-pilot, no-autopilot helicopter, this is a genuine fitness-for-flight concern. The FAA notes that approximately 80% of aviation accidents are caused by human factors. If the pilot's workload capacity is saturated by routine checklist tasks during an approach, they lack the mental reserve needed to handle unexpected deviations, ATC instructions, or system anomalies — all of which are foreseeable during an IFR approach. Under sound ADM, this pilot should not accept the IFR clearance until proficiency is restored through additional training. Once airborne, if this is discovered in flight, the pilot should request an ILS with the longest final available, declare intentions to ATC early, and consider landing VFR if conditions permit rather than pressing an approach they cannot safely manage.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM, SRM, workload management, automation management); 14 CFR 61.57 (IFR currency)

questions.question: During an ILS approach checkride, the examiner observes that you completed the approach checklist correctly but skipped the after-landing checklist entirely. You've landed safely and taxied to the ramp. Can this still result in a disapproval, and what does checklist discipline on a checkride demonstrate beyond just item completion?
questions.answer: Yes, omitting a required checklist — even after a safe landing — can result in disapproval under the ACS, which explicitly requires completing 'the appropriate checklist(s)' as a skills element. The ACS does not limit this to pre-approach checklists only; it encompasses all appropriate checklists for the task. Beyond item completion, checklist discipline demonstrates: (1) Habit patterns — examiners look for consistent, reliable behavior, not situational compliance; a pilot who skips checklists when the pressure is off will likely skip them in actual IMC when fatigued or distracted; (2) Professionalism and systems knowledge — knowing which checklists exist and when they apply reflects genuine understanding of the aircraft and operation; (3) SRM integration — it shows whether the pilot has internalized workload management as a continuous discipline rather than a performance-only behavior during high-stakes phases. The examiner is evaluating whether this behavior will carry into real-world IFR operations, not just whether the aircraft is parked safely.
questions.follow_up: If during the debrief you tell the examiner 'the after-landing checklist isn't safety-critical since we're already on the ground,' how should the examiner respond, and what FAA principle does that pilot attitude violate?
questions.follow_up_answer: The examiner should reject that rationalization directly. After-landing checklists often include critical items such as: turning off transponder altitude encoding, setting hydraulic or engine system switches to ground positions, fuel system reconfiguration, rotor brake application sequencing, and documenting anomalies — items with real consequences if omitted before shutdown or the next flight. More fundamentally, this attitude is a classic example of hazardous pilot attitudes identified in ADM — specifically 'invulnerability' or 'resignation,' believing that because nothing bad happened, the omission was acceptable. The FAA's ADM framework teaches that the absence of a negative outcome does not validate a poor decision. If a pilot habitually rationalizes skipping checklists based on perceived low risk, they are building a pattern that will eventually contribute to an error chain leading to an accident. The examiner should document this attitude as a deficiency even if a retest is not warranted solely for the missed checklist.
questions.regulatory_ref: ACS IH.VII.B.S7; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM, hazardous attitudes, error chain); individual helicopter POH/RFM

questions.question: What does 'helicopter configuration' mean in the context of setting up for a precision instrument approach, and what are the primary items you would configure before intercepting the glideslope?
questions.answer: Helicopter configuration refers to the aircraft's flight control, power, and systems setup for the approach. Before glideslope intercept, the pilot should establish the airspeed appropriate for the approach (per the Rotorcraft Flight Manual or operator's procedures), set power to maintain that airspeed, configure any anti-ice or deice systems as required by meteorological conditions, verify landing light and transponder are set, and confirm navigation equipment (ILS receiver, course, identification) is properly tuned and identified. The goal is to be stabilized in configuration early enough that the pilot can focus on tracking the localizer and glideslope rather than managing aircraft changes.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5; Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) — aircraft specific

questions.question: Why is airspeed selection on a precision approach more critical in a helicopter than in a fixed-wing aircraft?
questions.answer: Helicopters operate closer to their performance limits at low airspeeds and are more sensitive to power changes. Flying too slow on an ILS can result in settling with power or loss of effective translational lift, making altitude control difficult. Flying too fast makes it hard to descend at the required rate to track the glideslope without overshooting. The correct approach airspeed, as published in the RFM or operator procedures, provides the best balance of controllability, power margin, and the ability to execute a go-around. Additionally, helicopters must consider that at low airspeeds autorotation entry characteristics differ significantly from higher speed flight.

questions.question: How do icing meteorological conditions affect the configuration you establish before flying a precision approach in a helicopter equipped with anti-ice systems?
questions.answer: In known or forecast icing conditions, the pilot must activate all required anti-ice and deice systems — such as pitot heat, rotor blade anti-ice, windshield deice, and carburetor heat if applicable — prior to entering icing conditions and before beginning the approach. Ice accumulation on rotor blades changes their aerodynamic profile, increases weight, and can cause severe vibration or loss of lift. Ice on pitot-static probes will degrade airspeed and altitude indications, both critical instruments during an ILS approach. Activating these systems early is essential because they prevent ice buildup; most systems are not effective at removing existing ice. Reference 14 CFR 91.527 for flight into known icing conditions requirements.

questions.question: You are being vectored for an ILS approach. The reported weather is OVC 200, visibility 1/4 mile in freezing drizzle, surface temperature 28°F, and winds 310° at 18 knots gusting 28. Walk me through how those conditions specifically change the configuration and airspeed you establish compared to a standard VMC approach.
questions.answer: For these conditions I would make several configuration changes beyond a standard approach: (1) Airspeed — I would add a wind correction to my normal approach airspeed, typically half the gust factor (half of 10 knots = +5 knots), bringing my final approach airspeed up to account for gusts and possible wind shear near the surface. (2) Anti-ice systems — With freezing drizzle and OAT at 28°F, I would have pitot heat ON, all rotor blade and engine inlet anti-ice activated, and windshield deice running before entering IMC. (3) Power margin awareness — With ice potential and gusting winds, I'd be alert to the need for rapid power application on go-around and would not allow the aircraft to become critically slow. (4) Lighting — Landing light on, all external lights as required. (5) Navigation — ILS frequency confirmed, identified, and CDI/glideslope verified. I would brief the go-around point early given the low visibility, and be prepared for a missed approach given the conditions near minimums.

questions.question: ATC clears you for the ILS approach but you are currently at 180 knots on a radar vector. Your RFM recommends 70 knots on final. Describe your energy management and configuration sequencing to arrive at the final approach fix stabilized at 70 knots.
questions.answer: I would begin decelerating well before the final approach course intercept to avoid being fast and high on the glideslope intercept. Specific steps: (1) Inform ATC if I need a longer final or a slower vector speed to properly configure — helicopters often need more time/distance than fixed-wing to slow to approach speeds. (2) Reduce collective/power smoothly to begin deceleration while maintaining assigned altitude. (3) Run through any pre-approach or landing checklist items (anti-ice, transponder, lighting, navigation tuning) during the deceleration segment while workload permits. (4) Target being at or below approach speed before intercepting the localizer, and absolutely no later than the FAF. A stabilized approach means airspeed, configuration, and descent rate are all established by the FAF. (5) Avoid the temptation to carry excess speed to the glideslope and 'bleed it off' during descent — this technique results in glideslope overshoots and unstabilized approaches.
