If fuel and weather clearly support a localizer-only approach and you are already established, continuing with higher minimums is defensible. Document your reasoning.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.185; 14 CFR 91.175; FAA-H-8083-21B, Chapter 13; FAA-H-8083-15B, Chapter 9

questions.question: Approximately 80% of aviation accidents involve pilot error. In the context of a helicopter IFR loss-of-communications event, describe how SRM specifically reduces the probability of adding a second human-factor error to an already abnormal situation, and what personal minimums or SRM safeguards should be pre-established before the flight.
questions.answer: SRM recognizes that a comm failure is an abnormal event that immediately raises cognitive load and stress — conditions proven to increase the likelihood of additional errors. Pre-established SRM safeguards reduce the chance of compounding errors: (1) Pre-flight risk assessment identifies personal minimums — experience in type, currency, weather limits, route familiarity — so the pilot knows ahead of time what conditions warrant a divert or ground stop. (2) Briefing 91.185 procedures before departure builds mental models so execution under stress is automatic rather than improvised. (3) Workload management via pre-built automation (GPS route loaded, approach plates pre-pulled) reduces in-flight cognitive demand when the failure occurs. (4) Situational awareness checkpoints (fuel, position, weather trends) maintained throughout the flight mean the pilot isn't starting fresh when the comm failure happens. (5) The 'avoid probably' principle means the pilot pre-commits to actions (e.g., 'if I lose comm past this point, I proceed to XYZ; before that point, I turn back') rather than deciding under duress. These pre-established safeguards break the error chain before it can form, reducing the likelihood that the initial equipment failure becomes a fatal human-error sequence.
questions.follow_up: If you had pre-filed an alternate on your IFR flight plan and your comm failure occurs after passing the alternate's airport, does 91.185 require you to return to it, or do you continue to your destination?
questions.follow_up_answer: Under 14 CFR 91.185(c)(1), in the absence of assigned routing, you proceed via the route filed in your flight plan. The regulation does not require you to return to a previously passed alternate — you continue to your destination airport and execute the approach. The alternate on the flight plan is a filing requirement under 91.169 for dispatch planning purposes; it does not create an obligation to divert once airborne unless fuel, weather, or pilot judgment independently require it. SRM and ADM require you to continuously reassess whether continuing to destination remains the safest option given fuel state and weather trends.

tasks.title: Task B. Instrument Approach and Landing with an Inoperative Engine (Simulated) (Multiengine Helicopter Only)

questions.question: When executing an instrument approach with one engine inoperative in a multiengine helicopter, what is the primary concern regarding published landing minimums?
questions.answer: Published instrument approach minimums assume full operation of all aircraft systems and components. With an engine inoperative, performance is degraded, and the crew must consider whether the aircraft can execute a missed approach or go-around safely. Higher minimums may effectively apply because the crew must ensure sufficient visual references and performance capability exist before descending below DA/DH or MDA. The Inoperative Components Table in the Terminal Procedures Publication (TPP) addresses equipment-specific minimums, but OEI performance margins must also be evaluated per the Rotorcraft Flight Manual.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter on Instrument Approaches and Minimums; Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) OEI performance data

questions.question: What does the acronym MAP stand for in the context of instrument approaches, and what must you do if you reach the MAP without the required visual references during a single-engine inoperative approach?
questions.answer: MAP stands for Missed Approach Point. If you reach the MAP without having established the required visual references — at least one of the ten specified visual references identified and visible — you must immediately execute the published missed approach procedure. On an OEI approach, this means transitioning to the missed approach climb on one engine, following the published missed approach routing, and managing the remaining engine's performance per RFM OEI climb procedures. You should not continue below MDA/DA/DH without the required visual references regardless of engine status.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175; FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Approaches and Minimums

questions.question: During an instrument approach with one engine inoperative, why is early identification of the inoperative engine's effect on antitorque and directional control especially important during the approach and landing phase?
questions.answer: With one engine inoperative, the torque output of the operating engine is increased to compensate for lost performance. This increased torque creates a greater yaw tendency that the tail rotor must counteract. During a slow, instrument approach profile — particularly at low airspeeds near the decision point — antitorque pedal authority may become marginal or asymmetric. Additionally, during power changes on final (such as a go-around or landing flare), the abrupt torque change can create significant directional control challenges. Pilots must understand these dynamics in advance so inputs are precise and timely to maintain directional control.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (Helicopter Emergencies); RFM OEI procedures

questions.question: You are flying a multiengine helicopter ILS approach and lose one engine on the glideslope at 1,500 feet AGL. Your RFM shows OEI hover ceiling is below field elevation for current conditions. How does this performance limitation change your approach strategy?
questions.answer: If OEI hover capability does not exist at the destination field, a running or roll-on landing must be planned rather than a hover to landing. This means you must ensure the runway or landing area is long enough and clear of obstructions for a running landing, and you should not plan to transition to a hover at any point. You should also brief the missed approach early, because if visual references are not acquired at DA, the OEI missed approach climb performance must be verified against obstacle clearance requirements in the terminal area. The approach itself can still be flown to published ILS minimums, but the exit strategy changes entirely — you are committed to a running landing or must divert to a field where OEI performance supports the required operation.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; RFM OEI performance charts; 14 CFR 91.175

questions.question: When flying an OEI instrument approach, a procedure turn is published on the chart. Under what conditions are you NOT authorized to fly the procedure turn, and why does this matter more during an OEI approach than a normal approach?
questions.answer: You are not authorized to fly a procedure turn when: a NoPT symbol appears on the chart, ATC provides radar vectors to final, a holding pattern is published in lieu of a procedure turn, you are conducting a timed approach from a holding fix, or ATC directs otherwise. During an OEI approach, this matters more because flying an unnecessary procedure turn adds significant time, fuel burn on the good engine, and workload at a time when energy management and aircraft control are already demanding. Additionally, the additional maneuvering exposes the crew to prolonged flight at higher power settings on the operating engine, potentially exceeding single-engine time limits. Avoiding unnecessary maneuvering conserves performance margins and reduces crew workload.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Approaches and Minimums; AIM 5-4-9

questions.question: You are conducting an OEI RNAV (GPS) approach and the approach controller clears you for a straight-in. As you pass the final approach fix (FAF), you realize your groundspeed is significantly higher than planned due to a tailwind component. How does this affect your OEI approach management and decision-making?
questions.answer: Higher groundspeed on final shortens your time between the FAF and the decision altitude, reducing time available to manage the operating engine, monitor instruments, and identify the required visual references. With an engine inoperative, pilot workload is already elevated, so a compressed timeline increases error risk. You should consider requesting a longer final or a vector for spacing if workload is unmanageable. Additionally, higher groundspeed affects your energy state at DA — if a missed approach is initiated, you may need to account for higher airspeed during the initial climb. Descent rate must also be increased to maintain glidepath, which at OEI power settings may challenge the operating engine. Slowing to a safe approach speed consistent with OEI performance before the FAF is the preferred solution.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5 and Instrument Approaches; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM); RFM OEI approach speeds

questions.question: During an OEI missed approach from a precision approach, your RFM specifies a single-engine missed approach climb speed that is significantly different from the published missed approach climbing airspeed. Which takes precedence, and how do you brief this conflict before the approach?
questions.answer: The RFM-specified OEI missed approach climb speed takes precedence over the published procedure's recommended airspeed, because the RFM is aircraft-specific and provides the best climb performance for the actual aircraft configuration with one engine inoperative. The published missed approach climb gradient is calculated assuming a specific climb performance standard, but it is the pilot's responsibility to verify that the aircraft can meet that gradient OEI. If the RFM OEI best rate-of-climb speed differs from the published speed, use the RFM speed to maximize climb performance and ensure obstacle clearance. This conflict should be briefed before the approach begins — the crew should calculate OEI missed approach climb performance, note the applicable RFM speed, and pre-brief that the RFM speed will be flown regardless of what is depicted on the chart.
questions.follow_up: If you determine during the pre-approach brief that your OEI missed approach climb performance does not meet the published missed approach climb gradient, what are your options?
questions.follow_up_answer: If OEI climb performance does not meet the published missed approach gradient, you have several options: (1) Do not begin the approach — divert to an alternate where OEI missed approach performance is adequate; (2) Reduce weight (fuel dump if equipped, or reduce payload) to improve OEI performance before beginning the approach; (3) Request a different approach procedure with a lower or more favorable missed approach climb gradient; (4) Accept visual-only operations if weather permits landing with certainty before the MAP, though this eliminates the IFR safety net. Continuing the approach knowing a missed approach cannot be safely executed OEI is not an acceptable option — it violates sound ADM principles and may violate 14 CFR 91.175 requirements to have an alternate plan when visual references are not assured.
questions.regulatory_ref: RFM OEI climb performance data; 14 CFR 91.175; FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Approaches; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13

questions.question: A multiengine helicopter crew loses an engine shortly after passing the outer marker on an ILS approach in IMC. The PM (pilot monitoring) suggests continuing the approach since they are already established and close to the field. Walk me through the decision-making framework you would apply to determine whether to continue or go missed approach immediately.
questions.answer: This scenario requires immediate structured ADM, not task-saturation-driven continuation. The decision framework includes: (1) Aircraft control first — confirm engine failure is identified and secured per memory items, operating engine is stabilized, and the helicopter is flyable OEI; (2) Performance check — verify OEI approach power is within limits and that the aircraft can maintain glidepath and execute a missed approach climb if needed; (3) Obstacle clearance — confirm OEI missed approach climb performance meets the published gradient for existing conditions; (4) Landing area suitability — determine whether a hover landing or running landing is required based on OEI hover ceiling, and whether the landing area supports that; (5) Crew workload — assess whether workload is manageable for two pilots to fly the approach and manage the emergency simultaneously; (6) Weather — confirm ceiling and visibility give a reasonable probability of acquiring the required visual references. If all checks are satisfactory, continuation may be justified. If any check fails — especially missed approach climb performance or OEI landing capability — an immediate missed approach to an alternate is the safer choice. The Trescott principle applies: if continuation will 'probably' work out, that is not good enough — choose the option known to work.
questions.follow_up: The PM argues that because you are past the outer marker and low on fuel, diverting is not a real option. How does this change your analysis?
questions.follow_up_answer: Fuel state is a critical factor and changes the decision calculus significantly. If diverting to the alternate is no longer viable due to fuel, the crew is now in a situation where the approach at this field is the only practical option. However, this does not mean minimums or OEI performance limitations are waived — it means the crew must ensure the approach can be safely completed at this airport. If OEI hover capability is insufficient, a running landing must be planned immediately. The crew should declare an emergency if they have not already, which may allow ATC to provide equipment, clear conflicting traffic, and potentially extend fuel options. The lesson here is that this decision should not be made at the outer marker — OEI fuel analysis and alternate viability should be part of the pre-approach brief so the crew is never forced into a corner. The accumulation of a fuel shortage AND an engine failure AND IMC conditions illustrates the classic error chain, and the time to break that chain was before the approach began.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM, error chain, Trescott Tip); 14 CFR 91.175; FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Approaches; 14 CFR 91.185

questions.question: During a single-engine instrument approach in a multiengine helicopter, why is the approach and landing phase considered one of the highest-risk periods for an engine failure?
questions.answer: During the approach and landing phase, the helicopter is at low altitude with reduced airspeed, leaving minimal time and altitude to react to an engine failure. Power demands can be high, especially during final approach and deceleration. The combination of instrument conditions reducing situational awareness, constrained options for autorotation or go-around, and proximity to terrain and obstacles creates a compounded risk environment. Any failure at this stage leaves the crew with very little margin for error.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter on Instrument Approaches

questions.question: What is the immediate pilot action required upon recognition of an engine failure during a multiengine helicopter instrument approach?
questions.answer: Upon recognition of an engine failure, the pilot must immediately execute the emergency procedures for single-engine operations as specified in the RFM/POH — this typically includes confirming the failed engine, applying corrective inputs to maintain aircraft control, and deciding whether to continue the approach (if performance permits on the remaining engine) or initiate a missed approach/autorotation. Maintaining rotor RPM within limits is critical; if rotor RPM begins to decay, collective must be reduced immediately. The decision must be made quickly given the low altitude and instrument conditions.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; applicable Rotorcraft Flight Manual emergency procedures

questions.question: How does inoperative component status affect the instrument approach minimums when you are already flying a single-engine approach in IMC?
questions.answer: When components supporting the instrument approach are inoperative — such as approach lighting, VASI/PAPI, or certain NAVAID components — published minimums must be raised in accordance with the Inoperative Components Table in the Terminal Procedures Publication (TPP). This means the crew must verify that the approach can still be safely executed with the reduced visual reference requirements imposed by higher minimums. Attempting the approach at standard minimums when required components are inoperative is not authorized and increases risk significantly, especially when already managing a single-engine situation.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Approaches and Minimums; TPP Inoperative Components Table; 14 CFR 91.175

questions.question: You are flying a two-pilot IFR crew in a twin-engine helicopter conducting an ILS approach in solid IMC at night. At 500 feet AGL inbound, you lose the right engine. The aircraft performance charts confirm you can maintain level flight on one engine at current weight. What factors determine whether you continue the approach or execute a missed approach?
questions.answer: Even if single-engine level flight is confirmed, the decision to continue must weigh several factors: (1) Whether approach minimums can still be met — if any approach components are now inoperative due to the failure, minimums may have risen; (2) Aircraft configuration and energy state — can the helicopter maintain a stabilized approach profile on one engine through to a safe landing? (3) Airfield environment — is the runway environment suitable for single-engine operations, including go-around capability if a balk landing is needed? (4) Crew workload — managing the failure, flying instruments, communicating with ATC, and flying a precision approach simultaneously in IMC at night is an extreme workload; SRM and crew resource management are critical. (5) The 'error chain' principle — already managing a failure in IMC at night means the margin for additional error is near zero. If any factor creates doubt, a missed approach to a suitable airport for a single-engine approach or autorotation landing is the safer option.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13; FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Approaches; 14 CFR 91.175

questions.question: During a simulated single-engine instrument approach, you reach the missed approach point without acquiring the required visual references. You initiate the missed approach, and at that moment the simulated engine failure becomes more complex — the remaining engine's power is now also fluctuating. Describe the risk factors you are managing simultaneously and how ADM guides your next action.
questions.answer: At this point, multiple risk factors are compounding: (1) Instrument meteorological conditions eliminating outside visual reference; (2) One engine already inoperative; (3) Remaining engine unreliable — potential for complete power loss; (4) Low altitude at missed approach point; (5) Crew workload at maximum. ADM and the error chain concept from the Helicopter Flying Handbook apply directly — multiple poor outcomes are stacking. The appropriate ADM response is to avoid the word 'probably' — if you are not certain the remaining engine will sustain flight, treat it as failing. Immediately declare an emergency with ATC (7700 squawk), communicate your position and situation, and prioritize aircraft control including rotor RPM management above all else. Depending on altitude and terrain, an autorotation may be the only survivable option. Attempting to continue a missed approach procedure with a failing second engine compounds risk unacceptably.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13 (ADM/SRM); FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Approaches; 14 CFR 91.3

questions.question: How does a pilot's total flight time versus hours in a specific helicopter model affect risk during a single-engine instrument approach and landing scenario, and what does the FAA handbook say about this relationship?
questions.answer: The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook states that accident rates correlate more strongly with hours in a specific aircraft model than with total flight hours, and that accident rates decrease significantly after 100 hours in type. This is directly relevant to the single-engine instrument approach scenario because unfamiliarity with the specific helicopter's single-engine performance characteristics, power management techniques, emergency checklists, and cockpit layout under high stress dramatically increases risk. A pilot with 5,000 total hours but only 20 hours in a specific twin-engine helicopter is at significantly higher risk during a single-engine emergency than a pilot with 500 total hours and 200 hours in type. Currency and type-specific proficiency are critical risk mitigation factors.

questions.question: You are conducting an IFR approach to an airport with a circling approach as the only available procedure. During the circling maneuver at MDA, you lose one engine. The aircraft can maintain level flight on the remaining engine. However, the visibility drops momentarily and you lose visual contact with the runway environment. Walk me through every risk factor and decision point you must navigate, and explain what the FAA requires you to do if visual reference is lost during a circling approach.
questions.answer: This scenario compounds multiple high-risk elements simultaneously. First, regarding the loss of visual reference during circling: FAA instrument approach guidance states that if visual reference is lost during a circling-to-land approach, the pilot must make an initial climbing turn toward the landing runway and then intercept the missed approach course. This is not optional — it is a required procedure to ensure terrain clearance during the missed approach. Risk factors stacking in this scenario include: (1) Circling approach places the aircraft in a non-straight-in profile at low altitude, increasing exposure to terrain and obstacles; (2) Engine failure has reduced performance margin; (3) Loss of visual reference removes the ability to see and avoid terrain/obstacles; (4) Single-engine missed approach from a circling maneuver is exceptionally demanding — power demand at low altitude and low airspeed while turning toward the runway on one engine is near the performance limit of most helicopters; (5) Crew workload is at maximum. ADM requires committing immediately to the missed approach procedure — delaying to attempt to reacquire visual reference while already engine-out at MDA is unacceptable risk. Declare emergency, execute the circling missed approach procedure, and obtain ATC support for vectors to a straight-in approach or divert.
questions.follow_up: The missed approach procedure for the circling approach takes you back over mountainous terrain. You're now single-engine in IMC in a climb. What specific rotor system consideration becomes critical as you manage this situation, and why?
questions.follow_up_answer: On a single-engine missed approach in IMC over mountainous terrain, the pilot must be vigilant about rotor RPM management. With only one engine supplying power, the power available is reduced, and climbing demands can push the operating engine toward its limits. If power demand exceeds what the single engine can provide, main rotor RPM will begin to decay. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook is explicit that rotor stalls in helicopters are not recoverable — early recognition of low RPM is imperative. In a climbing single-engine profile, the pilot must monitor Nr continuously and be prepared to reduce collective if RPM begins to decay, even if it means temporarily leveling off or reducing climb rate. Attempting to maintain climb at the cost of rotor RPM in IMC over mountains is a fatal error chain. Additionally, any rapid roll or pitch input at low G conditions on some rotor systems can cause mast bumping — the pilot must use coordinated, smooth inputs throughout.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Approaches (circling missed approach); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (rotor stall, LTE); 14 CFR 91.175(e)

questions.question: A multiengine helicopter crew completes a thorough preflight risk assessment and determines the flight is acceptable. En route, weather deteriorates below published minimums at the destination, but an alternate is available. While executing the alternate's instrument approach, an engine fails inside the final approach fix. The crew decides to continue to a landing. After the flight, the chief pilot questions whether the decision to continue was appropriate. What risk management framework applies, and what factors would support or contradict the decision to continue past the FAF with a failed engine?
questions.answer: The risk management framework from the FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook's ADM chapter applies directly. The 'error chain' concept is central here — the crew had already experienced: weather below minimums at destination, a divert to alternate, and now an engine failure inside the FAF. Each event individually may be manageable, but the accumulation of adverse factors narrows the safety margin dramatically. Factors that might support continuing: single-engine performance confirmed sufficient for the approach profile; weather at or above minimums; runway environment suitable for single-engine landing; no go-around capability issue; crew trained and current in type. Factors contradicting a continue decision: accumulated stress and workload reducing crew performance; any performance uncertainty at landing weight; if a go-around on single engine was not clearly achievable; if MDA/DA was not yet reached (meaning the approach hadn't confirmed visual contact yet). The FAA handbook's 'Trescott Tip' applies — if the outcome of continuing will only 'probably' be acceptable, choose the option known to work. In this case, if single-engine performance is confirmed and visual contact is established, a landing may be the better option than a single-engine missed approach in IMC. However, if there is doubt about performance or visual contact, a missed approach and autorotation to a suitable site may be the safer known outcome. The chief pilot's question is valid — every link in the error chain should have triggered a reevaluation of go/no-go.
questions.follow_up: Suppose the crew had 800 total hours each but only 15 hours in this specific helicopter model. How does that fact change your risk assessment of their decision to continue?
questions.follow_up_answer: According to the FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook, accident rates are more strongly correlated with hours in a specific aircraft model than total hours, and decrease significantly after 100 hours in type. At 15 hours in type, both crew members are in the highest-risk category for this aircraft. In a high-stress, single-engine, instrument approach scenario, they are far more likely to mismanage power settings, misread aircraft-specific performance cues, struggle with emergency checklists under time pressure, and misinterpret the flight characteristics of the specific helicopter on one engine. This dramatically weakens any argument that continuing past the FAF was appropriate — crew inexperience in type is itself a major risk factor that should have weighed heavily toward the most conservative available option, which would have been initiating a missed approach immediately upon engine failure inside the FAF and declaring an emergency for ATC assistance.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM, error chain, SRM, Trescott Tip); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; 14 CFR 91.3

questions.question: When preparing to fly an instrument approach with one engine inoperative in a multiengine helicopter, where do you find the approved single-engine performance limitations for your specific aircraft?
questions.answer: The approved single-engine performance limitations are found in the Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) or Pilot's Operating Handbook (POH) for the specific aircraft, specifically in the Limitations section and Emergency/Abnormal Procedures section. These include single-engine power limits such as One Engine Inoperative (OEI) power ratings (e.g., 30-second, 2-minute, continuous OEI), airspeed limitations, maximum gross weight, density altitude performance charts, and any placarded restrictions. These are FAA-approved limitations and must be complied with.

questions.question: What does OEI stand for, and what are the typical OEI power ratings you would expect to see published in a multiengine helicopter RFM?
questions.answer: OEI stands for One Engine Inoperative. Typical OEI power ratings published in a multiengine helicopter RFM include: 30-second OEI (maximum emergency power, very limited use), 2-minute OEI (short-duration emergency power), and continuous OEI (maximum sustained power with one engine inoperative). Some aircraft also publish an intermediate contingency power rating. Each rating has associated torque, turbine temperature (ITT/TOT), and N1/N2 RPM limits that must not be exceeded, as exceeding them can cause engine damage or failure of the remaining engine.

questions.question: Why is gross weight a critical limitation to verify before attempting an instrument approach and landing with one engine inoperative?
questions.answer: Gross weight is critical because single-engine performance — including the ability to maintain altitude, execute a missed approach, and control the aircraft during final approach and landing — is directly tied to weight. Exceeding the published single-engine maximum gross weight (or the weight for which OEI performance data is charted) may mean the operating engine cannot produce enough power to maintain flight or execute a safe missed approach. At high gross weight, torque, ITT, and rotor RPM limits on the operating engine may be reached before adequate performance is achieved. Pilots must verify actual aircraft weight is within the single-engine performance envelope for the existing density altitude conditions.

questions.question: You are flying a twin-turbine helicopter on an ILS approach to minimums with the right engine failed. As you approach DA, you realize the operating engine ITT is already at its continuous OEI limit. What risk does this create, and what decision should you make?
questions.answer: This situation creates a critical risk: if a missed approach is required, you will need additional power beyond the continuous OEI limit (potentially 2-minute or 30-second OEI power), which means the engine is already at maximum sustainable output with no power reserve. If the approach goes wrong — wind shear, late visual acquisition, or ATC instruction to go missed — you may be unable to arrest a descent or climb away safely without exceeding engine limits or causing engine failure. The correct risk management decision is to execute the missed approach before reaching DA, while there is still altitude and energy to maneuver safely. Continuing to a landing attempt at the edge of the engine's limit with no margin remaining violates the principle of maintaining a known-good option.

questions.question: During preflight planning for an OEI instrument approach, you check the single-engine hover ceiling chart and find your helicopter cannot hover out of ground effect (OGE) at the destination airport's current density altitude at your current weight. How does this affect your approach planning and risk assessment?
questions.answer: If the helicopter cannot hover OGE on one engine at the destination density altitude and weight, it means you have very limited or no ability to arrest a descent and transition to a hover if needed during the approach or missed approach. This significantly increases risk because: (1) a missed approach may require substantial altitude gain the single engine cannot support for sustained periods; (2) any landing short of the runway could be unrecoverable if terrain or obstacles are present; (3) an aborted landing from low altitude with no OGE capability could be catastrophic. Risk management steps include: reducing weight if possible, waiting for density altitude to decrease (cooler temperature or lower pressure altitude), selecting an alternate airport at lower elevation, or reconsidering whether the flight should be conducted at all. The pilot must also confirm whether a running landing or roll-on landing is available to reduce power requirements.

questions.question: Your multiengine helicopter RFM specifies that a go-around from an OEI approach must be initiated no lower than 200 feet AGL and at a minimum airspeed of 60 knots. You are flying an ILS to a DA of 300 feet AGL. How do these powerplant limitations affect your decision point on the approach, and what happens if you delay the missed approach?
questions.answer: These RFM limitations mean that your effective go-around decision point is 200 feet AGL and 60 KIAS — which is actually higher than the published DA of 300 feet AGL if you are decelerating below 60 knots before DA. You must manage your approach so that if you initiate a missed approach, you still have the airspeed and altitude margins the RFM requires for a successful climb-out. If you delay the missed approach below 200 feet AGL or allow airspeed to drop below 60 knots, you may be operating outside the approved single-engine performance envelope, meaning the aircraft is not certificated to successfully complete the maneuver. This could result in a controlled flight into terrain. The practical risk management strategy is to treat the 200-foot AGL / 60-knot limitation as your personal decision altitude, not the published DA, unless the RFM limitation is less restrictive than the IAP DA.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; applicable aircraft RFM

questions.question: A pilot argues that because the 30-second OEI power rating exists in the RFM, it is available to use at any point during an OEI instrument approach whenever extra power is needed — for example, to correct for being low on the glideslope. How would you evaluate this reasoning from a risk management and aircraft limitation standpoint?
questions.answer: This reasoning is flawed and represents a significant misunderstanding of OEI power ratings and their intended use. The 30-second OEI rating exists specifically for emergency escape from imminent danger — it is a one-time or very limited-use contingency power setting, not a tool for routine power corrections during an approach. Using 30-second OEI power to correct glideslope deviations means: (1) you are consuming the emergency power margin that should be reserved for a genuine missed approach emergency; (2) turbine components are being exposed to extreme temperatures that accelerate wear and can cause unscheduled maintenance or failure; (3) once the 30-second limit is reached, you must reduce power or risk engine damage — potentially at the worst moment. From a risk management perspective, being low on glideslope during an OEI approach while needing 30-second power to correct indicates the approach is unstabilized and the proper response is to execute a missed approach, not to continue by exploiting emergency power ratings. The RFM limitations define the boundary of safe and certificated operation.
questions.follow_up: If a pilot does use 30-second OEI power during an approach and then lands safely, what are the required actions afterward?
questions.follow_up_answer: After using 30-second OEI power (or any time-limited OEI power rating), the pilot must comply with the engine manufacturer's maintenance requirements specified in the RFM and engine maintenance manual. Typically this requires a mandatory inspection or engine teardown before the next flight, regardless of whether the engine appears to be operating normally. The flight crew must document the event in the aircraft maintenance log, including the duration and level of power used. Operating the aircraft without completing the required inspection would be a violation of 14 CFR 91.7 (airworthiness) and 14 CFR 43 (maintenance requirements). In a commercial operation, the certificate holder's operations specifications and maintenance program would also dictate specific actions.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.7; 14 CFR Part 43; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; applicable RFM emergency procedures

questions.question: You are flying an IFR Part 135 air taxi flight in a multiengine helicopter. During the approach, the second engine fails unexpectedly, leaving you in single-engine IMC. The RFM single-engine performance charts show you are 400 pounds over the charted OEI maximum gross weight for the current density altitude. What are the risks, the regulatory implications, and what actions should you take?
questions.answer: This is a compounded emergency with multiple risk layers. Operationally, being 400 pounds over the OEI performance chart weight means the published performance data does not apply — you are operating in an uncertificated regime where climb rate, missed approach capability, and landing performance are unknown and likely degraded. The single operating engine may be unable to sustain level flight or provide a safe missed approach margin. Regulatory implications include: operating outside the aircraft's approved flight envelope may constitute a violation of 14 CFR 91.7 (airworthiness) and 14 CFR 135.185 (weight and balance compliance for Part 135 operations). However, 14 CFR 91.3 grants the pilot in command emergency authority to deviate from any rule to meet the emergency. Immediate actions: declare an emergency with ATC (7700 squawk, advise ATC of engine failure and weight situation); accept vectors to the nearest suitable airport with the best approach and landing surface available; fly the approach at the best-documented OEI airspeed from the RFM even if weight is over limits, as this gives the best aerodynamic efficiency from the operating engine; plan for a roll-on or running landing to reduce power demand at touchdown; avoid any maneuver that requires power above continuous OEI rating. After landing, report the deviation per 14 CFR 91.3(b) and comply with Part 135 incident/accident reporting requirements under 14 CFR 135.19.
questions.follow_up: After this emergency landing, your Part 135 operator asks you to fly the aircraft to a maintenance base 20 miles away with the same weight and one engine inoperative, arguing it is a short flight in VMC. What is your response?
questions.follow_up_answer: I would refuse the flight. The aircraft is outside its approved OEI performance envelope by weight, and that condition does not change based on weather conditions or distance. Flying in VMC does not change the powerplant limitation risk — if the operating engine fails or loses power on this ferry flight, I have no performance margin and no ability to safely execute a missed approach or avoid obstacles. Additionally, a ferry flight outside the RFM-approved weight envelope would require an FAA Special Flight Permit (ferry permit) under 14 CFR 21.197 and 91.209, which must be obtained before the flight. Without this permit, the flight would be illegal and the aircraft would not be in an airworthy condition as required by 14 CFR 91.7. I would ground the aircraft and coordinate with maintenance and the FSDO as necessary.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3; 14 CFR 91.7; 14 CFR 135.185; 14 CFR 21.197; 14 CFR Part 830 (NTSB reporting); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: During an instrument approach with a simulated engine failure, what does 'loss of situational awareness' mean in practical terms for the pilot?
questions.answer: Loss of situational awareness means the pilot no longer has an accurate mental picture of the helicopter's position, flight status, or the environment around them. In a single-engine instrument approach scenario, this could mean losing track of altitude, position on the approach, airspeed relative to best glide or autorotation entry speed, or the status of aircraft systems — any of which can quickly lead to a dangerous situation.

questions.question: What is the 'error chain' concept, and why is it especially relevant when executing an instrument approach with an inoperative engine in IMC?
questions.answer: The error chain is the concept that most aviation accidents result from a series of multiple poor decisions or events rather than one single catastrophic failure. During an instrument approach with an inoperative engine, multiple stressors exist simultaneously — workload is high, power margin is reduced, and IMC limits visual cues. Each poor decision or missed task (e.g., failing to configure on time, forgetting checklists, misidentifying the MAP) adds a link to the chain. Breaking any one link — such as going missed approach earlier, requesting vectors, or slowing down mentally — can change the outcome.

questions.question: Name at least three common sources of distraction during a simulated single-engine instrument approach that could compromise task prioritization.
questions.answer: Common distractions during a single-engine instrument approach include: (1) managing engine failure checklists or emergency procedures simultaneously with flying the approach, (2) radio communications with ATC requiring attention at critical phases such as the final approach fix or decision altitude, (3) passenger or crew communications inside the cockpit, (4) cockpit warning lights or audio alerts such as low rotor RPM warnings, (5) attempting to troubleshoot the failed engine instead of focusing on flying the approach, and (6) managing fuel or systems imbalances caused by the engine failure. Any of these can break focus from the primary task of maintaining instrument currency, airspeed, and course.

questions.question: You are flying a single-engine ILS approach in IMC and your copilot is running the engine-out checklist aloud while ATC calls with a revised missed approach clearance. At the same time, you notice the glideslope needle is one dot low. How do you prioritize these competing tasks, and what risk does poor prioritization create here?
questions.answer: The correct priority follows Aviate, Navigate, Communicate. First, immediately correct the glideslope deviation — being low on an ILS in IMC with reduced power margin is a terrain and obstacle clearance risk that must be addressed first. Second, acknowledge ATC with a brief 'Roger, standby' or have the copilot copy the clearance — do not attempt to fully process the new clearance while hand-flying a deviation. Third, allow the copilot to continue the checklist but pause if their readback requires your active confirmation. Poor prioritization here risks: (1) continued glideslope deviation leading to controlled flight into terrain, (2) missing the new missed approach instructions leading to airspace/terrain conflict, and (3) task saturation causing all three items to be handled poorly. The Trescott Tip applies — if multitasking will only 'probably' work, choose the one action known to keep you safe (correcting the deviation) first.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter (Instrument Approaches and Minimums)

questions.question: A multiengine helicopter crew is shooting a GPS approach with one engine inoperative. At the missed approach point, the required visual references are not in sight. The captain begins a climbing left turn immediately upon reaching the MAP. What situational awareness risk is present in this scenario, and what is the correct procedure?
questions.answer: The risk is spatial disorientation and terrain/obstacle conflict during an uncoordinated or premature turn. FAA guidance states that if a missed approach is initiated prior to the MAP, the pilot must continue to fly the instrument approach procedure to the MAP at or above MDA/DA before beginning a turn. Beginning a turn early in IMC with a degraded power margin on a single engine can lead to loss of separation from terrain, especially in mountainous or obstacle-rich environments. The correct procedure is to fly runway heading or the published missed approach course to the MAP, then execute the published missed approach climb gradient and turning instructions. With one engine inoperative, the crew must also verify the aircraft can meet the published missed approach climb gradient on the remaining engine — if not, this should have been assessed during approach briefing.

questions.question: How does reduced rotor RPM margin on a single-engine approach in IMC increase the risk of spatial disorientation, and what specific cockpit cues should the pilot monitor to prevent it?
questions.answer: On a single-engine approach, the pilot is already managing higher workload from checklist execution, asymmetric torque, and performance limitations. This cognitive load competes with instrument scan, making it easier to fixate on one instrument and neglect others — a classic setup for spatial disorientation. Additionally, if rotor RPM approaches a low-RPM condition, the resulting vibration or warning can startle the pilot and cause abrupt control inputs that worsen attitude. Key cockpit cues to monitor include: rotor tachometer (Nr) — keep within limits to avoid loss of control authority; attitude indicator — primary reference to prevent inadvertent bank; VSI and altimeter — detect unintended descent; torque gauge — confirm remaining engine is not exceeding limits; and airspeed — maintain best single-engine approach speed to preserve rotor energy and control margin. Systematic cross-check discipline is critical.

questions.question: During a coupled single-engine ILS in IMC, the autopilot disconnects at 600 feet AGL on final approach. The crew has been heads-down managing engine-out procedures and neither pilot has been actively hand-flying. What compounding situational awareness risks are now present, and how should the crew manage the transition to hand-flying?
questions.answer: Multiple compounding risks exist: (1) Automation complacency — after a period of autopilot-coupled flight, neither pilot may have maintained a current mental picture of aircraft attitude, trend, or position relative to the glideslope and localizer; (2) Startle effect from the autopilot disconnect — abrupt alerting at a critical altitude can cause task-saturated crews to react poorly; (3) Transition lag — manually taking control of a helicopter after an extended period of automation management, especially in IMC with one engine inoperative and potential torque asymmetry, requires deliberate reorientation before making control inputs; (4) Low altitude margin — at 600 feet AGL in IMC, there is very limited time to reestablish the approach before a go-around becomes the only safe option. Correct crew management: the pilot flying (PF) should announce assumption of manual control clearly, focus entirely on attitude and glidepath instruments, and verbalize any deviation; the pilot monitoring (PM) should call out deviations, manage ATC communications, and confirm checklist status is stable. Both pilots must resist fixating on the engine-out situation and redirect full attention to flying the approach. If deviations are not immediately recoverable, execute the missed approach without hesitation.
questions.follow_up: If the crew decides to continue the approach manually and reaches decision altitude still in IMC with one needle deflection on the localizer, what is the correct action, and does the reduced power margin from the engine failure change that decision?
questions.follow_up_answer: At decision altitude (DA/DH), if at least one of the ten required visual references specified in 14 CFR 91.175(c) is not distinctly visible and identifiable, the missed approach must be executed immediately — there is no discretion. The engine-out condition does not change the regulatory requirement to go missed at DA without required references. However, it does change the urgency and execution: with reduced climb performance on one engine, the crew must have pre-briefed the single-engine missed approach performance — specifically whether the helicopter can meet the published missed approach climb gradient. If it cannot, the crew should have identified an alternate plan (lower minimums alternate, different approach, divert) prior to commencing the approach. Continuing below DA in IMC without required references is a violation of 14 CFR 91.175 regardless of engine status.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175(c); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13; FAA-H-8083-15B (Instrument Approaches and Minimums)

questions.question: FAA research indicates that aviation accident rates decrease significantly after 100 hours in a specific aircraft type. How does this concept apply to the risk of disorientation and task saturation during a single-engine instrument approach for a pilot who is highly experienced in total hours but relatively new to the specific helicopter type?
questions.answer: FAA data from the Helicopter Flying Handbook indicates that accidents correlate more strongly with hours in a specific aircraft model than with total flight hours. A pilot with thousands of total hours but fewer than 100 hours in the specific helicopter type may have automation habits, rotor RPM decay rates, torque response characteristics, and instrument layout familiarity that differ significantly from the current aircraft. During a high-workload event like a single-engine instrument approach, the pilot may default to muscle memory or mental models from a previous aircraft type — leading to incorrect control inputs, delayed recognition of instrument deviations, or misjudgment of single-engine performance margins. This type-specific inexperience is especially dangerous in IMC because visual cues that might otherwise allow the pilot to correct are absent. The risk mitigation is to acknowledge this currency gap during pre-flight risk assessment, ensure thorough type-specific training and simulator time for single-engine IMC scenarios, and potentially increase personal minimums for single-engine approaches until type-specific proficiency is established.
questions.follow_up: If this same pilot uses the word 'probably' when briefing the approach — for example, 'we can probably make the single-engine missed approach climb gradient' — what does the Trescott Tip tell you about the safety of continuing that approach?
questions.follow_up_answer: The Trescott Tip, referenced in the FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook Chapter 13, states that the word 'probably' is a warning sign — if an action will only 'probably' work, the pilot should instead choose a course of action known to work. If the crew is uncertain whether the aircraft can meet the single-engine missed approach climb gradient, the correct decision is not to commence or continue the approach. The uncertain outcome means the known-safe action is to divert to an airport with lower climb gradient requirements, wait for a better power margin (e.g., lighter fuel load), or plan for a different approach procedure. Continuing an approach with unverified missed approach performance in IMC on one engine is accepting a risk that should not be accepted — especially given the reduced situational awareness already introduced by the engine failure.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (Trescott Tip, accident rate by hours in type); 14 CFR 91.175

questions.question: During an instrument approach with one engine inoperative, what is the primary reason collision hazards are considered higher risk than during a normal two-engine approach?
questions.answer: With one engine inoperative, the pilot faces significantly higher workload managing aircraft performance, asymmetric power, and abnormal checklists simultaneously with flying the approach. This divided attention reduces situational awareness and increases the likelihood of missing traffic advisories, TCAS alerts, or terrain warnings. Additionally, the single-engine helicopter may have limited ability to maneuver aggressively to avoid a conflict due to reduced power margins.

questions.question: What onboard systems are available to help the pilot of a multiengine helicopter detect collision hazards during an instrument approach in IMC?
questions.answer: The primary onboard collision hazard detection systems include TCAS (Traffic Collision Avoidance System), which provides traffic advisories (TAs) and resolution advisories (RAs) based on transponder returns, and ADS-B In, which displays nearby ADS-B Out equipped traffic on a moving map or traffic display. TAWS (Terrain Awareness and Warning System) addresses terrain and obstacle collision hazards. The pilot should also monitor ATC for traffic calls.

questions.question: What does TAWS specifically protect against during an instrument approach, and how does it differ from TCAS?
questions.answer: TAWS (Terrain Awareness and Warning System) provides alerts for controlled flight into terrain (CFIT) by comparing the aircraft's current position, altitude, and flight path against a terrain and obstacle database. It warns of potential ground or obstacle collisions. TCAS, by contrast, detects other transponder-equipped aircraft and advises on traffic conflicts. TAWS addresses terrain/obstacle collision hazards; TCAS addresses mid-air collision hazards. Both are important during an instrument approach, especially with degraded crew capacity due to engine failure.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5; 14 CFR 91.223 (TAWS requirements for turbine aircraft)

questions.question: You are flying a multiengine helicopter ILS approach in IMC with the left engine inoperative. At 500 feet AGL, you receive a TCAS Traffic Advisory (TA) for traffic at your 12 o'clock, same altitude, converging. How does the engine-out condition affect your ability to respond, and what is your priority sequence?
questions.answer: A TA does not mandate a maneuver but requires immediate heightened visual scanning and readiness to act. With one engine inoperative, your maneuvering capability is significantly reduced — aggressive climbs or turns may not be achievable within single-engine power margins. Priority sequence: (1) Maintain aircraft control — the engine-out condition means you cannot sacrifice control authority; (2) Notify ATC immediately of the TA and your engine-out status so they can provide separation; (3) Increase scan for the traffic; (4) If a Resolution Advisory (RA) follows, comply to the extent your single-engine performance allows while keeping ATC informed. Do not allow collision avoidance maneuvering to create a secondary emergency (e.g., exceeding single-engine OEI limits or entering an unsafe flight regime).
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and 13; 14 CFR 91.123 (compliance with ATC instructions)

questions.question: During an OEI instrument approach, your workload is extremely high managing checklists, communications, and aircraft control. How should you manage the collision hazard risk specifically caused by reduced situational awareness in this high-workload environment?
questions.answer: Workload management is the key mitigation. Strategies include: (1) Prioritize aviate-navigate-communicate — do not let radio or checklist tasks distract from aircraft control and collision scan; (2) Brief the approach thoroughly before commencing it, reducing in-flight cognitive load; (3) Delegate non-critical tasks to the copilot if crew-qualified; (4) Use automation (autopilot, FMS) to reduce manual flying demands, freeing mental capacity for threat monitoring; (5) Actively monitor TCAS and ADS-B displays and do not dismiss advisory alerts; (6) Inform ATC early of the engine-out condition so they can provide increased separation and priority handling, reducing the likelihood of traffic conflicts in the first place. The error chain concept from ADM applies — high workload is one link; allowing it to also degrade collision awareness creates multiple links toward an accident.

questions.question: You are conducting a simulated OEI instrument approach to a busy Class C airport. ATC issues a 360-degree heading turn for spacing immediately after you pass the final approach fix (FAF) inbound. What collision hazard considerations are specific to this OEI scenario, and how do you respond?
questions.answer: A 360-degree turn issued after the FAF is an unusual and high-risk instruction under any circumstances, but with an engine inoperative it is especially hazardous for several reasons: (1) The added drag and power demand of a banked turn in OEI configuration may exceed available performance; (2) The turn significantly increases exposure time in the terminal environment where traffic density is high; (3) Loss of the established instrument approach course increases CFIT risk. The pilot should immediately declare the engine-out condition to ATC if not already done, state inability to comply safely with the 360 in OEI configuration, and request an alternative such as a missed approach, hold, or immediate clearance to continue the approach. Under 14 CFR 91.123, ATC instructions should be followed unless, in the pilot's judgment, an emergency exists — an OEI condition limiting safe maneuvering qualifies. Declaring an emergency (7700 transponder, verbal declaration) is appropriate if needed to ensure priority handling and safe separation.

questions.question: During a simulated OEI instrument approach in actual IMC, your TCAS issues a Resolution Advisory (RA) commanding a climb at the same moment you break out of the clouds at minimums with the runway environment in sight. The single-engine performance of your helicopter is marginal. How do you evaluate this collision hazard scenario, and what is the correct action?
questions.answer: This is a direct conflict between two safety imperatives: TCAS RA compliance and landing at minimums. FAA guidance states pilots should comply with TCAS RAs; however, pilot authority under 14 CFR 91.3 always applies. With marginal OEI performance, an RA-commanded climb may be physically impossible without risking rotor stall, exceeding OEI limits, or a loss of control. The correct action requires rapid evaluation: (1) If the climb performance is available — comply with the RA, advise ATC immediately, and execute a missed approach; (2) If the climb is not safely achievable in OEI configuration — the pilot must exercise emergency authority, advise ATC of the conflict and inability to comply, and if the runway is clearly in sight and landing can be completed safely, that may be the safest outcome; (3) ATC must be notified of both the RA and the OEI condition so separation from the conflicting traffic can be managed. The key FAA ADM principle applies: never choose an option that only 'probably' works. If the RA climb is uncertain in OEI, the known-safe option (land on the visible runway) may be correct.
questions.follow_up: TCAS RAs are mandatory under FAA policy and some regulations — what is the regulatory basis for TCAS RA compliance, and does it override pilot-in-command authority?
questions.follow_up_answer: 14 CFR 91.221 requires TCAS equipment on certain aircraft, and FAA policy in AC 120-55 states pilots should comply with RAs. However, 14 CFR 91.3(b) explicitly states that in an emergency the PIC may deviate from any regulation to the extent necessary to meet that emergency. An OEI condition with marginal performance is an emergency that could make RA compliance physically impossible or unsafe. The TCAS RA does not override PIC authority — it is a strong safety guidance tool, not an absolute regulatory command that supersedes 91.3. The pilot must report any deviation to ATC as soon as practical, and if an emergency was declared, submit an ASAP or NASA ASRS report as appropriate.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3; 14 CFR 91.221; FAA AC 120-55; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13

questions.question: A multiengine helicopter crew is flying an OEI RNAV approach at night in IMC to a remote helipad. They have no TCAS, no ADS-B In display, and the airport is non-towered. What specific collision hazard mitigations are available to them, and how does the engine-out condition amplify those hazards?
questions.answer: Without TCAS or ADS-B In, the crew is relying on procedural separation, see-and-avoid (impossible in IMC), and radio self-announcement. Available mitigations include: (1) CTAF/UNICOM position announcements throughout the approach — call inbound at the IAF, FAF, and final; (2) Check NOTAMs for known traffic activity at the destination; (3) Monitor the CTAF frequency for other traffic; (4) Use TAWS to address terrain/obstacle collision hazards since those are still present; (5) Coordinate with approach control or center for traffic advisories as long as in radar coverage. The OEI condition amplifies these hazards in two ways: first, the crew's attention is necessarily split between managing the abnormal condition and maintaining SA on traffic; second, if a go-around or evasive maneuver becomes necessary due to traffic, the OEI helicopter has significantly degraded performance to execute it safely. This scenario also highlights the risk management decision of whether to continue to a non-towered, remote destination without adequate traffic conflict tools while OEI — a divert to a towered airport with full radar services may be the safer option.
questions.follow_up: If this crew decided to divert to the nearest towered airport while OEI in IMC, what airspace, communication, and priority handling considerations apply?
questions.follow_up_answer: Declaring an emergency (squawk 7700, verbal declaration on current frequency and 121.5 if needed) activates priority handling under ATC Order 7110.65. ATC is required to provide direct routing, priority sequencing, and reduced traffic conflict exposure. This is especially important in OEI IMC — the crew should not attempt to manage a complex arrival without ATC priority assistance. Upon declaring an emergency, ATC will assign an approach, clear the airspace, and coordinate with emergency services at the destination. The PIC must log the emergency declaration and may be asked to file a report with the FAA Administrator under 14 CFR 91.3(c). NTSB notification under 49 CFR Part 830 may also be required depending on damage or injury.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3; 14 CFR 91.123; 49 CFR Part 830; ATC Order 7110.65; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and 13

questions.question: When flying a multiengine helicopter instrument approach with one engine inoperative, what does 'configuring the helicopter' mean, and why does it matter for safety?
questions.answer: Configuring the helicopter means setting up all systems, controls, and power settings in the optimal state for continued flight on the operating engine — this includes securing the failed engine per the POH/RFM (fuel shutoff, throttle, engine controls), setting the operating engine to appropriate power, trimming the aircraft to reduce pilot workload, and ensuring all checklists are complete. It matters because an improperly configured helicopter increases pilot workload during the approach, risks asymmetric torque or yaw excursions, and can mask performance limitations of the remaining engine, all of which increase the chance of a flight control error or controlled flight into terrain.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; applicable Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) emergency procedures

questions.question: What is the purpose of completing emergency and abnormal checklists before beginning an instrument approach with an inoperative engine, rather than during the approach?
questions.answer: Completing all checklists prior to commencing the approach ensures the helicopter is fully configured and the pilot's mental workload is minimized during the highest-workload phase of flight. During the approach, the pilot must simultaneously manage navigation, communications, power monitoring, and flight controls. Attempting to run checklists during this phase distracts from flying the aircraft, increases the risk of missing a critical step, and can lead to an undetected configuration error at a critical altitude. The principle is: aviate, navigate, communicate — configure before you descend.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11 and Chapter 13 (ADM/workload management); applicable RFM

questions.question: When an engine fails during an instrument approach in a multiengine helicopter, what are the two immediate configuration priorities for the remaining operative engine?
questions.answer: The two immediate configuration priorities for the operative engine are: (1) ensuring it is set to the appropriate power level for continued flight — typically maximum continuous power or as specified by the RFM for OEI operations — to maintain altitude, airspeed, and rotor RPM within limits; and (2) verifying the engine is stable, with oil pressure, temperature, and rotor RPM in normal ranges before committing to the approach. Failure to confirm operative engine status before continuing the approach risks an inadvertent dual-engine failure scenario or an over-torque/over-temperature event that degrades the only remaining power source.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; applicable RFM OEI procedures

questions.question: You are flying a multiengine helicopter ILS approach in IMC and experience an engine failure at the final approach fix. You are single-pilot, hand-flying the approach. Walk me through your configuration priorities and explain the risk if you delay any of them.
questions.answer: Immediately upon engine failure: (1) Maintain aircraft control — collective, cyclic, and pedals to counter yaw and maintain airspeed and rotor RPM; (2) Execute the OEI memory items per the RFM (typically: identify failed engine, confirm, then secure — fuel off, throttle closed, or as specified); (3) Set the operative engine to OEI power rating as published in the RFM; (4) Trim the aircraft to relieve control forces and reduce workload; (5) Assess whether to continue the approach or execute a missed approach based on aircraft performance capability. Risks of delay: failing to trim allows control forces to fatigue or distract the pilot; delaying securing the failed engine risks a fire or continued fuel feed to a failed hot section; failing to set correct OEI power may result in performance below that needed to maintain glide path or execute a missed approach safely. At the FAF in IMC, terrain and obstacle clearance margins are already thin — any delay in proper configuration compounds the hazard.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5 (instrument approach); applicable RFM

questions.question: Landing minimums on an instrument approach procedure assume all components are fully operational. How does an inoperative engine affect your approach minimums, and what configuration steps must occur before you can legally descend to the published minimums?
questions.answer: An inoperative engine is a significant aircraft system change that can affect approach capability. Under 14 CFR Part 97 and TPP Inoperative Components Tables, minimums are raised when certain equipment is inoperative; however, an inoperative engine is an aircraft airworthiness issue governed by the RFM, not directly addressed in the TPP inoperative components table. The pilot must: (1) Confirm the aircraft is airworthy and within OEI performance limits for the approach per the RFM; (2) Complete all OEI checklists so the aircraft is fully configured before commencing or continuing the approach; (3) Verify the aircraft can perform the missed approach procedure on one engine at the applicable weight and density altitude — if it cannot, a lower or different approach minimum may effectively apply operationally even if not charted. Descending to minimums before confirming OEI configuration and performance capability is unsafe because the missed approach becomes the last safety net, and an unconfigured aircraft may not be able to execute it.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175; FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Approaches and Minimums; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; applicable RFM

questions.question: During a simulated OEI instrument approach training exercise, your instructor tells you to skip the trim configuration step to save time. What risk does this introduce, and how would you respond as pilot-in-command?
questions.answer: Skipping trim configuration in an OEI approach introduces the risk of increased pilot workload and physical fatigue from fighting sustained control forces, which can degrade precision on the approach. With an engine inoperative, asymmetric torque and yaw require constant pedal and cyclic input; if the aircraft is not trimmed, the pilot is simultaneously hand-flying precise instrument procedures while holding significant control pressures. This degrades situational awareness, increases error rate, and masks unusual attitudes. As PIC, I would respectfully but clearly decline the shortcut and explain that proper OEI configuration — including trim — is a non-negotiable safety step. Aeronautical decision-making principles (FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13) specifically warn against 'get-there-itis' and cutting steps to save time; if a configuration step would 'probably' be fine to skip, the correct answer is to do it — not to assume. The PIC has final authority under 14 CFR 91.3.

questions.question: You execute a missed approach from an OEI instrument approach and, during the climb, you realize you never secured the failed engine's fuel control — you only reduced power on it. The engine is windmilling and consuming fuel. What is the risk this configuration error creates, and what is your decision-making priority sequence at this point?
questions.answer: A windmilling engine consuming fuel creates multiple risks: (1) fuel exhaustion of the operative engine if they share a fuel system or cross-feed is open; (2) potential for a fire if the failed engine's hot section is still exposed to fuel flow; (3) asymmetric drag from the windmilling engine reducing overall performance on the missed approach; (4) potential for an uncommanded restart or further mechanical failure. The priority sequence is: (1) Maintain aircraft control — you are in IMC in a missed approach climb, so aviate first; (2) Communicate your situation to ATC and request vectors to a safe altitude and holding if needed; (3) Navigate to the published missed approach procedure; (4) Then complete the overdue OEI checklist to properly secure the failed engine. Do NOT attempt to run the checklist at low altitude in IMC while climbing — gain altitude and stability first. This scenario is a direct example of how an incomplete configuration creates a compounding chain of errors, consistent with the FAA's 'error chain' model in Chapter 13.
questions.follow_up: If securing the failed engine now requires pulling a fuel shutoff that also affects the operative engine's cross-feed, how do you manage that risk?
questions.follow_up_answer: Before touching any fuel shutoff, I must identify and confirm I am manipulating only the failed engine's controls — this is the 'identify, confirm, secure' procedure required by the RFM. If the fuel system architecture creates ambiguity about which shutoff affects which engine, I should reference the RFM systems section and verify with any available cockpit indications (fuel flow gauges, engine instruments) before acting. If I cannot positively identify the correct shutoff without risk to the operative engine, I hold configuration (leave it as is), communicate to ATC, and land at the nearest suitable airport with the windmilling engine — an imperfect configuration managed safely is preferable to an action that could extinguish the only working engine. This reflects the ADM principle: if an action will only 'probably' work, choose the option you know to be safe.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (OEI procedures, emergency), Chapter 13 (ADM, error chain); 14 CFR 91.3; applicable RFM

questions.question: A pilot argues that on an OEI approach to minimums in VMC conditions below the clouds, configuration is less critical because they can see and land visually. How would you challenge that reasoning as an examiner, and what specific risks does an improperly configured helicopter create even in visual conditions at minimums?
questions.answer: This reasoning is flawed and dangerous. Visual conditions at minimums do not eliminate the configuration risks — they simply change one variable. An improperly configured helicopter at minimums still presents: (1) asymmetric yaw or torque that requires constant pilot input, distracting from the landing flare and touchdown phase; (2) an improperly secured failed engine still poses fire risk regardless of visibility; (3) if the landing must be aborted for any reason (obstruction, traffic, unstabilized approach), the ability to execute a safe OEI go-around depends entirely on the aircraft being properly configured — a windmilling engine, incorrect power setting, or un-trimmed aircraft degrades go-around performance exactly when it is most needed; (4) at low altitude in the landing environment, there is zero margin for a configuration-related surprise. Additionally, FAA ADM principles (Chapter 13) warn against situational overconfidence — 'I can see, therefore I am safe' is a known cognitive trap. Proper configuration is not optional based on visibility; it is required for aircraft airworthiness and safe completion of any approach regardless of meteorological conditions.
questions.follow_up: If this pilot holds a helicopter ATP certificate and argues their experience justifies the shortcut, how does the FAA's accident research on experience versus aircraft type hours address that argument?
questions.follow_up_answer: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 specifically notes that accident rates correlate more strongly with hours in a specific aircraft model than with total flight hours. A pilot with high total time but low time in a specific multiengine helicopter type is statistically at higher risk — experience in other types does not transfer fully to OEI configuration proficiency in an unfamiliar aircraft. Furthermore, holding an ATP certificate increases the legal standard of care, not the license to skip procedures. Under 14 CFR 91.3, the PIC is responsible for the safe outcome regardless of certificate level. Complacency driven by experience is itself identified as a hazardous attitude ('invulnerability') in the FAA's hazardous attitude framework, and is one of the documented links in the error chain that leads to accidents.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM, hazardous attitudes, error chain); 14 CFR 91.3; 14 CFR 61.153 (ATP standards); applicable RFM

questions.question: During a go-around on a multiengine helicopter with one engine inoperative, what is the primary aerodynamic risk that distinguishes this maneuver from a go-around with both engines operating?
questions.answer: With one engine inoperative, the remaining engine must provide all power for both climb and torque compensation. The primary risk is that the available power margin is significantly reduced or may be insufficient to arrest the descent and establish a positive climb, especially at higher density altitudes or heavy weights. There is also increased asymmetric torque demand on the antitorque system. The pilot must recognize that performance charts for OEI go-arounds may show marginal or no climb capability depending on conditions.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) OEI performance charts

questions.question: What does the term 'rejected landing' mean in the context of a multiengine helicopter IFR approach, and at what point in the approach must the pilot commit to this decision?
questions.answer: A rejected landing is a decision to discontinue a landing attempt and transition to a go-around or missed approach after crossing the decision altitude/height (DA/DH) or minimum descent altitude (MDA) but before touchdown, or any time a safe landing cannot be assured. In a multiengine helicopter with an inoperative engine, this decision is critical because OEI performance may limit the ability to execute a go-around at very low altitude. The pilot should make this decision as early as possible — ideally at or before the MAP — because go-around capability decreases as the helicopter descends further toward the landing surface and airspeed bleeds off.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter on Instrument Approaches and Minimums; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: Why is low rotor RPM a particular concern during a go-around or rejected landing with one engine inoperative in a multiengine helicopter?
questions.answer: During a go-around with one engine inoperative, the pilot must rapidly increase collective to arrest descent and initiate a climb. This sudden collective increase places a high demand on the single operating engine. If the engine cannot supply sufficient power to meet this demand, rotor RPM will decay. Per the FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook, rotor stall in helicopters is not recoverable; once RPM decays below the stall threshold, recovery is impossible. Early recognition of a low RPM condition during this critical phase is therefore imperative, and the pilot must monitor rotor RPM closely throughout the maneuver.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; RFM rotor RPM limitations

questions.question: You are flying a two-pilot IFR approach in a multiengine helicopter. At 200 feet AGL on the ILS, one engine fails. The runway is in sight but the helicopter is slightly high and fast. What risk factors must you immediately evaluate before committing to either a go-around or a continued landing?
questions.answer: The pilot must rapidly assess: (1) OEI power available versus power required at current weight, altitude, and temperature — consult the RFM OEI performance charts mentally or by memory; (2) current airspeed — if above minimum controllable airspeed OEI, a go-around may be feasible; (3) height-velocity diagram — at 200 feet AGL, the helicopter may be within or near a dangerous region for OEI; (4) whether the aircraft can maintain controllable flight with the remaining engine during the go-around climb; (5) runway remaining and surface condition if continuing to land; and (6) whether remaining engine has reached any torque or temperature limits.
