Being 'slightly high and fast' may actually favor a continued approach to landing rather than a go-around if OEI climb performance is marginal, since a rejected landing initiated at very low altitude with insufficient power margin creates a higher-risk scenario than accepting the landing.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; RFM OEI procedures and performance charts; FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Approaches

questions.question: A helicopter crew is conducting a Category I ILS approach in IMC when an engine fails at the DA/DH. The crew elects to go around and enters the published missed approach procedure. What specific risk does transitioning from instrument conditions to the OEI missed approach procedure introduce that would not exist on a normal two-engine missed approach?
questions.answer: On a normal missed approach, the crew can climb at the published gradient using full power from both engines. With an engine inoperative, the risks introduced include: (1) reduced climb performance — the OEI climb rate may not meet the published missed approach obstacle clearance gradient, creating CFIT risk; (2) increased workload — the crew must simultaneously manage OEI checklists, aircraft control, and instrument navigation while transitioning from approach configuration; (3) asymmetric thrust effects requiring precise pedal and cyclic control; (4) the possibility that OEI ceiling and climb performance cannot maintain the missed approach routing in icing or mountainous terrain; and (5) increased time in IMC at low altitude with reduced performance reserve. Crews should be trained on the OEI missed approach specifically and know the aircraft's OEI single-engine service ceiling relative to the missed approach altitude.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Approaches and Minimums; 14 CFR 91.175

questions.question: During a practice OEI instrument approach, the simulating instructor reduces power on one engine at the missed approach point. The weather is at minimums and the runway environment is not in sight. Describe how the risk profile of the go-around changes compared to the same maneuver conducted in VMC at altitude during training.
questions.answer: The risk profile is significantly higher in actual IMC at minimums for several reasons: (1) there is no visual reference to detect bank or descent excursions — all corrections must be made by instrument scan alone while managing OEI; (2) the crew is at the lowest altitude in the approach with minimum obstacle clearance, so any delay in executing the go-around increases CFIT exposure; (3) workload peaks simultaneously — OEI control inputs, aviate/navigate/communicate priorities, and checklist execution must all compete at the same moment; (4) in VMC at altitude, a margin exists to recover from control errors; at minimums in IMC, that margin is essentially zero; (5) there is no option to visually identify terrain, obstacles, or alternate landing areas. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook emphasizes that situational awareness and early, decisive action are critical, and that accumulation of poor decisions (error chain) is most dangerous in these high-stress scenarios.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13 (ADM/SRM); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter on Instrument Approaches

questions.question: A multiengine helicopter crew has pre-briefed that if an engine fails below DA/DH with the runway in sight, they will continue to land rather than go around, based on OEI performance charts showing marginal climb capability at their current weight and density altitude. During the approach, an engine fails at 150 feet AGL — 50 feet below DA/DH — and the runway is in sight but a fuel truck is parked in the touchdown zone. What are the risk management considerations that should drive the crew's decision, and is their pre-briefed plan still valid?
questions.answer: The pre-briefed plan must be immediately re-evaluated because a critical variable has changed — the intended landing surface is now obstructed. The risk management considerations are: (1) The pre-brief assumed a clear, usable runway. An obstruction in the touchdown zone invalidates that assumption and requires a go/no-go re-evaluation in real time. (2) At 150 feet AGL OEI, a go-around may be possible if airspeed is adequate and power margin exists, but performance charts must be consulted mentally — the crew should know their OEI hover-out-of-ground-effect (HOGE) and climb capability by memory before the approach. (3) Attempting to land on a contaminated touchdown zone at low airspeed with one engine risks ground contact with the obstruction, dynamic rollover on uneven surface, or loss of tail rotor effectiveness during deceleration. (4) The FAA ADM principle warns against 'probably' solutions — landing with an obstruction present is not a known-safe outcome. (5) If an OEI go-around is initiated, it must be committed fully and immediately; a hesitant attempt that aborts halfway is likely worse than either firm option. The crew should execute the OEI go-around if performance permits and communicate immediately with ATC, or if go-around performance is definitively insufficient, identify an alternate clear surface (taxiway, overrun area) prior to touchdown.
questions.follow_up: Your RFM OEI performance chart shows the helicopter is approximately 200 lbs below the maximum OEI hover weight at current density altitude. Does this mean the go-around is safe to execute?
questions.follow_up_answer: Not necessarily. Being below maximum OEI hover weight means the helicopter can theoretically maintain hover OEI, but a go-around requires more than a hover — it requires a positive climb rate sufficient to clear obstacles on the missed approach. The OEI hover weight limit is a static calculation; the go-around requires transitioning through effective translational lift (ETL) while managing height loss during acceleration. At 150 feet AGL, there may not be sufficient altitude to absorb any height loss during the transition. The crew must also verify that the single operating engine is within all torque, temperature, and N1 limits and that no additional limiting factors (icing, turbulence, contaminated air data) are affecting performance. Being 200 lbs under the chart limit provides a margin but does not guarantee a successful go-around — it is a necessary condition, not a sufficient one.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13; RFM OEI Performance Charts; 14 CFR 91.175(c)

questions.question: During a multiengine helicopter IFR checkride, an examiner simulates an engine failure during the go-around portion of a circling approach. The applicant immediately pitches up and raises collective aggressively to arrest the descent. What specific hazards does this control input sequence create, and what does it reveal about the applicant's understanding of OEI go-around risk?
questions.answer: Aggressively pitching up and raising collective simultaneously creates several compounding hazards: (1) A sudden large collective increase demands maximum power from the remaining engine immediately — if torque limits are exceeded, engine damage or failure can occur, leaving the helicopter with no power. (2) Pitching up aggressively at low airspeed can reduce translational lift and push the rotor system toward lower RPM by increasing disk loading without the benefit of forward airflow — exactly opposite of what is needed. (3) Low rotor RPM risk is acute: per the FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook, once rotor stall occurs it is unrecoverable. (4) During a circling approach, the helicopter may be in a banked turn — aggressive back cyclic combined with collective in a banked attitude can introduce retreating blade stall risk if near Vne for the bank angle. (5) This input sequence reveals that the applicant is reacting instinctively rather than applying a systematic OEI go-around procedure — the correct technique is to apply power smoothly to OEI limits, establish the appropriate OEI best climb airspeed per the RFM, control yaw with pedals for the asymmetric torque change, and then execute the missed approach routing. The error chain initiated by a panic response at this phase of flight is one of the most dangerous scenarios in helicopter instrument operations.
questions.follow_up: The applicant says they were trained that 'power is your friend' during an engine failure go-around and that maximum collective is always correct. How do you address this as an examiner?
questions.follow_up_answer: The 'power is your friend' concept is partially correct — available power must be used — but it is dangerously incomplete without the qualifier 'within limits and at the correct airspeed.' Maximum collective at the wrong airspeed, wrong bank angle, or beyond engine torque limits is not safe. The correct teaching point is: apply collective to achieve the RFM-specified OEI go-around power setting (which may be maximum continuous OEI or takeoff OEI depending on the aircraft and phase), simultaneously establish the OEI best climb airspeed with cyclic, and control heading with antitorque pedals. The RFM defines the limit — exceeding torque or turbine temperature limits to 'use all available power' risks the only remaining engine. As an examiner, this misunderstanding represents a deficit in both systems knowledge and risk management judgment, and would require additional training before the practical test could be successfully completed.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; RFM OEI procedures and power limits; 14 CFR 61.43

questions.question: During an instrument approach in a multiengine helicopter, what are the primary indications that tell you an engine has failed?
questions.answer: Primary indications of engine failure in a multiengine helicopter include: a yaw or roll tendency toward the failed engine side, a drop in that engine's N1/N2 (gas producer/power turbine RPM), a decrease or loss of torque on the affected engine, a drop in TOT/TGT (turbine outlet/gas generator temperature) on the failed side, and possibly an engine failure warning light or audio alert depending on aircraft systems. In IMC, the pilot must cross-check these indications quickly because outside visual cues are not available to confirm the yaw or attitude change.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; POH/RFM for specific aircraft

questions.question: After recognizing an engine failure in IMC during an instrument approach, what is the immediate priority before any troubleshooting or checklists?
questions.answer: The immediate priority is to maintain positive helicopter control — meaning maintain the desired attitude on the flight instruments, counter any yaw with appropriate pedal input, adjust collective and cyclic as needed to maintain aircraft control and a stabilized flight path. Aircraft control always comes first. Troubleshooting or running emergency checklists comes only after the helicopter is under positive control, because losing control in IMC is immediately fatal regardless of engine status.

questions.question: On a multiengine helicopter, which flight control input is typically the first required to counteract the asymmetrical torque when one engine fails suddenly?
questions.answer: The antitorque pedals — specifically, a pedal input to counteract the yaw caused by the sudden change in torque. With one engine producing power and the other failing, the torque balance changes and the nose will yaw toward the failed engine side. The pilot must apply the appropriate pedal (toward the operating engine side) to maintain heading. Simultaneously, cyclic must be used to arrest any roll tendency and maintain attitude on the flight instruments.

questions.question: You are flying a twin-engine helicopter on the ILS final approach at 800 feet AGL in IMC. Your right engine suddenly fails. Walk me through the first five seconds of your response — what are you doing and in what order?
questions.answer: 1) Immediately apply left pedal (assuming right engine failure causes left yaw) to arrest the yaw and maintain heading. 2) Apply cyclic input as needed to arrest any roll and maintain the approach attitude on the attitude indicator — do not chase the glideslope yet, control the helicopter first. 3) Adjust collective to maintain desired power setting and rotor RPM with the remaining engine — avoid pulling too much collective and overloading the surviving engine. 4) Cross-check the engine instruments to confirm which engine has failed (do not shut down the wrong engine). 5) Communicate intent to ATC if workload permits and transition into the single-engine OEI approach profile per the POH. The approach may continue if performance allows, but the missed approach option must be assessed immediately based on single-engine performance charts.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; applicable aircraft RFM/POH OEI procedures

questions.question: During an instrument approach simulation of an engine failure, your instructor pulls the power on one engine and you notice the rotor RPM starting to decay. You are in the clouds at 1,200 feet AGL. What specifically causes rotor RPM to decay in this scenario, and what is your control response?
questions.answer: Rotor RPM decay occurs because the remaining engine may not immediately or fully compensate for the lost power, particularly if the collective is set too high for single-engine power available, or if the governor has not yet responded. The rotor system is being asked to produce more work than the surviving engine can sustain at that torque setting. The response is to immediately lower collective to reduce the load on the rotor system and allow RPM to recover. Once rotor RPM is back in the green arc, reset collective to the maximum single-engine torque limit per the OEI chart. In IMC, this must be done entirely on instruments — the pilot cannot look outside to verify attitude, requiring a disciplined instrument scan throughout the recovery.

questions.question: You are flying a twin-engine helicopter on an IFR approach at night in IMC. You receive an engine failure warning light but the torque gauges still appear nearly equal. How do you determine which engine has actually failed, and how does this affect maintaining positive control?
questions.answer: With ambiguous indications, cross-check all engine instruments: N1, N2/Ng, TOT/TGT, torque, and fuel flow for each engine. The failed engine will show a decaying trend across most or all of these parameters, even if the torque gauges momentarily appear similar due to lag. The yaw direction is also a cue — the helicopter will yaw toward the engine producing less thrust/torque. Do NOT pull a fuel cutoff or shut down an engine based on a single warning light alone. Maintain positive control — pedal, cyclic, and collective inputs to keep the helicopter on the approach path — while methodically verifying the failure. In IMC, a misidentification (shutting down the wrong engine) could cause a total power loss, so verification before action is critical. If in doubt, execute the missed approach on both engines while diagnosing.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; aircraft specific RFM emergency procedures

questions.question: During an OEI instrument approach practice, you notice the student consistently maintains heading and rotor RPM well but allows the aircraft to descend 150–200 feet below the glidepath within the first 10 seconds of the simulated failure before recovering. What specific error in instrument scan or control technique is most likely producing this pattern, and how do you address it?
questions.answer: This pattern indicates the student is fixating on the engine instruments or the failed-engine side of the panel to identify and confirm the failure rather than maintaining a prioritized instrument scan. During the identification process, the attitude indicator and VSI/altimeter are being neglected, allowing the helicopter to pitch down or the collective to drop excessively during the pedal input, causing the descent. The fix involves: (1) training the student to make attitude and rotor RPM recovery the first reflexive response before ANY instrument analysis — attitude, then altitude, then systems; (2) practicing a rapid scan cross-check that returns to the AI within 2–3 seconds; (3) using sim scenarios where the student verbalizes scan order aloud to make the fixation visible. The student must internalize that in IMC, 150 feet below glidepath at low altitude on an approach is a terrain/obstacle clearance issue, not just a deviation.
questions.follow_up: If this student is about to take a checkride and still shows this pattern in the last training session, are they ready, and what specifically would you document?
questions.follow_up_answer: No, they are not ready. This is a safety-of-flight deficiency — losing 150–200 feet below minimums in IMC during an emergency is not a minor deviation. I would document the specific unsatisfactory performance area in the training record, note the pattern and the sessions where it appeared, and withhold the endorsement until the pattern is corrected and demonstrated stable for at least two consecutive sessions. Under 14 CFR 61.39, the endorsement requires that I have found the applicant competent to pass the test; I cannot in good conscience sign off a student who loses altitude control in a simulated OEI approach. I would also consider whether this is a training methodology issue and change the approach — perhaps reducing the complexity of the scenario first, then building back up.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11, Chapter 13; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5; 14 CFR 61.39

questions.question: A multiengine helicopter has Category A performance capability, and the crew is flying an instrument approach with a published OEI missed approach procedure. At the critical decision point (CDP) during the approach, an engine fails. The pilot maintains positive control but the surviving engine immediately hits its OEI torque limit. What are the compounding risk factors in this specific moment, and what control discipline is required to avoid a secondary hazard?
questions.answer: At the CDP on a Category A approach, the pilot has the option to continue the approach to landing or execute the OEI missed approach — but both paths require the aircraft to stay within its performance envelope. The compounding risk factors at this moment include: (1) the surviving engine is already at torque limit, leaving zero margin for any collective increase; (2) any additional collective demand — such as flaring aggressively, attempting to arrest a sink rate, or reacting to a wind shear — could cause rotor RPM decay; (3) in IMC, the pilot cannot assess the visual environment to make a rapid land-or-go decision, adding cognitive load; (4) the transition from approach power to missed approach climb power puts peak demand on the engine precisely when it is most vulnerable. Control discipline required: hold collective at or below the published OEI torque limit regardless of sink rate temptation; use cyclic to manage attitude and airspeed to remain in the safe performance corridor; commit to the procedure (continue or go missed) without hesitation — indecision means exceeding the performance envelope. If rotor RPM begins to decay with the engine at limit, the only correct response is to lower collective and accept a higher sink rate rather than overtorque and lose rotor control.
questions.follow_up: If the aircraft's Category A performance chart shows the OEI missed approach climb rate at maximum gross weight barely meets the obstacle clearance gradient for this specific approach — say, 200 FPM required and the chart shows 210 FPM available at ISA — what additional real-world factors could erase that 10 FPM margin, and how should the crew have accounted for this before starting the approach?
questions.follow_up_answer: Real-world factors that could erase or exceed that 10 FPM margin include: temperatures above ISA (hot day reduces engine power output and reduces density altitude performance), pressure altitude higher than the chart reference, aircraft weight slightly over the chart reference due to fuel burn calculation errors or passenger weight estimates, engine performance degradation due to compressor fouling or normal wear (engines rarely perform exactly at chart values), and wind component — a tailwind on the missed approach track reduces climb gradient over the ground. The crew should have evaluated all of these during preflight planning: compute density altitude, use the correct weight, apply any engine power deterioration factor if known, and identify whether the published OEI missed approach gradient can actually be achieved under current conditions. If the margin is this thin, the crew should have selected an approach to an airport where single-engine performance provides adequate margin, or delayed the approach until conditions improved. This is exactly the risk management analysis required before committing to an instrument approach in IMC in a multiengine helicopter — Category A certification gives you options, but only if you plan to the actual performance numbers, not the chart maximums.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; AC 29-2C (Category A performance); applicable RFM OEI performance charts; 14 CFR Part 27/29

questions.question: When flying an instrument approach with one engine inoperative, what does 'best performance configuration' generally mean in terms of flight control inputs for a multiengine helicopter?
questions.answer: Best performance configuration means the pilot uses flight control inputs and aircraft configuration (such as airspeed, collective position, and any applicable checklists like feathering a failed engine or adjusting bleed air/generators) to achieve the optimal lift-to-drag ratio and maintain rotor RPM within limits. This typically involves flying the manufacturer-specified Vy or single-engine best rate-of-climb airspeed, keeping the remaining engine(s) at appropriate power settings, and reducing unnecessary drag. The specific configuration is always dictated by the RFM/POH for the aircraft type.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; applicable Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) for specific aircraft

questions.question: On a multiengine helicopter, why is it important to consult the RFM when configuring the helicopter after an engine failure during an instrument approach rather than relying on memory alone?
questions.answer: Different multiengine helicopter models have significantly different performance characteristics, power-matching systems, rotor systems, and OEI procedures. The RFM provides the manufacturer's tested and approved airspeeds, power settings, and control inputs for the specific aircraft. Using generic or recalled procedures could result in operating outside approved limits, degraded performance, rotor RPM exceedance or decay, or loss of control. The RFM is the authoritative source for all emergency and abnormal configurations.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 27.1585 / 29.1585 (Rotorcraft Flight Manual requirements); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: What is the purpose of maintaining the manufacturer-recommended airspeed during an OEI instrument approach, and what happens to performance if you fly significantly slower?
questions.answer: The manufacturer-recommended OEI airspeed is calculated to provide the best balance of lift, drag, and available power from the operating engine(s). Flying at this speed maximizes the helicopter's ability to maintain altitude or minimize descent rate. Flying significantly slower increases induced drag and power required, which can overload the remaining engine, cause rotor RPM decay, and reduce the helicopter's ability to arrest a descent or execute a missed approach — potentially leading to an uncontrolled descent below minimums.

questions.question: You are flying an ILS approach to minimums in a twin-engine helicopter when you lose one engine at the final approach fix. You complete the engine failure checklist and the operating engine is at its OEI power limit. Describe how you would configure your flight controls and the helicopter to continue the approach safely.
questions.answer: First, apply the OEI emergency checklist — confirm the failed engine is identified, secure it per the RFM (or leave in autorotation if directed), and verify the operating engine is within OEI time limits. Adjust cyclic to maintain the manufacturer-specified OEI approach airspeed (typically Vy or published OEI approach speed), use pedals to trim out yaw from asymmetric torque, and set collective to achieve the required descent gradient while keeping the operating engine at or below OEI power limits. Maintain instrument scan especially on torque, rotor RPM, and airspeed. Do not attempt to steepen the approach or slow below published minimums airspeed — if you cannot maintain the glideslope and airspeed simultaneously within power limits, execute the missed approach immediately.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter on Instrument Approaches; applicable RFM

questions.question: During an OEI instrument approach in IMC, you notice the operating engine is approaching its OEI maximum continuous power (MCP) limit but you are still above MDA with the helicopter slightly high on the glidepath. How do you use your flight controls to correct back to glidepath without exceeding engine limits?
questions.answer: Do not simply lower collective to descend if the engine is already near MCP — first, consider increasing airspeed slightly (within approved range) to reduce induced power required, which may allow a gentle collective reduction without spiking above the power limit. Use cyclic forward incrementally to allow airspeed to increase, then use a small collective reduction to come back down to the glidepath. Monitor torque and turbine temperature continuously. If you cannot get back on glidepath without exceeding engine limits or compromising airspeed, initiate the missed approach — do not descend below MDA without the required visual references regardless of glidepath position.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Approaches chapter; applicable RFM

questions.question: You are conducting a simulated OEI instrument approach for training and your instructor says 'maintain best performance.' You are flying a twin-engine helicopter with both pilots and 200 lbs of equipment on board. What specific flight control and configuration steps do you take to optimize performance for this approach?
questions.answer: Steps include: (1) Establish the RFM-published OEI approach airspeed on cyclic — typically the single-engine best rate-of-climb or published OEI approach speed; (2) Set collective to maintain the approach glidepath while keeping the simulated operating engine within OEI power limits; (3) Use anti-torque pedals to trim coordinated flight (ball centered or as directed by RFM for OEI trim); (4) If applicable, shut down non-essential electrical loads to reduce demand on the operating engine's generators; (5) Verify bleed air, environmental systems, and other engine-driven accessories are configured per the OEI checklist to reduce load; (6) Configure landing gear (if applicable) at the appropriate point per RFM to minimize drag until committed to landing. All steps reference the specific aircraft's RFM.

questions.question: During an OEI ILS approach, the operating engine is at OEI power and you are established on course and glideslope. As you pass through 300 feet AGL in IMC, a yaw oscillation begins that you cannot immediately suppress with pedal inputs. What does this indicate, and how do you respond with flight controls to maintain best performance and prevent loss of control?
questions.answer: Uncommanded yaw oscillation during OEI at high power on approach could indicate loss of tail rotor effectiveness (LTE), tail rotor damage or failure, or a dynamic control issue. Immediate response: do not fight it with large opposing pedal inputs, which can aggravate the situation. Apply pedal in the direction of rotation to reduce the yaw rate, lower collective to reduce torque load (reducing the demand on the tail rotor), and adjust cyclic to maintain controlled airspeed. If yaw cannot be controlled, execute the manufacturer's antitorque failure procedure immediately — which may require a running landing or autorotation depending on the aircraft and available power. At 300 feet AGL in IMC, the priority is preventing blade stall and rotor damage while flying toward terrain clearance. Declare emergency with ATC.
questions.follow_up: If you lower collective to arrest the yaw and the rotor RPM begins to decay, what is your priority — controlling the yaw or recovering rotor RPM, and why?
questions.follow_up_answer: Rotor RPM recovery takes priority. Without adequate rotor RPM, the helicopter loses the ability to generate lift regardless of yaw control — a rotor stall in a helicopter is not recoverable, and the aircraft will lose lift entirely. Raise collective only as needed to arrest RPM decay while simultaneously attempting to manage yaw. If RPM continues to fall below limits, the situation becomes unsurvivable regardless of yaw control; therefore maintaining rotor RPM in the green arc is the primary flight parameter. This is consistent with FAA-H-8083-21B which states 'rotor stalls in helicopters are not recoverable; early recognition of low RPM condition is imperative.'
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; applicable RFM antitorque failure procedures

questions.question: You are on an OEI RNAV approach with the helicopter configured per the RFM. At the missed approach point in IMC, you do not have the required visual references. As you apply power for the missed approach on one engine, the operating engine exceeds its OEI 2.5-minute time limit during the climb. How do you manage flight controls and configuration to balance performance and engine protection, and what are the consequences of exceeding the time limit?
questions.answer: At the MAP, initiate the missed approach immediately regardless of engine time limits — safety of flight is the priority. Apply OEI maximum continuous power (MCP) rather than 2.5-minute power if the time limit has been reached, accepting a reduced climb performance. Use cyclic to establish the published missed approach climb airspeed (typically Vx or Vy OEI), set collective at MCP, and trim coordinated flight with pedals. Reduce drag by retracting gear (if applicable) at a safe altitude. Advise ATC of the engine situation and declare an emergency. Exceeding the OEI 2.5-minute time limit risks catastrophic engine failure, hot section damage, turbine blade shedding, and compressor stall — the engine may fail entirely. The aircraft will require mandatory inspection and likely hot section replacement. However, the RFM may authorize exceeding limits in an actual emergency to save the aircraft — the pilot must exercise judgment and document the exceedance. The key takeaway is that during a real emergency, preserving the aircraft and occupants outweighs engine preservation, but the pilot must immediately manage power back to MCP as soon as climb performance allows.
questions.follow_up: After landing safely following that OEI missed approach where the engine exceeded its 2.5-minute limit, what are your regulatory obligations before flying that helicopter again?
questions.follow_up_answer: The pilot must make an entry in the aircraft maintenance logbook documenting the engine exceedance including the duration and power level exceeded, per 14 CFR 91.417 (maintenance record requirements). The helicopter is grounded — it cannot be returned to service until an FAA-certificated mechanic or repair station inspects the engine in accordance with the manufacturer's maintenance manual (which typically mandates a mandatory inspection or replacement of hot section components after a time-limit exceedance). The pilot should also file an ASRS (NASA) report if they feel appropriate and notify the operator. The aircraft is not airworthy until the maintenance action is complete and a return-to-service entry is made per 14 CFR 43.9.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.417; 14 CFR 43.9; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; applicable RFM engine limits section

questions.question: During an instrument approach with a simulated engine failure, when should you reference the emergency checklist — before, during, or after the critical phase of flight?
questions.answer: The manufacturer's emergency procedures are divided into memory items (immediate action items) and checklist items. Memory items must be completed immediately from recall during the critical phase. The written checklist is then referenced to confirm all steps were completed correctly once the helicopter is in a stabilized or controlled state. You never defer memory items to the checklist, but you never skip the checklist verification either.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; aircraft-specific RFM/POH Emergency Procedures section

questions.question: What is the general difference between an emergency checklist and an abnormal checklist in the context of a multiengine helicopter engine failure on approach?
questions.answer: An emergency checklist covers situations that require immediate action to prevent loss of life or the aircraft — such as an engine failure — and typically begins with bold-faced or capitalized memory items that must be performed without reference to written material. An abnormal checklist covers situations that are outside normal operations but do not require immediate action, such as a single generator failure. For an engine failure on approach, the emergency checklist is the applicable reference.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; aircraft RFM/POH Emergency vs. Abnormal Procedures sections

questions.question: After securing a failed engine during a single-engine instrument approach, what general category of checklist item should a pilot complete to address the inoperative engine's associated systems?
questions.answer: After the immediate action memory items — such as identifying the failed engine, reducing power or shutting down as directed, and maintaining aircraft control — the pilot should reference the engine shutdown or engine failure in-flight checklist. This typically includes items such as confirming the fuel condition lever or fuel shutoff, generator offline, crossfeed as required, and monitoring single-engine performance limits. The exact steps are aircraft-specific per the RFM/POH.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; aircraft-specific RFM/POH

questions.question: You are flying a multiengine helicopter on an ILS approach in IMC at 1,200 feet AGL when you receive a low oil pressure indication on the number two engine. At what point do you complete the emergency checklist, and how do you manage workload so the checklist doesn't compromise aircraft control or approach continuity?
questions.answer: At 1,200 feet AGL in IMC you still have time to assess the situation. First, maintain aircraft control and instrument scan. If the indication requires immediate action per your RFM, accomplish memory items first. Use crew resource management principles — if flying single pilot, prioritize aviate, navigate, communicate. After stabilizing the aircraft and confirming you are on profile, reference the written checklist. Consider whether continuing the approach is safe given single-engine performance margins. If workload is too high to safely complete the checklist and fly the approach simultaneously, execute the missed approach, level off, then complete the checklist in a controlled environment before attempting another approach.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapters 11 and 13; aircraft RFM/POH; 14 CFR 91.3

questions.question: During a simulated engine failure on an instrument approach, you notice you already briefed the approach with the single-engine missed approach procedure. How does having that briefing completed in advance support proper emergency checklist execution?
questions.answer: Pre-briefing the single-engine missed approach reduces cognitive workload at the critical moment of the failure, allowing the pilot to allocate mental resources to the emergency checklist execution rather than re-computing the missed approach route. This is consistent with good ADM and SRM practice — by loading the decision in advance, the pilot avoids the hazardous 'probably' thinking and follows a known, planned course of action. The reduced workload also reduces the risk of checklist errors or omissions, which is especially important when managing single-engine performance margins on approach.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 13 (ADM/SRM); FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Flying Handbook, Chapter on Instrument Approaches

questions.question: You are on a RNAV approach in IMC and experience a simulated engine failure just as you pass the final approach fix. You complete the memory items but the aircraft has drifted left of course. Describe how you prioritize completing the emergency checklist versus regaining course guidance.
questions.answer: Aircraft control and obstacle clearance always take priority. At the FAF in IMC with a known engine failure, the first action is to aviate — correct the deviation and maintain the published MDA/DA and course. Once back on profile and stabilized, complete the written checklist. If the workload prevents safe continuation of the approach — particularly if single-engine performance margins are tight and the deviation is significant — execute the missed approach immediately. The missed approach provides guaranteed obstacle clearance; attempting to simultaneously complete a checklist and correct a course deviation below the FAF introduces compounding risk. Resume the checklist after the missed approach is complete and the aircraft is in a safe, stable configuration.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Flying Handbook, Instrument Approaches and Minimums; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and 13; 14 CFR 91.175

questions.question: If you complete the manufacturer's emergency checklist after an engine failure on approach and later discover you performed a step out of sequence — for example, you secured the wrong engine fuel supply momentarily before correcting — what are the implications, and what is your obligation as pilot-in-command?
questions.answer: Performing an out-of-sequence or incorrect checklist step during an engine failure could have safety-of-flight implications, including inadvertent fuel interruption to the operating engine. As PIC under 14 CFR 91.3, you are responsible for the safe operation of the aircraft. You must immediately assess whether the operating engine was affected and confirm it is operating normally. After landing, a maintenance inspection is required before further flight if there is any doubt about engine or fuel system integrity. Additionally, if an incident or accident resulted, you may have reporting obligations under 14 CFR 830 (NTSB). This scenario underscores why the checklist must be performed methodically, with callouts, and why challenge-response technique exists.
questions.follow_up: What specific technique can a single-pilot IFR helicopter pilot use to reduce the chance of securing the wrong engine when completing an emergency checklist in IMC?
questions.follow_up_answer: A key technique is the 'confirm before shutting down' drill — physically placing your hand on the control for the identified engine (e.g., fuel condition lever or engine power lever) and verbally confirming the failed engine indication matches the control you are about to actuate before moving it. Some operators use the mnemonic 'identify, confirm, close' or similar flows. Cross-checking two independent failure indications (e.g., N1 decay AND low oil pressure on the same engine) before shutting down adds another layer of protection. This is reinforced in type-specific training and the RFM emergency procedures.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3; 14 CFR Part 830; FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; aircraft-specific RFM/POH

questions.question: At decision altitude on an ILS approach during a simulated engine failure scenario, the emergency checklist is still in progress and you do not have the required visual references. What is the correct action, and does the incomplete checklist change the missed approach procedure you must fly?
questions.answer: If visual references are not established at DA, you must execute the missed approach immediately per 14 CFR 91.175, regardless of checklist status. The incomplete checklist does not alter the published missed approach procedure — you fly the missed approach as charted (or as assigned by ATC) to ensure obstacle clearance. Once established on the missed approach and in a stable configuration, resume the checklist. However, single-engine missed approach performance must be confirmed adequate before continuing the approach; if the aircraft cannot meet published climb gradient on one engine, diverting to a suitable alternate or executing an emergency landing may be required. The checklist is a means to maintain safety — it never overrides the requirement to fly the aircraft safely.
questions.follow_up: If inoperative components related to the failed engine — such as a generator — would require higher instrument approach minimums per the Terminal Procedures Publication Inoperative Components Table, and you did not account for this before the approach, what are your options at this point?
questions.follow_up_answer: If you are already on the missed approach with the aircraft in a safe configuration, you must reassess whether you can legally and safely fly another approach at the higher minimums required by the inoperative components table. If the weather is at or above the revised minimums, you may elect to fly another approach with the appropriate MDA/DA adjustment. If weather is below the revised minimums, you cannot legally continue instrument approaches to that runway and must divert to an alternate where weather is at or above minimums accounting for all inoperative components. This illustrates why the pre-approach brief for a single-engine scenario should include confirming approach minimums based on actual aircraft equipment status.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175; FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Flying Handbook, Instrument Approaches and Minimums; TPP Inoperative Components Table; 14 CFR 91.187

questions.question: When flying a multiengine helicopter with one engine inoperative (OEI), what does the term 'OEI operating limitations' refer to, and where do you find them for your specific aircraft?
questions.answer: OEI operating limitations are the performance and operational boundaries published by the manufacturer for single-engine flight, including maximum continuous power (MCP), time-limited power ratings (such as 2.5-minute or 30-minute OEI power), OEI airspeed ranges, and maximum gross weight limits. These limitations are found in the FAA-approved Rotorcraft Flight Manual (RFM) for the specific helicopter, typically in the Limitations section and supported by the Performance section. Exceeding these limits can result in engine damage, structural failure, or loss of control.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 27.1585 / 14 CFR 29.1585; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Aircraft RFM Limitations Section

questions.question: What is the difference between an OEI maximum continuous power (MCP) rating and a time-limited OEI power rating such as a 30-minute or 2.5-minute rating on a multiengine helicopter?
questions.answer: OEI Maximum Continuous Power (MCP) is the highest power level the operating engine can sustain indefinitely following an engine failure without time restriction, subject to torque, temperature, and RPM limits. Time-limited OEI ratings — such as 30-minute or 2.5-minute ratings — allow the remaining engine to produce higher power levels than MCP, but only for the specified duration to handle the critical period immediately after engine failure (such as takeoff or missed approach). Exceeding the time limit at these elevated power settings can cause engine overtemperature, accelerated wear, or failure. The pilot must monitor the clock and engine instruments and reduce power to MCP before the time limit expires.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 29.45; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Aircraft RFM Limitations Section

questions.question: During an instrument approach with one engine inoperative, which flight instruments and engine instrument indications do you monitor to confirm you are staying within OEI operating limitations?
questions.answer: The pilot must cross-monitor: (1) Engine instruments on the operating engine — torque (%), turbine temperature (TOT/TGT/ITT), N1/N2 RPM, and fuel flow — to ensure none exceed OEI limits published in the RFM. (2) Rotor RPM (Nr) to confirm it remains in the normal operating range, as OEI power demands and pilot control inputs can allow Nr to decay. (3) Airspeed indicator, to maintain at or above published OEI minimum speeds (Vtoss, best rate of climb OEI, or instrument approach speeds). (4) OEI time limits if operating on a time-limited power rating. (5) Altitude and vertical speed to ensure the aircraft is performing within expected OEI climb or maintain capability for the approach.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5; Aircraft RFM Limitations and Performance Sections

questions.question: You are flying an ILS approach in IMC with one engine simulated inoperative. On final, you notice torque on the operating engine is creeping toward the OEI limit and your airspeed has decayed 10 knots below the published OEI approach speed. What actions do you take, and what are the consequences of allowing both conditions to continue?
questions.answer: Immediate actions: (1) Increase collective smoothly to arrest the airspeed decay, which requires simultaneously adding more anti-torque pedal input to maintain coordinated flight. (2) Adjust cyclic to establish and hold the published OEI approach airspeed — typically Vtoss or a manufacturer-specified minimum approach speed. (3) Monitor torque carefully; if approaching the OEI torque limit, recognize you may be at or near the aircraft's performance ceiling for this condition — weight, density altitude, and configuration must be assessed. If torque must exceed the limit to maintain safe flight, a go-around/missed approach must be initiated immediately while still above DA/DH. Consequences of continued airspeed decay: risk of entering the height-velocity (H-V) avoid curve on short final, loss of translational lift, and potential rotor RPM decay leading to unrecoverable low-Nr condition. Consequences of exceeding torque limit: engine damage, possible catastrophic failure of the operating engine, leaving the aircraft with no power source.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Aircraft RFM Limitations and Performance; 14 CFR 29.67

questions.question: You are on an OEI instrument approach and reach the missed approach point without acquiring visual references. Your operating engine has been on the 30-minute OEI power rating and you have 8 minutes remaining on that limit. Describe how you manage OEI power limitations during the missed approach climb and what you do if the time limit expires before reaching a safe altitude.
questions.answer: At the MAP, initiate the missed approach by applying power as required per the RFM missed approach climb procedure, which may initially use the time-limited OEI rating for obstacle clearance. Simultaneously start or confirm the OEI time limit clock. Fly the published missed approach procedure, climbing to the missed approach altitude while monitoring torque, TOT/TGT/ITT, and Nr. With 8 minutes remaining: (1) Prioritize climbing to the published missed approach altitude and proceeding to the holding fix. (2) If the 30-minute limit expires before reaching a safe altitude, reduce power to OEI MCP rating — expect some reduction in climb performance and compensate with airspeed adjustments. (3) If MCP is insufficient to maintain altitude with acceptable control, declare an emergency, communicate with ATC, and plan for an immediate landing at the nearest suitable area. Under no circumstances should the time limit be exceeded to avoid a potential engine failure — a controlled descent under MCP is preferable to losing the operating engine entirely.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Aircraft RFM Emergency and Limitations Sections; 14 CFR 91.3

questions.question: During a simulated OEI instrument approach, density altitude is higher than standard due to a hot, high-elevation airport. How does this affect your ability to stay within OEI operating limitations, and what specific technique adjustments do you make on the approach?
questions.answer: High density altitude reduces available engine power output and rotor efficiency. On an OEI approach, this means: (1) The operating engine may reach its torque or temperature limits at a lower collective pitch than it would in standard conditions — leaving less power margin for corrections or go-around. (2) OEI hover or low-speed performance may be marginal or unavailable, requiring a run-on or roll-on landing rather than a zero-ground-speed touchdown. Technique adjustments: (1) Calculate OEI performance from the RFM charts using actual density altitude before the approach — confirm whether a go-around is viable. (2) Fly at the upper end of the published OEI approach airspeed range to maximize energy and rotor efficiency. (3) Plan a shallow approach profile if performance data supports it, reducing the power required. (4) Establish a clear plan to transition to a roll-on landing if hover capability is not available at the destination. (5) Monitor engine instruments more frequently, as the engine is operating closer to its thermal limits under these conditions.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapters 11 and 9 (Performance); Aircraft RFM OEI Performance Charts

questions.question: During an OEI ILS approach in IMC, you break out at minimums and simultaneously notice that the operating engine's torque has exceeded the OEI limit by 5% for approximately 20 seconds while you were heads-down transitioning to visual. You complete the landing uneventfully. What are your regulatory and airworthiness obligations after landing, and how does this event affect your next flight?
questions.answer: An OEI torque exceedance is a maintenance-critical event. Obligations after landing: (1) The aircraft must be removed from service immediately — it is not airworthy until inspected per the RFM and engine manufacturer's maintenance manual. Operating an engine beyond published limits constitutes operating in an unairworthy condition in violation of 14 CFR 91.7. (2) A maintenance logbook entry must be made documenting the exceedance, including the magnitude (5% over limit), duration (approximately 20 seconds), and flight conditions. This is required under 14 CFR 91.417. (3) The engine manufacturer's overtemperature/overtorque inspection procedure must be completed before the next flight — this typically involves a borescope inspection, review of engine trend data, and possibly power assurance checks. (4) If the exceedance is beyond a certain threshold defined by the manufacturer, an engine teardown inspection may be required. (5) Depending on the operator's operations specifications (for Part 135 operators), the incident may require notification to the company director of maintenance and possibly the FAA. The next flight cannot occur until an A&P (or IA if required) signs off the aircraft as airworthy following the appropriate inspection.
questions.follow_up: What if you had not noticed the exceedance during the flight and only discovered it later reviewing engine trend monitoring data — does that change your obligations, and is there any regulatory reporting requirement to the FAA?
questions.follow_up_answer: The airworthiness obligation is identical regardless of when the exceedance is discovered — the aircraft must be grounded and inspected before the next flight once the event is known. The maintenance entry is still required under 14 CFR 91.417. Regarding FAA reporting: an overtorque alone does not automatically trigger a mandatory report under 14 CFR Part 830 (NTSB jurisdiction) unless it resulted in an accident or incident as defined. However, if the exceedance caused damage discovered during inspection — such as hot section damage or component failure — it may rise to the level of an incident requiring NTSB notification under 49 CFR 830.5. Additionally, the operator may voluntarily file an Aviation Safety Hotline report or NASA ASRS report. For Part 135 operators, company reporting requirements to the POI may apply independently of FAA Part 830 obligations.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.7; 14 CFR 91.417; 49 CFR Part 830; Aircraft RFM Limitations; Engine Manufacturer Maintenance Manual

questions.question: You are conducting an OEI instrument approach in IMC and, at 500 feet AGL on final, rotor RPM begins to decay below the lower limit of the normal range despite being at what appears to be the correct collective position and airspeed. The operating engine instruments are all within OEI limits. What is causing this, and what is your precise control response to recover Nr while maintaining aircraft control on instruments?
questions.answer: Nr decay below normal range in this scenario, with engine instruments within OEI limits, is most likely caused by one or more of the following: (1) Airspeed has decayed below translational lift speed, increasing induced flow and collective demand beyond what the single engine can sustain at the current power setting without Nr decay. (2) The collective has been unconsciously raised (a common instrument scan fixation error), increasing disk loading beyond OEI power available. (3) The OEI power available is at its margin for current weight and density altitude conditions. Recovery technique (precise sequence): (1) Immediately lower collective — this is the priority response to Nr decay; reducing collective reduces disk drag and allows the rotor system to accelerate back toward normal Nr. This is consistent with FAA-H-8083-21B guidance that lowering collective is the immediate action to arrest Nr decay. (2) Simultaneously apply forward cyclic to accelerate toward or above effective translational lift speed — this reduces induced flow and collective demand, further helping Nr recover. (3) Maintain instrument scan — do not fixate on Nr gauge; crosscheck attitude, airspeed, and altitude continuously. (4) If Nr recovers and airspeed increases, smoothly raise collective to arrest altitude loss and re-establish the approach profile. (5) If Nr continues to decay despite these inputs, execute a missed approach immediately — do not attempt to reach the runway with decaying Nr, as rotor stall is non-recoverable. The Helicopter Flying Handbook notes that rotor stall in helicopters is not recoverable; early recognition is imperative.
questions.follow_up: If you lower collective to recover Nr but you are now below MDA with the runway not yet in sight and altitude loss is occurring, what do you do and how do you prioritize rotor RPM recovery versus obstacle clearance?
questions.follow_up_answer: Rotor RPM recovery is the absolute priority — an unrecoverable Nr decay leads to loss of all rotor lift and is fatal. A controlled descent under low but recoverable Nr is survivable; a rotor stall is not. Regulatory and procedural guidance: You are already committed to executing a missed approach the moment you cannot maintain the approach profile within OEI limitations, per instrument approach procedure requirements that the pilot must execute the missed approach when visual references are not established by the MAP or when the approach cannot be continued. If Nr is in decay, the missed approach must begin immediately — lower collective to recover Nr, accept the altitude loss momentarily, then as Nr enters the normal range, apply collective smoothly to arrest descent and climb. Communicate the emergency to ATC. 14 CFR 91.3 grants the pilot in command authority to deviate from any rule to the extent necessary to meet the emergency. If terrain contact is imminent, the pilot must attempt to establish the best possible autorotative or OEI forced landing.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; 14 CFR 91.3; Instrument Approach Procedure requirements per 14 CFR 91.175

questions.question: During a simulated single-engine instrument approach, which engine instruments should you be monitoring on the operating engine, and what are you looking for?
questions.answer: On the operating engine, you must continuously monitor torque (or power setting), turbine temperature (TOT/TGT/ITT), N1/N2 RPM, fuel flow, and oil pressure/temperature. You are looking for any exceedance of operating limits, signs of overtorque or overtemperature from the increased demand placed on the remaining engine, and any trend toward an abnormal indication that could signal a developing problem on your only remaining powerplant.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; applicable RFM for the specific helicopter

questions.question: Why is torque management especially critical on the operating engine during a single-engine instrument approach compared to a normal two-engine approach?
questions.answer: During a single-engine approach, the one operating engine is carrying the entire power demand that would normally be shared between two engines. This significantly increases the torque required for any given maneuver, particularly during go-around or missed approach. The engine is operating much closer to its maximum continuous or single-engine service ceiling limits, meaning there is far less margin before an overtorque or overtemperature exceedance occurs. Constant monitoring and careful collective management are required to avoid exceeding manufacturer-published limits.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; applicable Rotorcraft Flight Manual

questions.question: What helicopter system, beyond the engine instruments, should you also monitor during a single-engine instrument approach, and why?
questions.answer: In addition to engine instruments, you must monitor the electrical system (bus voltage, generator load), hydraulic system (pressure and warning lights if equipped), rotor RPM (Nr), fuel quantity and balance, and any associated caution/warning annunciators. With one engine inoperative, the remaining engine's accessories are carrying a greater load, and certain systems such as generators or hydraulic pumps that may be engine-driven could be affected. Monitoring all systems ensures a secondary failure does not go undetected during an already high-workload instrument approach.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5

questions.question: You are on a single-engine ILS approach at 500 feet AGL in IMC and notice the operating engine's turbine temperature is approaching the maximum continuous limit. What adjustments do you make and how does this affect your approach management?
questions.answer: Immediately reduce collective slightly to lower the power demand and bring the temperature back within limits, while simultaneously adjusting cyclic to maintain approach profile and airspeed. If collective reduction causes you to drop below the glideslope or lose airspeed to an unsafe value, you must consider whether a go-around is the safer option before getting further committed at lower altitude. Document the exceedance if it occurred for maintenance. This situation also highlights the need to have pre-briefed single-engine go-around power settings and limits — if maintaining the approach requires exceeding engine limits, the approach must be discontinued.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapters 11 and 13; applicable RFM limitations section

questions.question: During a simulated single-engine instrument approach in actual IMC, you notice the hydraulic pressure caution light illuminates on the operating engine's hydraulic system. Walk me through how you manage this while continuing to monitor the engine and fly the approach.
questions.answer: Immediately acknowledge the caution light and cross-check the hydraulic pressure gauge if available. Refer to the abnormal checklist for the specific aircraft. If hydraulic pressure is confirmed low, flight control forces will increase — in some helicopters this can make precise attitude control very difficult, particularly on approach. Workload must be managed carefully: maintain aircraft control on instruments first, then address the abnormal procedure. If the checklist directs landing as soon as possible, evaluate whether breaking off the approach and declaring an emergency to obtain the most direct routing to landing is appropriate. The key principle is aviate, navigate, communicate — do not allow the secondary failure to distract you from maintaining aircraft control and approach parameters.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5; applicable RFM abnormal procedures

questions.question: How does fuel management on a twin-engine helicopter become more demanding during a prolonged single-engine instrument approach sequence, and what specific adjustments might you need to make?
questions.answer: The operating engine is consuming significantly more fuel than it would under normal two-engine operations because it is producing the total required power alone. On an extended approach sequence with holds or radar vectors, fuel burn rate is higher than planned. The pilot must monitor fuel quantity more frequently, cross-check fuel flow against expected burn, and consider fuel balance between tanks if the aircraft has an interconnect or crossfeed system. If one engine failed due to a fuel-related cause (e.g., fuel starvation from an imbalanced system), the remaining engine's fuel supply must be positively confirmed. Adjustments may include selecting crossfeed, balancing tanks, or advising ATC of fuel emergency if minimums are being approached.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapter 11; applicable RFM fuel system section

questions.question: You are conducting a single-engine ILS approach in IMC and, just inside the FAF at 1,200 feet AGL, the operating engine's oil pressure drops into the caution range. The approach is fully established with one mile visibility reported at the field. How do you prioritize your actions, what adjustments do you make to the engine, and at what point — if any — do you commit to landing versus executing a missed approach?
questions.answer: First priority is aircraft control — maintain the approach parameters while immediately cross-checking oil pressure and oil temperature to determine whether the indication is a transient or a developing failure. If oil temperature is also rising, this indicates genuine lubrication loss and engine failure may be imminent. Declare an emergency with ATC immediately to ensure priority handling. If the engine is still producing power and the field is achievable, continuing to the lowest practical minimums may be the best option — landing short of a full engine failure is better than a missed approach that could result in engine seizure in IMC. However, the RFM limitations for low oil pressure must be consulted during training to understand how much time is available. The key adjustment is to reduce collective to minimum power required to maintain approach, reducing engine stress. If oil temperature exceeds limits or power begins to decay, the engine may need to be secured and autorotation initiated — at 1,200 AGL in IMC, this is an extremely critical situation requiring immediate ATC coordination and the best available landing option.
questions.follow_up: If you had to execute a missed approach with the oil pressure now in the red range, what is your primary concern about the operating engine and how does that change your missed approach execution compared to a normal single-engine go-around?
questions.follow_up_answer: The primary concern is that the engine may seize or lose power at any moment during the go-around, which requires maximum collective input and the highest power demand — precisely the condition that would accelerate the failure. The missed approach must be executed with the minimum power necessary to achieve a positive climb and obstacle clearance, avoiding aggressive collective pulls. The pilot must be prepared for complete power loss immediately and ensure the helicopter is positioned for the best available autorotation landing area throughout the climb. ATC should be advised of the emergency and a landing should be achieved as quickly as possible after breaking out of the approach environment — dragging out the missed approach to fly the full published procedure is not appropriate given the imminent engine failure risk.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapters 11 and 13; FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Approaches chapter; applicable RFM emergency procedures

questions.question: During a single-engine practice instrument approach in VMC, your student consistently fixates on the flight instruments and stops cross-checking engine gauges after passing the FAF. As their instructor or as an examiner evaluating this, why is this fixation dangerous in actual single-engine IMC operations, and what scenario would you use to make this point?
questions.answer: Instrument fixation during the most demanding phase of a single-engine approach is dangerous because the operating engine is under maximum continuous stress just as the pilot's cognitive workload peaks. A developing engine problem — rising TOT, dropping oil pressure, increasing torque fluctuation — can go undetected for critical seconds or even minutes if the pilot abandons the engine scan. The failure may then manifest as sudden power loss at the worst possible moment: below MDA, slow airspeed, and close to terrain in IMC. A compelling training scenario to make this point: brief the student that during the next approach a simulated engine anomaly will be introduced at some point inside the FAF. Cover one or two engine gauges with sticky notes after the approach begins so the student realizes — only when asked to state current TOT — that they have no idea what the engine has been doing for the last two minutes. This demonstrates that monitoring cannot be suspended simply because the approach environment demands attention; rather, an efficient instrument scan must incorporate engine gauges as an integrated part of the overall scan, not an afterthought.
questions.follow_up: How would you structure the instrument scan for a multiengine helicopter pilot on a single-engine ILS approach so that engine monitoring is incorporated without sacrificing approach precision?
questions.follow_up_answer: The scan should be organized in a disciplined radial pattern anchored on the primary flight instruments — attitude indicator, altimeter, airspeed, and course deviation indicator — with periodic excursions to the engine cluster. A practical structure is to complete a full approach scan cycle every 10–15 seconds, with a deliberate glance at torque, TOT, and Nr included in every second or third scan cycle. Using the autopilot where authorized can reduce workload and allow more frequent engine monitoring. Verbalization helps: calling out engine values briefly during lower-workload segments (level segments, early approach) builds the habit so it carries through the high-workload final approach segment. The goal is that engine monitoring becomes part of muscle memory, not a separate cognitive task that gets dropped when the workload rises.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook, Chapters 11 and 13; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5 (instrument scanning techniques)

questions.question: When you receive an ATC approach clearance that includes 'cleared ILS runway 24, maintain 3,000 until established,' what does 'until established' mean, and what are you established on?
questions.answer: You must maintain the assigned altitude of 3,000 feet MSL until you are established on a published segment of the instrument approach procedure — in this case, the ILS localizer course. 'Established' means you are on the final approach course and within the lateral limits of the approach segment, allowing you to then descend on the glideslope or follow published step-down altitudes. You may not descend below 3,000 feet until that condition is met.

questions.question: What is the correct phraseology you should use when requesting an instrument approach clearance from approach control after declaring a simulated engine failure in training?
questions.answer: A proper request would be: '[Facility], [Callsign], request ILS runway [XX] approach, simulated single-engine.' You clearly state your aircraft identification, the specific approach type and runway you are requesting, and any special conditions relevant to your operation. In an actual emergency you would add the nature of the emergency and souls on board. ATC may then issue vectors or a clearance via a published route to the final approach fix.

questions.question: After receiving an approach clearance, ATC issues you a heading of 180 and says 'expect ILS runway 18 approach, vectors to final.' Are you required to fly the published procedure turn?
questions.answer: No. When ATC provides radar vectors to the final approach course, the procedure turn is not authorized. The published 'NoPT' restriction and vectoring instructions both negate the requirement for a procedure turn. You must follow ATC-assigned headings until established on the final approach course, then fly the approach as published from that point forward.

questions.question: You are flying a twin-engine helicopter with one engine failed (simulated) and ATC clears you for the RNAV (GPS) approach but then amends your altitude restriction while you are already established inbound on final. How do you handle this new clearance and what are your priorities at that moment?
questions.answer: You must acknowledge the amended clearance with your callsign, read back the new altitude restriction, and comply with it unless doing so would cause you to descend below a published segment altitude or the DA/MDA before you are authorized to do so. With a simulated engine failure your workload is elevated, so proper SRM and workload management are critical — aviate first (maintain aircraft control with asymmetric power), then navigate (stay on course), then communicate (read back the clearance). If the amended altitude conflicts with published minimums, query ATC immediately: '[Callsign] unable, request clarification — published segment altitude is [X].'

questions.question: You are cleared for the ILS approach and are on final with one engine inoperative (simulated) when ATC instructs you to 'go around, traffic on the runway.' Describe the sequence of actions you take to comply with this ATC instruction.
questions.answer: Immediately acknowledge: '[Callsign], going around.' Then execute the missed approach procedure while managing the single-engine configuration. Apply maximum available power on the operating engine, establish a positive climb attitude, arrest any descent, and follow the published missed approach procedure unless ATC issues different instructions. With only one engine, performance will be reduced — you must reference the helicopter's AFM/POH single-engine missed approach performance data. Maintain close communication with ATC, advise them of the engine-out condition if not already done, and request routing and altitude appropriate for single-engine climb capability. Do not delay acknowledgment or compliance due to cockpit workload.

questions.question: You receive this approach clearance: 'Helicopter 5 Tango Foxtrot, cleared RNAV runway 10 approach, cross DANLO at or above 2,800, circle to land runway 28.' You have one engine inoperative. What factors must you evaluate before accepting and executing this clearance?
questions.answer: Several factors must be evaluated: (1) Crossing restriction — can you cross DANLO at or above 2,800 feet with single-engine performance? Check AFM/POH climb/cruise data for one engine inoperative. (2) Circling — circling minimums are higher than straight-in minimums and require visual maneuvering; in a single-engine condition, the added workload and potential for asymmetric power during the circle increases risk significantly. (3) Weather — ensure ceiling and visibility meet circling minimums, not just straight-in minimums. (4) If unable to comply safely, you should advise ATC: '[Callsign] unable circling, request straight-in runway 10.' ATC must be informed of limitations. Accepting a clearance you cannot safely execute is not permissible under 14 CFR 91.123.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.123; 14 CFR 91.175; AIM 5-4-20; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter on Instrument Approaches

questions.question: You are cleared for an instrument approach with one engine simulated inoperative and you inadvertently read back the wrong final approach fix crossing altitude — you said '1,800' but the clearance was '2,800.' ATC did not catch the error and you begin descending to 1,800 feet. At what point does responsibility shift, and what should you do the moment you realize the error?
questions.answer: The pilot in command bears ultimate responsibility for safe operation and compliance with ATC clearances under 14 CFR 91.123. While ATC has a responsibility to catch readback errors under AIM 4-2-3, an uncorrected readback error does not relieve the pilot of responsibility. The moment you realize the discrepancy, immediately climb back to the correct altitude (2,800) and advise ATC: '[Callsign], correction, readback error — climbing back to 2,800.' Do not wait to see if ATC catches it. This is compounded in a single-engine scenario because the reduced performance margin means deviating below minimum safe altitudes poses an immediate terrain/obstacle threat.
questions.follow_up: If you had already descended to 1,800 feet and ATC then issues an immediate low-altitude alert, what are your obligations and what is the first thing you do?
questions.follow_up_answer: Your first obligation is to aviate — immediately initiate a climb using maximum available single-engine power. Then communicate: acknowledge the alert, state your intentions, and advise ATC of the engine-out condition if not previously communicated. Under 14 CFR 91.3, the PIC has final authority to deviate from any ATC clearance to the extent necessary to meet an emergency — but in this case, the deviation (descending too low) was the error, and the correct response is immediate corrective action. A pilot deviation report may be required if ATC requests one (AIM 7-6-4).

questions.question: During a simulated single-engine instrument approach in actual IMC, you are handed off from approach control to tower, but you lose two-way radio communication before receiving landing clearance. Walk me through exactly how you execute the approach and landing under lost communications procedures.
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.185, in IMC you continue the approach using the last received routing and altitude clearance. Squawk 7600 immediately. If you were already cleared for the approach, continue to fly the full published procedure to the MAP/DA. If you reach the MAP or DA and have the required visual references (one of the ten specified references per 14 CFR 91.175(c)), you may descend and land. You should land as soon as practicable. At a towered airport, watch for light gun signals if below the clouds — a steady green from the tower while on final means cleared to land. Document the communications failure and advise ATC after landing.
questions.follow_up: In this same scenario with one engine inoperative, you reach the DA with only marginal visual references — you can see approach lights but not the runway environment. Can you legally descend below DA?
questions.follow_up_answer: No. Approach lights alone only authorize descent to 100 feet above the touchdown zone elevation — you must see more of the runway environment (threshold, threshold markings, threshold lights, REIL, VASI/PAPI, touchdown zone, touchdown zone markings, or touchdown zone lights) to continue below that point. With one engine inoperative, the consequences of a missed approach and go-around are more serious, but that does not change the legal minimum visual reference requirements under 14 CFR 91.175(c). The correct action is to execute the missed approach at DA if the required references are not established, regardless of single-engine performance concerns.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175(c); 14 CFR 91.185; AIM 6-4-1; FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Approaches chapter

questions.question: During an instrument approach with a simulated engine failure, what are the ACS tolerances you must maintain for altitude, airspeed, and heading?
questions.answer: The ACS requires altitude within ±100 feet of the assigned or target altitude, airspeed within ±10 knots of the selected airspeed, and heading within ±10° of the selected heading. These tolerances apply throughout the approach procedure, not just at specific fixes.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-S-ACS-18 Instrument Helicopter ACS, Task IH.VIII.B.S7

questions.question: Why is maintaining the ±10-knot airspeed tolerance especially critical during a single-engine instrument approach compared to a normal two-engine approach?
questions.answer: With one engine inoperative, the helicopter is operating at reduced power margins. Allowing airspeed to decay beyond ±10 knots below the target approach speed can quickly reduce the safety margin against vortex ring state, loss of tail rotor effectiveness, or an inability to execute a missed approach. Conversely, excessive airspeed reduces your ability to land within the available area and increases workload. The tighter power margin means deviations compound faster than in two-engine flight.

questions.question: Which flight instruments are you primarily relying on to monitor and maintain your ±100-foot altitude tolerance during an IMC approach with a simulated engine failure?
questions.answer: The primary instrument for altitude is the altimeter (static system), with the VSI used to detect and correct trends before altitude deviates beyond ±100 feet. On aircraft equipped with EFIS or an autopilot altitude alerter, those systems can provide additional awareness. The altimeter reads static pressure only; a blocked static system would cause it to freeze at the altitude of the blockage, which is why alternate static source awareness is also important.

questions.question: You are flying a single-engine ILS approach in IMC and notice your altitude is creeping 80 feet high on the glide slope while your airspeed is simultaneously 8 knots fast.
