What is your sequence of control inputs to correct both deviations before they exceed ACS tolerances, and why does the order matter?
questions.answer: First, reduce collective slightly to arrest the altitude trend and simultaneously reduce airspeed — in a helicopter these two are coupled. A reduction in collective will lower both altitude gain and airspeed simultaneously. Follow with a slight forward cyclic adjustment only if needed after collective is stabilized. The order matters because in a single-engine helicopter, abrupt or large collective reductions can cause rapid RPM changes or torque transients on the remaining engine. Small, coordinated inputs prevent compounding the deviations. You must also monitor heading, as asymmetric torque from the power change may push you outside the ±10° heading tolerance if pedal trim is not maintained.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM/SRM); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5; FAA-S-ACS-18 IH.VIII.B.S7

questions.question: During a single-engine instrument approach, you are established on final and your heading drifts 12° off the selected approach course heading. At what point does this heading deviation become not just an ACS bust but also a safety-of-flight concern, and how would you recover without compounding your altitude and airspeed deviations?
questions.answer: The ACS tolerance is ±10°, so a 12° deviation is already a bust. From a safety standpoint, a heading deviation on final also means you are drifting off the approach course centerline, which in IMC could threaten obstacle clearance, since published approach minimums assume you are tracking the centerline. Recovery requires a shallow coordinated bank — typically no more than standard rate — to return to the selected heading. The key is to use the attitude indicator and heading indicator together and make the correction gradually. A steep bank on a single-engine approach will increase the power requirement, risk loss of altitude or airspeed, and can push either parameter outside ACS tolerances. Trim pedal inputs must keep the ball centered throughout the correction.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 7 (Instrument Approaches and Minimums); FAA-S-ACS-18 IH.VIII.B.S7

questions.question: You are flying a multiengine helicopter on a single-engine non-precision approach and are cleared to descend to MDA. As you level off at MDA, you notice your workload spikes and your altitude oscillates between MDA and MDA +120 feet. What specific technique should you use to stabilize at MDA within ACS tolerances while managing the increased single-engine workload?
questions.answer: The key technique is to establish a precise collective position for level flight at MDA and note the power setting (torque, N1, or manifold pressure as applicable) before the descent. As you level off, set that known power setting rather than chasing the altimeter. Use the VSI to detect trend early — if VSI shows any climb, reduce collective before the altimeter moves 100 feet. Trim the helicopter in pitch and yaw so hands and feet are not fighting to maintain heading and attitude. Pre-briefing the MDA level-off altitude and setting the altimeter alerter (if equipped) reduces workload at the critical moment. The SRM concept of workload management from ADM principles is directly applicable here — identify the high-workload phase in advance and shed unnecessary tasks before reaching MDA.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (SRM/ADM); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 7; FAA-S-ACS-18 IH.VIII.B.S7

questions.question: During a single-engine ILS approach in actual IMC, you switch to the alternate static source to address a suspected blocked primary static port. How does this affect your ability to maintain the ±100-foot altitude tolerance, and what specific correction do you apply to your altimeter reading?
questions.answer: Switching to alternate static source in most helicopters draws cabin air, which is typically at slightly lower pressure than outside static air due to the venturi effect of airflow around the fuselage. This causes the altimeter to read slightly higher than actual altitude, the VSI to show a momentary false climb, and the ASI to indicate slightly faster than actual. The magnitude varies by aircraft and is documented in the POH/RFM. For the altitude tolerance, you must know your aircraft's specific alternate static source error (from the POH) and mentally correct for it — for example, if the alternate source gives a +50-foot altimeter error, your 'actual' MDA is 50 feet lower than indicated. Failure to account for this could cause you to descend below published MDA while the altimeter shows you are at or above it, violating obstacle clearance.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5 (Alternate Static Source); FAR 14 CFR 91.205; Aircraft POH/RFM
questions.follow_up: If your POH does not list the altitude error for the alternate static source, what are your options to determine it before relying on it during an approach?
questions.follow_up_answer: If the POH does not specify the error, you have a few options: (1) Prior to the flight or in VMC, you can cross-check the altimeter reading on the alternate source against a known field elevation or against a GPS-derived altitude to estimate the error. (2) You can treat the alternate source altitude as an approximation and apply a conservative buffer — fly the approach at or above MDA with extra margin to account for the unknown error. (3) On the ground during preflight, you can select alternate static and note any deviation from the known field elevation. In all cases, if the error is unknown and significant IMC is involved, the safest decision is to not commence or continue the approach, consistent with the ADM principle of avoiding actions that will only 'probably' work out.

questions.question: On a single-engine instrument approach in a multiengine helicopter, you are consistently nailing altitude and heading but your airspeed keeps oscillating ±12 knots due to turbulence. At what point should you call the approach unstabilized and execute a missed approach, and how does the single-engine condition change that decision compared to a normal two-engine go-around?
questions.answer: An airspeed fluctuation of ±12 knots exceeds the ACS ±10-knot tolerance, making this a technical bust, but the more critical question is safety. In turbulence, you must distinguish between control-input-driven deviations (which indicate poor technique) and turbulence-induced momentary exceedances (which may be unavoidable). If you cannot maintain airspeed within ±10 knots consistently through your inputs — not just due to gusts — the approach is unstabilized and should be discontinued. On a single engine, the missed approach decision is more complex: the go-around itself requires significant power and precise collective/pedal coordination, and if the remaining engine is already at or near its single-engine power limit, a go-around may be marginal or require precise execution to avoid exceeding torque or temperature limits. However, continuing an unstabilized single-engine approach into IMC to a runway you cannot yet see is the higher-risk option. The missed approach should be executed early, while altitude and airspeed margins exist, rather than late when options narrow.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (Emergency Operations); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 7 (Missed Approach); FAA-S-ACS-18 IH.VIII.B.S7
questions.follow_up: If you execute a missed approach on a single-engine ILS and the published missed approach procedure requires a climbing turn, what consideration specific to single-engine helicopter performance must you verify before initiating that turn?
questions.follow_up_answer: Before initiating a climbing turn on a single-engine missed approach, you must verify that you have achieved a positive climb rate and are at or above the published climb gradient required by the missed approach procedure — typically expressed as feet per NM. In a single-engine helicopter, climb performance is significantly degraded, and the helicopter may not be capable of meeting the published climb gradient for the missed approach, particularly at higher density altitudes or heavy weights. Before the approach, the pilot should have calculated single-engine climb performance from the RFM and compared it to the required missed approach climb gradient. If single-engine performance is insufficient to meet the gradient, the approach should not have been commenced. During the turn itself, bank angle must be kept shallow (typically no more than 15°) to avoid increasing the load factor and reducing climb performance further on the single operating engine.

questions.question: What is the difference between a Decision Altitude (DA) and a Minimum Descent Altitude (MDA), and how does each affect when you must initiate a missed approach?
questions.answer: A Decision Altitude (DA) is used on precision approaches (e.g., ILS) and is expressed as an MSL altitude. At DA, you must have the required visual references to continue; if not, the missed approach is initiated immediately at that point. An MDA is used on non-precision approaches; it is the lowest altitude you may descend to and must remain at until you either acquire required visual references or reach the Missed Approach Point (MAP). You cannot descend below MDA unless you have at least one of the ten required visual references and are in a position to make a normal descent to the runway.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter on Instrument Approaches

questions.question: When planning a non-precision approach in a multiengine helicopter with one engine inoperative, what is the basic concept behind selecting a rate of descent so that you arrive at the MDA in a position to land?
questions.answer: The rate of descent must be calculated so that when you reach the MDA, the helicopter is close enough to the runway—both laterally aligned and at an appropriate distance—to make a continuous, normal descent to the landing point without a steep dive or an S-turn. If you descend too quickly, you arrive at MDA far from the runway and must level off and fly level while hoping to acquire the runway visually; if you descend too slowly, you may cross the MAP still above MDA with insufficient runway remaining. With an inoperative engine, performance is reduced, so the pilot must anticipate that a go-around or missed approach will be more demanding and plan the approach to maximize the chance of a successful landing from a stabilized position at MDA.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Approaches and Minimums; 14 CFR 91.175

questions.question: What are the ten visual references specified in 14 CFR 91.175 that a pilot must identify before descending below MDA or DA/DH?
questions.answer: According to 14 CFR 91.175(c), at least one of the following must be distinctly visible and identifiable: (1) approach light system, except that the pilot may not descend below 100 feet above the touchdown zone elevation using approach lights alone; (2) threshold; (3) threshold markings; (4) threshold lights; (5) runway end identifier lights (REIL); (6) visual approach slope indicator (VASI); (7) touchdown zone or touchdown zone markings; (8) touchdown zone lights; (9) runway or runway markings; (10) runway lights.

questions.question: You are flying a multiengine helicopter with the left engine inoperative conducting a VOR/DME approach. The FAF is at 3,000 feet MSL, the MDA is 1,200 feet MSL, and the MAP is 4.2 DME from the station. Your groundspeed is 90 knots. Walk me through how you would calculate and manage your rate of descent to arrive at the MDA in a position to make a normal descent to the runway.
questions.answer: First, determine the altitude to lose from FAF to MDA: 3,000 - 1,200 = 1,800 feet. Next, calculate the time from FAF to MAP at 90 knots groundspeed over 4.2 NM: (4.2 / 90) x 60 = 2.8 minutes. Divide altitude to lose by time: 1,800 / 2.8 ≈ 643 feet per minute required. However, you do not want to arrive at the MDA exactly at the MAP—you need to be at MDA early enough to visually acquire the runway and transition to a normal landing descent. A practical technique is to target arriving at MDA approximately 0.5–1 NM before the MAP, which means slightly increasing the ROD or beginning the descent earlier so you have horizontal distance remaining to assess the environment and make a landing. With an inoperative engine, confirm the helicopter can maintain the required ROD with available power on the operating engine, and cross-check that obstacle clearance is maintained during the descent.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Approaches and Minimums; 14 CFR 91.175

questions.question: During an ILS approach in a multiengine helicopter with one engine inoperative, you reach DA and have only the approach lights in sight—no runway environment. What must you do, and is there any condition under which you can descend further?
questions.answer: At DA on a precision approach, if you do not have the required visual references, you must immediately execute the missed approach—you cannot continue descending. However, 14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i) provides a limited exception: if you can see the approach lighting system (ALS), you may descend to 100 feet above the touchdown zone elevation (TDZE), but no lower, unless you then acquire additional runway environment references. If you reach 100 feet above TDZE and still have only approach lights without any runway environment, a missed approach is mandatory. With an inoperative engine, the missed approach must be executed promptly and precisely because single-engine go-around performance is limited, making early recognition and decisive action at DA especially critical.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175(c)(3)(i); FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Approaches and Minimums

questions.question: You are established on a RNAV (GPS) approach in a multiengine helicopter with the right engine failed. You reach the MDA at 1.8 NM from the runway threshold but you are not yet visual. The published MAP is at 0.5 NM. Describe exactly what you should do from this point forward.
questions.answer: You must level off at the MDA and continue flying toward the MAP while maintaining MDA. You cannot descend below MDA until you acquire the required visual references per 14 CFR 91.175(c). While flying level at MDA toward the MAP, you are searching for at least one of the ten required visual references. If you acquire the required visual references before the MAP and you are in a position from which a normal descent to the intended landing point can be made, you may descend and land. If you reach the MAP—in this case 0.5 NM from the threshold—without acquiring visual references, you must execute the missed approach immediately. With an inoperative engine, level flight at MDA may require significant power from the operating engine, so monitor engine instruments closely during this segment. Do not delay the missed approach decision at the MAP; a late initiation with reduced performance increases risk significantly.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175(c); FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Approaches and Minimums

questions.question: A candidate flying a multiengine helicopter OEI on a localizer approach reaches MDA 3 NM from the threshold, acquires the runway, and begins a visual descent. Halfway down, clouds close in and they lose visual contact. The MAP has already been passed. What must they do, and what does the regulation specifically require regarding the climbing turn?
questions.answer: Once visual reference is lost after passing the MAP, the pilot must execute an immediate missed approach. Per 14 CFR 91.175(e), if a missed approach is initiated prior to the MAP, the pilot must continue to the MAP at or above MDA before beginning any turn. However, since the MAP has already been passed in this scenario, the pilot should immediately apply go-around power on the operating engine, climb, and follow the published missed approach procedure. The key regulatory requirement under 91.175 is that if visual reference is lost during a circling approach, an immediate climbing turn toward the landing runway must be made, then intercept the missed approach course—but on a straight-in approach that has passed the MAP, the pilot initiates the missed approach directly. With an OEI helicopter, the missed approach must be flown precisely per the published procedure because the reduced climb performance leaves no margin for deviation. The pilot must also be aware that a descent below MDA after losing visual contact is a regulatory violation.
questions.follow_up: If the published missed approach requires a climbing turn to a fix, but the OEI performance data in the RFM shows the helicopter cannot achieve the required climb gradient on one engine, what options does the pilot have?
questions.follow_up_answer: If the helicopter cannot meet the published missed approach climb gradient OEI, the pilot faces a critical safety situation. Options include: (1) Declare an emergency (7700) and inform ATC immediately, requesting vectors or an alternative procedure with a more achievable gradient; (2) If performance allows any climb, climb straight ahead on the runway heading as long as possible to gain altitude before turning, even if this deviates from the published procedure—safety of flight takes precedence; (3) If a suitable landing area is visible, land immediately rather than attempting an impossible climb. Pilots should have reviewed OEI missed approach performance during preflight planning and should not have accepted the approach if single-engine missed approach climb performance was not achievable. This is a risk management failure that originates before the approach even begins.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175(e); FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Approaches and Minimums; Helicopter RFM OEI performance data

questions.question: During a checkride, a candidate flying a simulated OEI ILS approach intercepts the glideslope but allows airspeed to decay 15 knots below Vref while chasing the glideslope, arriving at DA on glidepath but slow. As an examiner, why is this specifically a problem related to the S8 skill standard, and what is the deeper aerodynamic hazard unique to a low-inertia rotor helicopter in this situation?
questions.answer: The S8 standard requires arriving at DA in a position from which a descent to the landing point can be made—this means not just being on glidepath geographically, but being stabilized in airspeed, power, and configuration to execute a safe transition to landing. Arriving 15 knots slow at DA means the helicopter is not in a position to safely continue, because a go-around or even a continued approach will be degraded: the pilot must accelerate while simultaneously managing altitude, reducing the chance of a successful landing from that point. The deeper hazard specific to low-inertia rotor helicopters is rotor RPM decay. At low airspeed and high power demand (as in a slow approach on one engine), if the pilot makes an abrupt collective input—such as attempting to arrest an unexpected sink rate at DA—rotor RPM can decay rapidly. Low-inertia rotor systems have very little stored energy and RPM decay can become unrecoverable within seconds, potentially leading to rotor stall, which the Helicopter Flying Handbook explicitly states is not recoverable. On a single-engine approach, the operating engine is already heavily loaded, and a slow airspeed condition narrows the margin further.
questions.follow_up: If rotor RPM begins decaying on short final during this OEI approach and the pilot recognizes it, what is the correct immediate action and why must it be taken before any other input?
questions.follow_up_answer: The immediate action is to lower collective to reduce blade pitch and allow the rotor to accelerate—this takes priority over every other control input including any attempt to arrest sink rate or maintain altitude. The reason is that rotor RPM is the fundamental source of lift and control authority in a helicopter; without adequate RPM, no other control input is effective. The Helicopter Flying Handbook states that early recognition of low rotor RPM is imperative because rotor stall in a helicopter is not recoverable. Once collective is lowered and RPM begins recovering, the pilot can then manage the descent and assess whether a landing or missed approach is possible. Attempting to maintain altitude or arrest sink rate by raising collective while RPM is decaying will accelerate the RPM loss and advance the aircraft toward an unrecoverable state.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Helicopter Flying Handbook Chapter 11; FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Approaches and Minimums; 14 CFR 91.175

questions.question: On a precision approach with one engine inoperative, what does '¾-scale deflection' mean in practical terms for the glide slope needle?
questions.answer: The glide slope indicator has a full-scale deflection of approximately 0.7° above or below center (full scale is typically marked by the needle reaching the outer dot). ¾-scale deflection means the needle must stay within 75% of that full travel — roughly within the inner ¾ of the indicator scale — on both the high and low side. In practical terms, the needle must not reach the outer dot or peg against the case; a small but visible deflection is acceptable, but the pilot must correct before the needle moves beyond that ¾ threshold.

questions.question: On a non-precision approach flown with one engine inoperative, does the ¾-scale deflection standard apply to vertical guidance?
questions.answer: On a non-precision approach, there is no electronic vertical guidance (no glide slope), so vertical guidance via a needle does not apply — hence the phrase 'as applicable' in the ACS standard. The pilot is expected to manage descent using step-down fixes, CDFA technique, or published crossing altitudes. The ¾-scale standard still applies to the lateral CDI needle regardless of approach type.
questions.regulatory_ref: ACS IH.VIII.B.S9; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter on Instrument Approaches

questions.question: Why is maintaining within ¾-scale deflection on final approach with an inoperative engine considered a more demanding standard than simply 'full-scale'?
questions.answer: Full-scale deflection means the needle has moved to its maximum travel, indicating the aircraft is significantly off the desired course or glide path — at that point obstacle clearance may be compromised. ¾-scale deflection is a tighter tolerance that ensures the pilot is actively correcting before deviations become large. With an inoperative engine, asymmetric thrust, increased pilot workload, and possible torque and yaw tendencies make it more challenging to hold this tighter standard, which is why the ACS specifically tests it as a skill element under OEI conditions.

questions.question: You are flying an ILS approach in a twin-engine helicopter with the left engine failed (simulated). On final, you notice a sustained half-dot low on the glide slope and a quarter-dot right of course. What corrective technique would you apply, and are you within the ACS standard?
questions.answer: A half-dot low on the glide slope exceeds the ¾-scale standard (since ¾ of full scale is approximately ¾ of a dot's travel, a half-dot deflection is still within tolerance — but if the full-scale deflection equals one dot, then half-dot is within ¾-scale). With a quarter-dot lateral deflection, the pilot is well within the ¾-scale lateral standard. Corrective technique: apply a small increase in collective/power to arrest the below-glide-slope trend while simultaneously applying a gentle lateral cyclic correction to the left to recenter the localizer. With an inoperative left engine, the pilot must be alert to asymmetric torque effects — the operating right engine may introduce a left yaw tendency depending on rotor system design, requiring right pedal input. Corrections should be small and coordinated to avoid over-controlling in the OEI regime.

questions.question: During an RNAV (GPS) approach to LPV minimums with one engine inoperative, how does the sensitivity of the lateral CDI change as you transition from the en route segment to the final approach fix, and how does this affect your ability to maintain ¾-scale deflection?
questions.answer: On an RNAV approach with LPV, the CDI sensitivity transitions from ±2 NM (en route) to ±1 NM (terminal) and then narrows to angular sensitivity similar to an ILS localizer (approximately ±350 feet at threshold) on the final approach segment. As sensitivity increases, the same physical aircraft deviation produces a larger needle deflection, making it easier to bust the ¾-scale standard with small positional errors. With an OEI condition, the pilot must anticipate this tightening sensitivity well before the final approach fix, cross-check LNAV/VNAV or LPV guidance frequently, and make increasingly small corrections. Waiting until the needle is moving rapidly to correct is a common failure mode in OEI approaches.
questions.regulatory_ref: ACS IH.VIII.B.S9; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5; FAA RNAV approach criteria

questions.question: You are shooting an ILS in IMC with one engine inoperative (simulated). At 500 feet AGL on final, workload spikes and your glide slope needle momentarily reaches full-scale deflection high before you recapture. The examiner is watching. Walk me through how you prioritize your recovery without destabilizing the approach or losing sight of your single-engine performance margins.
questions.answer: First priority is to avoid a rapid or large collective reduction to chase the glide slope — in OEI, any reduction in collective that drops power below the single-engine power setting needed for obstacle clearance is dangerous. Recognize the full-scale high deviation and apply a moderate, measured collective reduction combined with maintaining the approach airspeed with cyclic. Simultaneously verify the operating engine is within limits (torque, TOT/ITT). Do not allow airspeed to drop toward Vy or minimum single-engine airspeed while chasing the glide slope. The needle has already exceeded ¾-scale, which is an ACS bust, but the recovery technique matters — the examiner is assessing whether you manage the deviation without creating a secondary emergency. If the approach becomes unstabilized below the stabilization gate (typically 500 feet for instrument approaches per operator SOPs), the correct decision may be to execute the missed approach rather than continue to descend while chasing full-scale deflections.
questions.regulatory_ref: ACS IH.VIII.B.S9; FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Approaches and Minimums; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: An examiner asks: 'If the ¾-scale deflection standard exists to preserve obstacle clearance, explain exactly how the published instrument approach procedure guarantees that clearance — and where does that guarantee end if you are at ¾-scale deflection on both lateral and vertical guidance simultaneously?'
questions.answer: Published ILS procedures guarantee obstacle clearance based on full compliance with the published procedure, including maintaining the localizer centerline and glide slope centerline. The ILS obstacle clearance surface (OCS) is designed with a slope and width that assumes the aircraft will fly within certain lateral and vertical bounds. ¾-scale deflection on the glide slope represents approximately 0.525° off the glide path (¾ of ~0.7° full scale), and ¾-scale lateral deflection represents approximately ¾ of the localizer full-scale sensitivity at that point. The FAA designs the approach with a buffer — the obstacle clearance is not instantly compromised at ¾-scale — but the buffer diminishes as deflection increases and disappears at or beyond full-scale deflection, particularly on the low side of the glide slope where the aircraft could fly below the OCS. Being simultaneously at ¾-scale high laterally AND ¾-scale low vertically places the aircraft at the edge of the protected airspace in two dimensions at once — obstacle clearance is no longer guaranteed with the same confidence, particularly in mountainous or complex terrain environments.
questions.follow_up: If the approach had an inoperative glide slope (localizer-only minimums), and you are at ¾-scale lateral deflection on the localizer while flying the MDA step-down, what specific additional hazard exists that does not exist on a full ILS?
questions.follow_up_answer: On a localizer-only approach (no glide slope), the pilot is responsible for vertical navigation entirely — the MDA is the floor, and there is no electronic guidance to warn of premature descent. At ¾-scale lateral deflection, the aircraft may be outside the primary obstacle clearance area defined for the localizer procedure. Unlike the ILS glide slope, which keeps the aircraft on a precise descent path away from obstacles in the vertical plane, the localizer-only approach relies on step-down fixes and the MDA to provide vertical obstacle clearance over a wider lateral corridor. If you are also near the edges of that lateral corridor (¾-scale deflection), you are simultaneously approaching the edge of lateral protected airspace AND flying a flat approach profile with minimal vertical obstacle clearance margin — a combination that is especially dangerous in terrain or when obstacles exist off the extended centerline.
questions.regulatory_ref: ACS IH.VIII.B.S9; FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Approaches and Minimums; FAA Order 8260.3 (TERPS)

questions.question: During an OEI ILS checkride scenario, the pilot maintains ¾-scale or better on the glide slope but consistently allows the localizer to reach exactly ¾-scale deflection — always catching it right at the limit. As an examiner, how do you evaluate that performance, and what does it reveal about the pilot's skill level versus the ACS standard?
questions.answer: The ACS standard states the pilot must maintain within ¾-scale deflection — technically, a needle that repeatedly reaches exactly ¾-scale but does not exceed it meets the minimum standard. However, as an examiner, consistently flying to the edge of the tolerance reveals a reactive control technique rather than a proactive one. The pilot is chasing the needle instead of establishing a correction before the deviation develops. In OEI conditions, this technique is particularly concerning because any distraction — an engine parameter exceedance, an ATC call, a cockpit emergency — will push the deviation past ¾-scale before the pilot can respond. A proficient pilot should be making small corrections well before the needle approaches ¾-scale, keeping deviations within approximately ½-scale as a practical target. The examiner should note this as a performance trend, discuss it during the debrief, and may factor it into an overall assessment of whether the applicant demonstrates the level of precision appropriate for an instrument rating in a multiengine helicopter.
questions.follow_up: If the same pilot then executes the missed approach perfectly — climbing on course, maintaining single-engine performance, and following the published procedure — does the in-approach deviation still constitute a failure of this task element?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, if the needle exceeded ¾-scale deflection — even momentarily — at any point on the final approach segment, that is a specific and objective failure of ACS element IH.VIII.B.S9, regardless of how well the missed approach is executed. The missed approach performance is evaluated under its own ACS task element. The two are scored independently. The examiner cannot 'average' a failed approach against a successful missed approach to produce a pass. However, the examiner has discretion to evaluate whether the deflection was transient and immediately corrected versus sustained, and whether it resulted from a controllability issue (potential safety of flight concern) versus a momentary distraction — this context informs whether additional testing is warranted or whether a disapproval is issued.
questions.regulatory_ref: ACS IH.VIII.B.S9; FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Approaches and Minimums; FAA Order 8900.2 (Practical Test Standards evaluation criteria)

questions.question: When executing a landing at the conclusion of an instrument approach with one engine simulated inoperative, what is the primary consideration regarding touchdown point selection?
questions.answer: The pilot should plan for a landing area that allows a safe touchdown and rollout/deceleration with reduced go-around capability. With one engine inoperative (or simulated), the ability to execute a full missed approach or go-around from very low altitude may be severely limited or unavailable depending on helicopter performance. Therefore, the pilot must be committed to landing once below a safe single-engine go-around altitude, and the touchdown point must be within the available landing area with no obstacles in the approach path.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; applicable helicopter POH/RFM performance data

questions.question: During the landing phase following an instrument approach with a simulated engine failure, how does collective management differ from a normal two-engine landing?
questions.answer: With one engine inoperative, the operating engine is at or near its maximum power output throughout the approach and landing. The pilot must be cautious with collective inputs because demanding additional power — such as a large collective pull to arrest a high sink rate — may exceed the single engine torque limit or exceed the engine's available power, potentially causing a hard landing or main rotor RPM decay. Smooth, deliberate collective movements are essential, and the pilot must accept a slightly firmer landing rather than over-torquing the remaining engine.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; applicable POH/RFM single-engine performance limits

questions.question: At what point during the instrument approach with a simulated inoperative engine should the pilot transition from instrument scan to visual references in order to execute the landing?
questions.answer: The pilot must acquire at least one of the ten FAA-specified visual references before descending below the DA/DH or MDA. Once visual references are acquired and the pilot determines a normal landing can be made, the transition to visual flight for the landing phase begins. The instrument scan is reduced gradually as outside visual cues take over for glidepath and alignment control during the final flare and touchdown. If visual references cannot be acquired by the MAP or DA/DH, a missed approach must be executed instead of attempting a landing.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter on Instrument Approaches; 14 CFR 91.175(c)

questions.question: You are flying a twin-engine helicopter on an ILS approach to minimums with the left engine simulated inoperative. At 200 feet AGL you acquire the required visual references and continue the approach. On short final you notice the wind has shifted and you are drifting left of centerline. Describe how you correct and complete the landing safely.
questions.answer: With one engine inoperative, any aggressive cyclic or collective correction increases the risk of exceeding single-engine power limits or inducing rotor RPM decay. The pilot should apply smooth right cyclic to correct the drift, cross-checking torque and rotor RPM throughout. If the drift is minor, a slight crab or slip correction with cyclic can align the helicopter prior to touchdown. However, if the drift cannot be corrected while maintaining a stabilized approach profile and safe power margins, the pilot must initiate a go-around (if single-engine go-around performance permits at that altitude/weight) or accept an off-centerline but safe landing area. The pilot should never attempt to force the helicopter onto a specific spot at the cost of a dangerously steep or rushed final correction that could exceed power limits.

questions.question: You complete an instrument approach with a simulated engine failure and transition to a visual landing. During the flare, you notice your sink rate is higher than desired and you are running out of landing zone. How do you prioritize your inputs and what trade-offs must you consider with one engine inoperative?
questions.answer: The pilot must use the remaining collective available before reaching the single-engine torque limit to arrest the high sink rate. Aft cyclic can also be used to slow forward speed and redistribute lift, helping reduce sink rate. The trade-off is that pulling collective aggressively may exceed the engine's single-engine power limit or drain rotor RPM below a safe margin. If the landing zone is no longer safe and sufficient altitude and performance remain, a go-around is the preferred option. However, at very low altitude with a high sink rate, a committed landing — even if firm — is safer than an attempted go-around that cannot be completed. The pilot must know the helicopter's single-engine go-around capability at the current weight and density altitude before making that decision.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; applicable POH/RFM OEI performance charts

questions.question: After breaking out of the clouds during an instrument approach with one engine simulated inoperative, you have the runway environment in sight but the touchdown zone lights are not visible due to fog. Can you legally continue to a landing, and how does this affect your landing execution?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.175(c), the pilot must be able to identify at least one of ten specified visual references before descending below DA/DH or MDA. The touchdown zone lights (TDZ lights) are one of those ten references, but the regulation only requires at least one — not specifically the TDZ lights. If another qualifying reference is clearly visible (such as the approach light system, threshold, runway threshold markings, runway lights, PAPI/VASI, or the runway itself), the pilot may legally continue the approach and landing. However, limited visual cues in fog will affect the flare and landing judgment, especially with single-engine power constraints. The pilot must ensure the landing can be completed safely given reduced visual depth perception and must not allow uncertainty about the landing surface to cause delayed or abrupt control inputs.

questions.question: During a training flight, your student executes the landing phase of an instrument approach with one engine simulated inoperative and pulls maximum torque on the remaining engine during the flare, briefly exceeding the published OEI torque limit before touchdown. As the examiner, how do you evaluate this from a practical test standpoint, and what does it indicate about the student's understanding of OEI landing technique?
questions.answer: An exceedance of the OEI torque limit is a safety-critical error that must be noted on the practical test. It indicates the student did not properly plan the energy state (speed, altitude, and sink rate) on final approach to arrive at the flare with a manageable descent rate that could be arrested within single-engine power limits. It also suggests the student may not have internalized the fundamental principle that on single-engine approaches, the flare must be planned so that the maximum collective required at any point does not exceed the OEI limits. From a test standpoint, this may constitute an unsatisfactory performance depending on whether it presented a safety hazard, whether the student recognized and acknowledged the error, and whether it was a momentary exceedance vs. sustained. The examiner must consult the POH/RFM regarding maintenance action requirements for the torque exceedance.
questions.follow_up: If the student argues that the torque exceedance was only for half a second and the engine was not damaged, how do you respond as the examiner and what action is required after the flight?
questions.follow_up_answer: Duration does not negate the exceedance. Most POH/RFMs require a maintenance inspection any time a torque limit is exceeded, regardless of duration. The crew must complete a maintenance write-up documenting the exceedance, including the duration and peak value if recorded, and the aircraft must not be returned to service until a qualified mechanic reviews it per the manufacturer's instructions. From an airmanship standpoint, the pilot's dismissal of the exceedance also reflects poor aeronautical decision-making — the 'error chain' principle from ADM tells us that minimizing or rationalizing limit exceedances can lead to compounding consequences. The examiner must address both the technical requirement and the ADM concern during the debrief.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 and Chapter 13 (ADM); applicable POH/RFM maintenance procedures; 14 CFR 91.7

questions.question: You are flying a multiengine helicopter IFR at night with actual IMC. At the MAP, you have the runway environment in sight and begin the transition to land with one engine inoperative. As you cross the threshold, your remaining engine begins surging. Walk me through your immediate decision-making and landing execution.
questions.answer: Engine surging at threshold height is an emergency compounding an already high-workload single-engine night landing. The pilot must immediately assess whether sufficient rotor RPM and engine power remain to complete a controlled landing. With the runway environment already in sight and the helicopter at threshold height, the priority is to land immediately — a go-around attempt with a surging engine and already degraded performance would be extremely hazardous. The pilot should focus on maintaining rotor RPM above minimum, using smooth collective to cushion the touchdown, and controlling heading with pedals. If the engine fails entirely during flare, the pilot transitions to an autorotation flare technique — lowering collective to maintain rotor RPM and using available inertia to arrest sink rate for touchdown. After landing, the pilot should stop the aircraft safely, secure the engines, and notify ATC of the emergency. Post-landing, a full maintenance inspection is mandatory before the next flight.
questions.follow_up: If rotor RPM begins to decay rapidly during that final flare because the surging engine loses power entirely, and you are at 10 feet AGL, what is your one available option to prevent a hard landing and how does it work?
questions.follow_up_answer: At 10 feet AGL with decaying rotor RPM, the pilot must immediately execute the autorotation flare: apply aft cyclic to slow forward speed and momentarily increase angle of attack across the rotor disk, which temporarily arrests RPM decay by using stored rotor inertia, then time the collective pull during the final flare to convert remaining rotor inertia into lift to cushion touchdown. This is a time-critical maneuver — if the rotor RPM is too low when collective is applied, there is insufficient energy to soften the landing. This is why the handbook emphasizes that rotor stall is not recoverable and early recognition of low RPM is imperative. The ground will arrive quickly at 10 feet; there is no time to troubleshoot the engine — the entire focus must be on rotor RPM management and flare timing.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11 (Autorotation, Low Rotor RPM/Stall, Emergency Procedures); applicable POH/RFM emergency procedures

questions.question: During a simulated single-engine instrument approach, at what point in the procedure should you complete the engine-out checklist versus the approach checklist, and why does the order matter?
questions.answer: The engine-out emergency checklist should be completed first to stabilize the aircraft and confirm the failed engine is properly secured (fuel shutoff, fire suppression if applicable, appropriate systems isolated). Only after the aircraft is under control and the emergency is addressed should you complete the approach checklist. Reversing this order risks missing critical engine-out items while being distracted by approach tasks, which increases the chance of an unsafe configuration during one of the most demanding phases of flight.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; AFM/RFM Emergency Checklist procedures

questions.question: What is the difference between a memory (immediate action) checklist item and a reference (do-list) checklist item in the context of a single-engine instrument approach?
questions.answer: Memory items, also called immediate action items, are steps that must be performed from memory without referencing printed material because they require immediate response to prevent loss of aircraft control or further damage — examples include lowering collective at engine failure and maintaining rotor RPM. Reference or do-list items are steps performed by reading the checklist line by line after the immediate situation is stabilized, such as confirming fuel selectors, completing systems checks, and configuring for approach. During a single-engine instrument approach, immediate action items address the engine failure first, then the printed checklist is referenced to confirm all steps were completed correctly before continuing the approach.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; Aircraft Flight Manual (AFM) Emergency Procedures

questions.question: Name at least three checklists that could be required during a single-engine IFR instrument approach and landing in a multiengine helicopter.
questions.answer: During a single-engine instrument approach and landing, a pilot could be required to complete: (1) Engine Failure / Engine-Out Emergency Checklist — immediate and reference items to secure the failed engine and stabilize systems; (2) Single-Engine Approach Checklist — configures aircraft for reduced-power approach including power settings, limitations, and performance adjustments; (3) Before Landing / Landing Checklist — confirms gear (if applicable), systems, and configuration for landing; (4) After Landing / Shutdown Checklist — addresses securing systems following touchdown. Some aircraft also have a specific Inoperative Engine Securing checklist separate from the emergency checklist.
questions.regulatory_ref: AFM/RFM specific to aircraft; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: You are flying a two-pilot IFR crew in a twin turbine helicopter and experience a single-engine failure at the final approach fix (FAF) on an ILS. Describe how you would manage checklist completion between pilots without compromising approach control or crew resource management.
questions.answer: At engine failure on the FAF, the Pilot Flying (PF) calls out the failure and executes immediate action memory items to maintain control — lowering collective as needed, maintaining rotor RPM, and continuing the approach at single-engine power settings. The Pilot Monitoring (PM) calls out the failure, cross-checks instruments, and begins the engine-out reference checklist, reading each item aloud while the PF confirms completion or the PM performs non-flying tasks. The PF announces 'continue approach' or 'execute missed approach' based on performance and terrain. The PM manages the printed checklist while monitoring approach progress. Neither pilot should have their head down exclusively in the checklist at critical points such as DA/DH — checklist items must be paused at decision altitude until the missed approach or landing decision is made. This division of duties follows standard CRM principles for multiengine helicopter operations.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM/SRM/CRM); AFM Emergency Procedures; 14 CFR 91.3

questions.question: You are single-pilot IFR in a twin helicopter and an engine fails mid-approach. You are heads-down completing the engine-out checklist when you pass through MDA without having acquired the required visual references. What should you have done differently with checklist management, and what is the correct action now?
questions.answer: The error was allowing checklist completion to distract from approach monitoring and the visual reference requirement at MDA. Correct checklist management requires the pilot to pause checklist activity at MDA/DA to make the land-or-miss decision — checklist items do not override regulatory requirements. At MDA, at least one of the ten required visual references must be clearly visible before descending below that altitude per 14 CFR 91.175. Having passed MDA without visual references, the correct action now is to immediately execute the published missed approach procedure, climb to missed approach altitude, then complete any remaining checklist items once established on the missed approach. Continuing descent below MDA without visual references is a serious deviation.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175(c); Instrument Flying Handbook FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter on Instrument Approaches; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13

questions.question: The landing checklist for your multiengine helicopter requires selecting a fuel crossfeed position as part of a single-engine landing configuration. You skip this item under pressure and land without completing it. What are the potential consequences, and how does this scenario illustrate the importance of disciplined checklist use during single-engine approaches?
questions.answer: Skipping a fuel configuration item could result in fuel exhaustion to the operating engine if crossfeed is required to balance fuel load or supply the remaining engine — this could cause a double-engine failure on short final or during the landing roll, with almost no recovery options. In the broader sense, this illustrates that checklists exist precisely because high-workload, high-stress environments are where memory is least reliable. The systematic use of printed checklists — not memory alone — is the safeguard against missed items that seem insignificant in the moment but carry catastrophic consequences. The error chain concept from ADM teaches that skipping one item often precedes additional errors, and breaking any one link (by completing the checklist properly) can prevent the accident sequence.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (error chain, ADM); AFM Checklist procedures; 14 CFR 91.3

questions.question: During a single-engine instrument approach in IMC, you complete the engine-out checklist and notice the checklist directs you to reduce airspeed to the single-engine best rate of climb speed, but ATC has assigned a speed restriction of 160 knots until 5 miles from the FAF. The single-engine Vy for your aircraft is significantly below that. How do you resolve this conflict, and what is your obligation?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.3, the pilot in command has final authority for the safe operation of the aircraft. A declared or understood emergency situation — such as an engine failure in IMC — allows the PIC to deviate from ATC instructions to the extent necessary for safety. You should inform ATC immediately of the engine failure and inability to comply with the speed restriction, request priority handling, and advise of your intentions. ATC must give priority to emergency aircraft per FAA JO 7110.65 Air Traffic Control handbook. The checklist speed exists because flying above single-engine Vy while IMC could result in insufficient climb performance to maintain obstacle clearance on a missed approach or in the event of a go-around. Complying with ATC speed while ignoring aircraft limitations places the flight at risk. After landing or clearing the emergency, a report may be required per 14 CFR 91.3(c) if deviations were made.
questions.follow_up: What if ATC denies your request to reduce speed and you are already inside the FAF in IMC — do you have any obligation to comply with the speed restriction at that point?
questions.follow_up_answer: No. Once an emergency exists and the PIC has declared it or is operating under emergency conditions, 14 CFR 91.3(b) states the pilot may deviate from any rule to the extent necessary to meet the emergency. Inside the FAF in IMC on one engine, compliance with an operationally unsafe speed restriction is not required. The PIC should fly the aircraft at the appropriate single-engine approach speed per the AFM, advise ATC of the deviation, and file a report per 14 CFR 91.3(c) if requested by ATC. The key principle: fly the aircraft first, communicate second, comply with paperwork third.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.3(b) and (c); FAA JO 7110.65 (ATC emergency priority); AFM Emergency Procedures

questions.question: Your multiengine helicopter AFM has two separate engine-out checklists: one for 'Engine Failure Above Minimum Continued Takeoff Speed' and one for 'Engine Failure During Approach and Landing.' During a single-engine instrument approach checkride, you reach into the wrong section and complete the wrong checklist. How would an examiner evaluate this error, and what principle of checklist discipline does it highlight?
questions.answer: An examiner would consider this a significant procedural error because using the wrong checklist can result in incorrect system configurations — potentially securing systems that should remain active or failing to address items specific to the flight phase. For example, the approach/landing checklist may require different fuel, bleed air, or hydraulic configurations than a takeoff abort checklist. The examiner would evaluate whether the error was caught and self-corrected, how quickly it was identified, and whether it resulted in an unsafe aircraft state. The principle highlighted is phase-of-flight checklist discipline: checklists are keyed to specific operational phases for sound aeronautical reasons. Pilots must confirm they are in the correct section before executing, especially under high-workload or stress conditions when the error is most likely to occur. This also ties to the ACS requirement to complete the 'appropriate' checklist — not just any checklist.
questions.follow_up: If you completed the wrong checklist but the aircraft remained in a safe configuration, would this still be a potential unsatisfactory (bust) on a checkride, and why?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, it could still be evaluated as unsatisfactory or at minimum a significant deficiency, because the ACS standard specifically requires completing the 'appropriate' checklist. Completing the wrong checklist demonstrates a lack of procedural discipline and systems knowledge even if the outcome was incidentally safe — it means the pilot got lucky rather than correct. In a real emergency, wrong checklist use could produce an unsafe configuration. Examiners evaluate the process and adherence to standards, not just the outcome. A corrective action taken promptly and correctly after recognizing the error may allow the examiner to continue the evaluation, but the deviation itself is noteworthy and must be assessed in the context of the overall performance.
questions.regulatory_ref: ACS IH.VIII.B.S11; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM, error recognition); AFM Procedures

questions.question: You are flying a two-pilot multiengine helicopter on an ILS approach when an engine fails. What is the fundamental difference between SRM and CRM, and which applies to your situation?
questions.answer: SRM (Single-Pilot Resource Management) is the management of all onboard and external resources by one pilot flying alone. CRM (Crew Resource Management) involves the effective use of all available resources — human, hardware, and information — among a flight crew of two or more. In a two-pilot scenario with an engine failure on an instrument approach, CRM applies. This means clearly dividing tasks: one pilot flies the aircraft and manages the approach while the other handles checklists, radio calls, and monitoring. Both concepts are rooted in the same ADM framework but CRM explicitly leverages crew coordination and communication to manage workload.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter on ADM

questions.question: Name the five key components of Single-Pilot Resource Management as described in the FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook.
questions.answer: The five key components of SRM as described in the FAA-H-8083-21B are: (1) Risk Management — identifying and mitigating hazards; (2) Situational Awareness — knowing where you are and what is happening around you at all times; (3) Aeronautical Decision-Making (ADM) — using a systematic approach to evaluate options and choose the best course of action; (4) Controlled Flight Into Terrain (CFIT) Awareness — actively monitoring terrain proximity, especially during IMC; and (5) Automation Management — effectively using available automated systems without over-relying on them or losing manual proficiency. Workload management is also a closely integrated element.

questions.question: The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook states that approximately what percentage of aviation accidents are caused by pilot error, and what does that tell you about the importance of SRM and CRM during a high-workload event like a single-engine instrument approach?
questions.answer: Approximately 80% of aviation accidents are attributed to pilot error (human factors). This statistic directly underscores why SRM and CRM are critical — especially during high-workload events like a single-engine instrument approach in IMC. The accident chain in these events almost never involves a single catastrophic failure; it typically involves a series of poor decisions or lapses in coordination that compound. Applying SRM or CRM discipline helps break that chain by ensuring workload is distributed, checklists are completed, situational awareness is maintained, and no single decision point is left unmanaged.

questions.question: You are the pilot flying (PF) in a two-pilot IFR helicopter during an LPV approach to minimums with one engine shut down per the checklist. The PM has fallen behind on the approach briefing, ATC changes your clearance, and the checklist is only half complete. Walk me through how you would apply CRM principles to manage this situation without compromising aircraft control.
questions.answer: CRM requires clear task allocation and communication under pressure. As PF, my primary responsibility is to fly the aircraft — maintain approach profile, airspeed, and configuration. I would first announce clearly to the PM: 'I have the aircraft, stop the checklist, acknowledge the new ATC clearance.' This prevents dual-task fixation and re-establishes crew coordination. I would then assess whether the partial checklist leaves any safety-critical items incomplete — if so, I would consider requesting a hold or delaying the approach to allow time to complete it. I would use standard callouts ('1,000 above,' 'approach checks complete or incomplete,' 'minimums') to maintain shared situational awareness. The goal is to never allow workload accumulation — the 'error chain' — to reach a point where both crew members are saturated simultaneously. If needed, I would declare an emergency or request priority handling to reduce external pressure.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13; FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Approaches and Minimums

questions.question: You are flying single-pilot in a multiengine helicopter under IFR when an engine failure occurs at the final approach fix on an ILS. Describe specifically how SRM principles should guide your decision-making from the FAF to either landing or missed approach execution.
questions.answer: At the FAF with an engine failure, SRM requires immediate workload prioritization: aviate first, then navigate, then communicate. I would immediately verify the failed engine, cross-check the OEI power available against the approach requirements, and confirm I can maintain the approach profile within OEI performance limits per the AFM. Risk management means re-evaluating the go/no-go decision at the FAF: Can I execute a missed approach on one engine? Is the destination runway suitable for an OEI landing? I would use automation (autopilot if available) to reduce manual workload, reference the checklist from memory for immediate action items, and defer non-critical checklist items. I would brief myself out loud (a SRM technique for single-pilot operations) on the missed approach procedure and required visual references. I would not descend below MDA/DA unless I have the required visual references per 14 CFR 91.175. If any doubt exists about OEI approach capability, I execute the missed approach immediately — never allowing 'probably' thinking to substitute for a known-safe option.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13; 14 CFR 91.175; FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Approaches and Minimums

questions.question: During a two-crew OEI instrument approach, the PM suggests continuing below MDA because they 'think' they can see the runway environment through broken clouds. How does proper CRM application guide your response as the PF?
questions.answer: CRM does not mean deferring to the other crew member automatically — it means using all available resources and information to make the safest decision. In this case, the PM's use of 'think' is a red flag; the FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook specifically warns against 'probably' or uncertain thinking when a known-safe alternative exists. As PF, I am the final authority on the operation. At least one of the ten specified visual references required by 14 CFR 91.175(c) must be clearly visible and identifiable before descending below MDA/DA — not merely thought to be visible. I would respond: 'I don't have the required visual references identified — executing missed approach.' I would communicate this assertively but professionally, then initiate the missed approach without hesitation. After the approach, a CRM debrief is appropriate to reinforce decision-making standards.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175(c); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13; FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Approaches and Minimums

questions.question: During a two-crew OEI ILS approach, you notice your PM — who is more senior and highly experienced — has made two minor errors in sequencing the emergency checklist, and is now rushing the approach briefing. How do you apply CRM assertiveness principles without undermining crew coordination, and what is the risk if you say nothing?
questions.answer: CRM demands that every crew member, regardless of rank or experience, has both the right and the responsibility to raise safety concerns. I would use a structured assertiveness technique: state the concern factually and without judgment ('I noticed items 4 and 6 of the OEI checklist were sequenced differently than published — can we confirm both are complete?'), propose a solution ('I'd like to pause 60 seconds before the FAF to finish the briefing'), and request acknowledgment. The risk of saying nothing is classic crew-induced error chain — two unchallenged small errors can compound. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook notes that breaking even one link in an error chain can change the outcome. If the PM dismisses the concern and I remain genuinely unsure of aircraft configuration safety, I have the authority as a certificated pilot to request a holding pattern or go-around. Silence in CRM environments has historically been a contributing factor in fatal crew accidents.
questions.follow_up: After the flight, the PM says your challenge was unnecessary and slowed down the approach. How do you handle this debrief?
questions.follow_up_answer: A CRM debrief is not about assigning blame — it is about improving future safety outcomes. I would acknowledge the PM's experience respectfully, then present the objective facts: two checklist sequencing deviations occurred, and the approach briefing was incomplete at the FAF. I would reference the published checklist to confirm the correct sequence and note that the FAA standard holds both crew members accountable for safe outcomes regardless of seniority. The goal is to establish a shared norm: speaking up is a professional obligation, not a challenge to authority. If the PM remains resistant, that resistance itself is a CRM concern worth documenting in a NASA ASRS report or raising with the operator's safety management system.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter on ADM; NASA ASRS program

questions.question: You are flying single-pilot on an OEI RNAV approach. You have successfully managed the engine failure, are fully established on the approach, and are inside the FAF — but you realize your situational awareness has narrowed entirely to the primary flight display. What SRM discipline addresses this, and what specific actions should you take to recover broad situational awareness before reaching DA?
questions.answer: Tunnel vision — the narrowing of attention to a single instrument or task under stress — is a well-documented human factors failure mode. The SRM discipline that directly addresses this is situational awareness management, combined with workload management and CFIT awareness. To recover broad situational awareness before DA, I should deliberately force a scan expansion: cross-check the moving map for terrain and obstacle clearance, verify the missed approach point location and required visual references, confirm altimeter setting is current, check OEI power margins against the approach requirements, and review the missed approach procedure. Automation management is also key here: if the autopilot is flying the approach, I should use that workload reduction to accomplish the broader scan rather than monitor the autopilot passively. The FAA notes that accidents correlate with narrow task fixation during high-stress events — deliberately breaking the tunnel is an active SRM skill, not a passive one.
questions.follow_up: If you reach DA with broad situational awareness restored but still no visual reference, what is the exact regulatory standard governing your next action, and does being single-pilot change that standard?
questions.follow_up_answer: Per 14 CFR 91.175(c), a pilot may not operate below DA/DH or MDA unless at least one of the ten specified visual references for the intended runway is distinctly visible and identifiable to the pilot. Being single-pilot does not change this regulatory threshold — the legal and safety standard is identical regardless of crew complement. If no required visual reference is established at DA, the missed approach must be initiated immediately. If the missed approach is initiated prior to the missed approach point, the pilot must continue on the published instrument approach procedure to the MAP at or above MDA/DA before beginning any turn, per FAA instrument approach procedure guidance. Single-pilot operations may increase the temptation to 'push through' due to fatigue or pressure, which is precisely why SRM discipline must be applied proactively before reaching that decision point.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175(c); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13; FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Approaches and Minimums

tasks.title: Task C. Approach with Loss of Primary Flight Instrument Indicators

questions.question: Name the six basic flight instruments used for helicopter attitude instrument flying, and explain which one is considered primary for pitch control during straight-and-level flight.
questions.answer: The six basic flight instruments are: attitude indicator, altimeter, airspeed indicator (ASI), vertical speed indicator (VSI), heading indicator, and turn-and-slip indicator. During straight-and-level flight, the altimeter is the primary instrument for pitch control because it directly shows whether the helicopter is maintaining the desired altitude. The attitude indicator is the supporting pitch instrument in this phase.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Flying Handbook, Chapter 8 – Helicopter Attitude Instrument Flying

questions.question: What is the first indication a pilot should recognize that the attitude indicator may have failed or become unreliable during IMC flight?
questions.answer: The first indication is typically a conflict or disagreement between the attitude indicator and the other flight instruments. For example, if the attitude indicator shows wings level and a steady altitude, but the altimeter is unwinding, the VSI shows a descent, and the airspeed is increasing, the attitude indicator is suspect. A gyroscopic instrument failure may also present as a slow, continuous precession or a tumbled display. Any time instrument cross-check reveals one instrument disagreeing with two or more others, the conflicting instrument should be treated as unreliable.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Flying Handbook, Chapter 8 – Helicopter Attitude Instrument Flying

questions.question: If you suspect your airspeed indicator is inoperative during an IFR approach, what is your responsibility regarding ATC communication?
questions.answer: You are required to notify ATC as soon as practicable. Declaring the malfunction allows ATC to provide amended clearances, increased separation, or direct you to a suitable airport. Under 14 CFR 91.187, the pilot in command of an aircraft operated under IFR in controlled airspace must report any malfunctions of navigational, approach, or communication equipment that occur in flight to ATC. The airspeed indicator is a required instrument for IFR flight under 14 CFR 91.205(d), so its failure is a reportable equipment malfunction.

questions.question: During an ILS approach in IMC, you notice your VSI is pegged at a constant 500 fpm descent even though you've leveled off and your altimeter shows you holding altitude. What is the most likely cause, and how do you confirm the VSI is the faulty instrument rather than the altimeter?
questions.answer: The most likely cause is a VSI failure — either a stuck mechanism or a ruptured or blocked static line affecting only the VSI if it has its own static port, or ice or blockage in the shared static system. To confirm which instrument is faulty, cross-check with the altimeter and the attitude indicator. If the altimeter is stable and the attitude indicator shows a level pitch attitude consistent with cruise power settings, and the ASI is constant, then the VSI is the unreliable instrument. The altimeter and VSI share the static system, so if the static port is fully blocked, both instruments would be affected simultaneously — the altimeter would freeze and the VSI would read zero. A VSI reading that contradicts all other instruments while they agree with each other points to VSI-specific failure.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Instrument Flying Handbook, Chapter 8; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 9

questions.question: You are on a published instrument approach in a helicopter and your heading indicator begins slowly precessing — it drifts 5 degrees every minute with no apparent cause. How does this affect your instrument scan, and what backup instrument do you use to maintain directional control?
questions.answer: A slowly precessing heading indicator becomes unreliable as the primary bank instrument during straight-and-level flight. The pilot must shift to the magnetic compass as the primary directional reference, cross-checking it with the turn-and-slip indicator. The magnetic compass is usable in straight-and-level, unaccelerated flight when it has settled. The turn-and-slip indicator becomes the primary bank instrument during any turning maneuvers. The pilot should advise ATC of the malfunction under 14 CFR 91.187 and, if the approach requires precise tracking, should consider requesting vectors or declaring a higher workload situation. Fixation on the failing heading indicator must be avoided — per the IFH, a radial scan pattern that redistributes attention across reliable instruments is essential.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.187; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 8 – Helicopter Attitude Instrument Flying

questions.question: A student pilot describes the correct technique for instrument cross-check as 'focusing on the attitude indicator and glancing at the others.' As the instructor, how do you correct this, and why is this error especially dangerous during a partial-panel approach?
questions.answer: This describes fixation, which the IFH specifically identifies as a common error. Fixating on the attitude indicator means the pilot is not verifying that the instrument is actually functioning correctly and not detecting subtle failures in other instruments early enough to take corrective action. The correct technique is a radial scan — continuously moving attention across all instruments in a systematic pattern, with dwell time allocated based on the phase of flight and what information each instrument provides. During a partial-panel approach, where one or more primary instruments have failed, the remaining instruments become even more critical. If the pilot is over-relying on the attitude indicator and it then fails, spatial disorientation can occur extremely rapidly — particularly in a helicopter, which has a much lower inertia than fixed-wing aircraft and reacts more quickly to control inputs. Per the IFH, no single instrument should dominate the scan.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 8 – Helicopter Attitude Instrument Flying

questions.question: During a checkride, the evaluator covers your attitude indicator and VSI to simulate a partial-panel approach. You recognize the failure and correctly transition to partial-panel technique — but midway through the approach, you also notice the altimeter appears to be reading approximately 200 feet higher than the approach procedure's published altimeter check point. How do you determine whether the altimeter is accurate or inaccurate, and at what point does this require you to execute a missed approach?
questions.answer: First, cross-check the altimeter against all available corroborating sources: the published crossing altitude for the fix, any DME or GPS altitude data available in the cockpit, and the radar altimeter if installed. If the barometric altimeter setting (Kollsman window) was correctly set to the current ATIS/AWOS altimeter setting, and the altimeter still disagrees by 200 feet with an expected crossing altitude or with the radar altimeter, it must be considered potentially inaccurate. Per 14 CFR 91.205(d), a functioning altimeter is required for IFR flight. Per the Aeronautical Information Manual (AIM 5-3-3), if the altimeter cannot be verified against a known elevation (such as a published DME fix altitude), the pilot should treat it as unreliable. A missed approach is required when you cannot maintain the approach with confidence in terrain/obstacle clearance — if the altimeter cannot be cross-verified and the discrepancy is unexplained, continuing the approach below MDA/DA without reliable altitude data is not authorized. The pilot must advise ATC of the equipment issue per 14 CFR 91.187 and execute the published missed approach.
questions.follow_up: Suppose your GPS-derived altitude confirms the altimeter is accurate, but the discrepancy was caused by a cold temperature correction error. How does cold temperature affect altimeter accuracy on an approach, and is there a required correction for helicopter IFR operations?
questions.follow_up_answer: Standard altimeters are calibrated based on ISA (International Standard Atmosphere) pressure lapse rates. In extremely cold temperatures, the air is denser than standard, meaning the aircraft is actually lower than the altimeter indicates. The colder the temperature, the greater the error — the aircraft can be significantly below the indicated altitude, reducing obstacle clearance. The FAA has implemented cold temperature corrections in the AIM and on specific approach procedures designated with a 'C' symbol (cold temperature restricted airports). For helicopter IFR operations, when temperatures are at or below the published cold temperature restriction, pilots must apply the corrections published in AIM Table 7-2-3 to all altitude segments of the approach. Failure to apply this correction on a cold day could result in CFIT even though all instruments appear to be functioning normally. This is a case where instruments are technically accurate but the data they present requires pilot interpretation and correction.

questions.question: From an ADM perspective, explain how the 'error chain' concept applies specifically to a scenario where a pilot fails to recognize an inaccurate primary flight instrument during an approach, and what single action has the highest probability of breaking that chain before an accident occurs.
questions.answer: Per the FAA-H-8083-21B, approximately 80% of aviation accidents are caused by human factors, and the error chain typically involves multiple compounding poor decisions rather than a single catastrophic failure. In an instrument failure scenario, the chain might start with: (1) inadequate preflight instrument check, (2) failure to maintain a proper radial scan in flight, (3) fixation on the failing instrument, (4) subtle control inputs to match the false instrument rather than cross-checking others, (5) delayed recognition of the discrepancy, and (6) continued descent below safe altitude. Each of those is a link. The single highest-probability action for breaking the chain is maintaining a disciplined, continuous radial instrument scan — because it is the only habit that simultaneously prevents fixation, enables early detection of disagreement, and forces cross-verification before any false instrument can influence flight path control. The handbook also emphasizes that if an action will only 'probably' work out, choose the option known to work — continuing an approach with an unverified instrument failure rather than executing a missed approach violates this principle. The missed approach, though inconvenient, is always the option known to work.
questions.follow_up: The handbook states that accident rates decrease significantly after 100 hours in a specific aircraft type. How does this apply to instrument failure recognition, and what is the implication for a pilot transitioning to a new helicopter model with a glass cockpit after 2,000 hours total time in conventional-instrument aircraft?
questions.follow_up_answer: Per the FAA-H-8083-21B, accident statistics correlate more strongly with hours in a specific aircraft model than with total flight hours. A pilot with 2,000 hours in conventional-instrument helicopters transitioning to a glass cockpit (PFD/MFD) system effectively resets to a lower experience level for that aircraft type. Glass cockpit failures can present differently than analog failures — a PFD can go dark entirely, display incorrect data due to a data bus fault, or show partial failures that are less visually obvious than a spinning gyro. The pilot must receive specific training in recognizing glass cockpit anomalies, including reversionary mode operations, and should not assume that 2,000 hours of total experience translates directly to proficiency in recognizing instrument failures in the new aircraft. Until approximately 100 hours in the new type are accumulated, the pilot is statistically at higher risk, and should apply more conservative personal minimums and extra vigilance in the instrument cross-check specific to that avionics suite.
