If the MEL does not list it as deferrable, the helicopter is grounded for that discrepancy until repaired. If it is listed as deferrable, the MEL's conditions and placarding requirements must be followed precisely, and the deferral itself must be documented.

questions.question: A student asks you: 'If I notice a discrepancy in flight and the RFM doesn't specifically address it in the abnormal procedures section, what should I do in flight, and then what's my documentation obligation after landing?' How do you answer?
questions.answer: In flight: Apply sound aeronautical decision-making — if the discrepancy does not affect safety of flight, note it and continue monitoring; if it does, follow the closest applicable RFM guidance or treat it as an emergency as warranted. The ADM framework (DECIDE model or similar) should guide the response, and the pilot should prioritize aviate, navigate, communicate. After landing: Regardless of whether any RFM procedure was triggered, any malfunction or abnormality must be entered in the aircraft maintenance records per 14 CFR 43.9 requirements. The entry should be factual and descriptive — what the system did, when, under what flight conditions — so that a mechanic can investigate. The helicopter must not be dispatched for another flight until the discrepancy is evaluated and either repaired or legally deferred.

questions.question: You land after an IFR flight and log a discrepancy: 'Altimeter appeared to freeze momentarily at 3,500 feet MSL during descent — suspected blocked static system.' The next pilot reviews the log, decides it was likely moisture and probably cleared itself, puts a line through it, and departs IFR. What regulatory and safety failures occurred, and what should have happened?
questions.answer: Multiple failures occurred. First, the next pilot cannot unilaterally dismiss a logged maintenance discrepancy — only a certificated mechanic (A&P or IA as appropriate) can return an aircraft to airworthy status after a logged discrepancy, and doing so requires a signed maintenance record entry per 14 CFR 43.9. Second, a suspected blocked static system directly affects the altimeter, VSI, and ASI — all three are required IFR instruments under 14 CFR 91.205(d). Departing IFR with an unresolved static system discrepancy violates 91.205 and potentially 91.7 (airworthiness). Third, the Instrument Flying Handbook notes that a blocked static system freezes the altimeter at blockage altitude and renders the VSI useless — this is a genuine IFR safety hazard. The correct procedure: log the discrepancy clearly, ground the aircraft for IFR flight, have a mechanic inspect and operationally test the static system per the appropriate maintenance manual, document the finding and any corrective action per 43.9, and only return the aircraft to IFR service after a proper maintenance sign-off.
questions.follow_up: If the mechanic inspects the static system, finds no defect, and operationally tests the altimeter and it reads correctly — can the mechanic return the aircraft to service, and what must the maintenance record entry include?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, the mechanic can return the aircraft to service if the static system tests within tolerances and no defect is found. The maintenance record entry under 14 CFR 43.9 must include: a description of the work performed (inspection and operational test of the static system), the date, the aircraft total time in service, the mechanic's name, certificate number, certificate type, and their signature. The entry should state the result — e.g., 'Inspected static ports and lines, performed altimeter system check per [applicable maintenance manual section], system within tolerances, no defects found, aircraft returned to service.' Without this signed entry, the aircraft is not legally returned to airworthy status regardless of what the mechanic did.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 43.9; 14 CFR 91.7; 14 CFR 91.205(d); FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 8

questions.question: During a postflight check, you identify two separate discrepancies: (1) the cyclic trim system was inoperative throughout the flight, and (2) one fuel quantity gauge was reading erratically. How do you evaluate each one for deferability under 91.213, and how does the legal standard for the fuel gauge differ from what you might assume?
questions.answer: Cyclic trim: The FAA-H-8083-21B specifically identifies cyclic trim as an item that is NOT automatically deferrable — if it is not listed in an approved MEL as deferrable, it requires repair before the next flight. Under 91.213(d), the pilot must verify the item is not required by 91.205, the RFM, or the type certificate data sheet. If any of those require it, it cannot be deferred without an MEL that explicitly permits it. Log the discrepancy and ground the aircraft for repair or MEL evaluation. Fuel quantity gauges: This is counterintuitive — 14 CFR 27.1337(b)(1) requires fuel quantity gauges to be accurate only when reading empty. This means an erratically-reading fuel quantity gauge that is not reading empty may not constitute an airworthiness defect under the certification standard. However, the pilot must still log the discrepancy, and a mechanic must evaluate whether the gauge's behavior affects the ability to determine usable fuel. The pilot's preflight fuel check must always be accomplished by visual inspection or measuring — never by relying on gauges alone — and this becomes even more critical with a known gauge discrepancy. The discrepancy should still be logged and evaluated; the point is that the regulatory accuracy standard is more limited than most pilots assume.
questions.follow_up: If you're operating under an approved MEL and neither discrepancy is listed in the MEL at all — meaning there's no MEL entry for cyclic trim or fuel quantity gauges — what does that mean for your deferral options?
questions.follow_up_answer: If an item is not listed in the MEL, it means the MEL provides no authority to defer it. The MEL only permits deferral of items it explicitly addresses with conditions and limitations. An item absent from the MEL must be treated as if no MEL exists for that item — you fall back to 91.213(d) for that specific item, or the aircraft must be repaired before flight. This is a common trap: pilots assume a MEL gives blanket deferral authority. It does not. The MEL is a restrictive document — it can only expand deferral authority for items it specifically lists, not for items it omits.

questions.question: Who is legally responsible for ensuring the helicopter is in an airworthy condition before each flight, and where does that responsibility come from?
questions.answer: The Pilot in Command (PIC) is responsible for ensuring the helicopter is in an airworthy condition prior to flight. This responsibility is established in 14 CFR 91.7(b), which states the PIC of a civil aircraft is responsible for determining whether that aircraft is in condition for safe flight. The PIC must discontinue the flight when unairworthy mechanical, electrical, or structural conditions occur.

questions.question: After landing and discovering a hydraulic fluid leak during your postflight inspection, what is the correct way to document this discrepancy so the next crew or maintenance personnel is aware of it?
questions.answer: Discrepancies discovered during a postflight inspection must be entered in the aircraft's maintenance logbook or a dedicated aircraft discrepancy log. The entry should describe the nature of the discrepancy clearly and accurately so that a certificated mechanic can identify and address it. The helicopter should be grounded and placarded as appropriate until the discrepancy is evaluated and corrected or properly deferred. Under 14 CFR 91.409 and 91.7, the aircraft must not be flown until the discrepancy is resolved or legally deferred.

questions.question: Under 14 CFR 91.213(d), what two requirements must be met before an inoperative piece of equipment can be legally deferred without an approved MEL?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 91.213(d), inoperative equipment may be deferred without an approved MEL if: (1) the equipment is not required by the aircraft's VFR-day type certificate, applicable airworthiness directives, or 14 CFR part 91 operating rules; and (2) the inoperative equipment is either removed from the aircraft or deactivated and placarded as INOPERATIVE. If deactivation or removal involves maintenance, a certificated and appropriately rated maintenance person must perform that work.

questions.question: You just completed an IFR flight and during postflight inspection you notice the alternate static port cover was left in place the entire flight. You also notice the altimeter was reading slightly high throughout the flight but you just assumed it was a calibration issue. What risks does this reveal, and what documentation obligations do you now have?
questions.answer: This reveals a significant airworthiness and situational awareness failure. A blocked static system causes the altimeter to freeze at the altitude where the blockage occurred, the VSI to read zero continuously, and the airspeed indicator to become inaccurate. If the alternate static source was used during the flight, it introduces its own errors — higher altitude indication, faster airspeed, and a momentary false climb on VSI due to lower cabin pressure. The risk is that IFR altitude separation may have been compromised. Documentation obligations include: entering the discrepancy (blocked static source) in the aircraft logbook, notifying maintenance so the static system can be inspected and certified as required under 14 CFR 91.411, and if the flight was conducted under IFR, a safety report via NASA ASRS should be considered to preserve good faith protections.

questions.question: During your postflight walk-around, you notice a small chip in the tail rotor blade. The helicopter is based at a remote location and the next crew needs it in the morning for a medevac flight. How does the absence of an approved MEL affect your decision, and what is the correct risk management approach?
questions.answer: The tail rotor and its components are flight-critical and are not deferrable under 14 CFR 91.213(d) — they are required by the type certificate and their failure would be catastrophic. Without an approved MEL, there is no legal mechanism to defer a damaged tail rotor blade. The helicopter must be grounded. The correct risk management approach is to: (1) document the discrepancy clearly in the maintenance record; (2) notify the operator and maintenance personnel immediately; (3) not allow any flight, including the medevac, until a certificated A&P mechanic or IA evaluates the damage and determines airworthiness. Pressure from operational needs — including emergency missions — does not override the legal airworthiness requirement. This is a classic scenario where 'get-there-itis' and mission pressure can create a fatal error chain.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.7; 14 CFR 91.213(d); FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 8 and Chapter 13

questions.question: You discover during postflight that the rotor tachometer was intermittently fluctuating during the flight but you managed the flight safely. A fellow pilot says it's fine to log it and fly it again tomorrow since you made it back. What is the specific regulatory and safety risk with that reasoning?
questions.answer: This reasoning is flawed and potentially illegal. The rotor tachometer is specifically called out in FAA-H-8083-21B as a component that is NOT deferrable — it is not listed as deferrable in the MEL because it is essential for safe rotor RPM management. Flying with an intermittently unreliable tachometer means the pilot cannot verify rotor RPM is within limits, which is critical for avoiding overspeed, underspeed, and resonance conditions. Additionally, 14 CFR 91.7 requires the PIC to determine the aircraft is airworthy before each flight — a known discrepancy that was not properly documented and addressed means the next PIC cannot make that determination accurately. The discrepancy must be entered in the maintenance log immediately, and the aircraft must be evaluated by maintenance before further flight.

questions.question: You are flying for a part 91 operator and complete an IFR cross-country. During postflight, you discover a crack in the engine cowling and a fuel quantity gauge that was showing full the entire flight — never moving — even though you burned approximately 40 gallons. Rank these discrepancies by airworthiness risk, explain the regulatory basis for each, and describe how you document and communicate them differently.
questions.answer: The cracked engine cowling must be evaluated first for structural significance — if it affects engine cooling, fire containment, or structural integrity, it is an immediate grounding item requiring inspection by an A&P mechanic. It must be documented in the aircraft logbook with a detailed description of location and size, and cannot be deferred under 91.213(d) if it affects airworthiness-critical structure. The fuel quantity gauge discrepancy is actually lower immediate risk than it might appear: under 14 CFR 27.1337(b)(1), fuel quantity gauges are only required to be accurate when reading empty — they are not required to accurately reflect fuel quantity at other levels. However, a gauge stuck at 'full' is more insidious because it provides false confidence and could mask a true fuel emergency. It should still be documented as an inoperative instrument and may be deferrable under 91.213(d) if placarded INOPERATIVE and proper fuel management procedures are substituted. Both discrepancies must be entered in the logbook before the next flight. The cowling crack should be flagged as 'requires maintenance evaluation before further flight.' The fuel gauge should be flagged with the specific symptom so maintenance can differentiate a gauge failure from a fuel system issue.
questions.follow_up: If the next PIC reviews the logbook and sees the fuel gauge entry placarded as INOPERATIVE, but the aircraft also lacks any other reliable fuel measurement method — no fuel totalizer, no sight gauge — can they legally depart IFR under part 91?
questions.follow_up_answer: This becomes a judgment call with significant risk. Under 14 CFR 91.213(d), the fuel quantity gauge may technically be deferrable if not required by the type certificate for the intended operation. However, 14 CFR 91.151 requires specific VFR fuel reserves, and 14 CFR 91.167 requires IFR fuel reserves — both implicitly require the pilot to know how much fuel is on board. Without any reliable means to determine fuel quantity, the PIC cannot legally certify compliance with fuel reserve requirements, and departing without that knowledge violates 91.7 (airworthy condition) and creates a serious safety risk. The correct decision is to not depart until fuel quantity can be verified by physical measurement (draining and measuring, checking via fuel caps if designed to allow visual check) or until the gauge is repaired. No regulatory deferral eliminates the duty to know your fuel state.

questions.question: From an ADM and human factors perspective, explain why postflight inspections are frequently skipped or rushed, what specific risks this creates for helicopter operations specifically, and what is the FAA's documented position on the relationship between human error and aviation accidents?
questions.answer: Postflight inspections are frequently skipped or rushed due to complacency ('we just flew it and it was fine'), fatigue after a long flight, time pressure, and normalization of deviance — the mistaken belief that because nothing has gone wrong before, the risk must be low. In helicopter operations, postflight inspections are especially critical because helicopters have significantly more rotating components, dynamic systems, and wear-sensitive hardware than fixed-wing aircraft. Items like main rotor blade delamination, tail rotor pitch links, mast bumping evidence, hydraulic line chafing, and transmission chip detector indicators can only be caught on the ground. Missing these during postflight means the next PIC unknowingly departs with an undetected hazard — breaking the feedback loop that makes the maintenance system effective. The FAA's documented position, per FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13, is that approximately 80% of aviation accidents are caused by human factors/pilot error, and that accidents typically result from a chain of multiple poor decisions rather than a single catastrophic error. A skipped postflight is often one link in that error chain — it rarely kills by itself, but it removes a critical safety check. Thoroughly documenting discrepancies and performing consistent postflight inspections is one of the highest-value risk mitigation behaviors available to a pilot.
questions.follow_up: If you skip your postflight inspection today because you're tired, and the next day's pilot also skips it, and on day three a blade delamination that started on day one causes a fatal accident — what is the FAA's likely finding regarding the day-one pilot's culpability, and what regulatory action could result?
questions.follow_up_answer: The FAA could find the day-one pilot in violation of 14 CFR 91.7(b) for failing to properly determine the airworthiness condition of the aircraft following the flight where the delamination likely initiated, particularly if that pilot had an obligation as PIC and if evidence showed the damage was detectable on postflight. This could result in certificate action under 49 U.S.C. 44709 (suspension or revocation) and potentially civil liability. Even if the day-one pilot is not the proximate cause of the accident, failure to perform and document postflight inspection removes a critical safety check that could have prevented the fatal outcome. The NTSB accident report would likely cite 'improper maintenance' and 'inadequate preflight/postflight inspection' as contributing factors. This illustrates why the FAA treats postflight inspection not as optional courtesy but as a professional and legal obligation — it protects not just the next crew, but the entire operational chain of accountability.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.7(b); 49 U.S.C. 44709; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 8 and Chapter 13

questions.question: Who is responsible for ensuring the helicopter is in an airworthy condition before flight, and how does that responsibility connect to your postflight inspection?
questions.answer: The PIC is responsible for ensuring the helicopter is in an airworthy condition before each flight. The postflight inspection directly supports this by identifying discrepancies, damage, or servicing needs so they can be addressed before the next flight — effectively making the postflight inspection the first step in the next PIC's airworthiness determination.

questions.question: When you find an inoperative piece of equipment during your postflight inspection, what are the two primary methods under Part 91 for deferring that item so the helicopter can legally fly again?
questions.answer: The two primary methods are: (1) the deferral provision under 14 CFR 91.213(d), which allows deferral without an FAA-approved MEL by determining the equipment is not required by the kind of operations being conducted, not required by the VFR/IFR day/night equipment list, and can be deactivated and placarded INOPERATIVE; and (2) using an FAA-approved Minimum Equipment List (MEL) specific to that aircraft, which functions as a supplemental type certificate for the aircraft.

questions.question: During your postflight inspection, you notice the fuel gauges are reading higher than you'd expect based on your fuel burn calculations. Can you rely on the fuel gauges alone to document fuel quantity for the next flight?
questions.answer: No. Under 14 CFR 27.1337(b)(1), fuel quantity gauges are only required to be accurate when indicating empty. For all other readings, they may be inaccurate. Fuel quantity should be verified by direct measurement — visually checking or using a fuel measuring device — rather than relying solely on cockpit indications when documenting actual fuel state.

questions.question: You land at a remote fuel stop, and during your postflight walk-around you find a hydraulic fluid leak at the tail rotor servo that wasn't present before departure. The aircraft has an approved MEL, but the hydraulic servo is not listed as a deferrable item. Walk me through your decision-making and documentation process.
questions.answer: Since the hydraulic servo is not listed as deferrable in the MEL, it cannot be deferred — it requires repair before the next flight. I would: (1) document the discrepancy in the aircraft maintenance logbook with a clear description of the finding, location, and conditions observed; (2) placard the aircraft appropriately and secure it; (3) contact a certificated A&P mechanic or the operator's maintenance control; (4) not attempt to deactivate or remove the component myself unless I hold an A&P certificate, since any deactivation involving maintenance must be performed by a certificated maintenance person. The MEL functions as an STC for that aircraft — deviating beyond its provisions is not authorized.

questions.question: After an IFR flight in icing conditions, your postflight inspection reveals the pitot heat annunciator light was intermittently flickering during the approach. You're not sure if it actually failed or just vibrated loose. How do you document this and what are the implications for the next flight?
questions.answer: An intermittent discrepancy must still be documented in the maintenance logbook with as much detail as possible — conditions, frequency of occurrence, phase of flight when observed, and any associated cockpit indications. Even if the equipment appeared functional most of the time, an intermittent fault in pitot heat is a safety-critical item for IFR and known icing operations. The item should be written up and inspected by a certificated maintenance person before the next IFR or known icing flight. If operating under an MEL, verify whether pitot heat is listed and under what conditions it may be deferred. Undocumented squawks create liability and safety risk for the next crew.

questions.question: You've just completed a maximum performance takeoff and confined area operation in a turbine helicopter. What specific items would you prioritize checking during your postflight inspection given the demands of those maneuvers, and why?
questions.answer: After high-demand maneuvers like maximum performance takeoffs and confined area ops, I would prioritize: (1) Main and tail rotor blades — for strikes, FOD damage, or leading edge erosion from confined area debris; (2) Tail rotor and tail boom — confined areas increase tail strike risk; (3) Engine inlet and exhaust — for FOD ingestion from confined area surfaces; (4) Skids and belly — for hard contact with terrain or obstacles not noticed during operation; (5) Engine oil and transmission oil levels — high-power operations increase thermal stress; (6) Rotor head and hub — for unusual vibration-related wear or loose hardware. The confined area environment and OGE hover power requirements stress the drivetrain and expose the airframe to debris, so a thorough postflight catches problems before they become airworthiness issues.

questions.question: You discover during your postflight inspection that the rotor tachometer needle was slightly erratic during the last flight — you didn't write it up because it seemed minor and you weren't sure. Your company's MEL does not list the rotor tachometer as deferrable. What are the legal and safety implications of your decision not to document it, and what should you have done?
questions.answer: The rotor tachometer is a safety-critical instrument — it is specifically identified in FAA guidance as a component not deferrable under a standard MEL framework because it is directly tied to safe rotor RPM management. Failing to document an observed in-flight discrepancy violates the spirit and intent of 14 CFR 91.7 (airworthiness) and creates a false record of the aircraft's condition. Legally, undocumented known defects expose the PIC to enforcement action. Practically, the next crew has no knowledge of the discrepancy and may fly an aircraft with a degrading tachometer into a situation where accurate rotor RPM indication is critical — such as an autorotation. The correct action was to document the discrepancy in the maintenance log immediately after the flight with a full description, ground the aircraft pending inspection, and notify maintenance. In-flight discrepancies are handled by RFM emergency procedures during flight, but must be written up postflight without exception.
questions.follow_up: If you had documented it, but the A&P determined no fault could be found and signed it off as 'could not duplicate,' can the helicopter fly on that signoff alone?
questions.follow_up_answer: A 'could not duplicate' maintenance entry can return an aircraft to service, but the PIC must still make an independent airworthiness determination before flight under 14 CFR 91.7. If the PIC has reason to believe the discrepancy represents a real intermittent fault — especially on a safety-critical instrument like the rotor tachometer — they have the authority and responsibility to ground the aircraft until the root cause is identified. A maintenance logbook entry does not automatically override PIC judgment about airworthiness. The PIC should discuss concerns with maintenance and ensure the signoff addresses the specific conditions under which the fault occurred.

questions.question: You're conducting a postflight inspection after a flight where you used the alternate static source during an IFR approach because the primary static system appeared blocked. The approach went fine, but now postflight you're unsure whether the blockage was real or a momentary anomaly. How do you document this event and what does it mean for the aircraft's IFR airworthiness going forward?
questions.answer: This must be documented as a maintenance discrepancy in the aircraft logbook — specifically noting that the primary static system appeared blocked in flight, requiring use of the alternate static source, the phase of flight, altitude, and weather conditions. The aircraft should not be released for IFR flight until the static system is inspected and certified by an appropriately rated maintenance technician. Under 14 CFR 91.411, the altimeter and static system must be tested and inspected within the preceding 24 calendar months for IFR operations — a known or suspected blockage event warrants immediate re-inspection regardless of when the last 91.411 check was performed. The alternate static source affects instrument readings: it produces slightly higher altitude indications, slightly faster airspeed indications, and a momentary climb indication on the VSI due to lower cabin pressure. These deviations must be understood and noted, particularly if instrument approaches were flown on the alternate source, as the approach performance data may need to be reviewed.
questions.follow_up: You note in the logbook that the alternate static source was used in flight. Does this event reset the 24-calendar-month clock for the 14 CFR 91.411 altimeter/static system inspection?
questions.follow_up_answer: Using the alternate static source does not automatically reset the 91.411 inspection clock — however, if maintenance is required to inspect and repair the primary static system (which it is in this case given the suspected blockage), any maintenance action that opens or disturbs the static system typically requires a new 91.411 test and inspection before the aircraft can be used under IFR. The maintenance technician performing the repair must re-certify the system per 14 CFR 91.411 before IFR release. The PIC should confirm with maintenance that the 91.411 certification will be re-accomplished as part of the repair.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.411; 14 CFR 91.413; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 5; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 8

areas_of_operation.title: Appendix 1: Practical Test Roles, Responsibilities, and Outcomes

tasks.title: Addition of a Helicopter Rating to an Existing Instrument Rating Certificate

questions.question: If a pilot already holds an instrument rating for airplanes and now wants to add an instrument helicopter rating, does the evaluator test them on the full instrument ACS from scratch, or is there a reduced set of tasks?
questions.answer: There is a reduced set of tasks. The evaluator uses the Additional Rating Task Table, which identifies only the specific Areas of Operation and Tasks required for the additional helicopter instrument rating. The applicant is not retested on everything already demonstrated for the existing instrument rating.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 61.65; FAA Instrument Helicopter ACS, Appendix 1, IH.X.A.K1

questions.question: What document specifically identifies which Areas of Operation and Tasks an evaluator must cover when testing a pilot for an additional Instrument Helicopter rating who already holds an instrument rating in another category?
questions.answer: The Additional Rating Task Table, found in the FAA Instrument Helicopter Airman Certification Standards (ACS). It lists the specific tasks the evaluator is required to evaluate for applicants adding a helicopter instrument rating to an existing instrument rating in another category such as airplane or powered-lift.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Instrument Helicopter ACS, Appendix 1, Additional Rating Task Table

questions.question: Why does the FAA use a separate Additional Rating Task Table rather than requiring a full instrument checkride when a certificated instrument pilot adds a helicopter category rating?
questions.answer: Because the applicant has already demonstrated the foundational instrument knowledge and skills required for an instrument rating in another category. The Additional Rating Task Table focuses evaluation on helicopter-specific instrument tasks and knowledge areas — such as helicopter aerodynamics, RFM limitations, and helicopter-specific emergency procedures — that differ meaningfully from fixed-wing instrument operations, avoiding redundant testing of already-certificated competencies.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 61.65; FAA Instrument Helicopter ACS, Appendix 1

questions.question: You are an applicant holding an instrument airplane rating, and you show up for your instrument helicopter checkride. The evaluator says they plan to test you on every single task in the Instrument Helicopter ACS because 'helicopters are completely different.' Is the evaluator correct, and what should you know about your rights as an applicant?
questions.answer: The evaluator is not correct in requiring every task from the full ACS. Per IH.X.A.K1, when an applicant already holds an instrument rating in another category, the evaluator is required to evaluate only those Areas of Operation and Tasks listed in the Additional Rating Task Table. Conducting a full retesting of all ACS tasks would exceed the regulatory scope of the practical test for an additional rating. The applicant should be prepared to respectfully reference the ACS Appendix 1 and the Additional Rating Task Table to clarify the correct scope of evaluation.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 61.65; FAA Instrument Helicopter ACS, Appendix 1, IH.X.A.K1

questions.question: A pilot holds an instrument rating in the powered-lift category and applies for an instrument helicopter rating. During the oral, the evaluator asks about helicopter-specific emergency procedures under IMC, such as inadvertent IMC recovery and engine failure during instrument flight. Are these topics fair game even though the applicant is using the Additional Rating Task Table?
questions.answer: Yes, absolutely. The Additional Rating Task Table specifically identifies tasks that are unique to or significantly different in helicopter instrument operations. Helicopter-specific emergencies such as inadvertent IMC and engine failure procedures during IFR flight are areas where helicopter operations differ substantially from powered-lift, so these would be included in the required evaluation tasks. The Additional Rating Task Table does not eliminate helicopter-specific content — it focuses the evaluation on those helicopter-specific differences that the applicant has not yet demonstrated.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Instrument Helicopter ACS, Appendix 1; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: How does the evaluator's responsibility under IH.X.A.K1 change if the applicant holds an instrument rating in the airplane category versus someone seeking their very first instrument rating in helicopters?
questions.answer: For an applicant adding an instrument helicopter rating to an existing airplane instrument rating, the evaluator uses only the Additional Rating Task Table — a focused subset of tasks covering helicopter-specific instrument competencies. For an applicant seeking their first instrument rating ever in helicopters, the evaluator must test all Areas of Operation and Tasks in the full Instrument Helicopter ACS without reduction. The key difference is that prior certificated instrument experience in another category allows the evaluator to credit previously demonstrated knowledge and skills, narrowing the evaluation scope to only the helicopter-specific differences.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 61.65; FAA Instrument Helicopter ACS, Appendix 1, IH.X.A.K1

questions.question: During a checkride debrief, a DPE tells you that even though you hold an airplane instrument rating, they tested you on airspace and IFR chart interpretation because 'the task table doesn't explicitly exclude it.' As an instrument helicopter candidate, how do you evaluate whether this was appropriate, and what is the governing principle behind the Additional Rating Task Table's authority?
questions.answer: The governing principle is that the Additional Rating Task Table is not merely a suggestion — it defines the mandatory scope of evaluation for the additional rating practical test, as stated in IH.X.A.K1. Tasks not listed in the Additional Rating Task Table are outside the required evaluation scope for an applicant adding the helicopter instrument rating to an existing instrument rating. However, a DPE retains discretion to probe related knowledge during the oral exam to ensure overall competency, as long as a failure determination is based only on tasks within the applicable ACS scope. If the DPE based a failure determination on tasks outside the Additional Rating Task Table, that would be inconsistent with ACS guidance. The applicant's recourse would be to contact the FSDO that oversees the DPE.
questions.follow_up: What if the applicant voluntarily demonstrated those extra tasks without objection — does that change the DPE's authority to use that performance in the pass/fail determination?
questions.follow_up_answer: Even if an applicant voluntarily performs tasks outside the required scope, the DPE's pass/fail determination must still be grounded in the tasks specified by the applicable ACS and the Additional Rating Task Table for that certificate/rating. Performance on tasks outside the required scope should not form the basis for an unsatisfactory determination. The ACS defines what must be tested and to what standard; it does not authorize expanding the failure criteria based on voluntary demonstrations beyond that scope.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Instrument Helicopter ACS, Appendix 1, IH.X.A.K1; 14 CFR 61.65

questions.question: A pilot holds an instrument rating in the airplane category but has never flown IFR in a helicopter and has minimal helicopter time overall. The Additional Rating Task Table limits the scope of the practical test, but what are the evaluator's responsibilities and limitations if they believe the applicant, while technically meeting ACS minimums on required tasks, is genuinely unsafe in the helicopter instrument environment?
questions.answer: The evaluator's authority is bounded by the ACS task structure — they must evaluate the tasks in the Additional Rating Task Table and apply the performance standards defined therein. If the applicant meets all required task standards, the evaluator cannot issue a Notice of Disapproval solely based on a subjective overall impression. However, evaluators are not required to pass an applicant who demonstrates unsafe practices during any required task, as safety of flight is an overarching ACS standard that applies to every task. If the evaluator observes genuine unsafe behavior during a required task, that task can be graded unsatisfactory. Additionally, if the evaluator identifies a systemic safety concern beyond the checkride scope, they should document observations and may contact the supervising FSDO. The practical answer is that the aeronautical experience requirements in 14 CFR 61.65 — including instrument time and training — are prerequisites the applicant must meet before the test even begins.
questions.follow_up: What specific aeronautical experience requirements under 14 CFR 61.65 must an applicant meet before taking the instrument helicopter practical test, regardless of what prior instrument ratings they hold?
questions.follow_up_answer: Under 14 CFR 61.65(d), for an instrument helicopter rating the applicant must log: 50 hours of cross-country flight time as pilot in command (at least 10 of which must be in helicopters), 40 hours of actual or simulated instrument time (at least 15 of which must be in helicopters), and 3 hours of instrument flight training in helicopters from an authorized instructor within the 2 calendar months preceding the practical test. These requirements are not waived by holding an existing instrument rating in another category — only the practical test scope changes, not the experience prerequisites.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 61.65(d); FAA Instrument Helicopter ACS, Appendix 1, IH.X.A.K1

questions.question: When adding a helicopter rating to an existing instrument rating, the Additional Instrument Table specifies which Areas of Operation you must be tested on. What does 'Area of Operation IV – All' mean in practical terms for your checkride?
questions.answer: It means every task within Area of Operation IV is required for the helicopter add-on instrument checkride. You cannot skip or substitute any task in that Area of Operation — the examiner must evaluate all of them. This is in contrast to areas where only specific tasks (e.g., A and C) are listed, meaning the others from that area are already credited from the existing airplane/powered-lift instrument rating.

questions.question: The Additional Instrument Table shows Area of Operation I as 'None (Airplane/Powered-Lift)' for the helicopter add-on. What does that designation mean for a pilot who already holds an instrument rating in airplanes?
questions.answer: It means Area of Operation I tasks are not required for the helicopter instrument add-on checkride. The FAA has determined that those tasks — typically covering regulatory and flight planning knowledge common to all instrument ratings — are already demonstrated by the existing airplane instrument rating. The pilot receives credit for that entire area and is not re-tested on it.

questions.question: According to the Additional Instrument Table for the helicopter add-on, Area of Operation VII requires only tasks B and C. What does that tell you about task A in that area?
questions.answer: Task A in Area of Operation VII is not required for the helicopter instrument add-on checkride. The existing airplane or powered-lift instrument rating already satisfies that task. Only tasks B and C — which are either helicopter-specific or address unique helicopter instrument operations — must be demonstrated to the examiner.

questions.question: You hold an instrument rating for airplanes and are preparing for the helicopter instrument add-on checkride. Your examiner says you only need to prepare for Areas II, IV, VI, VII, and VIII. You argue that you also need Area III. Who is correct and why?
questions.answer: The examiner is correct. According to the Additional Instrument Table under IH.X.A.K2, Area of Operation III is listed as 'None,' meaning it is fully credited from the existing airplane instrument rating and is not required for the helicopter add-on. Area of Operation II requires tasks A and C; Areas IV, VI, and VIII require all tasks; Area VII requires tasks B and C. Area III is not tested.

questions.question: Area of Operation II requires only tasks A and C for the helicopter instrument add-on. Why would the FAA specifically require those two tasks but not others in that same area, rather than just crediting the whole area from the existing rating?
questions.answer: Tasks A and C in Area of Operation II are required because they address helicopter-specific instrument operations that are meaningfully different from their airplane equivalents. The FAA determined that skills or knowledge in those specific tasks cannot be assumed from an airplane instrument rating — helicopter systems, flight characteristics under IFR, or cockpit management may differ enough to warrant direct evaluation. Tasks not listed are considered sufficiently equivalent to what was already demonstrated in the airplane rating.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA ACS IH.X.A.K2; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 5; 14 CFR 61.65

questions.question: A helicopter CFI-I candidate tells you that for the helicopter instrument add-on, since Areas I, III, and V are all listed as 'None,' the checkride will be relatively short. Is that a reasonable assumption? What areas actually require full evaluation?
questions.answer: It is partially correct that Areas I, III, and V require no additional testing and are credited from the existing rating. However, 'relatively short' is debatable. Three entire areas still require ALL tasks: Area of Operation IV, VI, and VIII. Additionally, Area II requires tasks A and C, and Area VII requires tasks B and C. That is a substantial evaluation scope covering all tasks in three full areas plus selected tasks in two others. The checkride is significantly reduced from a full instrument rating practical test, but it is not a minor undertaking.

questions.question: As an examiner, I tell you that for your helicopter instrument add-on, Area of Operation VI requires 'All' tasks. What helicopter-specific factors make Area VI instrument tasks genuinely different from what you demonstrated in your airplane instrument checkride, and why can't those be credited from your existing rating?
questions.answer: Area of Operation VI typically covers instrument approaches and related procedures. Helicopters have unique instrument approach considerations: they can execute approaches to heliports with non-standard geometry, fly point-in-space (PinS) approaches, use vertically guided approaches to pads with steep vertical descent profiles, and execute copter-specific approach procedures not available to fixed-wing aircraft. Additionally, helicopter instrument flight involves unique control coordination — collective for altitude management simultaneously with cyclic and pedal inputs — and the absence of a stabilizer means the pilot must actively manage pitch attitude throughout. These helicopter-specific technique and judgment requirements mean direct re-demonstration is warranted rather than crediting the airplane rating.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA ACS IH.X.A.K2; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; 14 CFR 97.3 (copter approaches); AIM 5-4-18
questions.follow_up: You mentioned PinS approaches — if I asked you to fly a PinS approach during the checkride, what is the key decision point that distinguishes a PinS 'Proceed VFR' from a PinS 'Proceed Visual' approach, and how does each affect your minimums and subsequent flight path?
questions.follow_up_answer: A PinS 'Proceed VFR' approach requires the pilot to transition from the MAP to VFR flight conditions to reach the landing site — you must have weather at or above basic VFR minimums to continue. A PinS 'Proceed Visual' approach requires that you acquire the landing site visually before or at the MAP and then continue using visual references. The distinction affects how you evaluate weather before committing to the approach and what actions are required if visual contact is not established: 'Proceed VFR' mandates VFR weather exist; 'Proceed Visual' mandates actual visual acquisition of the landing site. Failure to meet the respective criteria requires execution of the missed approach procedure. This is unique to helicopter operations and has no direct fixed-wing equivalent.

questions.question: The Additional Instrument Table credits Areas I, III, and V entirely from an existing airplane instrument rating. As a practical examiner, I'm going to probe your understanding: if I discovered during the oral exam that your knowledge of Area I topics — regulatory requirements and flight planning — is dangerously deficient specific to helicopter IFR operations, can I still test you on those items even though the table says 'None'?
questions.answer: Yes. The 'None' designation in the Additional Instrument Table indicates that those areas are not required demonstration tasks for the add-on checkride — it does not prohibit an examiner from asking questions if safety-relevant deficiencies are revealed during the evaluation. Under 14 CFR 61.43 and the Examiner's Handbook, an examiner has the authority and responsibility to evaluate overall pilot competency. If during the oral exam a candidate demonstrates a clear lack of knowledge that poses a safety risk — such as not understanding IFR currency requirements specific to helicopters or helicopter-specific flight planning factors — the examiner can and should address those deficiencies. A 'None' credit assumes existing competency; it does not waive an examiner's safety discretion.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA ACS IH.X.A.K2; 14 CFR 61.43; FAA Order 8900.2 (Designated Pilot Examiner Handbook)
questions.follow_up: If I determine during the checkride that your demonstrated deficiency warrants discontinuing the test, what are your options and rights as an applicant, and does a Notice of Disapproval on the add-on test affect your existing airplane instrument rating?
questions.follow_up_answer: If the examiner discontinues the test, they issue a Notice of Disapproval (FAA Form 8710-1 or IACRA equivalent) specifying the areas not successfully completed. The applicant retains all areas already satisfactorily completed and only needs to retest on the failed areas — they do not restart from scratch. Critically, a Notice of Disapproval on the helicopter instrument add-on does NOT affect the existing airplane instrument rating; that certificate remains valid and intact. The add-on is a separate practical test for a rating addition; failure does not remove previously held privileges. The applicant may retest after additional training, with a new application and examiner.

questions.question: When adding a helicopter rating to an existing instrument rating, which area of operation contains the task that is only required if you bring a multiengine helicopter to the checkride?
questions.answer: Area of Operation VII, Emergency Operations. Specifically, Task B within that area does not apply unless the applicant supplies a multiengine helicopter for the practical test.

questions.question: Who bears the responsibility for determining whether Emergency Operations Task B in Area of Operation VII will be tested during an instrument helicopter rating addition checkride?
questions.answer: The applicant bears that responsibility by their choice of aircraft. If the applicant supplies a multiengine helicopter for the practical test, Task B applies and will be evaluated. If the applicant supplies a single-engine helicopter, Task B is not applicable and will not be tested.

questions.question: If you are adding an instrument helicopter rating to your existing instrument certificate and you show up with a single-engine helicopter, does Emergency Operations Task B need to be demonstrated?
questions.answer: No. Per the ACS, Emergency Operations Task B in Area of Operation VII does not apply unless the applicant supplies a multiengine helicopter. A single-engine helicopter applicant is not required to demonstrate that task.

questions.question: You are scheduled to add a helicopter rating to your existing instrument certificate and plan to use a twin-engine helicopter for the checkride. During your preflight, you discover a mechanical issue that requires you to substitute a single-engine helicopter at the last minute. How does this change the scope of your practical test regarding Emergency Operations?
questions.answer: Switching to a single-engine helicopter removes the requirement for Emergency Operations Task B in Area of Operation VII. Since Task B only applies when the applicant supplies a multiengine helicopter, the examiner cannot test that task using the single-engine aircraft. The rest of the applicable ACS tasks remain in effect. The applicant should brief the examiner on the aircraft change before the test begins.

questions.question: A pilot holds a single-engine instrument airplane rating and wants to add an instrument helicopter rating. They bring a twin-engine helicopter to the checkride. What is the practical implication of IH.X.A.K3 for this applicant's test?
questions.answer: Because the applicant supplied a multiengine helicopter, Emergency Operations Task B in Area of Operation VII is now applicable and must be evaluated. The examiner is required to test Task B as part of the practical test. The applicant must be prepared to demonstrate the knowledge and skills associated with multiengine helicopter emergency operations, including engine failure scenarios specific to that aircraft.

questions.question: Why does the ACS make Emergency Operations Task B conditional on the applicant supplying a multiengine helicopter, rather than simply requiring it for all instrument helicopter rating additions?
questions.answer: Emergency Operations Task B addresses emergency procedures specific to multiengine helicopters — such as single-engine failures, OEI operations, and related emergency checklists — that are not applicable or demonstrable in a single-engine helicopter. Requiring these tasks of a single-engine applicant would be impractical and irrelevant to the aircraft they are being certificated to fly. The ACS is designed to test only what is operationally relevant to the aircraft used for the test, ensuring standards are meaningful and safety-based.
questions.regulatory_ref: Instrument Helicopter ACS, Appendix 1, IH.X.A.K3; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: An applicant adds an instrument helicopter rating using a single-engine helicopter and is not tested on Emergency Operations Task B. Six months later, they begin flying a twin-engine helicopter IFR for an employer. What is the regulatory and safety implication of never having been evaluated on Task B?
questions.answer: The pilot is legally certificated to act as PIC of that multiengine helicopter under their instrument helicopter rating, since ratings are not type or category-restricted by number of engines for helicopters. However, they were never evaluated on multiengine emergency operations specific to instrument flight. The regulatory safety net is found in 14 CFR 61.31 for any type rating requirements on specific aircraft, and the employer's own training and qualification program (such as Part 135 or 91 subpart K requirements) should include multiengine helicopter emergency training. From a safety standpoint, the pilot should seek training and evaluation on OEI procedures before conducting IFR operations in a multiengine helicopter.
questions.follow_up: Would a flight instructor endorsement or additional checkride be legally required before that pilot flies the twin-engine helicopter IFR?
questions.follow_up_answer: Not necessarily for the instrument rating itself — no separate endorsement is required solely for transitioning from a single-engine to multiengine helicopter under the helicopter category rating. However, if the specific aircraft requires a type rating under 14 CFR 61.31, the pilot must hold that type rating. Additionally, if operating under Part 135, the operator's operations specifications and training program will impose their own currency and qualification requirements, which would typically include multiengine helicopter emergency procedures training before IFR line operations.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 61.31; 14 CFR Part 135; Instrument Helicopter ACS, Appendix 1, IH.X.A.K3

questions.question: As an examiner, if an applicant arrives with a multiengine helicopter for an instrument rating addition checkride and then requests mid-checkride to switch tasks away from Emergency Operations Task B due to a non-safety-of-flight maintenance concern with one engine, how should you handle this under the ACS framework?
questions.answer: If a genuine airworthiness concern exists mid-checkride, the examiner must prioritize safety and cannot require the applicant to continue operating with a system that may be unairworthy. The examiner should discontinue or defer that portion of the test. The applicant has not failed Task B — a discontinuance for a legitimate airworthiness or safety reason is not a failure. Per FAA guidance, the examiner would issue a notice of disapproval only for tasks already failed, and the applicant may return to complete the remaining tasks in a subsequent test with a different aircraft if needed. If the applicant returns with a single-engine helicopter for the re-test, Task B would no longer apply per IH.X.A.K3, but the examiner should document what occurred and consult FAA FSDO guidance on whether the previously uncompleted task can be waived or must be deferred.
questions.follow_up: If the applicant ultimately completes the rating addition using only a single-engine helicopter on the re-test, and Task B was never evaluated on either attempt, is the rating legally valid?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, the rating is legally valid. The ACS explicitly states that Task B does not apply unless the applicant supplies a multiengine helicopter. If neither test included a multiengine helicopter, Task B was never applicable, and the examiner had no authority to require it. The resulting instrument helicopter rating is fully valid and unrestricted by the number of engines, though the safety and operational implications of the pilot's limited multiengine IFR emergency training remain — addressed through employer training programs and the pilot's own professional responsibility.
questions.regulatory_ref: Instrument Helicopter ACS, Appendix 1, IH.X.A.K3; FAA Order 8900.2 (General Aviation Airman Designee Handbook); 14 CFR 61.39

tasks.title: Instrument Proficiency Check

questions.question: Under 14 CFR 61.57(d), when is a pilot required to complete an Instrument Proficiency Check (IPC)?
questions.answer: A pilot must complete an IPC when they have not met the instrument currency requirements of 14 CFR 61.57(c) — specifically, if they have not logged the required six instrument approaches, holding procedures and tasks, and intercepting and tracking courses within the preceding six calendar months, AND an additional six calendar months have passed beyond the initial lapse (a total of 12 calendar months). After that 12-month window, the pilot may not act as PIC under IFR or in IMC until completing an IPC.

questions.question: Who is authorized to conduct an Instrument Proficiency Check for a helicopter pilot under 14 CFR 61.57(d)?
questions.answer: Under 14 CFR 61.57(d), an IPC must be given by an examiner, an authorized instructor, or a person approved by the FAA Administrator. For helicopter pilots, this means an FAA-designated pilot examiner (DPE), an FAA Aviation Safety Inspector (ASI), or a flight instructor with an appropriate instrument rating (CFII) who is authorized to conduct the check in the rotorcraft category.

questions.question: After successfully completing an IPC, what instrument currency does the pilot receive, and when does it begin?
questions.answer: Upon successful completion of an IPC, the pilot is restored to instrument currency. The new six-calendar-month currency period begins at the end of the calendar month in which the IPC was completed. The pilot may then act as PIC under IFR or in IMC, provided they maintain the ongoing currency requirements of 14 CFR 61.57(c) — six instrument approaches, holding, and tracking/intercepting within each subsequent six-calendar-month period.

questions.question: A helicopter pilot completed their last instrument approaches 14 months ago and has flown no instrument time since. They want to fly IFR tomorrow. Walk me through exactly what is required before they can legally act as PIC under IFR.
questions.answer: Since more than 12 calendar months have passed since the pilot last met the 61.57(c) currency requirements, they are beyond the allowable lapse window and must complete a full IPC per 14 CFR 61.57(d). The IPC must be conducted by an authorized examiner or CFII and must cover the areas of operation and tasks specified in the instrument rating ACS appropriate for rotorcraft. Simply logging six approaches on their own is not sufficient — the IPC is mandatory. Once the IPC is successfully completed, the pilot is restored to currency and may fly IFR. The new six-calendar-month currency window begins at the end of the calendar month in which the IPC was completed.

questions.question: A helicopter pilot is 9 months beyond their last logged instrument currency tasks. Their CFII offers to log them 6 practice approaches in simulated IMC without formally conducting an IPC. Does this restore the pilot's instrument currency under 14 CFR 61.57?
questions.answer: No. Once a pilot has exceeded the initial six-calendar-month lapse window, logging approaches informally does not restore currency. Under 14 CFR 61.57(d), when the pilot is in the second six-month window (months 7–12) or beyond, they must complete a formal IPC administered by an authorized examiner or CFII. Simply logging approaches — even with a CFII present — does not satisfy the IPC requirement unless the CFII formally conducts and endorses the check as an IPC covering all required areas of operation per the applicable ACS. Without the formal IPC endorsement, the pilot remains unable to act as PIC under IFR.

questions.question: Can a helicopter pilot complete an IPC in a fixed-wing aircraft or a full-flight simulator approved for fixed-wing operations to restore their helicopter instrument currency?
questions.answer: No. The IPC must be conducted in the appropriate aircraft category. A helicopter pilot must complete the IPC in a helicopter or in a flight training device (FTD), aviation training device (ATD), or full-flight simulator that is approved for the rotorcraft category and rated for the appropriate tasks. Completing an IPC in a fixed-wing airplane or a fixed-wing simulator does not restore instrument currency for helicopter operations, because the instrument ACS requirements for rotorcraft are specific to that aircraft category.

questions.question: A CFII administers an IPC to a helicopter pilot and the pilot fails one area of operation — specifically, demonstrates unsatisfactory performance on a localizer approach. The CFII logs instrument approaches and notes the training but does not endorse an IPC completion. What is the pilot's legal status for IFR flight, and what options does the pilot have?
questions.answer: The pilot's legal status has not changed — they remain unable to act as PIC under IFR because the IPC was not successfully completed. An IPC is a pass/fail evaluation; partial credit or area-specific endorsements are not provided under 14 CFR 61.57(d). The CFII may log the flight as instrument training, and the pilot may log any instrument time and approaches flown, but no IPC endorsement can be given. The pilot's options are: (1) receive additional instrument training from a CFII to address the deficiency, then attempt the IPC again; (2) seek an IPC from another authorized examiner. The pilot may not fly as PIC in IMC or under an IFR flight plan until a complete, satisfactory IPC is endorsed.
questions.follow_up: If the same CFII who administered the failed IPC later provides remedial training and re-administers the IPC on the same day, is there any regulatory concern with that arrangement?
questions.follow_up_answer: Technically, the same CFII is authorized to both provide training and administer the IPC — there is no regulatory prohibition under 14 CFR 61.57(d) against the same instructor doing both. However, there is a practical and ethical concern: the CFII must ensure objectivity and that the pilot has genuinely corrected the deficiency before endorsing the IPC. The FAA expects CFIIs to exercise sound professional judgment. Additionally, if the same instructor administers both the training and the check repeatedly without genuine demonstrated improvement, this could raise questions about the validity of the endorsement and the instructor's standards if reviewed in an enforcement action.

questions.question: A helicopter pilot holds both a helicopter instrument rating and an airplane instrument rating. They are current in the airplane but have not flown instruments in the helicopter in over 18 months. Can they leverage their airplane IPC or currency to fly IFR in the helicopter?
questions.answer: No. Instrument currency and IPC completion are category-specific under 14 CFR 61.57. Currency logged in the airplane category — including approaches, holding, and any IPC — does not satisfy the instrument currency requirement for the rotorcraft category. The helicopter pilot must independently maintain and restore currency for rotorcraft instrument operations. Since 18 months have passed, they are beyond both the initial six-month currency window and the second six-month window, meaning a formal IPC in the rotorcraft category is required before acting as PIC under IFR in the helicopter. Each aircraft category requires its own separate instrument currency under 14 CFR 61.57(c).
questions.follow_up: If this same pilot logs six helicopter instrument approaches in simulated IMC under the hood with a safety pilot during the period between months 7 and 12 of their lapse, does that restore helicopter instrument currency?
questions.follow_up_answer: No. Once the pilot has entered the second six-calendar-month window (months 7 through 12 from the end of the last currency period), logging approaches alone — even in the helicopter — does not restore currency. Under 14 CFR 61.57(d), a formal IPC is the only way to restore currency once the pilot is in or beyond that second window. The six approaches logged would count as instrument training and could be entered in the logbook, but without the formal IPC endorsement from an authorized instructor or examiner, the pilot remains grounded from IFR PIC operations in the helicopter.

questions.question: When a CFII conducts an Instrument Proficiency Check for a helicopter pilot, what document defines the standards that pilot must meet to successfully complete the IPC?
questions.answer: The Instrument Rating – Helicopter Airman Certification Standards (ACS) defines the standards. The evaluator must ensure the pilot demonstrates the knowledge, risk management, and skill elements specified in the ACS to the required performance levels.

questions.question: Under 14 CFR 61.57(d), how does a pilot who has lost instrument currency regain the privilege to act as pilot in command under IFR?
questions.answer: A pilot who no longer meets the recency-of-experience requirements of 14 CFR 61.57(c) must pass an Instrument Proficiency Check (IPC) given by an authorized check pilot, a CFII, an instrument ground instructor (for the knowledge portion), or a person designated by the FAA. Once the IPC is satisfactorily completed, instrument currency is restored.

questions.question: An IPC is not a checkride for a new certificate, but the evaluator still has a specific obligation regarding standards. What is that obligation, and where does it come from?
questions.answer: The evaluator conducting the IPC must ensure the pilot meets every applicable standard established in the Instrument Rating ACS for helicopters. This obligation comes directly from the ACS itself (IH.X.B.K2) and from 14 CFR 61.57(d), which requires the IPC to be conducted in accordance with the areas of operation and instrument tasks that apply to the category and class of aircraft.

questions.question: You are a CFII administering an IPC to a helicopter pilot. During the oral portion, the pilot demonstrates solid knowledge of all systems, but during the flight portion she consistently fails to maintain instrument approach minimums within ACS tolerances. What must you do, and what happens to her instrument currency?
questions.answer: Because the pilot did not meet the standards established in the ACS, the IPC is unsatisfactory. You must not sign off the IPC as complete. Her instrument currency is not restored — she remains unable to act as PIC under IFR. You should debrief the deficiencies, conduct additional training as necessary, and administer another IPC when she is ready. The ACS requires the evaluator to ensure the pilot meets all applicable standards; partial completion does not satisfy the requirement.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 61.57(d); FAA-S-ACS-9; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 1 (evaluator responsibility context)

questions.question: A CFII who administers an IPC is not an FAA designated examiner. Does that change the standard the pilot must meet to complete the IPC successfully? Explain your reasoning.
questions.answer: No — the standard does not change. The ACS explicitly states that evaluators conducting an IPC must ensure the pilot meets the standards established in the ACS, regardless of whether the evaluator is a DPE or a CFII. The same knowledge, risk management, and skill tolerances apply. The difference is that a DPE issues a new certificate or rating on a successful checkride, while a CFII documents IPC completion in the pilot's logbook. The performance bar is identical.

questions.question: A helicopter pilot holds both a fixed-wing instrument rating and a rotorcraft-helicopter instrument rating. She completes an IPC in a Cessna 172 with a CFII. Does this IPC restore her helicopter instrument currency?
questions.answer: No. The IPC must be accomplished in each category for which instrument privileges are sought. An IPC completed in an airplane restores instrument currency for airplane operations only. To restore rotorcraft-helicopter instrument currency, she must complete an IPC in a helicopter (or an approved simulator/FTD representing a helicopter) that covers the applicable helicopter instrument areas of operation specified in the ACS.

questions.question: As a CFII administering a helicopter IPC, you observe that the pilot's ADM throughout the flight is consistently poor — she fixates on instrument failures, fails to communicate a deteriorating situation, and narrows her attention under workload. All numeric tolerances are technically within ACS limits. Are you required to pass her? Defend your answer.
questions.answer: No, you are not required to pass her. The ACS standards include risk management and ADM elements, not just numeric flight tolerances. The ACS specifically evaluates pilot ADM, risk management, and SRM as discrete task elements. If the evaluator determines the pilot did not meet these non-numeric standards — for example, failing to correctly identify or mitigate risks, or demonstrating unsafe decision-making patterns — the IPC may be unsatisfactory. The FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook notes that ~80% of accidents stem from human factors; poor ADM represents a real safety deficiency. Meeting altitude and heading tolerances alone does not constitute meeting 'the standards established in this ACS.'
questions.follow_up: What specific ACS areas would you cite to document why you found the IPC unsatisfactory based on ADM deficiencies rather than stick-and-rudder performance?
questions.follow_up_answer: You would reference the Risk Management (RM) and, where applicable, the Skills elements of the relevant ACS tasks — for example, tasks covering instrument approaches, holding, or unusual attitudes. Each task in the ACS includes risk management items such as identifying hazards, recognizing automation or system failures, and applying SRM. You would document in the logbook or on any internal training record which specific task's risk management elements were not met, citing the ACS task code (e.g., IH.VI.A.R1 or similar) to give the pilot clear feedback and a path for remediation.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 61.57(d); FAA-S-ACS-9; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM and SRM)

questions.question: A CFII conducts a helicopter IPC but only covers the approach and holding tasks because 'that's what the pilot really needed work on.' The pilot performs those tasks to ACS standards. Is the IPC legally complete? What is the evaluator's exposure?
questions.answer: No, the IPC is not legally complete. 14 CFR 61.57(d) requires the IPC to include the areas of operation and instrument tasks that are applicable to the category and class. The ACS defines those required areas — a CFII cannot selectively omit portions of the ACS and still certify that the pilot meets 'the standards established in this ACS.' If the CFII logs the IPC as satisfactory without covering all required areas, they have made a false logbook entry, which violates 14 CFR 61.51 and can be considered falsification under 14 CFR 61.59. The CFII could face certificate action, and the pilot could face enforcement action if they operate IFR based on an improperly administered IPC.
questions.follow_up: Is there any legitimate way a CFII can tailor or limit the scope of an IPC while still satisfying the regulatory requirement?
questions.follow_up_answer: The ACS does allow some flexibility in that an evaluator may combine tasks and does not have to demonstrate every procedure if the evaluator determines the pilot is proficient in areas not flown — but this is a judgment call that must be defensible and documented. In practice, the evaluator should still address all applicable areas of operation at minimum through oral examination or scenario-based discussion, and the rationale for omitting any flight demonstration should be noted. Any area the evaluator cannot assess as meeting ACS standards must be demonstrated or tested — selective omission without documented assessment is not acceptable and exposes the CFII to the enforcement risks described above.

questions.question: When a helicopter pilot undergoes an Instrument Proficiency Check, which Area of Operation in the Instrument ACS requires ALL tasks to be completed?
questions.answer: Areas of Operation VI and VIII both require all tasks to be completed during an IPC. Area of Operation VI covers instrument approaches, and Area of VIII covers emergency operations — no tasks within those areas may be skipped during the IPC.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 61.57(d); FAA-S-ACS-18 Instrument Rating ACS, IH.X.B.K3

questions.question: Which Areas of Operation require NO tasks to be completed during a helicopter Instrument Proficiency Check?
questions.answer: Areas of Operation I and II require no tasks during an IPC. This means the examiner or authorized instructor conducting the IPC is not required to evaluate any tasks from those two areas.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 61.57(d); FAA-S-ACS-18 Instrument Rating ACS, IH.X.B.K3

questions.question: For a helicopter IPC, Area of Operation VII requires specific tasks — which ones are they?
questions.answer: For Area of Operation VII, only Tasks B and C are required during an IPC. Not all tasks in Area of Operation VII must be demonstrated — only those two designated tasks.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 61.57(d); FAA-S-ACS-18 Instrument Rating ACS, IH.X.B.K3

questions.question: You are an authorized instructor conducting an IPC for a helicopter pilot. The pilot asks if you can skip Area of Operation VI — instrument approaches — because she just flew three approaches last week under actual IMC. How do you respond, and why?
questions.answer: You must decline to skip Area of Operation VI. The IPC task requirements under IH.X.B.K3 specify that ALL tasks in Area of Operation VI must be completed during the IPC. Recent actual IMC experience does not substitute for the IPC evaluation requirement. The IPC is a structured assessment with specific required tasks, not simply a currency flight. If she has recent instrument experience, it may reduce her preparation time, but it does not waive any required IPC tasks.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 61.57(d); FAA-S-ACS-18 Instrument Rating ACS, IH.X.B.K3

questions.question: A helicopter pilot completed an IPC but the authorized instructor only evaluated Task A in Area of Operation V. Was the IPC valid, and what does IH.X.B.K3 require for Area V?
questions.answer: Area of Operation V requires only Task A during an IPC, so evaluating Task A satisfies the requirement for that area. The IPC is valid with respect to Area V. The instructor must also confirm that all other required areas and tasks — particularly all of Areas VI and VIII, Task B of Area III, Task B of Area IV, and Tasks B and C of Area VII — were completed to make the overall IPC valid.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 61.57(d); FAA-S-ACS-18 Instrument Rating ACS, IH.X.B.K3

questions.question: A helicopter instrument pilot hasn't flown under IFR in 14 months. He asks why the IPC requires specific tasks from certain Areas of Operation rather than just any tasks the instructor chooses. What is the purpose of specifying required IPC tasks in the ACS?
questions.answer: The FAA specifies required IPC tasks to ensure that every pilot who completes an IPC has demonstrated proficiency in the most safety-critical areas of instrument flight — such as instrument approaches, partial panel operations, and emergency procedures. Standardizing the required tasks prevents instructors from conducting an IPC that only covers areas the pilot is already comfortable with, which would not adequately validate overall instrument proficiency. This structure ensures a consistent, minimum standard of competency regardless of who conducts the IPC.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 61.57(d); FAA-S-ACS-18 Instrument Rating ACS, IH.X.B.K3; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 1

questions.question: During an IPC debrief, a pilot argues that because Areas I and II have no required tasks, those subjects — preflight and ground operations — are completely irrelevant to the IPC and don't need to be discussed at all. Do you agree? Why or why not?
questions.answer: Not necessarily. While IH.X.B.K3 specifies that Areas I and II have no required tasks for the IPC, the authorized instructor or examiner retains discretion to evaluate or discuss any area they believe is relevant to the pilot's safe instrument operation. The 'no required tasks' designation means those areas are not mandatory, not that they are off-limits or irrelevant. Additionally, ADM and risk management — which are embedded throughout the ACS — may surface naturally during any phase of the IPC discussion, including topics that relate to preflight planning or weather evaluation. The FAA's intent is a minimum standard, not a ceiling.
questions.follow_up: If the pilot had a significant knowledge deficiency about IFR preflight weather planning during the IPC ground portion, what authority does the instructor have even though Area I has no required tasks?
questions.follow_up_answer: The authorized instructor conducting an IPC has the authority — and the responsibility — to decline to sign off the IPC if they observe a significant deficiency that affects the pilot's ability to operate safely in the IFR system, even if that deficiency falls in an area with no required tasks. Signing off an IPC certifies that the pilot is proficient in instrument operations per 14 CFR 61.57(d). If the pilot cannot demonstrate adequate knowledge of IFR preflight planning, the instructor is not obligated to complete the sign-off regardless of task completion status.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 61.57(d); FAA-S-ACS-18 Instrument Rating ACS, IH.X.B.K3; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM)

questions.question: A helicopter pilot completed an IPC where the instructor evaluated Task B in Area III and Task B in Area IV, but only one instrument approach in Area VI, arguing that one approach satisfies 'all tasks' since that was the only approach flown that day due to weather. Is this IPC valid under IH.X.B.K3?
questions.answer: This is likely not a valid IPC. 'All tasks' in Area of Operation VI means all of the tasks listed within that area of the ACS must be demonstrated — not just the number of approaches the weather permitted that day. If Area VI contains multiple tasks (such as precision approaches, non-precision approaches, circling, missed approach, etc.) and only one was evaluated, the IPC does not meet the standard regardless of weather conditions. The instructor should have either postponed, used a flight simulator/ATD for the remaining approaches, or documented why the IPC could not be completed, rather than signing it off as complete.
questions.follow_up: Can a flight simulator or Aviation Training Device be used to complete the required IPC tasks that could not be accomplished due to weather, and if so, what regulatory limitation applies to the device?
questions.follow_up_answer: Yes, 14 CFR 61.57(d) permits the use of an FAA-approved flight simulator or flight training device to complete IPC tasks, provided the device is representative of the helicopter category. The device must be approved for the specific maneuvers being evaluated, and the instructor must be authorized to conduct the IPC in that device. An ATD or FTD cannot be substituted for actual or simulated instrument flight in ways the device is not approved to replicate, and the overall IPC must still meet all required task standards.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 61.57(d); 14 CFR 61.4; FAA-S-ACS-18 Instrument Rating ACS, IH.X.B.K3

questions.question: During an Instrument Proficiency Check, which area of operation and task is waived if the applicant shows up in a single-engine helicopter?
questions.answer: Area of Operation VII, Emergency Operations, Task B is not required unless the applicant supplies a multiengine helicopter. If the applicant flies a single-engine helicopter, Task B in that area simply does not apply.
questions.regulatory_ref: IPC ACS IH.X.B.K4; FAA Instrument Rating ACS Appendix 1

questions.question: Who is responsible for determining whether the multiengine emergency operations task must be completed during an Instrument Proficiency Check?
questions.answer: The applicant determines this by virtue of the aircraft they supply for the check. If the applicant brings a multiengine helicopter, Task B under Emergency Operations applies and must be completed. If the applicant supplies only a single-engine helicopter, that task does not apply. The examiner cannot require multiengine tasks if the applicant has not provided a multiengine aircraft.
questions.regulatory_ref: IPC ACS IH.X.B.K4; FAA Instrument Rating ACS Appendix 1
