questions.answer: Evaluator discretion means the examiner — not the applicant — determines whether each non-precision approach will be completed with a landing or a missed approach. This allows the evaluator to test both skills in any combination and prevents the applicant from anticipating which outcome will be required, ensuring a more realistic evaluation of both procedures.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Instrument Rating ACS (FAA-S-ACS-8), Task IH.XII.D.S1

questions.question: Why is it important as a helicopter instrument pilot to be fully prepared to execute either a landing or a missed approach at the completion of every non-precision approach, without advance notice?
questions.answer: Because the evaluator has discretion to call either outcome without prior notice, the applicant must maintain situational awareness, proper aircraft configuration, and mental readiness for both contingencies throughout the approach. In real IFR operations, conditions at minimums may suddenly require a missed approach even when a landing was expected, so this evaluation reflects real-world demands.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Instrument Rating ACS (FAA-S-ACS-8), Task IH.XII.D.S1; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: You are flying a VOR non-precision approach to a heliport during your checkride. You reach the MDA and have the touchdown area in sight. The evaluator says nothing. How do you determine whether to land or go missed, and what are the key standards you must meet for whichever outcome is required?
questions.answer: Since the evaluator has discretion over the outcome, you should fly the approach to decision point at MDA while maintaining required obstacle clearance and not descending below MDA until conditions allow a normal landing. Absent a clear instruction to land or go missed, fly the approach to the missed approach point (MAP) as published. If landing is required, you must transition from instrument conditions to a stabilized approach to the helispot, maintaining appropriate airspeed and descent profile. If a missed approach is required, you must immediately apply power, arrest descent, establish climb attitude, and follow the published missed approach procedure — including climbing to the specified altitude and navigating per the chart. Standards include maintaining MDA ±50 feet, heading ±10°, airspeed ±10 knots, and completing all required callouts.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Instrument Rating ACS (FAA-S-ACS-8) Task IH.XII.D; 14 CFR 91.175; FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 1

questions.question: You have just completed a GPS non-precision approach to minimums and made a smooth landing. The evaluator then says 'let's do another approach — this time be ready for anything at the end.' What does this instruction tell you about how you should fly the second approach differently?
questions.answer: The evaluator's comment is a reminder that evaluator discretion applies to every non-precision approach, meaning either a landing or a missed approach may be called at any point at or before the MAP. You should fly the second approach with equal mental preparation for both outcomes. Practically, this means keeping the missed approach procedure readily accessible in memory or on the chart, ensuring the aircraft is configured so a go-around can be initiated immediately at the MAP, and not mentally 'committing' to a landing until the evaluator confirms it. Complacency from a successful first landing is a human factors trap — ADM discipline requires treating each approach as a fresh scenario.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Instrument Rating ACS (FAA-S-ACS-8) Task IH.XII.D.S1; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM)

questions.question: During a checkride, you fly a helicopter NDB non-precision approach and reach the MAP. The evaluator has not said anything. You do not see the runway environment. What must you do, and what specific actions constitute a proper missed approach execution in the helicopter?
questions.answer: If you reach the MAP without the required visual references, you are legally required to execute a missed approach regardless of evaluator instruction — 14 CFR 91.175 prohibits descending below MDA or continuing past the MAP without the required visual references. A proper missed approach in the helicopter begins with simultaneous application of collective to initiate climb, coordinated pedal input to maintain torque balance, and forward cyclic or pitch attitude adjustment as appropriate for the climb profile. You then follow the published missed approach procedure — climbing to the specified altitude on the specified course or heading, notifying ATC, and complying with any holding or alternate instructions. Throughout, you maintain positive rate of climb, published heading ±10°, and airspeed within ±10 knots of target.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175(c); FAA Instrument Rating ACS Task IH.XII.D.S1; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11

questions.question: An applicant argues during a debrief that they should have been told in advance whether they would land or go missed so they could 'properly configure the helicopter.' How would you respond as an examiner, and what does this objection reveal about a potential gap in the applicant's instrument pilot skills?
questions.answer: The evaluator's discretion is intentional and reflects real-world IFR operations — a pilot flying in actual IMC never knows with certainty whether they will land or go missed until they are at minimums. The objection reveals a potential overreliance on predictability and a lack of mental agility in maintaining dual readiness throughout an approach. A competent IFR helicopter pilot must configure the aircraft to support both outcomes simultaneously as they approach minimums: power available for a go-around, missed approach procedure memorized or on the chart, and descent rate managed to allow immediate response. If the applicant cannot maintain that readiness without advance notice, they are not yet demonstrating the standard required for an instrument rating.
questions.follow_up: What specific helicopter characteristic makes it especially important to be ready for a missed approach at any point during a non-precision approach, compared to a fixed-wing aircraft?
questions.follow_up_answer: Helicopters generally have lower inertia rotor systems that can lose RPM rapidly if power application is delayed or poorly timed — especially at low altitudes and low airspeeds near MDA. Additionally, the transition from instrument scan to visual landing in a helicopter requires precise coordination of collective, cyclic, and pedals, and any hesitation at the MAP can result in a rate of descent that cannot be arrested before ground contact. The evaluator's 'surprise' element tests whether the pilot's habit patterns are robust enough to respond immediately without cognitive delay — a requirement that is more safety-critical in helicopters than in many fixed-wing aircraft due to the proximity of the rotor system to translational lift boundaries at approach speeds.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Instrument Rating ACS Task IH.XII.D.S1; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapters 11 and 13; 14 CFR 91.175

questions.question: You are evaluating a helicopter instrument applicant who consistently flies technically precise non-precision approaches but always hesitates for 2–3 seconds at the MAP before initiating the missed approach when called. The approaches are otherwise within ACS tolerances. Do you pass or fail this applicant, and why?
questions.answer: This is a judgment call requiring careful evaluation. A 2–3 second hesitation at the MAP in a helicopter can be safety-critical — it represents continued flight below or at MDA without a clear decision, which in actual IMC at low altitude could result in controlled flight into terrain or obstacles. If the hesitation results in the aircraft descending below MDA or past the MAP without a positive missed approach initiation, it would constitute a unsatisfactory performance item. However, if the aircraft remains at or above MDA and within published obstruction clearance throughout the hesitation, the evaluator must determine whether this reflects a systemic decision-making deficiency versus a one-time occurrence. Per the ACS, the applicant must demonstrate 'positive, timely' action — consistent hesitation suggests a habit pattern that does not meet the 'positive' standard, and the evaluator would be justified in a disapproval based on risk management and ADM deficiency, even with technically accurate instrument flying.
questions.follow_up: If you disapprove this applicant solely based on the hesitation pattern, what documentation and debrief obligations do you have as an examiner?
questions.follow_up_answer: As the examiner, you must complete a Notice of Disapproval (FAA Form 8060-5) specifying the task(s) failed — in this case IH.XII.D and potentially related ADM/risk management tasks. The debrief must clearly articulate the specific deficiency observed (consistent delayed initiation of missed approach) and reference the ACS standard not met. You must advise the applicant that on re-test, only the failed task areas need to be re-evaluated within 60 days per 14 CFR 61.43. You should also document your reasoning clearly, as an examiner decision that disapproves an otherwise technically accurate performance will be scrutinized — your notes should reflect the safety basis for the determination, citing the helicopter-specific risk of delay at low altitude and the ACS 'positive' action requirement.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA Instrument Rating ACS Task IH.XII.D.S1; 14 CFR 61.43; FAA Order 8900.2; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13

questions.question: At the completion of a precision approach during your checkride, who decides whether you land or execute a missed approach?
questions.answer: The evaluator has discretion to determine whether the applicant performs a landing or a missed approach at the completion of each precision approach. The applicant should be prepared to perform either without advance notice until the evaluator communicates the requirement.

questions.question: What does 'precision approach' mean in the context of IFR helicopter operations, and why is the landing-versus-missed-approach decision significant?
questions.answer: A precision approach is an instrument approach that provides both lateral and vertical guidance to a defined decision altitude (DA), such as an ILS or LPV approach. The landing-versus-missed-approach decision is significant because each option demands a completely different set of immediate actions — one requires a controlled transition to landing while the other requires an immediate climb, turn to missed approach heading, and configuration change. A pilot must be equally proficient at both, since the evaluator can require either one at any time.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9; FAA Instrument Rating ACS IH.XII.D.S2

questions.question: At what point in a precision approach does the evaluator typically communicate whether they want a landing or a missed approach?
questions.answer: The evaluator typically communicates the requirement at or before the decision altitude (DA) on the approach. However, the evaluator may call for a missed approach at any point, including at DA if the required visual references are not established, or may allow a landing if visual references are acquired and conditions permit. The applicant must be mentally prepared for either option throughout the entire approach.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175(e); FAA Instrument Rating ACS IH.XII.D.S2

questions.question: You are flying an ILS to minimums in a helicopter and the evaluator says 'go missed' at DA even though you have the runway clearly in sight. What do you do, and does having visual contact with the runway change anything?
questions.answer: You execute the missed approach immediately as directed by the evaluator. The evaluator's instruction takes priority during a checkride — evaluators use their discretion to assess missed approach proficiency regardless of visual conditions. From a regulatory standpoint, a pilot may continue below DA only if the required visual references are established and the aircraft is continuously in a position to make a normal landing; however, the evaluator is not bound to allow a landing simply because you have the runway in sight. Execute the published missed approach: simultaneously apply power, establish a climb attitude, and follow the published missed approach procedure (climb heading, altitude, and fixes).
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175(c); FAA Instrument Rating ACS IH.XII.D.S2

questions.question: During your checkride, the evaluator has you fly two ILS approaches back to back. On the first they call for a missed approach; on the second they say 'make a full stop landing.' Describe the key differences in how you transition from the approach to each respective outcome.
questions.answer: For the missed approach: at DA, simultaneously apply maximum or appropriate power, transition to a positive climb attitude, retract unnecessary drag (if applicable), follow the published missed approach route (climb heading, altitude, and fixes), and notify ATC. In a helicopter, maintain rotor RPM in the normal range throughout. For the full stop landing: as visual references are confirmed at DA, transition smoothly from instrument scan to outside visual references, adjust collective and cyclic for a stabilized approach to the landing area, reduce power progressively, and bring the helicopter to a hover or ground contact using normal landing technique. The key difference is that the missed approach demands an immediate aggressive power increase and attitude change to climb, while the landing demands a continued power reduction and deceleration to a controlled stop.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 11; FAA Instrument Rating ACS IH.XII.D.S2

questions.question: You are briefing for your checkride ILS approach. How should you mentally and physically prepare so that you can perform either a landing or a missed approach with equal competency, knowing the evaluator will choose?
questions.answer: During the approach briefing, brief both outcomes explicitly: state the DA, the missed approach point, the full missed approach procedure (heading, altitude, fixes), and the landing plan (runway, touchdown point, taxi plan). Confirm that the missed approach is loaded and available in the navigation system. During the approach, maintain a stabilized profile and keep your instrument scan active all the way to DA — do not begin transitioning visually until you are confident the approach is stable and you have the required visual references. Keep your hand near the collective for an immediate power increase if a missed approach is called. Mentally rehearsing both outcomes reduces reaction time and decision error.
questions.regulatory_ref: FAA-H-8083-15B Chapter 9; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13 (ADM/SRM); FAA Instrument Rating ACS IH.XII.D.S2

questions.question: A student you are mentoring insists that once the runway is visible at DA and conditions are above minimums, the examiner must allow a landing and cannot call a missed approach. How do you respond, and what is the underlying principle the student is misunderstanding?
questions.answer: The student is confusing the regulatory authorization to continue below DA with an obligation on the evaluator's part. 14 CFR 91.175(c) gives the pilot the authority to descend below DA if the required visual references are established and the aircraft is in a position to make a normal landing — it does not require an evaluator to permit it. The ACS explicitly gives the evaluator discretion to require a missed approach at the completion of each precision approach regardless of visual conditions. The evaluator is assessing the applicant's ability to execute a safe, proficient missed approach, which is a critical skill. The student must be equally prepared for both outcomes and must never assume a landing will be the result.
questions.follow_up: If the student argues further that requiring a missed approach when the runway is in sight creates an unsafe situation because it forces an unnecessary go-around, how do you address that argument?
questions.follow_up_answer: A missed approach when visual is not inherently unsafe — it is a standard maneuver practiced routinely in instrument training. The evaluator's call for a missed approach at DA with the runway in sight mirrors real-world scenarios such as a runway incursion, a preceding aircraft not clearing, or an unstabilized final. The ability to immediately abandon a landing and execute a clean missed approach is a core instrument competency. If anything, the scenario tests the pilot's ability to avoid channelized attention (fixating on the runway) and transition back to instruments and the missed approach procedure without hesitation — which is exactly the kind of ADM and workload management tested on a checkride.
questions.regulatory_ref: 14 CFR 91.175(c); FAA Instrument Rating ACS IH.XII.D.S2; FAA-H-8083-21B Chapter 13

questions.question: During a simulated ILS checkride in a helicopter, the evaluator calls for a missed approach at DA. As you apply power and begin the climb, rotor RPM briefly decays. What does this tell the evaluator about your skill, and what corrective action is required?
questions.answer: A rotor RPM decay at the missed approach transition point reveals that the applicant was not adequately prepared for the rapid power application required or failed to properly manage collective and throttle (in piston/turbine aircraft with manual throttle correlation) during the critical transition. In a helicopter, low rotor RPM is a serious hazard — the FAA Helicopter Flying Handbook notes that rotor stall is not recoverable, making early recognition imperative. The correct response is to simultaneously lower collective slightly to arrest the decay, increase throttle if applicable, then smoothly re-apply collective as RPM recovers to the normal operating range, all while maintaining a positive climb attitude. The evaluator will note this as a deficiency in power management and rotor RPM control, which are core helicopter instrument skills.
questions.follow_up: If rotor RPM decays significantly below the minimum power-on limit during the missed approach transition, at what point would this constitute a unsatisfactory performance on the checkride, and what would the evaluator's next action be?
questions.follow_up_answer: Any exceedance of an aircraft operating limitation — including rotor RPM falling below the published minimum power-on RPM limit — constitutes an unsatisfactory performance that ends the practical test. Per the ACS, an applicant who fails a task or places the aircraft in an unsafe situation receives a notice of disapproval. The evaluator would take control of the aircraft if safety was at risk, ensure the aircraft is safe, and then inform the applicant that the test is discontinued. A retest would require the applicant to only repeat the tasks that were failed, though the evaluator has discretion to require all tasks be reperformed depending on the severity of the failure.
